knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasible primal-dual recovery from a positive SP1 solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling a positive SP1 solution into a feasible pair for the original primal and dual LPs with an explicit gap bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(y,x,\kappa,\vartheta)\) be a positive solution of \(SP_1\), and set \(\widetilde x=x/\kappa\) and \(\widetilde y=y/\kappa\). Then \(\widetilde x\) is feasible for \(P\), \(\widetilde y\) is feasible for \(D\), and \(c^T\widetilde x-b^T\widetilde y\leq\vartheta/\kappa\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dividing a positive SP1 solution's primal and dual coordinates by κ yields a feasible pair for the original primal and dual LPs, whose duality gap is at most θ/κ.
assumptions_latex: z=(y,x,\kappa,\vartheta)\text{ is a positive solution of }SP_1
\widetilde x=x/\kappa
\widetilde y=y/\kappa
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widetilde x\in\operatorname{Feas}(P),\quad \widetilde y\in\operatorname{Feas}(D),\quad c^T\widetilde x-b^T\widetilde y\leq\frac{\vartheta}{\kappa}

children.title: Turing Machine Models
children.top_down_role: Turing-machine accounting for LP computation over finite encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Turing Machine Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bit-complexity model for explicitly encoded rational linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Turing-machine model represents an LP instance by a finite binary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{*}\), with every rational coefficient encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. An algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine that halts with an encoded answer or status certificate. Its running time \(T(w)\) is the number of state transitions before halting, and its space is the maximum number of tape cells visited. Polynomial time means that some polynomial \(p\) satisfies \(T(w)\le p(|w|)\) for every valid input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP algorithm is polynomial-time in the Turing model when its transition count is polynomial in the binary length of the explicitly encoded rational input.
assumptions_latex: \(w\) is a valid finite binary encoding of a rational LP.
Numerators use signed binary notation, and denominators use positive binary notation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(w)\le p(|w|)\) defines polynomial Turing time.

source_refs.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

children.title: Bit-Operation Models
children.top_down_role: Bit-level cost accounting for arithmetic on encoded LP data.

knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Operation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boolean-operation accounting for exact algorithms on binary rational encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the bit-operation model, input and output are binary strings, and cost is the total number of elementary operations on individual bits. An elementary operation may read, write, copy, or apply a fixed Boolean function to a constant number of bits. Arithmetic on an \(s\)-bit integer is charged by the bit operations actually used rather than one unit; consequently, an algorithm's cost depends on both its arithmetic-operation count and the bit lengths of all intermediate operands. Bit complexity is polynomial when this total is bounded by a polynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bit complexity counts elementary Boolean work, so exact arithmetic cost reflects both the number of arithmetic operations and the sizes of intermediate integers.
assumptions_latex: The LP has an explicit finite binary encoding.
Each primitive manipulates only \(O(1)\) bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B(w)\le p(|w|)\) defines polynomial bit complexity.

notation.meaning: total bit-operation count on input w

children.title: Exact Rational Models
children.top_down_role: Exact rational arithmetic as a computational regime for LP algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost exact arithmetic over rational registers, distinguished from bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact rational arithmetic model stores elements of \(\mathbb{Q}\) without rounding and permits the operations \(+,-,\times,\div\), rational comparison, and copying, with division restricted to nonzero divisors. Its arithmetic cost is the number of such primitive operations. In the unit-cost version, each primitive costs one regardless of numerator and denominator lengths; therefore this count alone does not bound Turing or bit complexity. An output is exact when every returned rational and every stated comparison agrees with arithmetic in \(\mathbb{Q}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The model performs exact rational arithmetic and counts rational operations, often at unit cost; this operation count alone ignores operand bit growth.
assumptions_latex: All inputs and register values belong to \(\mathbb{Q}\).
Division is performed only by a nonzero rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathbb Q}\) counts exact rational primitives, not their bit-level implementation cost.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Encoding size and polynomial-time algorithms for rational linear programs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The size of a rational depends on its fraction representation; running time is measured in bit-level computation steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $i\in\mathbb Z$, let $\langle i\rangle=\lceil\log_2(|i|+1)\rceil+1$. For a rational represented as $r=p/q$ with $q\ne0$, let $\langle r\rangle=\langle p\rangle+\langle q\rangle$; vector and matrix sizes are sums of entry sizes. For $L=\{\max c^Tx:Ax\le b\}$ with rational data, $\langle L\rangle=\langle A\rangle+\langle b\rangle+\langle c\rangle$. An algorithm is polynomial for LP if a polynomial $p$ exists such that, for every such $L$, it produces a correct solution within $p(\langle L\rangle)$ bit-level computation steps. An arithmetic operation on long operands is not necessarily one such step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer size is signed binary length. The size of a represented rational is the combined size of its numerator and denominator, and vector, matrix, and LP sizes are obtained by summing component sizes. A polynomial LP algorithm uses polynomially many bit-level steps in this encoded input size; long-integer arithmetic is not automatically a single step.
assumptions_latex: i\in\mathbb Z
r=p/q,\quad p,q\in\mathbb Z,\ q\ne0
A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb Q^m,\quad c\in\mathbb Q^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists p\ \forall L:\ T_{\mathrm{bit}}(L)\le p(\langle L\rangle)

children.title: Exact-Model Cost Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relationships among Turing, bit-operation, and exact-rational complexity measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Model Cost Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-equivalence and non-equivalence boundaries among exact computational cost models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite binary inputs, standard Turing time and bit-operation cost simulate one another with polynomial overhead, so polynomial-time classifications agree up to conventional machine choices. If an exact rational algorithm performs \(N\) arithmetic primitives and every intermediate numerator and denominator has at most \(L\) bits, then implementing those primitives by integer algorithms yields bit cost bounded by \(Nq(L)\) for some polynomial \(q\). Without a polynomial bound on \(L\), a polynomial unit-cost rational-operation count need not imply polynomial Turing or bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Turing and bit models agree polynomially. Unit-cost rational bounds transfer only when intermediate rational bit lengths are also polynomially controlled.
assumptions_latex: Inputs and outputs have finite binary encodings.
Exact rational primitives use conventional integer-arithmetic implementations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\le\operatorname{poly}(|w|)\) and \(L\le\operatorname{poly}(|w|)\) imply polynomial bit and Turing cost.

notation.meaning: maximum intermediate numerator or denominator bit length

source_refs.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated-Squaring Separation of Rational and Bit Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-growth witness separating unit-cost exact rational operations from bit and Turing cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For unary input \(1^k\), set \(x_0=2\) and compute \(x_{i+1}=x_i^2\) for \(i=0,\ldots,k-1\). Then \(x_k=2^{2^k}\). This uses \(k\) exact integer, hence rational, multiplications, while the ordinary binary encoding of \(x_k\) has \(2^k+1\) bits. Any implementation explicitly outputting \(x_k\) therefore requires at least \(2^k+1\) bit or Turing steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated squaring uses only k exact rational multiplications but produces an exponentially long explicit binary output.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is \(\Theta(k)\).
The output is the ordinary explicit binary encoding of \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\mathbb Q}(1^k)=O(k),\qquad T_{\mathrm{bit}}(1^k)\ge 2^k+1.

notation.meaning: bit running time including explicit output

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Squaring Separation of Rational and Bit Cost

children.title: Real-Arithmetic Models
children.top_down_role: Unit-cost computation over real-valued LP data.

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Arithmetic Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost real-register model used for arithmetic complexity of LP algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real-arithmetic machine has finitely many control states and registers containing arbitrary elements of \(\mathbb{R}\). In one unit-cost step it may copy a register, apply \(+,-,\times,\div\) with nonzero divisor, or branch on an exact comparison. An LP over real data is supplied directly as register values rather than as a finite binary encoding. Running time is the number of executed unit-cost steps, independently of the magnitude, algebraic degree, or finite encodability of intermediate real numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-arithmetic machine stores arbitrary exact reals and charges one unit for each arithmetic operation, copy, or exact comparison.
assumptions_latex: Input coefficients are elements of \(\mathbb{R}\).
Division occurs only with a nonzero divisor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathbb R}\) is the number of unit-cost real-register steps.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

source_witnesses.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

children.title: Algebraic-Operation Models
children.top_down_role: Complexity measured through counted algebraic operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic-Operation Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count measure for algorithms expressed by real algebra and comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an algorithm whose data lie in \(\mathbb{R}\), its algebraic-operation complexity is the number of executed scalar additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions by nonzero quantities, and exact order or equality tests. Assigning unit cost to every listed primitive produces an operation count \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\); vector and matrix operations must be expanded into scalar primitives unless separately declared. This measure records the algebraic decision structure of an LP algorithm but does not charge for representing real numbers or for finite-precision evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraic complexity counts scalar arithmetic and comparison primitives, expanding compound linear-algebra operations unless the model explicitly declares otherwise.
assumptions_latex: Every permitted primitive is exact over \(\mathbb{R}\).
Compound operations are reduced to scalar primitives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\) equals the total number of executed scalar algebraic primitives.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

source_witnesses.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

children.title: Real-Arithmetic Cost Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of translating real-arithmetic guarantees into finite-encoding costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Arithmetic Cost Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits on transferring unit-cost real-arithmetic bounds to finite-bit computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) denote the problem dimension and let \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\) be the number of exact real-arithmetic and comparison primitives executed by an algorithm. A bound \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\le\operatorname{poly}(n)\) is only a real-arithmetic bound and does not by itself imply polynomial bit complexity. Arbitrary real inputs may lack finite encodings, while finitely encoded rational or algebraic inputs may generate intermediate values with superpolynomial descriptions or require superpolynomial work to implement exact arithmetic and branches. For a finitely encoded input \(w\), transfer to a Turing bound requires polynomial control of intermediate representation lengths and of the bit cost of every arithmetic operation and comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial unit-cost real-operation bound does not automatically imply an efficient finite-bit algorithm; finite encoding, intermediate representation growth, and implementation costs must also be controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\) counts exact real arithmetic and comparisons at unit cost.
Whenever bit complexity is discussed, \(w\) is a finite encoding of the input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{alg}}\le\operatorname{poly}(n)\) alone does not imply \(T_{\mathrm{bit}}(w)\le\operatorname{poly}(|w|)\).

notation.meaning: finite input encoding used for the bit-complexity comparison
finite-bit running time on encoding w

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between unit-cost access to arbitrary real data and finite-string exact computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) be noncomputable. A real-arithmetic machine receiving \(\alpha\) directly in an input register can copy it to an output register in one unit-cost step. No Turing machine can receive a finite effective exact description of \(\alpha\) and compute arbitrarily requested binary digits of \(\alpha\). Hence constant real-arithmetic cost need not correspond to any exact finite-bit realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real machine can copy an arbitrary noncomputable real in one step, although no finite effective encoding supports exact Turing computation of that real.
assumptions_latex: The real-arithmetic model permits arbitrary real input-register values.
A finite exact representation must effectively determine every requested output digit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathbb R}(\alpha)=O(1),\quad\text{while no exact finite-encoding Turing realization exists for noncomputable }\alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncomputable-Real Input Boundary

children.title: Separation Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Complexity interfaces based on separating queries for represented feasible regions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A norm-explicit approximate variant that separates points outside a prescribed neighborhood of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, fix a norm \(\|\cdot\|\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). A tolerance separation oracle queried at \(x\) either certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\varepsilon\), or returns a dual-unit vector \(a\), \(\|a\|_*=1\), such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\ge\sup_{y\in K}a^{\mathsf T}y+\varepsilon\). The norm, tolerance encoding, and permitted numerical error are part of the oracle specification; changing them changes the computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate separation model may certify proximity within a stated tolerance or return a normalized hyperplane separating the query by at least that tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
A norm and a positive encoded tolerance \(\varepsilon\) are fixed.
The displayed response is exact unless an additional numerical-error convention is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,K)>\varepsilon\implies \exists a:\|a\|_*=1,\ a^{\mathsf T}x\ge\sup_{y\in K}a^{\mathsf T}y+\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the selected primal norm.
Distance from the query to K in the selected norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance Separation Oracle Model
Separation Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation-oracle access to an implicitly represented convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be a nonempty closed convex set. A strong separation oracle for \(K\), queried at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), either certifies \(x\in K\) or returns \((a,\beta)\in(\mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(y\in K\). Oracle complexity counts queries; a complete cost model additionally charges the computation between queries and specifies whether returned quantities are exact or approximate and how they are encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle either confirms membership in a closed convex set or returns a hyperplane strictly separating the query point from it.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
Queries satisfy \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\notin K\) yields \(a^{\mathsf T}y\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}x\) for all \(y\in K\).

source_refs.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

children.title: First-Order Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Complexity interfaces based on objective or constraint first-order information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional unbiased stochastic subgradient access with a second-moment parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) contain the history before query \(x^k\). A stochastic first-order oracle returns \(G_k=G(x^k,\xi_k)\) satisfying \[\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\in\partial f(x^k),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert G_k\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M^2.\] Query complexity under this probabilistic contract is distinct from exact deterministic oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbiased stochastic first-order oracle returns a random vector whose conditional mean is a true subgradient and whose conditional second moment is bounded.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is convex and subdifferentiable at queried points}
x^k\text{ is }\mathcal F_k\text{-measurable}
M<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\in\partial f(x^k),\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert G_k\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M^2.

notation.meaning: History before the kth oracle response.

review_flags: Complexity claims must declare their probabilistic success criterion.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbiased Stochastic First-Order Oracle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit additive inexact value-and-affine-model convention for convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), a deterministic \(\delta\)-inexact first-order oracle queried at \(x\in D\) returns \((\widetilde f(x),g_x)\) such that \[|\widetilde f(x)-f(x)|\le\delta,\qquad f(y)\ge\widetilde f(x)+g_x^T(y-x)-\delta\quad\forall y\in D.\] The parameter \(\delta\ge0\) is part of the oracle contract; at \(\delta=0\), this convention reduces to exact value-and-subgradient access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This additive inexact oracle returns an approximate value and a global affine lower model valid up to a declared error.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex}
f:D\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex}
\delta\ge0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widetilde f(x)-f(x)|\le\delta,\qquad f(y)\ge\widetilde f(x)+g_x^T(y-x)-\delta\quad\forall y\in D.
review_flags: This is one inexact-oracle convention; other conventions require separate error accounting.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Additive Inexact First-Order Oracle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable specialization of exact first-order oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:D	o\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable at every queried point. An exact smooth first-order oracle queried at \(x\in D\) returns \((f(x),
abla f(x))\). Convexity gives \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle
abla f(x),y-xangle\qquad orall y\in D,\] and differentiability gives \(\partial f(x)=\{
abla f(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable convex objective, exact first-order access returns its value and gradient, which is its unique subgradient.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex}
f\text{ is convex and differentiable at every queried point}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\},\qquad f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in D.

notation.meaning: Gradient returned by the smooth first-order oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Smooth First-Order Oracle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical deterministic nonsmooth first-order oracle contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex. At a query \(x\in D\), an exact first-order oracle returns \((f(x),g_x)\) with \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\), equivalently \[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in D.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact nonsmooth first-order oracle returns a function value and a globally valid subgradient at the query point.
assumptions_latex: D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex}
f:D\to\mathbb R\text{ is convex and subdifferentiable at queried points}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_x\in\partial f(x)\iff f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in D.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Value-and-Subgradient Oracle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Query Complexity Is Not Total Computational Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-model boundary for first-order-oracle results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound of \(Q(n,\varepsilon)\) first-order-oracle calls controls only interactions with the declared oracle. A total arithmetic or Turing bound additionally requires bounds on computation between calls, oracle-response cost, response representation and precision, and intermediate operand lengths. Thus polynomial query complexity alone does not imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting first-order queries is incomplete unless arithmetic, response, precision, and encoding costs are also controlled.
assumptions_latex: Q(n,\varepsilon)\text{ counts calls under a declared oracle contract}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\in\operatorname{poly}(n,\log(1/\varepsilon))\centernot\implies\text{polynomial total bit complexity without additional cost bounds}.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Query Complexity Is Not Total Computational Complexity
First-Order Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact value-and-subgradient oracle access for convex optimization formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be convex and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. An exact first-order oracle, queried at \(x\in D\), returns the pair \((f(x),g)\), where \(g\in\partial f(x)\); equivalently, \(f(y)\ge f(x)+g^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\) for every \(y\in D\). Oracle complexity counts such queries. A full computational bound must also state the cost of arithmetic between queries and the representation or accuracy requirements for returned values and subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order oracle returns a convex function value and a subgradient satisfying the global subgradient inequality at the query point.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is convex.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and subdifferentiable at each queried point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\in\partial f(x)\) means \(f(y)\ge f(x)+g^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\) for every \(y\in D\).

source_refs.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

children.title: Oracle Capability Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relative information strength of separation and first-order access.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separation Responses Need Not Determine First-Order Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete information-theoretic boundary for the converse from epigraph separation to exact first-order access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0(x)=0\) and \(f_1(x)=1\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), and query either epigraph at \((0,-2)\). The inequality \(s\ge-1\) strongly separates this query from both \(\operatorname{epi}f_0\) and \(\operatorname{epi}f_1\). Thus the same valid separation response is compatible with two different values at the query point, so one generic separation response cannot determine \(f(0)\), and hence cannot in general reproduce a value-and-subgradient response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two different constant convex functions can give the same valid epigraph-separation response even though their exact values differ, demonstrating the generic non-converse.

Only the response to the stated query is available.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Responses Need Not Determine First-Order Data
Oracle Capability Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction from first-order information to separation of a convex epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and let \(E=\{(y,s)\in D\times\mathbb{R}:s\ge f(y)\}\). One exact first-order query at \(x\) separates any \((x,t)\notin E\): if the oracle returns \((f(x),g)\) and \(t<f(x)\), then \(g^{\mathsf T}y-s\le g^{\mathsf T}x-f(x)<g^{\mathsf T}x-t\) for all \((y,s)\in E\). Thus a first-order oracle implements epigraph separation, subject to access to \(D\). Conversely, a generic separation oracle for \(E\) need not return either \(f(x)\) or a selected subgradient without additional structure or further queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A value-and-subgradient query yields an epigraph separator. Generic epigraph separation does not automatically reveal an exact value and subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) and \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
An exact first-order oracle for \(f\) and required domain access are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f(x),g)\) implements strong separation of \((x,t)\) from \(\operatorname{epi}f\) whenever \(t<f(x)\).

children.title: Explicit Rational Encodings
children.top_down_role: Finite binary representations of rational LP coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Rational Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite binary representation and length measure for rational LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write each rational coefficient as \(r=p/q\), where \(p\in\mathbb{Z}\), \(q\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\), and \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\). An explicit rational LP encoding lists matrix dimensions, relation types, and every coefficient's sign together with binary encodings of \(|p|\) and \(q\), using a fixed decodable convention. For any standard self-delimiting convention, the coefficient length satisfies \(\ell(r)=\Theta\!\left(1+\log_{2}(|p|+1)+\log_{2}(q+1)\right)\), and the instance length is, up to constant factors, the structural metadata length plus the sum of the coefficient lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each rational coefficient is stored as a reduced signed numerator and positive denominator in binary; under a fixed decodable convention, total input length is asymptotically the metadata length plus the coefficient encoding lengths.
assumptions_latex: Every LP coefficient belongs to \(\mathbb{Q}\).
Each rational uses its reduced numerator and positive denominator.
The binary coding convention is fixed and uniquely decodable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|w|=\Theta\!\left(\operatorname{metadata}(w)+\sum_{r\text{ in }w}\ell(r)\right)\).

notation.meaning: length of dimensions, relation types, and other structural data

knowledge_statements.title: Standard-Form Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit rational encoding of equality-form LPs with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational LP in standard form is encoded as \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}\). Its finite encoding records \((m,n)\), followed in a fixed order by reduced binary numerator-denominator representations of all entries of \(A\), \(b\), and \(c\). The encoding length is the structural overhead plus the sum of the rational coefficient lengths; feasibility, unboundedness, or an optimizer must be interpreted relative to this stated minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A standard-form LP records dimensions and all rational entries of the equality system, nonnegative variables, and linear objective in a fixed binary order.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^{m}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}\).
The optimization convention is minimization with \(x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w=\operatorname{enc}(m,n,A,b,c)\) represents \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit slack-variable and free-variable splitting conversion to equality standard form.

source_refs.locator: 2.3. Polyhedra in standard form p. 53

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace each free coordinate by \(x_j=x_j^+-x_j^-\), where \(x_j^+,x_j^-\ge0\), and replace \(Ax\le b\) by \(Ax^+-Ax^-+u=b\), where \(u\in\mathbb R_+^m\). The resulting equality-standard-form LP has \(2n+m\) nonnegative variables and \(m\) equality constraints. Its matrix contains at most \(2s+m\) nonzeros. Copying rational coefficients, changing signs, and inserting unit coefficients can be performed in \(O(L+s+m+n)\) bit operations under a sequential explicit-encoding model, and the output encoding length obeys the same bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slack variables and splitting free variables convert an explicit rational LP to standard form with only linear encoding and processing overhead.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation condition under which slack insertion and free-variable splitting have linear encoded-size overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bound \(O(L+s+m+n)\) for converting \(Ax\le b\) to equality standard form applies when the output uses a sparse or otherwise zero-omitting serialization. If the output instead lists every entry of the \(m\times(2n+m)\) standard-form matrix, its structural coefficient count is \(m(2n+m)\), so a bound linear in \(L+s+m+n\) need not hold for a sparsely encoded input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear conversion overhead requires a compatible sparse output encoding; a dense output layout may explicitly store quadratically many zero positions.
assumptions_latex: The input matrix has \(s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) and may be stored sparsely.
The conversion produces \(m\) rows and \(2n+m\) nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Sparse output gives }O(L+s+m+n),\quad\text{whereas dense entrywise output stores }m(2n+m)\text{ matrix positions}.

notation.meaning: number of nonzero entries of the original matrix

children.title: Sparse Matrix Encodings

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary CSR/CSC representation with bit length separated from fixed-word structural storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) have \(s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\), and let \(B\) be the total bit length of its stored nonzero rational values. A CSR encoding records \((m,n)\), the values in a fixed within-row order, \(s\) column indices, and \(m+1\) row pointers; CSC interchanges rows and columns. With fixed-width binary fields, a CSR representation has length \[B+\Theta\!\left(\log(m+1)+\log(n+1)+s\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil +(m+1)\lceil\log_2(s+1)\rceil\right)\] bits, up to the fixed framing convention. In a machine-word model whose words hold all indices and pointers, the structural arrays instead occupy \(\Theta(m+s)\) words, in addition to the stored values. The bit and word counts are distinct cost models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CSR and CSC store values, indices, and pointer arrays; their binary bit length includes index widths, while their fixed-word structural storage is linear in dimensions and nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: Matrix dimensions and all rational values use a fixed decodable binary convention.
Within-row or within-column ordering is fixed.
The word-model summary assumes one index or pointer fits in one machine word.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exact binary length must charge index and pointer bit widths; \(\Theta(m+s)\) describes structural machine-word storage, not the same bit count.

notation.meaning: total binary length of stored nonzero rational values

assumptions_latex: The matrix is \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) with \(s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\).

children.title: Structure-Exploitation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which encoded matrix structure does or does not reduce computational work.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Input with Dense Normal Matrix
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete family showing that a sparse encoding can produce a quadratically larger derived matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge2\), let \[A_n=\begin{pmatrix}I_n\\ \mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb Q^{(n+1)\times n}.\] Then \(\operatorname{nnz}(A_n)=2n\), but \[A_n^{\mathsf T}A_n=I_n+\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}\] has every entry nonzero and hence \(n^2\) structural nonzeros. Thus an algorithm that explicitly forms this normal matrix expands linear sparse input storage to quadratic matrix storage before factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix with only twice as many nonzeros as columns can have a completely dense normal matrix.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm explicitly forms \(A_n^{\mathsf T}A_n\).
Structural nonzeros are counted before any special low-rank treatment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{nnz}(A_n)=2n\) while \(\operatorname{nnz}(A_n^{\mathsf T}A_n)=n^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Input with Dense Normal Matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary resource accounting for algorithms operating on sparse or compact matrix descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite descriptor \(D\) represent \(A(D)\). Compact storage yields an end-to-end bound polynomial in \(\operatorname{len}(D)\) only when every matrix primitive actually invoked by the algorithm is implemented from \(D\) within the claimed resource bound and all finite-precision intermediates have appropriately bounded encoding length. If a required stage materializes the expanded matrix, forms a dense derived matrix, incurs dense fill, or otherwise destroys the represented structure, that expanded work and storage must be charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact input storage improves end-to-end complexity only when every required operation preserves and efficiently uses the represented structure.
assumptions_latex: The computational model charges all invoked matrix operations and finite representations.
The claimed input size is based on a sparse or compact descriptor \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A storage bound in \(\operatorname{len}(D)\) alone does not imply an algorithmic bound in \(\operatorname{len}(D)\).
knowledge_statements.title: End-to-End Structure-Exploitation Boundary

assumptions_latex: A compact descriptor \(D\) represents \(A(D)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\).
An LP method invokes entry access, matrix products, or linear-system solves involving \(A(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound polynomial in \(\operatorname{len}(D)\) requires polynomial-time structured implementations of every invoked primitive and polynomially bounded intermediate bit lengths.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: representation-sensitive complexity must charge all required primitives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between compact input storage and genuine algorithmic speedup.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compact storage alone does not yield a running-time bound polynomial in \(\operatorname{len}(D)\). Such a bound is justified only when every primitive requested by the LP algorithm can be executed from \(D\) in polynomial bit time and produces intermediates of polynomial bit length. If some required primitive must materialize \(A(D)\), incurs dense fill-in of size \(\Omega(mn)\), or solves a structure-destroying system, then the valid bound must charge that expanded work. Thus sparsity or structure improves complexity only to the extent preserved by the complete computational pipeline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact matrix storage accelerates an LP algorithm only when all required operations preserve the structure and control intermediate size.
knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Exploitation Boundaries

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homogeneous embedding of the primal-dual LP data \((A,b,c)\) introduces scalars \(\tau,\kappa\ge 0\) and imposes \[Ax-b\tau=0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\tau=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y-\kappa=0,\] with \(x,s\ge0\) and \(y\in\mathbb R^m\). If \((x,y,s,\tau,\kappa)\) satisfies these equations, then so does \(\lambda(x,y,s,\tau,\kappa)\) for every \(\lambda\ge0\). Thus the representation is homogeneous; normalization must be supplied separately when a nonzero representative is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous embedding introduces homogenizing and gap variables so that every nonnegative scalar multiple of an embedded solution remains a solution.

children.title: Homogeneous Self-Dual Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations combining homogeneity with self-dual structure.

assumptions_latex: The rational primal-dual data satisfy \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\).
The embedded variables satisfy \(x,s\in\mathbb R^n_+\), \(y\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\tau,\kappa\in\mathbb R_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When \(\tau>0\), scaling by \(1/\tau\) yields primal-dual feasible points with duality gap \(\kappa/\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation of the positive-scaling branch of the homogeneous self-dual system.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The homogeneous self-dual encoding is the system \[Ax=b\tau,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\tau,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=\kappa,\qquad x,s,\tau,\kappa\ge0.\] Its skew-symmetric block representation gives \(x^{\mathsf T}s=\tau\kappa\). If \(\tau>0\), then \(x/\tau\) is primal feasible, \((y/\tau,s/\tau)\) is dual feasible, and their objective gap equals \(\kappa/\tau\). Consequently, a point with \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\) encodes an optimal primal-dual pair after scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogeneous self-dual system jointly encodes primal and dual feasibility; when the homogenizing scalar is positive, scaling recovers feasible points whose duality gap is the encoded gap scalar divided by the homogenizing scalar.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Self-Dual Encodings

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate branch in which normalization by the homogeneous scale is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Recovery of original primal-dual variables by division by \(\tau\) requires \(\tau>0\). If \(\tau=0\), normalization is undefined, and that equality alone determines no status of the original LP. In particular, the all-zero embedded vector satisfies the homogeneous equations with \(\tau=\kappa=0\) but supplies neither an optimum nor an infeasibility or unboundedness certificate. Any zero-scale status interpretation therefore requires a nonzero embedded ray and additional certificate-specific sign conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero homogeneous scale cannot be normalized, and tau equal to zero alone is not a solution-status certificate.
assumptions_latex: The embedded system is homogeneous and contains its zero solution.
Positive-scale recovery divides the embedded variables by \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau=0\) alone implies neither optimality, infeasibility, nor unboundedness of the original LP.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Scale Decoding Boundary

children.title: Feasibility Decision Tasks
children.top_down_role: Determining whether an encoded LP feasible region is nonempty.

assumptions_latex: The input is an explicitly encoded rational system \(Ax\le b\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rational feasibility decision task maps an explicit pair \((A,b)\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\times\mathbb Q^m\) to \[\mathrm{FEAS}(A,b)=\begin{cases}\mathrm{YES},&\text{if there exists }x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ with }Ax\le b,\\ \mathrm{NO},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\] The required output is only this Boolean value. Producing a feasible rational point in the YES case or an alternative certificate in the NO case is a distinct search task, although an algorithm may internally construct either object. Running time is measured against the complete binary encoding length of \((A,b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasibility decision task returns only whether a rational linear inequality system has a real solution; producing a witness or certificate is a separate task.

Such a certificate is verifiable in polynomial bit time.

assumptions_latex: \(A,b\) are explicitly encoded rational data.
\(Ax\le b\) is infeasible.

children.title: Decision-to-Certificate Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions between deciding status and producing verifiable output.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconditional reduction from total witness production to decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm for \(Ax\le b\) always returns either a rational feasible point \(x\) or a rational Farkas certificate \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Exact verification of the returned object decides feasibility. If \(T_{\mathrm{prod}}(L)\) is the production time and \(S(L)\) bounds the returned encoding length, then \(T_{\mathrm{dec}}(L)\le T_{\mathrm{prod}}(L)+\operatorname{poly}(L+S(L))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total producer of either a feasible point or a Farkas witness yields a decision algorithm after polynomial-time exact verification.
assumptions_latex: Inputs and outputs use binary rational encodings.
The producer always returns one of the two specified verifiable outcomes.
Exact rational arithmetic is charged in the bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{dec}}(L)\le T_{\mathrm{prod}}(L)+\operatorname{poly}(L+S(L)).
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Production Implies Feasibility Decision
Decision-to-Certificate Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-to-decision reduction for rational feasibility certificates under bounded encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the binary length of \((A,b)\), and suppose a known polynomial \(B(L)\) bounds the encoding length of a feasible point or normalized Farkas certificate. An exact feasibility-decision oracle applicable to rational systems augmented by additional linear constraints can recover the relevant certificate by polynomially many adaptive oracle queries and polynomial-time rational reconstruction. Apply the reduction to \(Ax\le b\) when feasible and to \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-1\) otherwise. Thus decision and certificate production are polynomial-time equivalent under these assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With polynomial certificate-size bounds and augmented feasibility queries, exact feasibility decisions can be converted into feasible points or Farkas certificates in polynomial time.
assumptions_latex: Certificate encoding length is bounded by a known polynomial \(B(L)\).
The decision oracle accepts rational systems with added linear constraints.
Bit operations and oracle calls are charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{cert}}(L)\le \operatorname{poly}(L,B(L),T_{\mathrm{dec}}(\operatorname{poly}(L)))\).

children.title: Solution-Value Accuracy Relations
children.top_down_role: Connections between solution accuracy and objective-value accuracy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a uniform converse from objective error to optimizer distance across LP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(P=[0,1]\) and \(\min\{\varepsilon x:x\in P\}\). Its unique optimizer is \(x^*=0\), but the feasible point \(x=1\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*=\varepsilon\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)=1\). Hence no instance-independent bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\phi(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*)\), with \(\phi(t)\to0\) as \(t\downarrow0\), holds uniformly over LP instances without conditioning or sharpness data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small objective error can coexist with unit optimizer distance across LP instances, so a reverse accuracy bound needs instance-dependent sharpness information.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The proposed modulus is required to hold uniformly over LP instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*=\varepsilon\to0\) while \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)=1\).
knowledge_statements.title: No Instance-Independent Value-to-Solution Modulus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-dependent linear value-to-solution bound for a fixed LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), suppose \(v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\) is finite and attained, and set \(X^*=\{x\in P:c^Tx=v^*\}\). For every norm there exists a finite constant \(H>0\), depending on \((A,b,c)\) and the norm, such that every \(x\in P\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le H\bigl(c^Tx-v^*\bigr).\] Equivalently, the fixed instance has weak-sharpness constant \(\alpha=H^{-1}>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed LP with an attained finite optimum admits an instance-dependent linear bound from objective error to distance from its optimal face.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\ne\varnothing
v^*>-\infty
X^*\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists H<\infty\ \forall x\in P:\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le H(c^Tx-v^*).

notation.meaning: Instance- and norm-dependent polyhedral error-bound constant.

review_flags: The constant is instance dependent and need not be uniformly bounded over encoded LP families.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Weak-Sharpness Error Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward Lipschitz relation for a linear objective on the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*=\arg\min_{u\in P}c^Tu\ne\varnothing\), \(v^*=\min_{u\in P}c^Tu\), and let \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_*\) be dual to \(\lVert\cdot\rVert\). Every feasible \(x\in P\) satisfies \[0\le c^Tx-v^*\le\lVert c\rVert_*\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to the optimal set bounds linear-objective error through the dual norm of the objective vector.
assumptions_latex: X^*\ne\varnothing
x\in P
\lVert\cdot\rVert_*\text{ is dual to }\lVert\cdot\rVert
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le c^Tx-v^*\le\lVert c\rVert_*\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*).

notation.meaning: Distance to the optimal set in the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution Distance Implies Objective Accuracy
Solution-Value Accuracy Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based implications between solution distance and objective accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\ne\varnothing\), with optimal value \(v^*\), and let \(\|\cdot\|_*\) be dual to \(\|\cdot\|\). Every feasible \(x\) satisfies \(0\le c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\le\|c\|_*\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\). Conversely, objective accuracy implies solution accuracy only under an error-bound condition: if \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\) for all \(x\in P\) and some \(\alpha>0\), then an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal feasible point satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closeness to the optimal set controls objective error; the reverse implication requires a positive sharpness or error-bound constant.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty and \(X^*\ne\varnothing\).
The stated converse additionally assumes an error-bound constant \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\le\|c\|_*\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\), and under sharpness, \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon/\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Distance to the optimal set in the chosen norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boolean Detection Alone Does Not Identify a Separator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-information boundary for an unrestricted Boolean detection oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An oracle that, for the complete constraint family and fixed query \(q\), returns only \(\mathbf 1[\exists i:A_{i:}q>b_i]\) reveals neither a violated index nor a separating inequality. Thus Boolean output conversion alone does not implement separation. A reduction requires additional access, such as inspection of explicit rows, subset-restricted detection queries, or another search self-reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Boolean violation answer alone does not identify a separator; row access or a self-reducible oracle interface is needed.
assumptions_latex: The detector returns only one Boolean answer for the complete constraint family.
No explicit-row inspection, subset-query interface, or other search access is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{Detection}\not\Rightarrow\mathrm{Separation}\) by output conversion alone.

notation.meaning: Boolean indicator returned by the detector.

knowledge_statements.title: Boolean Detection Alone Does Not Identify a Separator

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case deterministic query lower bound for locating one violated row from Boolean subset queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume exactly one of \(m\) indexed constraints is violated and a query on \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) returns the bit \(\mathbf 1[j\in S]\), where \(j\) is the violated index. Any deterministic adaptive algorithm that identifies \(j\) for every instance requires at least \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) subset queries in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with arbitrary subset queries, locating one violated row from Boolean answers needs at least logarithmically many deterministic queries.
assumptions_latex: m\ge1
\text{Exactly one violated index }j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}
\text{Each oracle response is one Boolean bit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{id}}(m)\ge\lceil\log_2m\rceil.

notation.meaning: Worst-case deterministic subset-query count for identification.

review_flags: The lower bound concerns deterministic identification with one-bit subset responses.
knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Detection Identification Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction from arbitrary-subset Boolean detection to violated-row identification and strong separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:A_{i:}x\le b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\). Suppose a detector accepts any subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and reports whether some \(i\in S\) satisfies \(A_{i:}q>b_i\). Query the full set. If positive, repeatedly split a currently positive subset into two parts, query one part, and retain a part known to contain a violation. After at most \(\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) further calls, obtain a violated index \(i\) and return \(A_{i:}x\le b_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary-subset violation detection identifies a violated row by binary search and thereby implements strong separation.
assumptions_latex: \text{The detector accepts arbitrary indexed subsets}
\text{Detector answers and comparisons are exact}
A_{i:}x\le b_i\text{ is valid for }P\text{ for every }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{sep}}(m)\le1+\lceil\log_2m\rceil\quad\text{detection calls}.
knowledge_statements.title: Subset-Detection Binary-Search Reduction
Detection-to-Separation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-search reduction when detection accepts arbitrary constraint subsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a violation-detection oracle accepts any indexed subset \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and reports whether \(A_{i:}q>b_i\) for some \(i\in S\). Query the full set; if a violation exists, repeatedly partition the current positive subset into two parts and query one part, retaining a part known to contain a violation. After at most \(\lceil\log_2 m\rceil\) additional queries, a violated index \(i\) is isolated. Returning \(A_{i:}x\le b_i\) then gives a separator for \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset violation detection yields an explicit separating row through binary search using logarithmically many additional oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: The oracle may be queried on arbitrary indexed subsets.
The constraints are explicit and comparisons are exact.
A returned violated row is valid for the represented polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q_{\mathrm{sep}}(m)\le1+\lceil\log_2m\rceil\) detection queries, plus polynomial bookkeeping.

notation.meaning: Detection-query count for producing a separator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subset-query binary search and its logarithmic query count are coherent under the stated stronger oracle interface, but no citation is supplied. A source specifically supporting this search reduction or an inspectable reduction theorem is required.

children.title: Exact Solution Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovering an exact optimal primal or dual solution.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and \(v^*\in\mathbb{Q}\).
The LP has an attained finite optimum with exact value \(v^*\).
An exact rational feasible-point procedure is available for rational linear inequality systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), \(Ax^*\le b\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=v^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of an exact rational optimizer from the exact finite optimal value.

source_refs.locator: Moving to a Solution from an Interior Point p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and the finite exact optimal value \(v^*\in\mathbb{Q}\), form the rational feasibility system \(Ax\le b\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x\le v^*\), and \(-c^{\mathsf T}x\le-v^*\). Apply an exact rational feasible-point procedure to this system and return its point \(x^*\in\mathbb{Q}^n\). The output conditions are \(Ax^*\le b\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^*=v^*\), both checked by exact rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover an exact optimizer by applying rational feasibility to the original constraints together with two inequalities enforcing the exact optimal value.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Solution Recovery

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Dual-Solution Recovery from the Optimal Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual counterpart of exact primal recovery for a rational standard-form LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\), suppose the finite exact optimum \(v^*\) is known and attained. Apply an exact rational feasible-point procedure to \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y\le v^*\), and \(-b^{\mathsf T}y\le-v^*\). Any returned \(y^*\) is an exact dual optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover an exact dual optimizer by imposing dual feasibility together with equality to the known exact optimal value.
assumptions_latex: \(A,b,c\) and \(v^*\) are rational.
The primal has a finite attained optimum and strong LP duality applies.
An exact rational feasible-point procedure is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^{\mathsf T}y^*\le c,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y^*=v^*.

notation.meaning: Known exact common primal-dual optimal value.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Dual-Solution Recovery from the Optimal Value

children.title: Optimal-Face Recovery
children.top_down_role: Identifying the optimal face or its encoded description.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery of the optimal face in standard form through coordinate-vanishing tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) and let \(z^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), solve the auxiliary problem \(u_j=\max\{x_j:x\in P,\ c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\}\), allowing the value \(+\infty\). Set \(Z=\{j:u_j=0\}\). Output the rational polyhedral face \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\}\), together with the description \(F^*=\{x\in P:x_j=0\text{ for every }j\in Z\}\). The procedure stops after computing \(z^*\) and solving \(n\) exact auxiliary LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve coordinate-maximization problems over the real optimal set. The coordinates whose maxima are zero are precisely those fixed at zero throughout that set, and they give an exact description of the optimal face.
assumptions_latex: The rational standard-form LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) is feasible and has a finite optimum \(z^*\).
The optimum and all auxiliary LPs are solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0,\ c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\}=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0,\ x_j=0\ \text{for every }j\in Z\}\).

notation.meaning: Real feasible polyhedron of the standard-form LP.
Indices forced to zero throughout the optimal face.

children.title: Optimal Basis Recovery
children.top_down_role: Recovering a basis associated with an optimal basic solution.

assumptions_latex: The rational standard-form minimization LP has rank \(m\), is feasible, and has a finite optimum.
Exact rational linear algebra and comparisons are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned set \(B\) is an optimal basis, and \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\) is an optimal basic feasible solution.

notation.meaning: Candidate set of basic column indices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exact basis recovery for a standard-form minimization LP, including degenerate optima.

source_refs.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), enumerate subsets \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) of cardinality \(m\). Discard \(B\) unless \(A_B\) is nonsingular. For each remaining set, put \(N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus B\), compute \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\), \(y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), and \(\bar c_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\). Stop and output the first \(B\) satisfying \(x_B\ge0\) and \(\bar c_N\ge0\). If the stated feasibility and boundedness assumptions hold, such a basis exists, and the enumeration terminates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enumerate nonsingular candidate bases and return one whose basic solution is feasible and whose nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative. Such a basis represents an exact optimal basic solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal Basis Recovery

source_witnesses.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case candidate count for the accepted exact enumeration algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the accepted rank-\(m\) standard-form assumptions, exhaustive optimal-basis recovery examines at most \(\binom{n}{m}\) column subsets. Each candidate requires exact nonsingularity, basic-feasibility, and reduced-cost tests. Thus the method terminates, but its candidate count can be exponential in the dimensions and does not establish polynomial-time basis recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact basis enumeration tests at most n choose m candidates and can therefore take exponentially many candidate checks.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has rank \(m\) and \(m\le n\).
Candidates are all cardinality-\(m\) column subsets.
Exact rational candidate tests are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{cand}}\le\binom{n}{m},\qquad \binom{n}{m}\text{ may be exponential in the encoded dimensions.}

children.title: Recovery-Output Complexity
children.top_down_role: Output-size and computational distinctions among exact recovery targets.

assumptions_latex: The output uses a fixed injective binary encoding.
The algorithm must explicitly write its exact recovery result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(I)\ge L_{\mathrm{out}}(I)\), and therefore \(T(I)=\Omega(L_{\mathrm{out}}(I))\).

notation.meaning: Number of output bits for instance I.
Bit-operation running time on instance I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive lower bound for explicit exact LP recovery under a bit model.

source_refs.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP instance \(I\), let \(L_{\mathrm{out}}(I)\) be the number of bits in the prescribed explicit encoding of the recovered exact solution, optimal basis, or optimal-face description. In a deterministic multitape Turing-machine model in which one transition writes at most one output symbol, every algorithm producing that encoding has running time \(T(I)\ge L_{\mathrm{out}}(I)\). Consequently, polynomial-time exact recovery requires the selected output representation itself to have length polynomial in the input encoding length; an exponentially long explicit output cannot be produced in polynomial total time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any exact-recovery algorithm needs at least one writing step per output bit. Thus its running time is at least the encoded length of the recovered object.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery-Output Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts compact exact recovery outputs with potentially exponential enumerative descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an explicitly encoded rational LP of binary input length \(L\), some exact optimal rational solution has encoding length \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\), and a basis index set has length \(O(m\log n)\) under a standard index encoding. An optimal face has a compact description using the original constraints and the exact optimal-objective equality. In contrast, a contract requiring every optimal vertex, every optimal basis, or another enumerative expansion may contain exponentially many entries. Polynomial output size therefore depends on the prescribed representation, not only on the underlying optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact solutions, basis indices, and implicit optimal-face descriptions can be compact, whereas enumerating every optimal vertex or basis may require exponential output.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational and explicitly encoded with binary length \(L\).
Outputs use fixed injective binary encodings.
The optimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_{\mathrm{out}}=\operatorname{poly}(L)\text{ for suitable compact representations, whereas enumerative contracts may have exponential }L_{\mathrm{out}}.

notation.meaning: Length of the prescribed recovery output.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Sensitive Recovery Output Size

children.title: Arithmetic-Operation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational cost measured by arithmetic operations.

assumptions_latex: The real-arithmetic model assigns unit cost to each scalar arithmetic operation and comparison.
The algorithm performs \(K\) iterations before termination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{arith}}=C_0+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}W_k+C_{\mathrm{out}}\).

notation.meaning: Arithmetic work performed during iteration k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost real-arithmetic accounting, distinct from bit complexity.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Count each scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, square root, and ordered comparison as one unit-cost operation. If initialization costs \(C_0\), iteration \(k\) costs \(W_k\), termination occurs after \(K\) iterations, and output formation costs \(C_{\mathrm{out}}\), then the arithmetic-operation complexity is \(C_{\mathrm{arith}}=C_0+\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}W_k+C_{\mathrm{out}}\). In particular, if \(W_k\le W\) for every \(k\), then \(C_{\mathrm{arith}}\le C_0+KW+C_{\mathrm{out}}\). This count does not charge for operand bit length or numerical precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total arithmetic complexity is initialization work plus the sum of per-iteration operation counts plus output work. Uniform per-iteration work yields the bound initialization plus iterations times work plus output.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-Operation Complexity

children.title: Iteration Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational cost measured by major algorithmic iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case update count relative to a specified LP stopping predicate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a deterministic iterative algorithm generate states \(z^0,z^1,\ldots\) on LP instance \(I\), and let \(S(z;I,\varepsilon)\) be its stated termination predicate for \(\varepsilon>0\). Its instancewise iteration complexity is \(K(I,\varepsilon)=\min\{k\ge0:S(z^k;I,\varepsilon)\text{ holds}\}\), with \(K(I,\varepsilon)=+\infty\) when termination never occurs. For the class \(\mathcal I_L\) of instances having encoding length at most \(L\), the worst-case iteration complexity is \(K(L,\varepsilon)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_L}K(I,\varepsilon)\). Iteration counting excludes initialization, output formation, and the internal arithmetic cost of an update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration complexity is the first update index satisfying a fixed stopping test. Worst-case complexity takes the supremum over inputs of bounded encoding length and excludes work inside each update.
assumptions_latex: A deterministic iterative LP algorithm and a precise stopping predicate are fixed.
The accuracy parameter satisfies \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(I,\varepsilon)=\min\{k\ge0:S(z^k;I,\varepsilon)\text{ holds}\}\), with value \(+\infty\) if the set is empty.

notation.meaning: Instance class with encoding length at most L.

If the principal system has order \(d\), contains \(s\) stored nonzeros, and the chosen solver costs at most \(L(d,s)\) operations, then \(W_k\le W_k^{\mathrm{form}}+L(d,s)+W_k^{\mathrm{update}}+W_k^{\mathrm{test}}\). The function \(L\) must reflect the specified dense or sparse factorization model.

knowledge_statements.title: Input Encoding Length
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete dense self-delimiting binary encoding for rational standard-form LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an injective self-delimiting binary code for signed integers, and let \(\ell(z)\) denote the length of the codeword for \(z\in\mathbb Z\). For a reduced rational \(r=p/q\) with \(q>0\), encode the ordered pair \((p,q)\) by concatenating its two self-delimiting codewords and define \(\ell(r)=\ell(p)+\ell(q)\). For rational data \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\), stored densely in a fixed order, define the input encoding length by \(L(A,b,c)=\ell(m)+\ell(n)+\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(A_{ij})+\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(b_i)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(c_j)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a self-delimiting binary code for integers and encode each reduced rational by its numerator and positive denominator. For dense LP data, input length is the sum of the codeword lengths of the dimensions and all entries.
assumptions_latex: Every rational is stored in reduced numerator-denominator form with positive denominator.
A fixed injective self-delimiting binary code is used for every signed integer.
The matrix is stored densely in a fixed row-major order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(A,b,c)=\ell(m)+\ell(n)+\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(A_{ij})+\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(b_i)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(c_j)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) have \(s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) nonzero entries, listed once in lexicographic order as triples \((i,j,A_{ij})\). Under fixed self-delimiting integer and reduced-rational codes, a sparse encoding has length \[L_{\mathrm{sp}}=\ell(m)+\ell(n)+\ell(s)+\sum_{A_{ij}\ne0}\bigl(\ell(i)+\ell(j)+\ell(A_{ij})\bigr)+\sum_{i=1}^m\ell(b_i)+\sum_{j=1}^n\ell(c_j).\] For standard binary index codes this is \[O\!\left((s+m+n)\log(m+n)+\sum_{A_{ij}\ne0}\ell(A_{ij})+\sum_i\ell(b_i)+\sum_j\ell(c_j)\right).\]
