notation.meaning: Intermediate reduced rational produced at time t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operand-growth accounting for exact rational LP computations.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r_0,r_1,\ldots,r_M\) be all reduced rational quantities stored during an exact LP computation, and set \(H=\max_{0\le t\le M}\ell(r_t)\). If the computation executes \(N\) rational additions, multiplications, divisions, and comparisons, then its Turing bit cost depends on both \(N\) and \(H\). With an integer-arithmetic cost bound \(M_{\mathbb Z}(H)\) for multiplying \(H\)-bit integers, a direct implementation has cost bounded by a polynomial in \(N\), \(H\), and \(M_{\mathbb Z}(H)\). Hence a polynomial arithmetic-operation count alone does not establish polynomial bit complexity unless \(H\) is polynomially bounded by the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rational complexity depends on both the number of arithmetic operations and the largest intermediate numerator or denominator. Polynomial operation count alone does not guarantee polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Number Growth

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated Squaring Produces Exponential Operand Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic family showing that operation count alone does not control intermediate bit length.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(r_0=2\), perform \(r_{k+1}=r_k^2\) for \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\). Then \(r_N=2^{2^N}\), whose ordinary binary encoding has \(2^N+1\) bits although only \(N\) multiplications were performed. Thus no polynomial in the arithmetic-operation count alone bounds intermediate encoding length for unrestricted exact computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated squaring uses only N multiplications but creates a number with exponentially many bits.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic is exact.
Integers use ordinary binary positional encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\text{ multiplications can produce }H_N=2^N+1\text{ bits, so }H_N\notin\operatorname{poly}(N).

notation.meaning: Binary length of the final integer.

review_flags: This is an exact-arithmetic obstruction illustrating the local operand-growth pathology; it is not asserted to be an LP algorithm trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Squaring Produces Exponential Operand Growth

children.title: Working-Precision Requirements
children.top_down_role: Precision budgets needed to support LP complexity guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Working-Precision Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision bound under an explicit forward-error model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a finite-precision LP computation returns \(\widehat z\) for an exact target \(z\), and its verified forward-error estimate is \(\|\widehat z-z\|\le K2^{-p}\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) is the binary working precision and \(K>0\) includes conditioning and accumulated-error factors. To guarantee \(\|\widehat z-z\|\le\eta\) for \(\eta>0\), it suffices to choose \(p\ge\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(K/\eta)\rceil\}\). If exact rational reconstruction additionally requires error strictly below a threshold \(\tau>0\), it suffices to choose a nonnegative integer \(p\) satisfying \(K2^{-p}<\tau\). The value of \(K\) must be established for the particular algorithm and instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a verified forward-error estimate, a nonnegative working precision at least the nonnegative rounded logarithm of the amplification-to-tolerance ratio guarantees the requested accuracy. A strict reconstruction threshold requires choosing precision so that the error bound is strictly below it.
assumptions_latex: At precision \(p\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\), the computed quantity satisfies \(\|\widehat z-z\|\le K2^{-p}\) for a known \(K>0\).
The requested absolute error tolerance satisfies \(\eta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\ge\max\{0,\lceil\log_2(K/\eta)\rceil\}\) implies \(\|\widehat z-z\|\le\eta\).

notation.meaning: Nonnegative integer number of working binary precision bits.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

children.title: Rounding Error Control
children.top_down_role: Complexity effects of finite-arithmetic rounding.

assumptions_latex: The exact update maps satisfy \(\|F_k(u)-F_k(v)\|\le L_k\|u-v\|\).
The computed update has local error at most \(\delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_K\le e_0\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}L_j+\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}\delta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^{K-1}L_j\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz factor of exact update k.
Local rounding error in update k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic propagation bound for normwise rounding errors across LP iterations.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let exact iterates satisfy \(z^{k+1}=F_k(z^k)\), and computed iterates satisfy \(\widehat z^{k+1}=F_k(\widehat z^k)+r_k\), where \(\|r_k\|\le\delta_k\). If \(F_k\) is Lipschitz with factor \(L_k\), then \(e_{k+1}\le L_ke_k+\delta_k\) for \(e_k=\|\widehat z^k-z^k\|\). Consequently, after \(K\) updates, \(e_K\le e_0\prod_{j=0}^{K-1}L_j+\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}\delta_i\prod_{j=i+1}^{K-1}L_j\), where an empty product equals \(1\). Controlling the right-hand side controls accumulated rounding error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each update amplifies prior error and adds local rounding error. Iterating this recurrence gives an explicit bound on total error after any fixed number of LP iterations.
knowledge_statements.title: Rounding Error Control

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

children.title: Rational Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of exact rational output from sufficiently accurate numerical information.

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar continued-fraction reconstruction from a rational approximation with a known denominator bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational approximation \(\widetilde x\in\mathbb Q\) and an integer \(Q\ge1\), compute the finite continued-fraction expansion of \(\widetilde x\) and its convergents. Among the reduced convergents \(p/q\) with \(1\le q\le Q\), output the unique one satisfying \(|\widetilde x-p/q|<1/(2Q^2)\); report failure if no such convergent exists. If an exact reduced rational \(x=a/b\) satisfies \(1\le b\le Q\) and \(|\widetilde x-x|<1/(2Q^2)\), then \(a/b\) is a convergent of \(\widetilde x\), is the unique rational with denominator at most \(Q\) satisfying the strict test, and is output by the procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a finitely encoded rational approximation, a target rational with denominator at most Q is uniquely recoverable when the error is less than one over twice Q squared. Continued fractions provide the finite reconstruction procedure.
assumptions_latex: The approximation \(\widetilde x\) is a finitely encoded rational number.
The exact value is a reduced rational \(x=a/b\) with \(1\le b\le Q\).
The approximation satisfies \(|\widetilde x-x|<1/(2Q^2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rational \(x\) is uniquely determined among rationals of denominator at most \(Q\) and is recovered from the continued-fraction convergents of \(\widetilde x\).

notation.meaning: Finitely encoded rational approximation to the exact value.

source_refs.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite bit-complexity bound for scalar bounded-denominator reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde x=u/v\) be reduced with \(v>0\), and let \(B=\ell(u)+\ell(v)\). Its finite continued fraction and all convergents with denominator at most \(Q\) can be computed by the Euclidean algorithm with total bit complexity polynomial in \(B+\ell(Q)\). Thus scalar bounded-denominator reconstruction is polynomial-time in its finite input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continued-fraction rational reconstruction runs in polynomial bit time in the encoded approximation and denominator bound.
assumptions_latex: The approximation is supplied as a finitely encoded reduced rational \(u/v\).
The denominator bound \(Q\geq1\) is encoded in binary.
Standard finite-integer arithmetic is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{recon}}\in\operatorname{poly}(B+\ell(Q)).

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the rational approximation.
Bit cost of scalar continued-fraction reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.title: Continued-Fraction Reconstruction Complexity

children.title: Precision-to-Reconstruction Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Accuracy regimes that permit reliable rational output recovery.

assumptions_latex: Every target coordinate is a reduced rational with denominator at most \(Q\ge1\).
The approximation obeys a certified coordinatewise error bound \(\|\widetilde x-x\|_\infty\le2^{-p}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2^{-p}<1/(2Q^2)\) guarantees unique coordinatewise rational reconstruction of \(x\).

notation.meaning: Number of certified accurate binary bits.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise precision threshold implied by a uniform denominator bound.

source_refs.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathbb Q^n\) have reduced coordinates whose denominators do not exceed \(Q\), and suppose \(\|\widetilde x-x\|_\infty\le2^{-p}\). The coordinatewise reconstruction condition is \(2^{-p}<1/(2Q^2)\). Under this strict inequality, each coordinate of \(x\) is the unique rational with denominator at most \(Q\) lying within \(1/(2Q^2)\) of the corresponding coordinate of \(\widetilde x\). A convenient integer sufficient condition is \(p\ge\lceil\log_2(2Q^2)\rceil+1\). Applying scalar rational reconstruction to every coordinate then recovers \(x\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every denominator is at most Q, certified coordinate error below one over twice Q squared permits exact coordinatewise recovery. One extra bit beyond the rounded logarithmic threshold suffices.
knowledge_statements.title: Precision-to-Reconstruction Thresholds

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Reconstruction Threshold Without a Denominator Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessity of denominator or separation information for exact reconstruction from absolute error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\delta>0\), choose an integer \(q>1/(2\delta)\). The distinct rationals \(0\) and \(1/q\) are both within \(\delta\) of \(\widetilde x=1/(2q)\). Therefore no positive absolute-error threshold independent of a denominator or separation bound can guarantee unique rational reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a denominator or separation bound, arbitrarily close distinct rationals make every fixed positive reconstruction tolerance ambiguous.
assumptions_latex: The target may be any rational with no denominator bound.
Only an absolute approximation-error guarantee is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\delta>0\ \exists x_1\ne x_2\in\mathbb Q,\ \widetilde x:\ |\widetilde x-x_1|<\delta\ \land\ |\widetilde x-x_2|<\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Reconstruction Threshold Without a Denominator Bound

assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses an LP instance only through a specified oracle \(\mathcal O\).
The accuracy requirement and oracle response convention are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle-call complexity is \(N_{\mathcal O}(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I)}q(e)\), with worst-case size bound \(N_{\mathcal O}(L,\varepsilon)=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}N_{\mathcal O}(I,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: number of oracle queries in execution e
binary encoding length of instance I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts oracle invocations independently of the arithmetic cost of producing or processing oracle responses.

source_refs.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP algorithm interacting with an oracle \(\mathcal O\), let \(\mathcal E(I)\) be the admissible executions on instance \(I\), including allowed internal randomness or oracle choices, and let \(q(e)\) count invocations of \(\mathcal O\) before the prescribed output condition is met. The oracle-call complexity on \(I\) is \(N_{\mathcal O}(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I)}q(e)\). For inputs of encoding length at most \(L\), the worst-case complexity is \(N_{\mathcal O}(L,\varepsilon):=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}N_{\mathcal O}(I,\varepsilon)\). Each call counts once, irrespective of its internal implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-call complexity is the worst-case number of invocations of a specified oracle needed to meet a fixed LP output and accuracy requirement.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic information lower bound for deterministic finite-answer oracle models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a deterministic LP oracle algorithm receives at most \(B\ge2\) possible answers to each query. If admissible instances contain \(N\) classes requiring different outputs, then every correct oracle decision tree has at least \(N\) leaves and worst-case oracle-call complexity \(q\ge\lceil\log_BN\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With at most B possible answers per query, distinguishing N output classes requires at least logarithm base B of N oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic.
Each oracle query has at most \(B\) possible encoded responses.
Different instance classes require different valid outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q\ge\lceil\log_BN\rceil.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of possible answers to one query.
Number of instance classes requiring distinct outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Decision-Tree Lower Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary of unit-cost oracle-call accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an execution make \(q\) oracle calls whose implementation costs are \(a_1,\ldots,a_q\ge0\), and incur nonoracle work \(W_0\). Its implemented work is \(W_0+\sum_{i=1}^qa_i\). Therefore, a bound \(q\le Q\) implies an end-to-end work bound only if the nonoracle work and individual oracle costs are also bounded; call complexity alone permits arbitrarily large total work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Few oracle calls do not imply low runtime unless the cost of each response and all nonoracle work are bounded separately.
assumptions_latex: Oracle invocations count at unit cost in the oracle-call measure.
Implemented oracle and nonoracle work may have nonuniform costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{impl}}=W_0+\sum_{i=1}^qa_i;\quad q\le Q\ \not\Rightarrow\ W_{\mathrm{impl}}\le\operatorname{poly}(Q).

notation.meaning: Implementation cost of oracle call i.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Count versus Implementation-Cost Boundary

children.title: End-to-End Work Complexity
children.top_down_role: Total computational work across all phases of an LP solution process.

assumptions_latex: The LP input, output requirement, computational model, and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) are fixed.
All preprocessing, oracle implementation, numerical linear algebra, and output verification are included.
All admissible executions, including allowed internal randomness or implementation choices, are included in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The end-to-end work is \(W(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)}\sum_{j=1}^{T(e)}c_{e,j}\), and its size-dependent worst case is \(W(L,\varepsilon)=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}W(I,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: set of admissible executions on instance I at accuracy epsilon
cost of charged action j in execution e
number of charged actions in execution e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes every charged stage from reading the encoded LP through producing and validating the requested output.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a computational model assigning a nonnegative cost \(c_{e,j}\) to charged action \(j\) in each admissible execution \(e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)\) on LP instance \(I\) at accuracy \(\varepsilon\). If execution \(e\) performs \(T(e)\) charged actions, define \(W(e):=\sum_{j=1}^{T(e)}c_{e,j}\) and \(W(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)}W(e)\). The accounting includes input decoding, preprocessing, all iterations and oracle implementations, numerical linear algebra, recovery of the requested LP output, and verification. For encoding bound \(L\), define \(W(L,\varepsilon):=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}W(I,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: End-to-end work is the worst-case sum of all model-dependent costs from decoding an LP instance through computing, recovering, and verifying the requested approximate output.
knowledge_statements.title: End-to-End Work Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive accounting across disjoint phases of an LP computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every execution \(e\) is partitioned into disjoint charged phases \(P_1(e),\ldots,P_m(e)\), then \(W(e)=\sum_{k=1}^mW_k(e)\), where \(W_k(e):=\sum_{j\in P_k(e)}c_{e,j}\). Hence \(W(I,\varepsilon)\le\sum_{k=1}^m\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)}W_k(e)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: End-to-end work decomposes additively by execution phase, and separate worst-case phase bounds sum to an overall upper bound.
assumptions_latex: The charged actions of each execution are partitioned into disjoint phases.
All phase costs use the same computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W(I,\varepsilon)\le\sum_{k=1}^m\sup_eW_k(e).

notation.meaning: Charged actions in phase k of execution e.

knowledge_statements.title: Phase Decomposition of End-to-End Work

children.title: Memory Complexity
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements of LP algorithms and their intermediate data.

assumptions_latex: A concrete machine model and representation of LP data are fixed.
Every admissible execution on instance \(I\) terminates after satisfying the prescribed accuracy requirement \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The memory complexity is \(M(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)}\max_{t\in\mathcal T(e)}S_{e,t}\), with worst-case bound \(M(L,\varepsilon)=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}M(I,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: set of admissible executions on instance I at accuracy epsilon
execution times or configurations of execution e
charged storage occupied by execution e at time t

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak-space accounting includes input, iterates, factorizations, oracle state, and output under one fixed storage unit.

source_refs.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each admissible execution \(e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)\) of an LP algorithm on instance \(I\) with accuracy requirement \(\varepsilon\), let \(S_{e,t}\) be the number of charged storage units simultaneously occupied at time \(t\in\mathcal T(e)\). Define \(M(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_{e\in\mathcal E(I,\varepsilon)}\max_{t\in\mathcal T(e)}S_{e,t}\). Charged storage includes retained input data, current and auxiliary iterates, matrix factors, oracle state, and output buffers, but excludes immutable program text when the machine convention does so. For inputs satisfying \(\ell(I)\le L\), define \(M(L,\varepsilon):=\sup_{\ell(I)\le L}M(I,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory complexity is the worst-case maximum charged storage simultaneously occupied during an LP computation, under a fixed machine and data representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

children.title: Communication Complexity
children.top_down_role: Data-movement costs in distributed or hierarchical computing environments.

assumptions_latex: The LP data are partitioned among specified processors or parties.
The communication topology, message encoding, and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Communication complexity is \(C(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_e\sum_{r=1}^{R(e)}b_{e,r}\); round complexity is \(R(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_e R(e)\).

notation.meaning: number of communicated bits in message r of execution e
number of communication rounds in execution e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates transmitted information from local arithmetic; message bits and synchronization rounds are distinct resources.

source_refs.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed LP algorithm, let an admissible execution \(e\) send \(R(e)\) messages or synchronized message batches, and let \(b_{e,r}\) be the encoded bit length of its \(r\)-th transmission. Its communication cost is \(\sum_{r=1}^{R(e)}b_{e,r}\). The communication complexity on instance \(I\) is \(C(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_e\sum_{r=1}^{R(e)}b_{e,r}\), while its round complexity is \(R(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_e R(e)\). Local computation is not charged to \(C\), and replicated input is counted only according to the stipulated initial-distribution convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication complexity counts worst-case transmitted bits for distributed LP solution; round complexity separately counts synchronization stages under a fixed data distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: 3 Complexity Theory p. 49

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information lower bound for a fixed binary deterministic communication model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a deterministic distributed LP protocol represented by a binary protocol tree. If a set \(\mathcal I\) of admissible distributed inputs contains \(N\) classes such that inputs from different classes require different outputs, then every correct protocol has at least \(N\) leaves. Consequently, its worst-case communication satisfies \(C\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil\) bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic protocol must communicate at least the logarithm of the number of input classes requiring distinguishable outputs.
assumptions_latex: Communication follows a deterministic binary protocol tree.
Inputs in different classes require different valid outputs under the fixed LP task.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\ge\lceil\log_2N\rceil.

notation.meaning: Number of input classes requiring distinguishable outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Transcript-Counting Lower Bound

children.title: Parallel Complexity
children.top_down_role: Parallel work, depth, and processor requirements for LP computation.

assumptions_latex: A parallel machine with \(p\) processors and a fixed communication model is specified.
Each execution must meet the same LP output and accuracy requirement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Parallel time is \(T_p(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_e\sum_{r=1}^{D(e)}\max_{1\le i\le p}w_{e,r,i}\), with work \(W_p(I,\varepsilon)=\sup_e\sum_{r,i}w_{e,r,i}\).

notation.meaning: local work of processor i in parallel stage r

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records critical-path time and aggregate processor work under an explicit parallel and communication model.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP execution \(e\) on \(p\) processors, partition computation into \(D(e)\) dependency-respecting parallel stages and let \(w_{e,r,i}\) be the charged local work of processor \(i\) in stage \(r\), including communication according to the machine model. The parallel time is \(T_p(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_e\sum_{r=1}^{D(e)}\max_{1\le i\le p}w_{e,r,i}\). The aggregate work is \(W_p(I,\varepsilon):=\sup_e\sum_{r=1}^{D(e)}\sum_{i=1}^{p}w_{e,r,i}\). Speedup is \(S_p:=T_1/T_p\) whenever both times use compatible accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel LP complexity records critical-path time and aggregate processor work for a fixed processor count, scheduling convention, and communication model.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Complexity

source_witnesses.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal inequalities under the seed's stage-based parallel accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every execution on \(p\) processors, \(T_p(e)\le W_p(e)\le pT_p(e)\). Consequently, compatible worst-case bounds satisfy \(T_p(I,\varepsilon)\le W_p(I,\varepsilon)\le pT_p(I,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time never exceeds aggregate work, and aggregate work is at most the processor count times parallel time.
assumptions_latex: Parallel time and work use the seed's common stage decomposition and nonnegative local costs.
The same execution set is used in both worst-case quantities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_p\le W_p\le pT_p.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Work–Time Inequalities

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic scheduling theorem for an LP computation represented by a unit-time dependency DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a computation DAG have \(W\) unit-time operations and depth \(D\). A greedy schedule on \(p\ge1\) identical processors completes it in time \(T_p\le W/p+D\). Every schedule satisfies \(T_p\ge\max\{W/p,D\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computation with work W and depth D can be greedily scheduled in time at most W/p plus D, while work and depth give universal lower bounds.
assumptions_latex: The computation is a finite dependency DAG of unit-time operations.
Processors are identical; scheduling overhead and communication absent from the DAG are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max\{W/p,D\}\le T_p\le W/p+D.

notation.meaning: Number of operations in the computation DAG.

knowledge_statements.title: Brent Work–Depth Scheduling Bound

children.title: Resource Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among work, storage, communication, and parallel depth.

assumptions_latex: Every algorithm is evaluated on the same LP instance class and accuracy convention.
Each resource coordinate uses a fixed, comparable computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The nondominated resource profiles form \(\mathcal P=\{r\in\mathcal R:\nexists s\in\mathcal R,\ s\preceq r,\ s\ne r\}\); a regime selects profiles minimizing its prescribed scalar objective or constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes algorithm comparison when work, memory, communication, and parallel time cannot all be minimized simultaneously.

source_refs.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate each admissible LP algorithm with a resource profile \(r=(W,M,C,T_p,N_{\mathcal O})\in\mathbb R_+^5\) under common input and accuracy conventions, and let \(\mathcal R\) be the attainable profiles. Write \(s\preceq r\) when every coordinate of \(s\) is no larger than the corresponding coordinate of \(r\). The Pareto frontier is \(\mathcal P:=\{r\in\mathcal R:\nexists s\in\mathcal R,\ s\preceq r,\ s\ne r\}\). A resource regime is specified by weights, budgets, or processor parameters and selects profiles minimizing its resulting scalar objective or satisfying its resource constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resource regime fixes weights or budgets for work, memory, communication, time, and oracle calls; nondominated algorithms form the corresponding Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.title: Resource Tradeoff Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite example showing that positive weighted sums need not enumerate a nonconvex Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal R=\{(0,2),(1,3/2),(2,0)\}\), all three profiles are Pareto efficient. However, for every \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0\), the profile \((1,3/2)\) does not minimize \(\lambda_1x+\lambda_2y\): choosing it over \((0,2)\) requires \(\lambda_1\le\lambda_2/2\), while choosing it over \((2,0)\) requires \(\lambda_1\ge3\lambda_2/2\), which is impossible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A three-profile nonconvex resource set has a Pareto point that no positive weighted sum can select.
assumptions_latex: Both resource coordinates are minimized.
Scalarization weights are strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (1,3/2)\in\mathcal P\quad\text{but}\quad(1,3/2)\notin\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal R}\lambda^Tr\ \text{for every }\lambda>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsupported Pareto Profile

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-constraint formulation that can recover every Pareto-efficient resource profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r^*\in\mathcal R\subseteq\mathbb R_+^d\) be Pareto efficient. For any coordinate \(j\), \(r^*\) minimizes \(r_j\) over \(\{r\in\mathcal R:r_i\le r_i^*\text{ for all }i\ne j\}\). Conversely, any such minimizer is Pareto efficient if it is the unique minimizer in coordinate \(j\), or if a Pareto-efficient minimizer is selected among ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every Pareto profile can be recovered by minimizing one resource while budgeting all the others at that profile; ties must be resolved without selecting a dominated point.
assumptions_latex: All resource coordinates are minimized.
The comparison uses the same attainable set and resource conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^*\in\mathcal P\implies r^*\in\arg\min\{r_j:r\in\mathcal R,\ r_i\le r_i^*\ (i\ne j)\}.

notation.meaning: Resource coordinate chosen as the objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Constrained Characterization of Pareto Profiles

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Scalarization and Supported Pareto Profiles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relationship between positive weighted objectives and the Pareto frontier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathbb R_+^d\) be the attainable resource profiles. If \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_{++}^d\) and \(r^*\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal R}\lambda^Tr\), then \(r^*\) is Pareto efficient. Conversely, a Pareto-efficient profile need not minimize any positive weighted sum when \(\mathcal R\) is nonconvex; weighted sums recover only supported efficient profiles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every minimizer of a strictly positive weighted resource sum is Pareto efficient, but nonconvex tradeoff sets can contain efficient profiles that no weighted sum selects.
assumptions_latex: All resource coordinates are minimized.
Every scalarization weight is strictly positive for the forward implication.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^*\in\arg\min_{r\in\mathcal R}\lambda^Tr,\ \lambda>0\implies r^*\in\mathcal P.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic ellipsoid algorithm for strict linear inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-center implementation of ellipsoid feasibility; the update formulas are referenced as (A.15)-(A.16) in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(B=n4^D I\), \(c=0\), and \(v=(2^{D+1}\sqrt n)^n\). If \(Ac<b\), return \(c\). Otherwise choose \(i\) with \(a_i^Tc\ge b_i\), and compute the updated ellipsoid matrix, center, and volume quantity from (A.15)-(A.16). If the updated volume quantity is less than \(2^{-(n+1)D}\), declare \(Ax<b\) infeasible; otherwise replace \((B,c,v)\) by the updated quantities and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the ellipsoid matrix, center, and volume scalar as specified. Return the center if it satisfies all strict inequalities. Otherwise select a violated inequality, apply the algebraic ellipsoid update formulas, and either declare infeasibility when the updated volume falls below 2^{-(n+1)D} or continue with the updated ellipsoid.
assumptions_latex: B_0=n4^D I
\text{Updates are computed by (A.15)-(A.16)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either returns }c\text{ with }Ac<b\text{ or stops with the declaration that }Ax<b\text{ has no solution.}

The added objective inequalities have common normal }c.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First find a feasible point using the ellipsoid method. At each iterate, test whether a feasible point with strictly smaller objective value exists. If none exists, the current point is optimal; otherwise use a returned improving point as the next iterate. All added objective boundaries are parallel.

x_t\in P

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-cut feasibility procedure under known inner and outer volume bounds; correctness is stated separately by the accompanying theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Tx\ge b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), a known \(v>0\) such that \(P=\varnothing\) or \(\operatorname{Vol}(P)>v\), and \(E_0=E(x_0,r^2I)\supseteq P\) with \(\operatorname{Vol}(E_0)\le V\), set \(t^*=\lceil2(n+1)\log(V/v)\rceil\), \(D_0=r^2I\), and \(t=0\). At iteration \(t\), declare \(P=\varnothing\) if \(t=t^*\); return \(x_t\) if \(x_t\in P\); otherwise choose \(i\) with \(a_i^Tx_t<b_i\), set \(H_t=\{x:a_i^Tx\ge a_i^Tx_t\}\), and update \[x_{t+1}=x_t+\frac{1}{n+1}\frac{D_ta_i}{\sqrt{a_i^TD_ta_i}},\qquad D_{t+1}=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(D_t-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{D_ta_ia_i^TD_t}{a_i^TD_ta_i}\right).\] Increment \(t\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a known ellipsoid containing P. Return its center when feasible; otherwise use a violated inequality to make a cut through the center and replace the current ellipsoid by the stated enclosing ellipsoid. At the prescribed iteration limit, declare P empty.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:a_i^Tx\ge b_i,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}
P=\varnothing\ \lor\ \operatorname{Vol}(P)>v
P\subseteq E_0=E(x_0,r^2I),\quad \operatorname{Vol}(E_0)\le V
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The specified output is a center }x_t\in P\text{ when one is encountered, or the declaration }P=\varnothing\text{ when }t=t^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential construction of the index sets J and I
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-order construction using feasibility tests; no additional property of the returned sets is asserted by this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(j=1,\ldots,n\), let \(J^*=J\setminus\{j\}\) and replace \(J\) by \(J^*\) if \(\sum_{k\in J^*}a_{ik}x_k\le b_i\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\) is solvable. Then initialize \(I=\varnothing\). For \(i=1,\ldots,m\), let \(I^*=I\cup\{i\}\) and replace \(I\) by \(I^*\) if there exists \((x_j)_{j\in J}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j\in J}a_{kj}x_j\le b_k\) for every \(k=1,\ldots,m\) and \(\sum_{j\in J}a_{kj}x_j\ge b_k\) for every \(k\in I^*\). Return \(J\) and \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inspect the variable indices in order, deleting an index when the system using the remaining variables is feasible. Then inspect the constraint indices in order, adding an index when all inequalities remain feasible and all selected inequalities can simultaneously hold at equality. Return the resulting sets J and I.
assumptions_latex: A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
b\in\mathbb R^m
x_j\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\quad\text{and}\quad I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\text{ are returned after the stated feasibility tests.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric ellipsoid algorithm for strict linear inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric feasibility procedure using enclosing ellipsoids and the source's localization-volume threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\{x:Ax<b\}\), let \(R_{13}\) be the region defined by (A.13), and set \(S=H\cap R_{13}\). Initialize \(E=\{x:x^Tx\le n4^D\}\), which encloses \(S\). If the center \(c\) of \(E\) lies in \(H\), stop with \(c\). Otherwise construct a smaller ellipsoid \(\widetilde E\) enclosing \(S\). If \(\operatorname{vol}(\widetilde E)<2^{-(n+1)D}\), stop and declare \(H=\varnothing\); otherwise set \(E\leftarrow\widetilde E\) and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the specified sphere enclosing the localized feasible set. Stop with the current center if it satisfies every strict inequality. Otherwise replace the ellipsoid by a smaller one still enclosing that set; declare the strict system infeasible if the new volume is below the localization threshold, and otherwise continue.
assumptions_latex: S=R_{13}\cap\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax<b\}
S\subseteq\{x:x^Tx\le n4^D\}
\widetilde E\supseteq S\text{ at every update}
Ax<b\text{ solvable}\implies\operatorname{vol}(S)\ge2^{-(n+1)D}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure either finds }c\text{ satisfying }Ac<b\text{ or declares }\{x:Ax<b\}=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-cut ellipsoid algorithm for bounded epsilon-thick feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Promise-style feasibility procedure with an outer-radius bound, an inner-radius threshold, and explicit permitted behavior for thin feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $A,b$ and rational $R>\varepsilon>0$, suppose $P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\subseteq B(0,R)$. Set $E_0=B(0,R)$. At iteration $k$, return the center $s_k$ if $s_k\in P$. Otherwise choose a violated inequality $a_i^Ts_k>b_i$ and let $E_{k+1}$ be the minimum-volume ellipsoid containing $E_k\cap\{x:a_i^Tx\le a_i^Ts_k\}$. If $\operatorname{vol}(E_{k+1})<\operatorname{vol}(B(0,\varepsilon))$, return NO SOLUTION; otherwise continue. Each $E_k$ contains $P$. If $P$ contains a ball of radius $\varepsilon$, the algorithm returns a point in $P$; if not, it may return either a point in $P$ or NO SOLUTION.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the known radius-R ball and test each ellipsoid center. A violated inequality supplies a central cut, after which the minimum-volume covering ellipsoid becomes the next iterate. The method reports no solution when its volume falls below that of an epsilon-ball. It must find a feasible point if the feasible set contains an epsilon-ball, but may report no solution when the feasible set is thinner.
assumptions_latex: R,\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q
R>\varepsilon>0
P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\subseteq B(0,R)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\exists z:\ B(z,\varepsilon)\subseteq P\bigr)\Rightarrow\text{the algorithm returns }y\in P;\quad \neg\exists z:\ B(z,\varepsilon)\subseteq P\Rightarrow\text{it may return }y\in P\text{ or NO SOLUTION}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $B^n=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:x^Tx\le1\}$. If $M\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ is nonsingular and $s\in\mathbb R^n$, then $E=\{Mx+s:x\in B^n\}=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:(y-s)^TQ^{-1}(y-s)\le1\}$, where $Q=MM^T\succ0$. Conversely, every $Q\succ0$ admits such a factorization. The vector $s$ is the center. In an orthogonal eigenbasis of $Q$, the ellipsoid is in axial position and its semiaxis lengths are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ellipsoid is an affine image of the unit ball, equivalently a positive-definite quadratic sublevel set. Its translation vector is its center. An orthogonal eigenbasis puts it in axial position, where the square roots of the shape-matrix eigenvalues are its semiaxis lengths.

s\in\mathbb R^n
Q=MM^T\succ0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{Mx+s:x\in B^n\}=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:(y-s)^TQ^{-1}(y-s)\le1\}

children.title: Ellipsoidal Localization
children.top_down_role: Geometric localization of candidate points within enclosing ellipsoids.

assumptions_latex: The current ellipsoid is \(E_k=\{x:(x-c_k)^\mathsf TQ_k^{-1}(x-c_k)\le1\}\) with \(Q_k\succ0\).
The convex target set \(K\) satisfies \(K\subseteq E_k\).
If \(c_k\notin K\), the oracle returns \(a_k\ne0\) with \(a_k^\mathsf T(x-c_k)\le0\) for every \(x\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The central-cut update defines an ellipsoid \(E_{k+1}\) satisfying \(E_k\cap\{x:a_k^\mathsf T(x-c_k)\le0\}\subseteq E_{k+1}\), and consequently \(K\subseteq E_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-cut ellipsoid update in dimension \(n\ge2\), maintaining an outer localization of a convex feasible set.

source_refs.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\). Given \(E_k=\{x:(x-c_k)^\mathsf TQ_k^{-1}(x-c_k)\le1\}\) and a central separating cut with normal \(a_k\), set \(u_k:=Q_ka_k/\sqrt{a_k^\mathsf TQ_ka_k}\), \(c_{k+1}:=c_k-u_k/(n+1)\), and \(Q_{k+1}:=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(Q_k-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{Q_ka_ka_k^\mathsf TQ_k}{a_k^\mathsf TQ_ka_k}\right)\). The ellipsoid determined by \((c_{k+1},Q_{k+1})\) contains \(E_k\cap\{x:a_k^\mathsf T(x-c_k)\le0\}\), and therefore contains \(K\). Stop when the center is accepted or the prescribed localization threshold is reached.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separating cut through the current center determines a lower-volume enclosing ellipsoid that continues to contain every feasible point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate invariance of the central-cut containment update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=Tz+d\) with nonsingular \(T\). Transform an ellipsoid and its central separating halfspace to \(z\)-coordinates, perform the standard central-cut update there, and map the resulting ellipsoid back. The result equals the ellipsoid obtained by applying the standard update directly in \(x\)-coordinates. Hence the containment localization update is invariant under nonsingular affine coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central-cut ellipsoid update commutes with every nonsingular affine change of coordinates.
assumptions_latex: x=Tz+d\text{ with }T\text{ nonsingular}.
The ellipsoid shape matrix is positive definite and the central cut normal is nonzero.

children.title: Ellipsoid Volume Reduction
children.top_down_role: Volume decrease as the progress measure behind ellipsoid complexity.

assumptions_latex: The central-cut update is applied in dimension \(n\ge2\).
The current shape matrix satisfies \(Q_k\succ0\), and the cut normal satisfies \(a_k\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update satisfies \(\operatorname{vol}(E_{k+1})/\operatorname{vol}(E_k)=\left(\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right)^{n/2}\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n+1}}\le e^{-1/(2(n+1))}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact determinant ratio and standard exponential bound for the central-cut enclosing ellipsoid.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the central-cut update in dimension \(n\ge2\), \(\det(Q_{k+1})/\det(Q_k)=\left(\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right)^n\frac{n-1}{n+1}\) and \(\operatorname{vol}(E_{k+1})/\operatorname{vol}(E_k)=\left(\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right)^{n/2}\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n+1}}\le\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2(n+1)}\right)\). After \(k\) unsuccessful central cuts, \(\operatorname{vol}(E_k)\le\exp\left(-\frac{k}{2(n+1)}\right)\operatorname{vol}(E_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each central ellipsoid cut reduces localization volume by an exact dimension-dependent factor bounded above by exp(-1/(2(n+1))).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimum-Volume Ellipsoid for a Central Cut
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Löwner-ellipsoid characterization underlying the standard central-cut volume factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), \(E=\{x:(x-c)^{\mathsf T}Q^{-1}(x-c)\le1\}\) with \(Q\succ0\), and \(H=\{x:a^{\mathsf T}(x-c)\le0\}\) with \(a\ne0\). The standard central-cut update ellipsoid is the unique minimum-volume ellipsoid containing \(E\cap H\). Its volume ratio to \(E\) is \(\left(\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\right)^{n/2}\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n+1}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard central-cut update is the unique minimum-volume ellipsoid enclosing the retained half of the current ellipsoid.

Q\succ0.
a\ne0\text{ and the cut hyperplane passes through }c.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Central-Cut Ellipsoid Containment and Volume Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit enclosing-ellipsoid update for the half of an ellipsoid retained by a hyperplane through its center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge2\), let \(E=E(z,D)\subset\mathbb R^n\) be an ellipsoid, and let \(a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\). Define \(H=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:a^{\mathsf T}x\ge a^{\mathsf T}z\}\), \[\bar z=z+\frac{1}{n+1}\frac{Da}{\sqrt{a^{\mathsf T}Da}},\qquad \bar D=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(D-\frac{2}{n+1}\frac{Daa^{\mathsf T}D}{a^{\mathsf T}Da}\right).\] Then \(\bar D\) is symmetric positive definite, so \(E'=E(\bar z,\bar D)\) is an ellipsoid, and \[E\cap H\subseteq E',\qquad \operatorname{Vol}(E')<e^{-1/(2(n+1))}\operatorname{Vol}(E).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a central halfspace cut of an ellipsoid in dimension at least two, the stated center and shape-matrix update produces a positive-definite enclosing ellipsoid containing the retained half, with volume strictly less than exp(-1/(2(n+1))) times the original volume.

a\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}

children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes where full-dimensional volume accounting requires refinement.

assumptions_latex: The ellipsoid method uses full-dimensional Lebesgue volume in \(\mathbb R^n\).
The feasible convex set \(K\) may be nonempty but have empty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No positive inner radius \(r\) exists and volume decay alone cannot distinguish \(K=\varnothing\) from \(K\ne\varnothing\); one must reduce to \(\operatorname{aff}(K)\), thicken the set, or adopt weak feasibility.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the failure of full-dimensional volume certification for nonempty lower-dimensional LP feasible regions.

source_refs.locator: Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a nonempty convex feasible set \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\) has \(\operatorname{affdim}(K)<n\), then \(\operatorname{vol}_n(K)=0\) and no \(r>0\) satisfies \(B(z,r)\subseteq K\). Thus the inference from a sufficiently small enclosing volume to emptiness is invalid: a sequence of full-dimensional ellipsoids can localize a nonempty lower-dimensional set while their volumes tend to zero. A valid complexity argument must instead work in \(\operatorname{aff}(K)\), use a thickening \(K_\delta:=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x,K)\le\delta\}\), or formulate weak feasibility with tolerance \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty lower-dimensional feasible region has zero ambient volume, so volume shrinkage cannot certify emptiness without affine reduction, thickening, or weak feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Localization Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write the rows of \(A\) as \(a_i^\mathsf T\). Given \(y\), compute every residual \(r_i:=a_i^\mathsf Ty-b_i\). If \(r_i\le0\) for all \(i\), output the membership certificate \(y\in P\). Otherwise choose any \(i\) with \(r_i>0\) and return \((a_i,b_i)\). Every \(x\in P\) satisfies \(a_i^\mathsf Tx\le b_i<a_i^\mathsf Ty\), so this row strongly separates \(y\) from \(P\). Direct residual evaluation uses \(O(mn)\) rational arithmetic operations; bit cost additionally depends on operand lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For explicit inequalities, scan their residuals: either all constraints accept the query or any violated row is a strong separating hyperplane.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strong separation oracle for an implicitly represented rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a procedure that, on rational query \(y\), either certifies \(y\in P\) or returns rational \(a\ne0\) and \(\beta\) such that \(a^\mathsf Tx\le\beta<a^\mathsf Ty\) for every \(x\in P\). The oracle is polynomial-time when its running time and the binary encoding length of \((a,\beta)\) are bounded by a polynomial in the implicit instance encoding and \(\ell(y)\). This resource control permits separation calls to participate in a polynomial bit-complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit-polyhedron oracle must either confirm membership or return a polynomial-size rational inequality strongly separating the query, within polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational separation-oracle transcript encodes a query \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\) and a tagged response. The response is either the finite tag \(\mathrm{IN}\) or a rational tuple \((a,\beta)\in\mathbb Q^n\times\mathbb Q\). Each rational is represented by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in lowest terms, and the transcript length is the sum of the tag, dimension, and coordinate encoding lengths. In a bit-cost model, parsing the query and writing and reading the complete response are charged operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational separation-oracle transcript finitely encodes the query and either a membership tag or rational separator, and bit cost includes processing the full transcript.
assumptions_latex: y\in\mathbb Q^n
\text{Any separator response has rational coefficients}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(\text{transcript})=\ell(y)+\ell(\text{tag})+\ell(a,\beta)\text{ for a separator response}.
review_flags: validity semantics are defined in the strong-oracle and implicit-separation leaves
knowledge_statements.title: Binary Oracle Transcript Encoding
Oracle Encoding
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary encoding for a rational strong separation oracle used by an ellipsoid algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a rational polyhedron and let \(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) be a query. A binary-encoded strong separation oracle returns either \(\mathrm{IN}\), asserting \(y\in K\), or rational \((a,b)\in\mathbb{Q}^n\times\mathbb{Q}\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\). The encoding length of the query or response is the total binary length of its rational coordinates, with each rational represented by signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in lowest terms. Oracle running time includes producing and reading this response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational separation oracle encodes membership or a valid separating inequality in binary, and its computational cost includes the complete query and response lengths.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a rational polyhedron.
Queries and separating coefficients are rational.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle interface has a finite binary input-output encoding whose bit length contributes to complexity.

children.title: Oracle Precision Control
children.top_down_role: Accuracy requirements imposed on oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Precision Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-controlled weak separation suitable for finite-bit ellipsoid computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta>0\), a \(\delta\)-controlled weak separation oracle for a closed convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) must, on rational input \(y\), return either \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), or rational \((a,b)\) with \(a\ne0\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) for every \(x\in K\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge b+\delta\lVert a\rVert_2\). The requested tolerance is encoded in binary, and the oracle must terminate in time polynomial in the query length and \(\log(1/\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precision control requires either approximate membership or a valid cut having the requested normalized margin, with cost polynomial in the tolerance’s bit length.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and convex.
\(y\in\mathbb{Q}^n\) and \(\delta>0\) are supplied to the oracle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every response has a correctness guarantee explicitly parameterized by \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from the query to the set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalized weak-separation interface is standard, but the exact convention requires an authoritative locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the precision-control leaf, but weak separation has several non-equivalent normalization conventions. The exact alternative involving distance at most delta, a normalized margin of delta, and polynomial dependence on log(1/delta) needs an authoritative source before the formulation can be relied upon.

children.title: Oracle Output-Size Control
children.top_down_role: Encoding-length bounds for separators, witnesses, or other oracle outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Output-Size Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial bit-length requirement for separation-oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an oracle query have binary length \(L\), dimension \(n\), and requested tolerance \(\delta>0\). Oracle output-size control holds if there is a fixed polynomial \(p\) such that every returned rational separator \((a,b)\) has encoding length at most \(p(n,L,\log(1/\delta))\). Together with polynomial oracle running time, this condition ensures that writing, reading, storing, and applying each cut costs polynomially many bit operations; geometric validity of the cut alone does not imply this resource bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every rational oracle response must have polynomially bounded binary length; otherwise even a geometrically correct cut can be computationally unusable.
assumptions_latex: Queries, tolerances, and oracle responses use binary rational encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bit cost of processing every oracle answer is polynomial in \(n\), \(L\), and \(\log(1/\delta)\).

children.title: Uncontrolled Oracle Responses
children.top_down_role: Complexity failures caused by insufficient precision or excessive response size.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample showing that approximate-membership acceptance is not an exact feasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{0\}\subset\mathbb R\) and \(\delta>0\). Under a weak-membership convention permitting an affirmative response whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\), the query \(y=\delta/2\) may be accepted because \(\operatorname{dist}(\delta/2,K)=\delta/2\), although \(y\notin K\). Thus treating fixed-tolerance acceptance as exact membership can return an infeasible point; exact feasibility requires exact verification or an instance-dependent accuracy-and-recovery guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A delta-weak oracle may accept a point delta over two away from a singleton feasible set, so approximate acceptance cannot certify exact feasibility.
assumptions_latex: The oracle convention permits approximate-membership acceptance when \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\;\not\Rightarrow\;y\in K.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Tolerance False Feasibility
Uncontrolled Oracle Responses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bit-polynomial complexity without bounded oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a separation oracle may return an arbitrary rational scaling of a valid inequality. If \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b<a^{\mathsf T}y\) is valid at iteration \(t\), then \((2^{2^t}a)^{\mathsf T}x\le2^{2^t}b<(2^{2^t}a)^{\mathsf T}y\) defines the same cut but requires \(\Omega(2^t)\) additional output bits. Thus an oracle can remain geometrically correct while forcing exponential transcript length. Without polynomial response-size and precision bounds, the usual polynomial iteration count for the ellipsoid method does not establish polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrary rescaling lets a correct oracle emit exponentially long cuts, so polynomially many ellipsoid iterations need not yield polynomial running time.
assumptions_latex: The oracle is required to return valid cuts but has no response-length bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Geometric correctness alone is insufficient for polynomial-time oracle computation.
