children.title: Feasibility-to-Optimization Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations that use optimization capability to resolve feasibility tasks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-call reduction from feasibility search to a total optimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a total optimization oracle that reports \(K=\varnothing\) or returns an attained optimizer for every rational objective, query it with \(c=0\). An emptiness response decides infeasibility; otherwise the returned optimizer lies in \(K\) and is a feasibility witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Query the total optimization oracle with the zero objective; it either reports emptiness or returns a feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \text{The optimization oracle is total on empty and nonempty inputs}
\text{On a nonempty input it returns an actual optimizer}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{FEAS}(K)\le_T\operatorname{OPT}(K)\text{ using one oracle call}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Objective Feasibility Reduction
Feasibility-to-Optimization Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of convex feasibility to an optimization oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) through an optimization oracle that either reports \(K=\varnothing\) or, for a rational objective \(c\), returns \(x_c\in K\) minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). Query the oracle once with \(c=0\). If it reports emptiness, output \(K=\varnothing\); otherwise output the returned point \(x_0\), which is feasible because every point of \(K\) minimizes the zero objective. Hence feasibility reduces to one optimization-oracle call, aside from encoding and verification costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Call the optimization oracle with the zero objective: emptiness proves infeasibility, while any returned optimizer is a feasible point.
assumptions_latex: The optimization oracle detects an empty feasible set and returns an attained optimizer otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility over \(K\) is decided using one optimization-oracle call.

notation.meaning: Optimizer returned for objective vector c

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the zero-objective reduction is immediate but no supplied locator addresses oracle reductions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, and the zero-objective reduction is correct under the explicitly strong assumption that the optimization oracle detects emptiness and returns an attained optimizer otherwise. No cited source supports this oracle convention or reduction.

children.title: Optimization-to-Feasibility Reductions
children.top_down_role: Transformations that use feasibility capability to resolve optimization tasks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive optimization through feasibility queries on objective sublevels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v^*=\min_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\), let \(\ell\le v^*\le u\), and first obtain a witness \(x^u\in K\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}x^u\le u\). While \(u-\ell>\varepsilon\), query feasibility of \(K\cap\{x:c^{\mathsf T}x\le(\ell+u)/2\}\); on success replace \(u\) and the retained witness, and on failure replace \(\ell\). The final retained witness is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Retain a feasible point at the upper bound and bisect objective thresholds until the bracket has width at most epsilon.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is nonempty and }v^*\text{ is finite and attained}
\ell\le v^*\le u
\text{A successful feasibility query returns a witness}
x^u\in K,\ c^{\mathsf T}x^u\le u
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}\hat x\le v^*+\varepsilon\text{ after at most }\max\{0,\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\}\text{ bisection calls}.
knowledge_statements.title: Initialized Additive Threshold Bisection

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Rational Recovery After Threshold Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-value variant when a reduced-denominator bound is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the rational optimum \(v^*\) has reduced denominator at most \(D\), threshold feasibility can shrink a bracket containing \(v^*\) to width less than \(D^{-2}\). The bracket then contains at most one rational with denominator at most \(D\); rational reconstruction identifies \(v^*\), and feasibility at threshold \(v^*\) returns an exact optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A denominator bound turns sufficiently accurate threshold bisection into exact rational recovery.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a nonempty rational polyhedron}
v^*\text{ is finite and attained}
\operatorname{den}(v^*)\le D
\ell\le v^*\le u
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^*\text{ and an optimizer are recovered with }O(\log((u-\ell)D^2)+1)\text{ feasibility calls}.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Recovery After Threshold Search
Optimization-to-Feasibility Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate linear optimization by feasibility queries on objective sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex, let \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and suppose known rational bounds satisfy \(\ell\le v^*:=\inf_{x\in K}c^{\mathsf T}x\le u\). For tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), repeatedly query feasibility of \(K\cap\{x:c^{\mathsf T}x\le\tau\}\) at \(\tau=(\ell+u)/2\). Replace \(u\) by \(\tau\) and retain the returned feasible point when the query succeeds; otherwise replace \(\ell\) by \(\tau\). Stop when \(u-\ell\le\varepsilon\) and output the retained point \(\hat x\), for which \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat x\le v^*+\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary search on objective thresholds converts feasibility queries into an epsilon-optimal solution when finite initial value bounds are known.
assumptions_latex: Feasibility of each objective sublevel intersection can be decided and returns a point when nonempty.
Finite rational bounds \(\ell\le v^*\le u\) are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After at most \(\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) queries, an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal feasible point is returned.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: threshold bisection is standard, but no supplied source locates the oracle reduction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the stated procedure can lack a retained feasible point when the initial interval already has width at most epsilon or when no threshold query succeeds. It also defines the value as an infimum without explicitly ensuring the output mechanism needed for an epsilon-optimal feasible witness. An authoritative reduction theorem is needed to settle the initialization, attainment regime, and exact query bound.

children.title: Reduction Overhead
children.top_down_role: Query, encoding, and precision costs introduced by task reductions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-model accounting for query count, oracle cost, and local processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a reduction makes \(q(I)\) calls, uses queries of length at most \(L_q(I)\), receives answers of length at most \(L_a(I)\), and performs \(W(I,L_q,L_a)\) local bit operations, then \(T_{\rm red}(I)\le q(I)T_{\mathcal O}(L_q(I))+W(I,L_q(I),L_a(I))\). Polynomially many calls preserve polynomial time only when query construction, oracle time, answer length, and answer processing are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total reduction cost is oracle-call cost plus local encoding and processing work; polynomial query count alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \text{All costs use one binary computation model}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\rm red}(I)\le q(I)T_{\mathcal O}(L_q(I))+W(I,L_q(I),L_a(I)).
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Reduction Cost Composition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specialization to the two feasibility–optimization reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero-objective reduction uses one optimization call. Given a retained feasible upper-bound witness, additive threshold bisection uses at most \(\max\{0,\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\}\) additional feasibility calls. These are polynomial bit reductions when the bracket, tolerance, queries, responses, and local processing have polynomial encoding and cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward reduction costs one call; initialized additive bisection costs logarithmically many calls, subject to binary-size control.
assumptions_latex: \ell\le v^*\le u
\varepsilon>0
\text{A feasible upper-bound witness is retained}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_{F\to O}=1,\qquad q_{O\to F}\le\max\{0,\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Query Overheads
Reduction Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call and bit-complexity overhead of feasibility–optimization reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The reduction of feasibility to optimization uses one call with objective \(0\). Given \(\ell
e u\) bracketing the finite optimum, the threshold-bisection reduction of optimization to feasibility uses at most \(\lceil\log_2((u-\ell)/\varepsilon)\rceil\) feasibility calls for additive error \(\varepsilon>0\). If forming each augmented inequality, processing each witness, and each oracle call take time polynomial in \(n\), the input length, and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), and if \(u-\ell\) has polynomial encoding length, then both reductions have polynomial bit overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility needs one optimization call; epsilon-optimization needs logarithmically many feasibility calls, with polynomial bit overhead under controlled encodings.
assumptions_latex: Finite rational objective bounds are available for bisection.
Oracle queries and responses have polynomially bounded encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reductions preserve polynomial-time solvability in the controlled binary oracle model.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows from the stated reductions, but an authoritative oracle-complexity locator is missing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind is appropriate. The displayed ceiling bound should account for the zero-query case when u-l is at most epsilon, and the stated encoding hypotheses need a precise bit-model formulation. Because no source is supplied and the record depends on the preceding reduction's initialization issue, the claimed overhead is not yet reliable.

children.title: Reduction Validity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation or oracle conditions governing the validity of reductions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Validity Conditions for the Reduction Pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive oracle and geometric conditions for the two directional reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The zero-objective reduction requires a total optimization oracle that detects emptiness and returns an optimizer otherwise. Threshold-feasibility optimization requires a nonempty region, a finite attained optimum, a finite initial bracket, and witness-producing feasibility queries. Exact recovery further requires rational discreteness, such as a known denominator or value-gap bound of polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each reduction needs an explicit oracle contract; threshold search additionally needs bounded, attained values, and exact recovery needs rational discreteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{These contracts distinguish valid exact, additive, and invalid reduction regimes.}
knowledge_statements.title: Validity Conditions for the Reduction Pair

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure without a finite lower objective bound or unboundedness contract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R\) and objective \(c=1\), every finite sublevel set \(K\cap\{x:x\le\tau\}\) is nonempty although \(\inf_{x\in K}x=-\infty\). Finite successful threshold queries therefore neither certify a finite optimum nor yield an additive optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the objective is unbounded below, every finite threshold may be feasible, so ordinary bisection cannot detect unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: K=\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A finite lower bracket or separate unboundedness contract is necessary.}
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Objectives Defeat Threshold Bisection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment boundary outside closed rational-polyhedral LP regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(K=(0,1]\subset\mathbb R\) and objective \(c=1\), the finite infimum is \(v^*=0\), but no feasible point attains it. Thus exact threshold recovery at \(v^*\) cannot return an optimizer, even though every threshold \(\tau>0\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite infimum need not be attained on a nonclosed convex set, so exact value recovery need not produce an optimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Attainment or an explicitly approximate output contract is necessary.}
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Infimum Without an Optimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Optimization Oracles Do Not Decide Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empty-input contract boundary for the zero-objective reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization oracle specified only on nonempty feasible regions does not decide whether its input is empty. Consequently, one zero-objective call reduces feasibility to optimization only when the oracle must correctly report emptiness and otherwise return an actual feasible optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero-objective reduction fails for an oracle whose behavior on empty inputs is unspecified.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal O_{\rm opt}\text{ is otherwise unrestricted on empty inputs}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{FEAS}\le_T\mathcal O_{\rm opt}\text{ by one call only under a total-oracle contract}.
knowledge_statements.title: Partial Optimization Oracles Do Not Decide Feasibility
Reduction Validity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions distinguishing exact rational reductions from approximate weak-oracle reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The feasibility–optimization reduction pair is polynomially valid when \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) has a controlled binary description or oracle interface, finite objective bounds are available, and oracle answers have polynomial size. Threshold bisection yields only additive \(\varepsilon\)-optimization in a weak numerical model. Exact optimization additionally requires a rational polyhedral regime with a known polynomial bound on optimal-value encoding length, so that an interval narrower than the minimum possible gap identifies the exact rational optimum. Without boundedness, attainment, or encoding control, the corresponding reduction may be invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate equivalence needs bounded values and controlled oracles; exact equivalence additionally needs rational discreteness and a polynomial solution-size bound.
assumptions_latex: The feasible region is convex and accessed through a controlled binary interface.
The objective is rational and has finite known bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Approximate reductions are broadly valid, whereas exact reductions require additional rational encoding and attainment hypotheses.

notation.meaning: Allowed additive error in the weak regime

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact and weak oracle regimes require distinct hypotheses

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits Reduction Validity Regimes and the approximate-versus-exact distinction is directionally sound. The minimum rational gap, solution-size bound, attainment requirements, and meaning of a controlled oracle interface are not quantified sufficiently to establish the exact reduction. These claims require a specific authoritative source.

children.title: Weak Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Approximate or tolerance-based oracle access for polyhedral computation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit Euclidean-distance convention; other weak-oracle normalizations are conventionally equivalent only after quantitative translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. A distance-tolerance weak separation oracle accepts \(y\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\delta>0\). It returns either \(\mathrm{NEAR}\), which certifies \(\operatorname{dist}_2(y,K)\le\delta\), or a vector \(a\) with \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}y\ge\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x+\delta\). At distance exactly \(\delta\), either valid response may be allowed. The model need not distinguish membership from nonmembership inside the \(\delta\)-neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a fixed distance convention, a weak oracle certifies proximity within the requested tolerance or returns a normalized separator with that margin; exact boundary membership is not required.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
\delta>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{NEAR}\Rightarrow \operatorname{dist}_2(y,K)\le\delta,\quad a\Rightarrow \lVert a\rVert_2=1\ \land\ a^{\mathsf T}y\ge h_K(a)+\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Tolerance Weak Separation Model

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic dependence on requested accuracy; machine encoding and response-size control remain in the resource-interface leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a binary accuracy model, requesting tolerance \(\delta\) contributes \(\Theta(\log(1/\delta))\) bits when \(\delta\) is specified dyadically. Polynomial-time weak access therefore means polynomial cost in the instance and query encodings and in the encoded precision, not polynomial cost in \(1/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-oracle complexity is measured in the encoded precision, typically logarithmic in the inverse tolerance.
assumptions_latex: 0<\delta\le1
\delta\text{ is supplied by a finite binary accuracy encoding}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell(\delta)=\Theta(\log(1/\delta))\text{ for dyadic accuracy requests}.

notation.meaning: binary length of the accuracy request

knowledge_statements.title: Precision-Input Semantics
Weak Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-dependent weak separation model for convex bodies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex. A weak separation oracle accepts rational \(y\) and tolerance \(\delta>0\). It may certify \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\); otherwise it returns a rational nonzero vector \(a\) such that \(a^{\mathsf T}y>a^{\mathsf T}x\) for every \(x\in K\) with a normalized separation margin prescribed by \(\delta\). Answers inside the tolerance boundary need not determine exact membership. Complexity is measured in the query length and \(\log(1/\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak oracle answers only to requested tolerance, allowing ambiguity near the boundary and measuring cost in the precision’s binary length.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is closed and convex.
The tolerance \(\delta\) is positive and binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle supplies approximate membership or tolerance-certified separation, not exact boundary classification.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: tolerance-dependent boundary ambiguity is standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits Weak Oracle Models, but the statement leaves the normalized separation margin merely 'prescribed by delta' rather than giving the actual inequality. Since weak-oracle conventions differ materially, a source is needed to determine the intended definition and normalization.

children.title: Strong Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Exact or fully separating oracle access for polyhedral computation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership-or-separation semantics; transcript encoding and output-size bounds are owned by the resource-control leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A strong separation oracle for a convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) accepts a query \(y\) and returns either \(\mathrm{IN}\), which is permitted only when \(y\in K\), or a nonzero pair \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in K\). Thus every query is classified without a tolerance band. In a rational oracle model, admissible queries and returned separators are rational.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle exactly confirms membership or returns a valid inequality strictly violated by the query, with no tolerance band.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex}
\text{The chosen computational model admits the required separator representation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{IN}\Rightarrow y\in K,\qquad (a,\beta)\Rightarrow \forall x\in K:\ a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation Oracle Model
Strong Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership-and-separation interface for rational convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a strong separation oracle accepts a rational point \(y\) and returns either the exact assertion \(y\in K\), or rational \((a,b)\) satisfying \(a\ne0\), \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) for every \(x\in K\), and \(a^{\mathsf T}y>b\). Unlike a weak oracle, it has no indeterminate boundary band. In a bit-complexity model, polynomial strength also requires polynomial running time and polynomial encoding length for \((a,b)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong oracle decides exact membership or supplies an exact rational separating inequality, with no tolerance band.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
Queries are rational, and rational separators exist whenever separation is requested.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every rational query is classified exactly or strictly separated from \(K\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact strong separation is standard, but no supplied locator supports this oracle definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and exact membership-or-separation role fit the leaf. The assumptions explicitly restrict the model to cases where rational separators exist, but no authoritative locator supports this particular strong-oracle convention or its polynomial output-size requirement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Delayed column generation through an improvement oracle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex column generation and its dual oracle interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP with too many variables to store explicitly, suppose that at each basic feasible solution an improvement oracle either returns an improving entering variable together with its tableau column or certifies optimality. Then the simplex method can proceed while generating only needed columns; this is delayed column generation. The improvement oracle is interpretable as a separation oracle for the dual LP, so the ellipsoid method can alternatively solve the LP using only a polynomial number of calls to that oracle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Column generation solves an LP with an implicit, very large variable set by asking an oracle for one improving entering column at each simplex step, or for an optimality certificate. The same oracle acts as a separation oracle for the dual, allowing an ellipsoid implementation with polynomially many oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \text{The LP variable set is available implicitly rather than stored in full}
\text{At each current basic feasible solution, an exact improvement oracle returns an entering column or certifies optimality}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The LP can be handled by delayed simplex column generation; equivalently, dual separation permits an ellipsoid solution with polynomially many improvement-oracle calls.}

children.title: Weak-to-Strong Oracle Reductions
children.top_down_role: Conditions permitting simulation of stronger oracle access from weaker responses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local necessity boundary for the stated one-query precision conversion; general oracle-separation examples belong to the sibling boundary leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the permitted exterior queries can approach \(P\) arbitrarily closely, then no fixed positive tolerance \(\delta\) makes a proximity response imply exact membership. Consequently, the gap-promised conversion cannot yield strong separation without an additional exact-recovery mechanism or an adaptive precision guarantee tied to a finite encoding bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a positive query-class gap or another exact-recovery mechanism, a weak proximity response cannot certify exact membership.
assumptions_latex: \inf\{\operatorname{dist}_2(y,P):y\in Q\setminus P\}=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\delta>0\text{ such that }\operatorname{dist}_2(y,P)\le\delta\Rightarrow y\in P\text{ for all }y\in Q.
knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform-Gap Conversion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional conversion for a prescribed rational query class under the distance-tolerance weak-separation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a rational polyhedron and let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb Q^n\) be the permitted query class. Suppose a computable \(\gamma>0\) satisfies \(y\notin P\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}_2(y,P)\ge\gamma\) for every \(y\in Q\). A distance-tolerance weak separation oracle queried with any \(0<\delta<\gamma\) simulates strong separation on \(Q\): a \(\mathrm{NEAR}\) response implies \(y\in P\), while a returned normalized margin inequality is a strong separator. If \(\log(1/\gamma)\), oracle runtime, and response encoding length are polynomially bounded, the simulation is polynomial-time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak separation oracle becomes exact on a query class having a known positive membership gap, provided the required precision and responses have polynomial encoding cost.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
Q\subseteq\mathbb Q^n\text{ is the permitted query class}
\forall y\in Q:\ y\notin P\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}_2(y,P)\ge\gamma>0
0<\delta<\gamma
\text{Weak-oracle outputs satisfy the selected distance-tolerance convention}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SEP}_{\mathrm{strong}}(P;Q)\le_T\operatorname{SEP}_{\mathrm{weak}}(P;\delta),
knowledge_statements.title: Gap-Promised Weak-to-Strong Reduction
Weak-to-Strong Oracle Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional conversion of weak answers into exact rational decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a rational polyhedron whose defining data have encoding length at most \(B\), and suppose a polynomially computable separation-gap bound \(\gamma(n,B)>0\) is known: every rational query in the prescribed encoding class that lies outside \(K\) admits a valid rational separator with normalized margin at least \(\gamma(n,B)\). Querying a weak separation oracle at tolerance \(\delta<\gamma(n,B)/2\), followed by rational reconstruction of its controlled-size output, implements strong separation on that query class. The reduction is polynomial only when \(\log(1/\gamma(n,B))\) and all output lengths are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation becomes exact only when rational data provide a known inverse-polynomial-bit separation gap and outputs can be reconstructed efficiently.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is rational polyhedral with data-size bound \(B\).
A computable positive separation-gap bound applies to the permitted queries.
Weak-oracle outputs have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak separation simulates strong separation on the restricted query class using polynomially many bit operations.

notation.meaning: Encoding-length bound for the polyhedral data

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind is suitable, but the reduction depends critically on the exact weak-oracle convention, the prescribed query class, and a uniform gap that prevents an outside query from receiving an approximate-membership answer. The rational-reconstruction step is also not specified. A theorem-level source is required before the hypotheses or conclusion can be validated.

children.title: Oracle-Strength Separation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where weak and strong oracle guarantees diverge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information condition permitting exact recovery from a quantitatively accurate weak answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose admissible instances satisfy the dichotomy \(m\le0\) in the exact yes case and \(m\ge\gamma>0\) in the exact no case, and a weak oracle returns \(\hat m\) with \(|\hat m-m|<\gamma/2\). Then the two output ranges are disjoint and the exact case is recoverable. Without a positive uniform \(\gamma\), no fixed positive accuracy gives this conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate answers determine an exact binary decision when the two exact regimes have a known positive gap exceeding twice the error.
assumptions_latex: \gamma>0
|\hat m-m|<\gamma/2
m\le0\text{ or }m\ge\gamma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \hat m<\gamma/2\text{ identifies the yes regime and }\hat m>\gamma/2\text{ identifies the no regime}.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Gap Condition for Exact Classification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-explicit example showing that tolerance membership does not determine exact membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an oracle permitted to answer IN whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\le\delta\). For \(K_0=\{0\}\), \(K_1=\{\eta\}\), \(0<\eta<\delta\), and query \(y=0\), the answer IN is valid for both sets, although \(0\in K_0\) and \(0\notin K_1\). Thus this fixed-tolerance response cannot determine exact membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two singleton sets closer than the tolerance admit the same approximate membership answer but different exact answers.
assumptions_latex: \delta>0
0<\eta<\delta
\text{IN is permitted throughout the outer }\delta\text{-neighborhood}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Fixed-tolerance membership does not generally simulate exact membership}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Tolerance Membership Ambiguity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization boundary for weak membership and separation information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the rescaling \(x=Mz\) with \(M\ne0\), Euclidean distances are multiplied by \(|M|\). An absolute tolerance \(\delta\) in \(x\)-coordinates therefore corresponds to \(\delta/|M|\) in \(z\)-coordinates. Oracle strength is not invariant under equivalent scaling unless tolerances transform with the coordinates or geometry is normalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed absolute weak-oracle tolerance changes under coordinate scaling, so meaningful strength comparisons require normalization.
assumptions_latex: \delta>0
M\ne0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,MK)\le\delta\iff\operatorname{dist}(x/M,K)\le\delta/|M|.
knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Tolerances Are Scale Dependent
Oracle-Strength Separation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information boundary preventing unconditional recovery of exact answers from weak oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix tolerance \(\delta>0\). Weak-oracle answers within a \(\delta\)-boundary band need not distinguish closed convex sets whose boundaries differ by less than that tolerance. For example, in \(\mathbb{R}\), the singleton sets \(K_0=\{0\}\) and \(K_1=\{\eta\}\) with \(0<\eta<\delta\) permit overlapping approximate answers at the query \(y=0\), although exact membership differs. Consequently, without arbitrarily refinable precision plus a rational separation-gap bound, no finite weak-oracle transcript generally determines the exact strong-oracle answer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sets differing below the oracle tolerance can produce compatible weak answers but different exact memberships, preventing unconditional weak-to-strong conversion.
assumptions_latex: The weak oracle permits ambiguity within distance \(\delta\) of the boundary.
No positive rational separation-gap bound is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed-precision weak oracle cannot generally simulate exact strong membership or separation.

notation.meaning: Set displacement smaller than the oracle tolerance

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed tolerance cannot encode exact boundary information

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and the singleton example illustrates fixed-tolerance ambiguity under an oracle permitted to certify any point within distance delta. Its force depends on that precise weak-oracle convention, however, and no source is supplied for either the example or the broader finite-transcript impossibility claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes original-space inequality count from extended-formulation size and usable oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exponential original-space inequality complexity neither means that the compact instance itself is exponentially long nor, by itself, proves exponential extension complexity. Polynomial oracle tractability additionally requires polynomial running time and polynomial output length for every separating response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Facet count, compact input length, extension complexity, and oracle complexity are different measures and cannot be substituted for one another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Original-space size}\not\equiv\text{extension size}\not\equiv\text{oracle cost}.
knowledge_statements.title: Description-Measure Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-level definition relative to a compact instance encoding; it does not assert exponential extension complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A compactly indexed family \(\{P_I\subseteq\mathbb R^{n(I)}\}\) has exponential original-space inequality complexity if there are a constant \(c>0\) and infinitely many instances \(I\) for which every exact description of \(P_I\) in its original variables requires at least \(2^{c|I|}\) inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is exponentially described in its original space when infinitely many compactly encoded members require exponentially many inequalities in every exact original-variable formulation.
assumptions_latex: I\text{ has a finite binary encoding}
P_I\text{ is a rational polyhedron}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ic}(P_I)\ge 2^{c|I|}\text{ on an infinite subfamily for some }c>0.

notation.meaning: binary length of the compact instance
minimum number of inequalities in an exact original-space description

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Original-Space Description

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical instance family separating original-space facet count from separation-oracle tractability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The perfect-matching polytope has an exponential family of odd-set inequalities in its original edge variables, while violated odd-set inequalities can be separated in polynomial time. It therefore exemplifies exponential original-space description with polynomial-time separation and optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perfect matching is the standard example of exponentially many original-space inequalities coexisting with polynomial-time separation and optimization.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is an encoded graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Exponential original-space facet complexity can coexist with polynomial-time separation.}
knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Polytope Exemplar

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic consequence of a polynomial-time strong separation interface for well-described rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P_I\) is a well-described rational polyhedron and admits polynomial-time strong separation returning polynomial-size rational cuts, then rational linear optimization over \(P_I\) is polynomial-time reducible to that oracle, independently of the number of inequalities in an explicit original-space description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponentially many original-space inequalities do not prevent polynomial-time optimization when strong separation and rational encoding are polynomially controlled.
assumptions_latex: P_I\text{ is well described in the rational binary model}
\text{Strong separation runs in polynomial time and returns polynomial-size cuts}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}(P_I)\le_T^{\mathrm{poly}}\operatorname{SEP}(P_I).
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Tractability Without Facet Enumeration

assumptions_latex: The family consists of rational polyhedra \(P_I\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n(I)}\) indexed by finitely encoded instances \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_I\) is exponentially described when its explicit facet description may have size \(2^{\Omega(|I|)}\), while access is supplied through an oracle polynomial in \(|I|\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard oracle-model definition for implicitly represented polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-model definition; exponential size refers to explicit inequality encoding, not dimension alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of rational polyhedra \(\{P_I\}\) is exponentially described if some members require \(2^{\Omega(|I|)}\) inequalities in an explicit irredundant description, but membership violations can be exposed implicitly: given rational \(y\), a separation oracle either confirms \(y\in P_I\) or returns rational \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in P_I\), using time and output bit length polynomial in \(|I|\), \(n(I)\), and the encoding length of \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponentially described polyhedron may have exponentially many explicit facets but admits polynomial-time access through a separation oracle.
knowledge_statements.title: Exponentially Described Polyhedra

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No inspectable citation is supplied, and the formulation “some members require” does not define an asymptotic family lower bound. The plain statement also weakens “require exponentially many inequalities” to “may have exponentially many facets.”

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial Reduction from Linear Optimization to Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the oracle-based polynomial-time implication for a family of polyhedra; the extract refers to condition (8.2) without reproducing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a family of polyhedra, if the separation problem can be solved in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log U\), then linear optimization over members of the family can also be solved in time polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log U\). If condition \((8.2)\) holds, the linear-optimization running time is also polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log U_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a family of polyhedra, a separation algorithm polynomial in n and log U yields a linear-optimization algorithm polynomial in the same parameters. Under the source's condition (8.2), the running time is also polynomial in n and log U0.
assumptions_latex: \text{The separation problem for the polyhedron family is solvable in time }\operatorname{poly}(n,\log U).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Linear optimization over the family is solvable in time }\operatorname{poly}(n,\log U);\quad (8.2)\Longrightarrow \operatorname{poly}(n,\log U_0).

children.title: Separation-to-Feasibility Reductions
children.top_down_role: Complexity-preserving routes from separation access to feasibility tasks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-dimensional strong-oracle reduction under explicit outer-radius and nonempty inner-radius promises.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and convex, contained in a known initial ball of radius \(R\), and promised either empty or to contain a Euclidean ball of radius \(r>0\). Starting from a containing ellipsoid, query a strong separation oracle at each center. A membership response returns a feasible point; otherwise intersect with the returned containing halfspace and replace the intersection by its standard central-cut covering ellipsoid. If no feasible center is found after \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) rejected centers, the volume bound contradicts the promised inner ball, so the algorithm declares \(K=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under inner- and outer-radius promises, the central-cut ellipsoid method converts strong separation into feasibility using polynomially many oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
K\subseteq B(x_0,R)
K=\varnothing\ \text{or}\ \exists z:\ B(z,r)\subseteq K
\text{A strong separation oracle for }K\text{ is available}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{FEAS}(K)\text{ is decided with }O\!\left(n^2\log(R/r)\right)\text{ strong-separation calls}.

notation.meaning: promised inner radius in the nonempty case

knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Separation-to-Feasibility Ellipsoid Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of ambient-volume emptiness certification for lower-dimensional or arbitrarily thin nonempty sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without a known positive lower bound on the volume of every admissible nonempty feasible region, ellipsoid volume shrinkage alone cannot certify emptiness. In particular, a nonempty lower-dimensional convex set has zero ambient volume and violates every positive ambient inner-ball promise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Volume exhaustion proves emptiness only with a positive-volume promise; lower-dimensional feasible sets require affine reduction, thickening, or weak feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \text{No positive ambient inner-radius promise is available}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{vol}_n(E_k)\to0\not\Rightarrow K=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Ball Promise Boundary

assumptions_latex: A strong separation oracle is available for a closed convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
A known ball of radius \(R\) contains \(K\), and every nonempty admissible \(K\) contains a ball of radius \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is decided using a number of oracle calls polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log(R/r)\).

notation.meaning: known outer and promised inner radii

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical central-cut ellipsoid feasibility reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-oracle reduction under explicit outer-radius and full-dimensional inner-radius promises.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize an ellipsoid \(E_0\) of radius \(R\) containing \(K\). At its center \(y_k\), query the separation oracle. If \(y_k\in K\), output \(y_k\). Otherwise use the returned separating halfspace to replace \(E_k\) by an ellipsoid \(E_{k+1}\) containing \(E_k\cap\{x:a_k^{\mathsf T}x\leq\beta_k\}\) and having a fixed dimension-dependent volume reduction. If no feasible center is found before the ellipsoid volume becomes smaller than that of an \(r\)-ball, declare \(K=\varnothing\) under the promise. The oracle-call count is polynomial in \(n\) and \(\log(R/r)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ellipsoid method converts strong separation into feasibility using polynomially many oracle calls when valid inner and outer radii are known.

children.title: Optimization-to-Separation Reductions
children.top_down_role: Complexity relationships that recover separation capabilities from optimization access.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural characterization underlying recovery of separators from optimization values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty closed convex set \(K\), with \(h_K(a)=\sup_{x\in K}a^{\mathsf T}x\), one has \(y\in K\) if and only if \(a^{\mathsf T}y\le h_K(a)\) for every \(a\). Any \(a\) with \(a^{\mathsf T}y>h_K(a)\) therefore supplies a strong separating inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to a closed convex set exactly when it satisfies every support-function inequality; a violated one is a separator.
assumptions_latex: K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y\in K\iff \forall a,\ a^{\mathsf T}y\le h_K(a).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Separation Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational-polyhedral reduction under controlled strong-oracle conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty well-described rational polyhedron \(P\) with a known polynomial facet-complexity bound, strong separation of a rational point is polynomial-time Turing reducible to exact strong optimization over \(P\). The reduction returns either membership or a polynomial-size rational inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) valid for all \(x\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact optimization over a well-described rational polyhedron yields exact strong separation in polynomial oracle time.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is nonempty, rational, and well described}
\text{The optimization oracle returns exact outcomes with polynomial-size encodings}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{SEP}(P)\le_T^{\mathrm{poly}}\operatorname{OPT}(P).
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Optimization-to-Separation Equivalence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact rational-polyhedral reduction under the standard well-described-polyhedron oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonempty well-described rational polyhedron \(P\) with a polynomial facet-complexity bound, strong separation of a rational query is polynomial-time Turing reducible to exact linear optimization over \(P\), provided the optimization oracle reports exact status and polynomial-size rational outcomes. The reduction returns either membership or rational \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta<a^{\mathsf T}y\) for every \(x\in P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard well-described rational-polyhedron assumptions, exact linear optimization yields exact strong separation in polynomial oracle time.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is nonempty, rational, and well described}
\text{A polynomial facet-complexity bound is known}
\text{The optimization oracle reports exact status and polynomial-size rational outcomes}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform relaxation preserves emptiness and creates full dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation bridge from integer-data feasibility to the empty-or-full-dimensional regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\}\), where \(A\) and \(b\) have integer entries bounded in absolute value by \(U\). Define \[\epsilon=\frac{1}{2(n+1)}((n+1)U)^{-(n+1)},\qquad P_\epsilon=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b-\epsilon e\},\] where \(e=(1,\ldots,1)\). If \(P=\varnothing\), then \(P_\epsilon=\varnothing\); if \(P\ne\varnothing\), then \(P_\epsilon\) is full-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer inequality data of magnitude at most U, relax every right-hand side by the stated epsilon. The relaxed polyhedron remains empty when the original is empty and is full-dimensional whenever the original is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b\}
A,b\text{ have integer entries with }|A_{ij}|,|b_i|\le U
P_\epsilon=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\ge b-\epsilon e\},\quad e=(1,\ldots,1)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\varnothing\Rightarrow P_\epsilon=\varnothing;\qquad P\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow P_\epsilon\text{ is full-dimensional}

knowledge_statements.title: Rational Solution Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential output-size bound for explicitly encoded rational LPs in the Turing model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the linear program maximizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) subject to \(Ax\leq b\), where all entries are rational and the complete binary encoding has length \(L\). If its feasible set is nonempty and its optimal value is finite, then it has an optimal rational solution \(x^*\) whose total binary encoding length is bounded by a polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible explicitly encoded rational linear program with a finite optimum has an exact optimal solution whose binary encoding length is polynomially bounded in the input length.
assumptions_latex: The rational linear program has total binary input length \(L\), is feasible, and has a finite optimal value.
All variables, constraints, and objective coefficients are explicitly encoded over \(\mathbb{Q}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists an optimal rational solution \(x^*\) whose total binary encoding length is bounded by a polynomial in \(L\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit determinant representation underlying polynomial bit size for vertices of rational polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\), where \(A\) and \(b\) are integral and every entry has absolute value at most \(\Delta\). If \(v\) is a vertex of \(P\), then some nonsingular \(n\times n\) active submatrix \(B\) and corresponding right-hand side \(d\) satisfy \(v=B^{-1}d\). In reduced form, every coordinate of \(v\) has denominator at most \(n^{n/2}\Delta^n\) and numerator of absolute value at most \(n^{n/2}\Delta^n\), hence polynomial binary length in the encoded data.

children.title: Rational Certificate Size
children.top_down_role: Encoding-length bounds for rational certificates of LP status.

assumptions_latex: The system \(Ax\leq b\) and objective \(c\) are explicitly encoded over \(\mathbb{Q}\) with total length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever the relevant alternative holds, a feasibility, infeasibility, or optimality certificate exists with encoding length polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-size Farkas and primal-dual certificates for rational LP data.

source_refs.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For infeasibility of \(Ax\leq b\), a rational vector \(y\geq0\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) is directly verifiable and proves inconsistency. For finite optimality of \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax\leq b\}\), a feasible primal point \(x\) together with a dual-feasible multiplier \(y\geq0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\) certifies optimality. When such alternatives apply, certificates can be chosen with binary length polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational LP infeasibility and optimality admit polynomial-size multiplier certificates checkable by exact rational arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational Certificate Size

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-size and encoding-size refinement for rational infeasibility certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(Ax\le b\), with \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), is infeasible, then it has a rational Farkas certificate \(y\ge0\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y=0\), \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-1\), and \(|\operatorname{supp}(y)|\le n+1\). If the input encoding length is \(L\), such a certificate can be chosen with total binary encoding length polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible rational inequality system has a polynomial-size normalized Farkas certificate with at most n+1 nonzero multipliers.
assumptions_latex: Ax\le b\text{ is an infeasible rational system in }n\text{ variables}.
The complete binary input encoding has length L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\in\mathbb Q_+^m:\ A^{\mathsf T}y=0,\ b^{\mathsf T}y=-1,\ |\operatorname{supp}(y)|\le n+1,\ \operatorname{size}(y)\le\operatorname{poly}(L).

children.title: Solution-Certificate Size Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Relationships between solution encodings and certificate encodings.

assumptions_latex: An explicitly encoded rational LP has binary input length \(L\).
The LP alternative being certified is feasible optimum or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both exact solution encodings and exact certificate encodings admit polynomial bounds in \(L\), though their coordinate counts and bounds need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares existential bit-size bounds, not numerical conditioning or algorithmic time.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There are polynomials \(p\) and \(q\), depending only on the chosen explicit LP encoding convention, such that a feasible finite rational LP possesses an optimal solution \(x^*\) with \(\operatorname{size}(x^*)\leq p(L)\), while infeasible or finitely optimal instances possess appropriate Farkas or primal-dual certificates \(w\) with \(\operatorname{size}(w)\leq q(L)\). These are parallel polynomial bounds; they do not assert identical dimensions, identical denominators, or equality of the two encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact rational solutions and verification certificates both have polynomial-size representatives, but their dimensions and detailed size bounds may differ.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solution and Certificate Roles Are Not Interchangeable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical comparison of solution witnesses and status certificates, independent of their parallel polynomial-size bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a rational LP, a feasible point certifies feasibility but generally does not by itself certify optimality. Finite optimality is certified by primal-feasible and dual-feasible witnesses with equal objective values, whereas infeasibility is certified by an alternative multiplier and admits no primal feasible-solution witness. Thus polynomial bounds on solution and certificate encodings are parallel size statements, not interchangeability statements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solutions and certificates can both be polynomially small, but they certify different assertions and are not interchangeable.
assumptions_latex: The LP data and proposed witnesses are rational and explicitly encoded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{feasible solution witness}\not\Rightarrow\text{optimality certificate};\quad \text{optimality uses a zero-gap primal-dual pair};\quad \text{infeasibility uses an alternative multiplier}.
knowledge_statements.title: Solution and Certificate Roles Are Not Interchangeable

children.title: Polynomial Output-Size Regimes
children.top_down_role: LP settings where rational outputs admit polynomial encoding length.

assumptions_latex: Input and required output are represented by finite binary strings in the Turing model.
All LP coefficients are explicitly rational with total input length \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact polynomial-time solution is meaningful when a required solution or certificate has encoding length bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(L)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Turing-model condition separating exact polynomial output from real-oracle or uncontrolled-precision regimes.

source_refs.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52
Linear Programming and Rational Numbers p. 54

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact-output LP problem lies in a polynomial output-size regime when every instance of length \(L\) for which an output is required admits a valid rational output \(w\) satisfying \(\operatorname{size}(w)\leq p(L)\) for some fixed polynomial \(p\). Explicit rational linear programs satisfy this condition for optimal solutions and standard infeasibility or optimality certificates. The condition can fail to be defined, or fail outright, for arbitrary real coefficients, unrestricted oracle outputs, or representations demanding exponentially many output bits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact polynomial-time LP algorithms require finitely encoded outputs whose bit lengths are polynomially bounded by the rational input size.
knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Output-Size Regimes

children.title: Numerical Rounding
children.top_down_role: Conversion of sufficiently accurate numerical output into discrete candidate data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure boundary for coordinatewise nearest-grid rounding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For grid spacing \(\Delta>0\), the midpoint \(\widetilde x=(k+\tfrac12)\Delta\) is at distance \(\Delta/2\) from both adjacent grid points \(k\Delta\) and \((k+1)\Delta\). Thus an error bound of at most \(\Delta/2\) does not make nearest-grid recovery unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a grid midpoint, two adjacent grid values are equally near, so nearest-grid recovery needs a strict half-spacing error bound or an additional tie-resolving certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta>0\) is the grid spacing.
\(k\in\mathbb Z\) and \(\widetilde x=(k+\tfrac12)\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(\widetilde x,k\Delta)=\operatorname{dist}(\widetilde x,(k+1)\Delta)=\Delta/2.
knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Grid Tie Boundary

assumptions_latex: The unknown exact vector satisfies \(x^*\in\Delta\mathbb{Z}^n\) for a known rational grid spacing \(\Delta>0\).
An approximation \(\widetilde{x}\) satisfies \(\|\widetilde{x}-x^*\|_\infty<\Delta/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise nearest-grid rounding returns \(x^*\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nearest-grid recovery; ordinary decimal rounding without a known grid has no such guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each coordinate, compute \(k_i=\operatorname{round}(\widetilde{x}_i/\Delta)\) using the unique nearest integer and output \(\widehat{x}_i=\Delta k_i\). Since \(|\widetilde{x}_i-x_i^*|<\Delta/2\) and \(x_i^*/\Delta\in\mathbb{Z}\), the nearest grid point is unique and \(\widehat{x}_i=x_i^*\) for every \(i\). After rounding, feasibility and optimality must still be checked exactly against the rational LP data; absent the grid hypothesis and error bound, coordinatewise numerical rounding need not preserve either property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A known rational grid and an error below half its spacing make coordinatewise rounding exact; otherwise feasibility and optimality require verification.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Rounding

children.title: Rational Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of exact rational values from numerical approximations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar continued-fraction recovery from a finitely encoded rational approximation; vector reconstruction is coordinatewise when bounds are certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=p/q\) be reduced with \(1\le q\le Q\), and let \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) satisfy \(|\alpha-x|<1/(2Q^2)\). Then \(x\) is the unique reduced rational with denominator at most \(Q\) satisfying this error bound. It occurs among the continued-fraction convergents of \(\alpha\) and is recovered by enumerating convergents with denominator at most \(Q\) and applying the exact denominator and error tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational with denominator at most Q is uniquely recoverable by continued fractions from an approximation closer than 1/(2Q squared).
assumptions_latex: x=p/q\text{ is reduced and }1\le q\le Q.
\alpha\in\mathbb Q\text{ and }|\alpha-x|<1/(2Q^2).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is the unique admissible bounded-denominator rational and is recovered among the convergents of }\alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Denominator Rational Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity of scalar reconstruction when the approximation and denominator bound are binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb Q\) given in binary and \(Q\ge1\) given in binary, the continued-fraction reconstruction procedure, including exact candidate validation, runs in time polynomial in \(\operatorname{size}(\alpha)+\log Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continued-fraction reconstruction and exact validation have polynomial bit complexity in the encoded approximation and denominator bound.
assumptions_latex: \alpha\in\mathbb Q\text{ is represented in binary}.
Q\ge1\text{ is represented in binary}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{reconstruct}}\le\operatorname{poly}(\operatorname{size}(\alpha)+\log Q).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the rational approximation

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Bit Complexity of Reconstruction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample family showing that bounded denominators alone cannot support substantially coarser worst-case accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every integer \(Q\ge2\), the distinct reduced rationals \(r=1/Q\) and \(s=1/(Q-1)\) have denominators at most \(Q\). Their midpoint \(\alpha=(r+s)/2\) satisfies \(|\alpha-r|=|\alpha-s|=1/(2Q(Q-1))\). Thus an approximation error allowance of this order can be consistent with two admissible rationals; a denominator bound without a sufficiently small error bound does not ensure unique reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Farey-neighbor rationals give ambiguity at order 1/Q squared, so denominator bounds alone do not ensure unique recovery.
assumptions_latex: Q\ge2.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists r\ne s:\operatorname{den}(r),\operatorname{den}(s)\le Q,\quad |\alpha-r|=|\alpha-s|=\frac1{2Q(Q-1)}.
review_flags: The example establishes the necessary Q^{-2} order; it does not claim that 1/(2Q^2) is the exact largest universal threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Order-Q-Squared Ambiguity Boundary

assumptions_latex: A rational number \(x=p/q\) is in lowest terms with \(1\leq q\leq Q\).
The approximation satisfies \(|\alpha-x|<1/(2Q^2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bounded-denominator rational \(x\) is unique and recoverable from continued-fraction convergents of \(\alpha\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical continued-fraction rational reconstruction theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar bounded-denominator reconstruction; vector recovery applies the rule coordinatewise with certified bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute the continued-fraction convergents of \(\alpha\) and inspect those whose denominators do not exceed \(Q\). Return the unique reduced fraction \(p/q\) satisfying \(|\alpha-p/q|<1/(2Q^2)\). Uniqueness holds because two distinct reduced fractions with denominators at most \(Q\) differ by at least \(1/Q^2\). Under the stated strict error bound, the exact fraction is therefore the only admissible candidate and occurs among the relevant continued-fraction convergents. For a rational vector, apply this procedure coordinatewise using certified denominator bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rational with denominator at most Q is uniquely recoverable from an approximation closer than one over twice Q squared.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational Reconstruction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-denominator reconstruction threshold is plausible and appropriately scoped, but the continued-fraction recovery assertion has no inspectable citation and the statement includes proof text.

children.title: Optimal-Face Recovery
children.top_down_role: Identification of the exact optimal face from approximate solution information.

assumptions_latex: The rational polyhedron is \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b\}\), and \(z^*=\max_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is known exactly and attained.
Exact rational feasibility is available for linear systems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The system \(Ax\leq b\), \(c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\) represents the optimal face and yields an exact optimal point when feasible.

notation.meaning: feasible polyhedron and its optimal face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery after the exact optimal value is known; approximate gaps alone do not identify the face.

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After recovering the exact finite optimum \(z^*\), form the rational system \(Ax\leq b\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\). Its feasible region is exactly the exposed optimal face \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=z^*\}\). Solving this system by an exact rational feasibility procedure returns an exact optimal point. To test whether an original inequality \(a_i^{\mathsf T}x\leq b_i\) contains all of \(F^*\) at equality, optimize its slack \(b_i-a_i^{\mathsf T}x\) over this recovered face and check whether the maximum equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the exact optimum is known, adding its objective equality recovers the optimal face and permits exact feasibility and activity tests.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Recovery

children.title: Approximation-to-Exactness Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Accuracy levels needed for exact LP output recovery.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness of strict half-separation accuracy for exact-value identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two admissible exact values be \(r_1<r_2\), and let \(\widetilde z=(r_1+r_2)/2\). Then \(|\widetilde z-r_1|=|\widetilde z-r_2|=(r_2-r_1)/2\). Hence a non-strict error guarantee at half their separation does not identify a unique exact value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the midpoint of two admissible exact values, half-spacing accuracy leaves both values equally consistent, so strict inequality is necessary for unconditional unique recovery.
assumptions_latex: \(r_1<r_2\) are both admissible exact values.
\(\widetilde z=(r_1+r_2)/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\widetilde z-r_i|\leq (r_2-r_1)/2\ (i=1,2)\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad\text{unique exact recovery}.
knowledge_statements.title: Half-Spacing Ambiguity Boundary

assumptions_latex: All candidate exact values are rational numbers whose reduced denominators are at most \(Q\).
The numerical approximation \(\widetilde{z}\) is within \(1/(2Q^2)\) of the intended value \(z^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interval \((\widetilde{z}-1/(2Q^2),\widetilde{z}+1/(2Q^2))\) contains at most one admissible exact value, namely \(z^*\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rational separation bound from bounded denominators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic rational isolation threshold; LP-specific use requires deriving \(Q\) from input-size and determinant bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Distinct reduced rational numbers with denominators at most \(Q\) are separated by at least \(1/Q^2\). Consequently, if an exact LP value \(z^*\) is known a priori to have denominator at most \(Q\) and \(|\widetilde{z}-z^*|<1/(2Q^2)\), then no second admissible rational value can satisfy the same strict error bound. Thus rational reconstruction identifies \(z^*\) uniquely. For rational LPs, a polynomial bit-length bound on basic solutions or objective values produces a bound \(Q\) whose logarithm is polynomial in the input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An error below half the minimum spacing between bounded-denominator rationals isolates the exact value and enables rational reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-to-Exactness Thresholds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic isolation threshold is standard, but the LP-specific claim that a polynomial input bound yields the required denominator bound needs a precise source. The statement also contains proof-style explanation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the ellipsoid polynomial-time argument under oracle-based separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be accessed by a separation oracle. For every rational query \(y\notin K\), an exact oracle must return rational \((g,\beta)\) satisfying \(g^Tz\leq\beta<g^Ty\) for every \(z\in K\). The standard polynomial-time ellipsoid guarantee requires both the oracle running time and the encoding length of \((g,\beta)\) to be polynomial in the query and instance lengths. If either quantity is superpolynomial, or if an inexact cut has error without a polynomially controlled tolerance ensuring validity and separation, the ellipsoid iteration bound alone yields no polynomial bound for solving the LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid polynomiality can fail as a guarantee when separation calls are superpolynomial, return excessively long cuts, or have errors too uncontrolled to preserve valid separation.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and represented through a separation oracle.
Queries and returned cuts use rational encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ellipsoid iteration bound does not imply polynomial total bit complexity without polynomial oracle cost, output size, and accuracy control.

children.title: Numerical Practice Regime

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Practice Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision operational regime distinct from the Turing bit-complexity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A numerical-practice regime for an LP algorithm consists of a floating-point format with unit roundoff \(u\), a scaling rule, linear-algebra solvers, and declared feasibility and optimality tolerances \(\tau_f,\tau_o>0\). A computed point \(\widehat{x}\) is accepted only according to residual tests such as \(\|A\widehat{x}-b\|\leq\tau_f\), bound-violation tests, and an objective or duality-gap test at tolerance \(\tau_o\). Runtime is measured by realized arithmetic, memory, and numerical-refinement costs rather than solely by exact rational bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Practical numerical performance is assessed in finite precision using scaling, residual tolerances, solver behavior, arithmetic work, memory, and refinement costs.
assumptions_latex: An LP implementation uses finite-precision arithmetic.
Feasibility and optimality are judged by declared tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime is specified by \((u,\tau_f,\tau_o)\), scaling, numerical kernels, and operational resource measures.

children.title: Guarantee-to-Practice Gap
children.top_down_role: Structural sources of divergence between polynomial theory and numerical performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Guarantee-to-Practice Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical distinction between asymptotic polynomiality and observed numerical performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound \(T(I)\leq p(\ell(I))\), where \(p\) is a polynomial and \(\ell(I)\) is binary input length, controls worst-case asymptotic growth in a specified computational model. It does not determine polynomial coefficients, performance on a particular instance distribution, memory traffic, finite-precision stability, or implementation overhead. Consequently, polynomial-time membership alone neither orders two implementations on finite instances nor guarantees that the theoretically polynomial method is faster or more reliable than a method lacking a polynomial worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial worst-case theorem does not by itself predict finite-instance speed, numerical reliability, memory use, or comparative implementation performance.
assumptions_latex: The complexity guarantee is asymptotic and model-specific.
Practical evaluation concerns finite, implemented computations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time classification alone is insufficient to rank practical LP solvers.

notation.meaning: Worst-case resource use on instance I

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Applicability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision conditions under which exact-arithmetic ellipsoid guarantees cease to transfer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an ellipsoid implementation computes a cut \((\widehat g,\widehat\beta)\) and update in finite precision. The exact-arithmetic guarantee transfers only if accumulated errors preserve cut validity for every feasible \(z\), maintain the localization invariant, and keep representation lengths and refinement work polynomially controlled. If rounding permits some feasible \(z\) with \(\widehat g^Tz>\widehat\beta\), the update may discard the feasible region. If no verified error margin, precision schedule, or backward-error bound prevents this event, exact-arithmetic polynomiality supplies no correctness or polynomial-work guarantee for that numerical implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite precision lies outside the exact guarantee when rounding can invalidate cuts, discard feasible points, or require uncontrolled precision and refinement.
assumptions_latex: Cuts and ellipsoid updates are computed in finite precision.
The theoretical method assumes valid separating cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without certified error control, exact-arithmetic polynomiality does not certify the numerical implementation.
