children.title: Projective LP Geometry
children.top_down_role: Projective geometric structure used in scaling-based LP complexity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convention-independent projective geometry of positive diagonal normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(d\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), define \(T_d(y)=D_dy/(d^{\mathsf T}y)\) on \(\Delta^n=\{y\geq0:e^{\mathsf T}y=1\}\). Then \(T_d\) is a bijection of \(\Delta^n\), preserves every coordinate face, maps \(\Delta_{++}^n\) onto itself, and has inverse \(T_{d^{-1}}\), where \(d^{-1}\) denotes componentwise reciprocals. Moreover, \(T_d(e/n)=d/(e^{\mathsf T}d)\); hence \(T_a(e/n)=a\) when \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal scaling followed by normalization is a simplex automorphism with an explicit reciprocal-scaling inverse and sends the center to a normalized positive vector.
assumptions_latex: \(d\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_d^{-1}=T_{d^{-1}},\qquad T_d(e/n)=d/(e^{\mathsf T}d).
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Diagonal Simplex Automorphisms
Projective LP Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex-preserving projective coordinates used in Karmarkar-style scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_{++}^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n:e^Tx=1\}\). For \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\), set \(D_a=\operatorname{Diag}(a)\) and define \(P_a(y)=D_ay/(a^Ty)\) for \(y\in\Delta_{++}^n\). Then \(P_a\) is a bijection of \(\Delta_{++}^n\), its inverse is \(P_{a^{-1}}\), and \(P_a(e/n)=a\). Thus the current interior point becomes the simplex center in projective coordinates, while rays in the positive orthant represent the same normalized simplex point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal projective map bijectively preserves the open simplex and sends its center to the chosen interior iterate.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\).
Projective coordinates are normalized by \(e^Tx=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_a:\Delta_{++}^n\to\Delta_{++}^n\) is bijective and \(P_a(e/n)=a\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulas are internally consistent and the representation kind fits, but no source or locator is supplied for this exact normalization and projective-map convention.

children.title: Special-Form LP Representation
children.top_down_role: The restricted LP representation underlying the projective-scaling route.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and Attainment in Homogeneous Simplex Form
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence of intersecting a homogeneous subspace with the unit simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=0,\ e^{\mathsf T}x=1,\ x\geq0\}\). Then \(P\) is compact. Consequently, if \(P\neq\varnothing\), every linear objective attains its minimum and maximum on \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous-subspace slice of the unit simplex is compact, so every linear objective attains an optimum when it is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}
c\in\mathbb R^n
P\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is compact and }\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\text{ is attained}.

notation.meaning: Homogeneous-subspace slice of the unit simplex

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness and Attainment in Homogeneous Simplex Form
Special-Form LP Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical homogeneous simplex form for the projective-scaling route.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A projective special-form LP is \[\min\{c^Tx:Ax=0,\ e^Tx=1,\ x\geq0\},\] where \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\), and a strictly positive feasible point is known. In the normalized Karmarkar interface, the known point is \(e/n\), the optimal value is known to be \(0\), and the objective is positive at nonoptimal interior iterates. Homogeneity of \(Ax=0\) permits positive rays to be renormalized onto the simplex without changing feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Karmarkar’s canonical interface minimizes a rational linear objective over a homogeneous linear subspace intersected with the simplex, with a known positive center and normalized optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(c\) have rational entries.
A strictly positive feasible point is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{x\geq0:Ax=0,\ e^Tx=1\}\), with the normalized interface using center \(e/n\) and optimum value \(0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The special-form representation is plausible, but the known-center, zero-optimum, positivity, and reduction assumptions are convention-dependent and have no cited source or locator.

children.title: Projective Transformation Interface
children.top_down_role: Interaction between projective transformations and the special-form representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential interface for transferring centered feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(T_a(y)=D_ay/(a^{\mathsf T}y)\), the differential is \[DT_a(y)[h]=\frac{D_ah\,(a^{\mathsf T}y)-D_ay\,(a^{\mathsf T}h)}{(a^{\mathsf T}y)^2}.\] Thus tangent directions in transformed simplex coordinates are transported to tangent directions at the corresponding original point; finite projective steps remain valid only while the transformed point stays in the simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of the projective map transfers feasible centered-coordinate directions, while finite-step validity still requires simplex feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: h\mapsto DT_a(y)[h]\ \text{is the local direction-transfer map}.

notation.meaning: directional derivative of the projective map

knowledge_statements.title: Projective Tangent Transfer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constraint and Objective Transfer Under Recentering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic interface between original and centered projective coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\), \(D_a=\operatorname{Diag}(a)\), and \(x=T_a(y)=D_ay/(a^{\mathsf T}y)\). For \(y\in\Delta^n\), the denominator is positive, \(Ax=0\) if and only if \(AD_ay=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=(c^{\mathsf T}D_ay)/(a^{\mathsf T}y)\). The inverse transfer is \(y=D_a^{-1}x/(e^{\mathsf T}D_a^{-1}x)\). Consequently, transformed feasible points map bijectively to original feasible points, and a centered-coordinate iterate can be returned exactly whenever the positive scaling vector is retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projective recentering transforms homogeneous equalities linearly, the objective fractionally, and feasible iterates bijectively through an explicit inverse.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\).
The special-form equalities are homogeneous: \(Ax=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax=0\iff AD_ay=0,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x=\frac{c^{\mathsf T}D_ay}{a^{\mathsf T}y}.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint and Objective Transfer Under Recentering
Projective Transformation Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change-of-coordinates formulas connecting a current interior point to centered coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(a>0\) satisfy \(Aa=0\) and \(e^Ta=1\). With \(D_a=\operatorname{Diag}(a)\), define \(x=P_a(y)=D_ay/(a^Ty)\) for \(y\in\Delta_{++}^n\). Then \(Ax=0\) is equivalent to \(AD_ay=0\), and \[c^Tx=\frac{c^TD_ay}{a^Ty}.\] Conversely, \(y=P_{a^{-1}}(x)\). Hence a direction or iterate computed around \(e/n\) in transformed coordinates can be mapped back to the original simplex, provided denominators remain positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal projective coordinates center the current iterate, transform homogeneous constraints linearly, transform the objective fractionally, and provide an explicit inverse map.
assumptions_latex: \(a\in\Delta_{++}^n\) and \(Aa=0\).
\(x,y\in\Delta_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maps \(P_a\) and \(P_{a^{-1}}\) transfer feasible interior points bijectively between the two coordinate systems.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The transformation formulas are algebraically consistent and fit the representation leaf, but the exact Karmarkar coordinate convention lacks a source and inspectable locator.

children.title: Special-Form Applicability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Representation restrictions limiting direct use of projective scaling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates direct use of the normalized projective formulas from a reduction of a general LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normalized projective-scaling interface applies directly only after the feasible set has the form \(\{x\geq0:Ax=0,\ e^{\mathsf T}x=1\}\), the required interior initializer is known, and any objective-value normalization assumed by the selected algorithm has been established. An affine system \(Ax=b\) with \(b\neq0\), an unavailable interior initializer, or an unestablished target-value normalization requires a separate correctness- and size-controlled reduction before the corresponding complexity theorem can be invoked.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general affine LP does not enter the normalized projective formulas directly; its embedding, initialization, and objective normalization must first be justified.
assumptions_latex: The invoked projective algorithm is stated for a normalized homogeneous-simplex instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Failure of a required normalization blocks direct invocation of that algorithm's guarantee.}
knowledge_statements.title: Direct-Interface Versus Reduction Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Positivity Boundary for Diagonal Projective Recentering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain boundary of the diagonal projective automorphism used to recenter a simplex point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a\in\Delta_n\), the diagonal projective map \(T_a(x)=D_a x/(e^{\mathsf T}D_a x)\) is a simplex automorphism with an inverse of the same form only when \(a>0\). If \(a_i=0\) for some \(i\), then \(D_a\) is singular and no positive-diagonal projective automorphism maps \(e/n\) to \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal projective recentering requires a strictly positive simplex point; a boundary point makes the diagonal scaling singular.
assumptions_latex: a\in\Delta_n
D_a=\operatorname{diag}(a)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\notin\mathbb R_{++}^n\Longrightarrow T_a\text{ is not a simplex automorphism with the required inverse}.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity Boundary for Diagonal Projective Recentering
Special-Form Applicability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions required for the centered projective special-form interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The centered projective interface requires a feasible \(a\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) with \(e^Ta=1\), homogeneous equalities, and a valid objective normalization. If every feasible point has some zero component, then \(D_a^{-1}\) does not exist and no projective map based on that point sends the simplex center to it. Likewise, affine constraints \(Ax=b\) with \(b\neq0\), an unknown objective shift, or absent initialization cannot be inserted into the canonical formulas without a separate homogeneous embedding or reduction whose size and correctness are controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical projective formulas do not directly apply without a strictly positive feasible initializer, homogeneous constraints, and a justified objective normalization or embedding.
assumptions_latex: The proposed method uses diagonal projective centering.
The canonical representation requires an interior simplex point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of strict feasibility or normalization blocks direct application of the special-form projective interface.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the claimed requirements and available remedies for affine constraints, initialization, and objective normalization require a cited special-form reduction or homogeneous-embedding source.

children.title: Projective Potential
children.top_down_role: The potential measure used to assess projective-scaling progress.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale-invariant primal potential for the normalized zero-optimum projective formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) with positive normalized objective gap \(g(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x>0\), define \(\Phi(x)=n\log g(x)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i=\log\!\left(g(x)^n/\prod_i x_i\right)\). For every \(\alpha>0\), \(\Phi(\alpha x)=\Phi(x)\). The real-valued formula is undefined when \(g(x)\leq0\), and it diverges to \(+\infty\) when a coordinate approaches zero while the gap remains bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal projective potential is the logarithm of the objective-gap power divided by the coordinate product; it is scale invariant and finite only for positive coordinates and positive gap.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
The normalized optimum is zero and \(c^{\mathsf T}x>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Phi(\alpha x)=\Phi(x)\quad(\alpha>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Projective Potential and Domain
Projective Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal projective potential for a normalized LP with zero optimal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an interior feasible point \(x>0\) of the normalized special-form LP with \(c^Tx>0\), define the projective potential by \[\Phi(x)=n\log(c^Tx)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i=\sum_{i=1}^n\log\!\left(\frac{c^Tx}{x_i}\right).\] The expression is invariant under positive rescaling: \(\Phi(\alpha x)=\Phi(x)\) for every \(\alpha>0\). It therefore depends only on the represented positive ray and combines reduction of the objective gap with a barrier against approaching coordinate hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projective potential is the log objective gap multiplied by dimension minus the sum of coordinate logarithms; it is invariant under positive scaling.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}_{++}^n\) is feasible.
The normalized optimal value is \(0\) and \(c^Tx>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(x)=n\log(c^Tx)-\sum_i\log x_i\) is well-defined and satisfies \(\Phi(\alpha x)=\Phi(x)\) for \(\alpha>0\).

children.title: Polynomial Iteration Complexity
children.top_down_role: Iteration-level polynomial guarantees associated with potential reduction.

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration bound obtained from uniform potential decrease and polynomial potential range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0,x^1,\ldots\) be feasible interior iterates, and let \(N\) be the number of nonterminal iterations performed before an iterate with objective gap at most \(\varepsilon\) is obtained. Suppose every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi(x^{k+1})\leq\Phi(x^k)-\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\), and every iterate whose objective gap exceeds \(\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\Phi(x^k)\geq B_\varepsilon\). If \(N=0\), the initial iterate is already terminal; otherwise, \[N\leq\left\lfloor\frac{\Phi(x^0)-B_\varepsilon}{\delta}\right\rfloor+1.\] In particular, if \(\delta^{-1}\), \(\Phi(x^0)-B_\varepsilon\), and the per-iteration cost in the selected computational model are polynomial in \(n\), input length \(L\), and \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), then the total complexity is polynomial in those quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform potential decrease yields at most the potential range divided by the decrease, rounded down and increased by one, nonterminal iterations; polynomial parameter and per-iteration bounds therefore give polynomial total complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi(x^{k+1})\leq\Phi(x^k)-\delta\) on every nonterminal iteration, where \(\delta>0\).
An objective gap greater than \(\varepsilon\) implies \(\Phi(x^k)\geq B_\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the initial iterate is not already terminal, then \(N\leq\left\lfloor(\Phi(x^0)-B_\varepsilon)/\delta\right\rfloor+1\).

notation.meaning: Number of nonterminal iterations before epsilon-termination

children.title: Potential-to-Complexity Link
children.top_down_role: How potential progress supports a polynomial complexity bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-to-Complexity Link
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Telescoping conversion of potential progress into an iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_\varepsilon\) be the set of acceptable \(\varepsilon\)-solutions, and let \(\Phi\) be a real-valued potential on feasible interior iterates. Assume that \(x^k\notin S_\varepsilon\) implies both \(\Phi(x^{k+1})\leq\Phi(x^k)-\delta\) for some \(\delta>0\) and \(\Phi(x^k)\geq B_\varepsilon\). Then no sequence can contain more than \(\left\lfloor(\Phi(x^0)-B_\varepsilon)/\delta\right\rfloor+1\) consecutive nonacceptable iterates. Thus a polynomial bound on the potential range divided by guaranteed per-step progress gives a polynomial iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Telescoping a uniform potential decrease over a bounded nonterminal potential range converts local progress into a global iteration-complexity bound.
assumptions_latex: Nonacceptable iterates have potential at least \(B_\varepsilon\).
Each nonacceptable step decreases potential by at least \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of consecutive iterates outside \(S_\varepsilon\) is at most \(\left\lfloor(\Phi(x^0)-B_\varepsilon)/\delta\right\rfloor+1\).

notation.meaning: Lower potential threshold outside the target set

children.title: Potential Progress Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where potential decrease does not directly control total computational cost.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of termination and polynomial iteration inference from strict potential decrease alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi_k=1+1/(k+1)\) and let termination require \(\Phi_k\leq1\). Then \(\Phi_{k+1}<\Phi_k\) for every \(k\), but no finite iterate is terminal. Thus strict monotonicity, without a sufficient accumulated or inverse-polynomial progress guarantee, implies neither finite termination nor polynomial iteration complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential can decrease strictly forever while never reaching its target, so monotonicity alone gives no iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: Termination is defined by \(\Phi_k\leq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall k,\ \Phi_{k+1}<\Phi_k\ \text{and}\ \Phi_k>1.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Decrease Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of what a potential-decrease argument controls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Even when a potential argument yields polynomially many iterations, polynomial arithmetic or Turing complexity follows only after separately bounding the work per iteration; bit complexity additionally requires polynomial bounds on working precision and intermediate encoding lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Potential progress controls iteration count only; per-step work and finite precision require independent bounds.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial iteration bound has been established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{polynomial iterations}\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{polynomial bit complexity without additional bounds}.
knowledge_statements.title: Iteration-to-Work Boundary
Potential Progress Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform potential decrease is the boundary needed for polynomial iteration accounting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi_k\) be a projective potential and let termination mean \(\Phi_k\leq \Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\). If every nonterminal iteration satisfies \(\Phi_{k+1}\leq\Phi_k-\delta\) for a constant \(\delta>0\), then termination occurs after at most \(\left\lceil(\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}})/\delta\right\rceil\) iterations. If only decreases \(\delta_k>0\) are known, with no inverse-polynomial lower bound on \(\delta_k\), potential monotonicity alone supplies no polynomial iteration bound; the accumulated condition \(\sum_{j<k}\delta_j\geq\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\) may require superpolynomially many iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial potential analysis requires a uniform inverse-polynomial decrease. Mere strict decrease can converge too slowly to establish polynomial complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi_k\in\mathbb R\) is finite for all iterates before termination.
\(\Phi_0>\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N\leq\left\lceil(\Phi_0-\Phi_{\mathrm{tar}})/\delta\right\rceil\) under uniform progress; without such progress, no polynomial bound follows.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic progress calculation is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no source identifies the projective potential, input-size dependence of the progress threshold, or the intended Karmarkar variant.

children.title: Homogeneous Extensions
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous reformulations extending projective-scaling applicability.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions not supplied merely by homogenizing an LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Homogenization alone does not produce the normalized Karmarkar starting configuration. Direct application of a special-form projective method additionally requires a bounded normalization section, a strictly positive feasible point in that section, and whatever centering and objective-value conventions the selected method assumes. These properties need not follow from \(P\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous cone is not automatically an admissible centered Karmarkar instance; strict positivity, normalization, and method-specific objective conventions remain necessary.
assumptions_latex: A projective method requiring a strictly positive normalized starting point is being considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\neq\varnothing\ \not\Rightarrow\ \text{direct admissibility of the normalized projective instance}.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Projective-Format Admission Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous representation of an equality-form feasible set and the exact positive-scale recovery boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), let \(K=\{(u,\tau):Au=b\tau,\ u\geq0,\ \tau\geq0\}\). Then \(K\) is a cone, \(P=\{u/\tau:(u,\tau)\in K,\ \tau>0\}\), and every nonzero ray of \(K\) has a unique representative satisfying \(e^{\mathsf T}u+\tau=1\). Points of that section with \(\tau=0\) encode nonzero recession directions \(u\geq0\), \(Au=0\), and cannot be dehomogenized to finite points of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homogenization turns affine feasibility into a cone whose positive-scale rays recover finite feasible points; zero-scale rays are recession directions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\{u/\tau:(u,\tau)\in K,\ \tau>0\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous Cone and Projective Sections
Homogeneous Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogenization of equality-form LP feasibility into a polyhedral cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), define the homogeneous cone \(K=\{(u,\tau)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:Au-b\tau=0,\ u\geq0,\ \tau\geq0\}\). Every \(x\in P\) yields \((\tau x,\tau)\in K\) for each \(\tau>0\), and every \((u,\tau)\in K\) with \(\tau>0\) yields \(u/\tau\in P\). Thus the slice \(\tau=1\) recovers the original feasible set, whereas points with \(\tau=0\) represent homogeneous recession directions satisfying \(Au=0\) and \(u\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a nonnegative scale variable converts affine feasibility into a homogeneous cone; every positive-scale cone point normalizes to an original feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogenization identity is correct for the displayed feasible set, but no citation confirms that this generic cone construction is the homogeneous extension intended by the Karmarkar projective-scaling container.

children.title: General-Form LP Extensions
children.top_down_role: Extensions from special-form instances to general LP representations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit equality-form treatment of a variable with two finite bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a variable satisfying \(\ell\le x\le u\) with \(\ell<u<+\infty\), introduce \(z,w\ge0\) and impose \[x=\ell+z,\qquad z+w=u-\ell.\] Eliminating \(x\) gives a nonnegative equality-form representation. In every original row, the term \(ax\) becomes \(az+a\ell\), and an objective term \(cx\) becomes \(cz+c\ell\). The mappings \(x\mapsto(z,w)=(x-\ell,u-x)\) and \((z,w)\mapsto x=\ell+z\) are inverse on their feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boxed variable is encoded exactly by a shifted nonnegative variable and one complementary nonnegative slack whose sum equals the box width.
assumptions_latex: \ell,u\in\mathbb Q
\ell<u<+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell\le x\le u\iff\exists z,w\ge0:\quad x=\ell+z,\quad z+w=u-\ell.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Boxed-Variable Standard-Form Encoding

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inconsistent Finite Bounds Are an Immediate Infeasibility Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary case for variable-bound conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a variable has finite bounds \(\ell>u\), no scalar satisfies \(\ell\le x\le u\), and no equality \(z+w=u-\ell\) with \(z,w\ge0\) is feasible. If \(\ell=u\), the variable is fixed and may be eliminated by substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversed bounds certify infeasibility, while coincident bounds define a fixed variable.
assumptions_latex: \ell,u\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell>u\Rightarrow\{x:\ell\le x\le u\}=\varnothing,\qquad \ell=u\Rightarrow x=\ell.
knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Finite Bounds Are an Immediate Infeasibility Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete Mixed-Form to Nonnegative Equality-Form Conversion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elementary conversion covering mixed row senses and standard variable-bound types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite rational mixed-form LP can be converted to \(\min\{\bar c^Tz+\kappa:\bar Az=\bar b,\ z\ge0\}\). Replace \(a^Tx\le\beta\) by \(a^Tx+s=\beta\), and \(a^Tx\ge\beta\) by \(a^Tx-s=\beta\), with \(s\ge0\). Replace a free variable by \(x=x^+-x^-\); a lower-bounded variable by \(x=\ell+z\); an upper-bounded variable by \(x=u-z\); a boxed variable by \(x=\ell+z\), \(z+w=u-\ell\); and a fixed variable by its fixed value. All introduced variables are nonnegative. Translation constants are moved to \(\bar b\), and objective constants are accumulated in \(\kappa\). Projection maps every transformed feasible point to an original feasible point with the same objective up to \(\kappa\), and every original feasible point has a transformed lift; hence feasibility, objective ordering, and optimality are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slacks, splitting, translations, box slacks, and fixed-variable elimination convert every finite mixed-form rational LP to an equivalent nonnegative equality-form LP.
assumptions_latex: \text{The LP has finitely many linear rows and variables}
\text{All coefficients and finite bounds are rational}
\text{Inconsistent bounds are detected before conversion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ feasible}\iff\exists z\ge0:\bar Az=\bar b\text{ projecting to }x,\qquad c^Tx=\bar c^Tz+\kappa.

notation.meaning: Aggregate vector of transformed nonnegative variables.
Objective constant produced by translations and eliminations.

This is the elementary conversion, not homogeneous or projective normalization.

General-Form LP Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact conversion of mixed linear constraints and unrestricted variables to nonnegative equality form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an LP with equality rows, inequality rows, lower or upper bounds, and unrestricted variables. Replace every unrestricted variable \(x_j\) by \(x_j^+-x_j^-\) with \(x_j^+,x_j^-\geq0\); translate a finite lower bound by \(x_j=\ell_j+z_j\), \(z_j\geq0\), and convert each inequality to an equality using a nonnegative slack, after reversing signs when necessary. Substitution gives \(\min\{\bar c^{\mathsf T}z+\kappa:\bar A z=\bar b,\ z\geq0\}\). Feasible points and objective values correspond under the substitutions, and an optimal transformed point maps to an optimal point of the original LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable splitting, bound translation, and slack variables convert a general LP exactly into equality form with nonnegative variables.
assumptions_latex: All coefficients and finite bounds are rational.
The original objective and constraints are linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The transformed standard-form LP preserves feasibility and objective values up to the constant \(\kappa\).

notation.meaning: constant objective shift caused by translations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The standard-form substitutions are broadly correct, but the treatment of finite upper bounds and the exact transformed row structure are not fully specified and no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Special-to-General Form Reduction
children.top_down_role: Encoding and complexity effects of transferring guarantees to general-form LP.

knowledge_statements.title: Special-to-General Form Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial preprocessing transfers a special-form interior-point method to general rational LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a rational general-form LP, first reverse inequality signs as needed, introduce one nonnegative slack per inequality, split every unrestricted variable, and translate finite lower bounds. This produces \(\min\{\bar c^{\mathsf T}z:\bar A z=\bar b,\ z\geq0\}\), possibly with an additive objective constant. Next form the homogeneous equations \(\bar A u-\bar b\tau=0\), \(u\geq0\), \(\tau\geq0\). Apply the special-form projective method to an appropriate normalized positive-scale slice. If its output has \(\tau>0\), normalize \(z=u/\tau\) and invert the preprocessing substitutions; otherwise the zero-scale output must be interpreted separately as a recession or infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: General LPs reduce by standard-form conversion and homogenization; positive-scale solutions normalize back, while zero-scale outputs require certificate analysis.
assumptions_latex: The input LP has rational data encoded in binary.
The special-form method accepts the resulting normalized homogeneous instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A positive-scale transformed solution maps algorithmically to a solution of the original LP.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the normalized slice accepted by the special-form method and the interpretation of zero-scale outputs are essential, version-dependent parts of the reduction that require a source.

children.title: Extension Overhead
children.top_down_role: Dimension, encoding, and numerical costs introduced by representation extensions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension and binary-encoding growth for free-variable splitting, slack introduction, homogenization, and optional affine normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an explicitly encoded rational LP with \(n\) variables, of which \(f\) are unrestricted, \(m\) inequality rows, and \(p\) equality rows. Replacing each unrestricted variable by a difference of two nonnegative variables and adding one nonnegative slack per inequality produces \(n+f+m\) nonnegative variables and \(p+m\) equality rows. Homogenizing these equations adds one scale variable and no row; if an affine ray-normalization equation is materialized, it adds one row. Thus this elementary extension has at most \(n+f+m+1\) variables and \(p+m+1\) rows. It uses only coefficient copies, sign changes, zeros, ones, and existing right-hand sides, so its construction work and binary encoding length are polynomial in the original encoding length and dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting free variables, adding slacks, homogenizing, and optionally normalizing increase dimensions only linearly and preserve polynomial binary encoding size.
assumptions_latex: All input coefficients are rational and explicitly binary encoded.
m counts all inequality rows that receive slacks, while p counts equality rows.
The extension does not enumerate an implicit exponential family of rows or columns.
Any additional centering or target-value gadget is not included in the displayed exact counts and must be accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n'\leq n+f+m+1,\qquad r'\leq p+m+1,\qquad L'=\operatorname{poly}(L,n,m,p).

notation.meaning: numbers of inequality and equality rows under the stated convention
input and extended binary encoding lengths

Extension Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension and encoding growth under standard-form conversion and one-variable homogenization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an LP has \(n\) variables, of which \(f\) are unrestricted, \(m\) inequality rows, and \(p\) equality rows. Splitting unrestricted variables and adding slacks produces at most \(n+f+m\) nonnegative variables and \(p+m\) equality rows. Homogenization then adds one scale variable and changes no row count. Under binary encoding, sign changes, copies, zeros, ones, and existing right-hand-side coefficients enlarge the total encoding length by at most a polynomial in the original length and \(n+m+p\); hence a polynomial-time special-form algorithm remains polynomial after the reduction.

No preprocessing step explicitly enumerates exponentially many constraints or variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Short-Step Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual short-step method in a narrow Euclidean central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), maintain strict feasibility and \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). Fix \(0<\theta<1\) and require \(\|XSe-\mu e\|_2\leq\theta\mu\). At iteration \(k\), set \(\sigma=1-\beta/\sqrt n\), solve the primal-dual Newton equations with complementarity right-hand side \(\sigma\mu e-XSe\), and take the full Newton step when it remains in the prescribed neighborhood. Stop when \(x^{\mathsf T}s\leq\varepsilon\). For suitable absolute constants \(\theta,\beta>0\), the method needs \(O(\sqrt n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon))\) Newton steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Short-step path following takes conservative full Newton steps inside a narrow central neighborhood and reaches the target duality gap in order square-root-n logarithmic iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank and a strictly feasible primal-dual point is supplied.
\(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is primal-dual feasible with \(x^{\mathsf T}s\leq\varepsilon\) after \(O(\sqrt n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon))\) iterations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duality-gap iteration guarantee under strict primal-dual feasibility and the stated initial centrality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the primal path-following algorithm use
\[
\alpha=1-\frac{\sqrt{\beta}-\beta}{\sqrt{\beta}+\sqrt n},
\]
with \(0<\beta<1\). Suppose the initial triple \((x^0,s^0,p^0)\) is primal-dual feasible, \(x^0>0\), \(s^0>0\), and

knowledge_statements.title: Long-Step Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual path following in a wider one-sided central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), consider \(Ax=b\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), with \(x,s>0\). Define \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\) and, for fixed \(0<\gamma<1\), maintain \(x_i s_i\geq\gamma\mu\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). At each iteration choose the standard long-step centering parameter, solve the primal-dual Newton equations, and take a damped step that preserves feasibility, positivity, and this neighborhood. With fixed admissible parameters ensuring \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\eta/n)\mu_k\) for an absolute constant \(\eta>0\), stop when \(x^{\mathsf T}s\leq\varepsilon\). The method then requires \(O\!\left(n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon)\right)\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible long-step method takes damped Newton steps in a wide central neighborhood. Standard fixed parameters reduce complementarity by a factor of order one minus a constant over n, giving an order n logarithmic iteration bound.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank, and a strictly feasible primal-dual starting point in the stated neighborhood is supplied.
\(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\).
The fixed parameters satisfy the standard long-step neighborhood-invariance and progress conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Predictor-Corrector Path Following
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mehrotra-type affine predictor followed by a centered second-order correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(r_p=Ax-b\), \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), and \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\), with \(x,s>0\). First solve the primal-dual Newton system with centering parameter \(\sigma=0\) to obtain \((\Delta x^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta y^{\mathrm{aff}},\Delta s^{\mathrm{aff}})\). Compute the maximum positivity-preserving affine step and its predicted complementarity \(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}\), and set \(\sigma=(\mu_{\mathrm{aff}}/\mu)^3\). Then solve the corrected Newton system with complementarity right-hand side \(\sigma\mu e-XSe-\Delta X^{\mathrm{aff}}\Delta S^{\mathrm{aff}}e\), combine the predictor and correction, and take a fixed fraction of the maximum positivity-preserving step. Stop when \(\|r_p\|\), \(\|r_d\|\), and \(x^{\mathsf T}s\) satisfy their prescribed tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mehrotra's method computes an affine predictor, estimates the resulting complementarity, and then adds adaptive centering and a second-order correction before taking a positivity-preserving step.
assumptions_latex: The primal-dual Newton systems are solvable.
The current vectors satisfy \(x>0\) and \(s>0\).
Positive feasibility and complementarity tolerances are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted update preserves \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), and termination reports the prescribed primal-residual, dual-residual, and complementarity tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Potential Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal potential descent using an objective lower bound and logarithmic barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(p^*=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) be finite. Given \(x>0\) with \(Ax=b\) and a valid lower bound \(z\leq p^*\) satisfying \(z<c^{\mathsf T}x\), define \(\Phi_\rho(x,z)=\rho\log(c^{\mathsf T}x-z)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\), where \(\rho>n\). At each iteration choose \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(Ad=0\) and a step \(\alpha>0\) such that \(x+\alpha d>0\) and the prescribed potential decrease holds; the lower bound may be increased only while remaining at most \(p^*\). Stop when \(c^{\mathsf T}x-z\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal potential method preserves primal feasibility while reducing a logarithmic function of the objective-gap upper bound and the positive-variable barriers.

The optimal value \(p^*\) is finite, and \(z\leq p^*\) is a valid lower bound.

If \(z>p^*\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}x-z\) can underestimate the true suboptimality and may be nonpositive even at a nonoptimal feasible point, so it neither provides the logarithm's required positive argument nor certifies \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a strictly feasible \(x\) with \(g=c^Tx-z>0\), let \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\), \(q=X\nabla_x\Phi_\rho(x,z)=\rho Xc/g-\mathbf1\), and let \(P\) be the Euclidean projector onto \(\ker(AX)\). If \(Pq\ne0\), choose \(v=-Pq/\lVert Pq\rVert_2\), \(d=Xv\), and use backtracking to find \(\alpha>0\) such that \(x+\alpha d>0\) and \[\Phi_\rho(x+\alpha d,z)\le\Phi_\rho(x,z)-\eta\alpha\lVert Pq\rVert_2\] for fixed \(\eta\in(0,1)\). Then \(Ad=0\), strict feasibility is preserved, and the potential decreases.

Primal-Dual Potential Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible primal-dual descent for a complementarity potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), consider the primal-dual pair \(Ax=b\), \(x\geq0\), and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s\geq0\). For a strictly feasible triple \((x,y,s)\), define \(\Psi_\rho(x,s)=\rho\log(x^{\mathsf T}s)-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(x_i s_i)\), where \(\rho>n\). At each iteration compute a direction satisfying \(A\Delta x=0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and choose a positivity-preserving step that gives the prescribed decrease in \(\Psi_\rho\), unless \(x^{\mathsf T}s\leq\varepsilon\). Primal and dual feasibility are preserved, and \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal-dual potential reduction preserves strict primal-dual feasibility while decreasing a complementarity potential; a small complementarity product is therefore a small duality-gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has full row rank, and a strictly feasible primal-dual point is supplied.
Every accepted step preserves positivity and gives the prescribed potential decrease.
\(\varepsilon>0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Bound from Uniform Potential Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic stopping bound for a feasibility-preserving primal–dual algorithm using the gap-barrier potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0>0\) be primal feasible and let \((p^0,s^0)\) be dual feasible with \(s^0>0\). Let \(\epsilon>0\), and let \(G\) be the primal–dual potential with parameter \(q>n\). If an algorithm maintains primal and dual feasibility and decreases \(G\) by at least \(\delta>0\) at every iteration, then it obtains iterates satisfying \[(s^K)^{\top}x^K\leq\epsilon\] after \[K=\left\lceil\frac{G(x^0,s^0)+(q-n)\log(1/\epsilon)-n\log n}{\delta}\right\rceil\] iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from strictly positive primal- and dual-feasible iterates, any feasibility-preserving algorithm that decreases the primal–dual potential by at least δ per iteration reaches duality gap at most ε after the displayed ceiling number of iterations.

(p^0,s^0)\text{ is dual feasible and }s^0>0
\epsilon>0
\delta>0
q>n
G(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})\leq G(x^k,s^k)-\delta\quad\text{for every iteration}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (s^K)^{\top}x^K\leq\epsilon,\qquad K=\left\lceil\frac{G(x^0,s^0)+(q-n)\log(1/\epsilon)-n\log n}{\delta}\right\rceil

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the potential-reduction algorithm with \(\beta<1\) and \(\gamma<1\): if \(\lVert u^k\rVert\geq\gamma\), then \[G(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})-G(x^k,s^k)\leq-\beta\gamma+\frac{\beta^2}{2(1-\beta)};\] if \(\lVert u^k\rVert<\gamma\), then \[G(x^{k+1},s^{k+1})-G(x^k,s^k)\leq-(q-n)+n\log\frac qn+\frac{\gamma^2}{2(1-\gamma)}.\] For \(q=n+\sqrt n\), \(\beta\approx0.285\), and \(\gamma\approx0.479\), every iteration decreases \(G\) by at least \(0.079\).

knowledge_statements.title: Strictly Feasible Start Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization regime for feasible primal-dual interior-point complexity analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), consider the primal LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\). Define \(r_p(x)=Ax-b\) and \(r_d(y,s)=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\). A strictly feasible start is a triple \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(r_p(x_0)=0\), \(r_d(y_0,s_0)=0\), \(x_0>0\), and \(s_0>0\). Its average complementarity is \(\mu_0=x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0/n>0\). Directions satisfying \(A\Delta x=0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\) preserve the two affine feasibility equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible start satisfies the primal and dual equations exactly and has strictly positive primal variables and dual slacks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A phase-I solution initializes the original affine-scaling iteration only when its recovered original variables are strictly positive and the artificial variable is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose any \(u>0\) and set \(v=b-Au\). If \(v=0\), then \(x^{(0)}=u\) is strictly feasible for \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\). If \(v\ne0\), solve the phase-I problem \(\min y\) subject to \(Ax+vy=b\), \(x\ge0\), and \(y\ge0\), initialized at \((u,1)>0\). A returned point with \(y=0\) is feasible for the original equalities and inequalities; if additionally \(x>0\), it supplies the strictly feasible start required by phase II.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a positive vector u and form v=b-Au. If v is zero, u is already a strictly feasible start. Otherwise introduce one nonnegative artificial variable y, minimize y subject to Ax+vy=b, and start the auxiliary affine-scaling run from (u,1), which is strictly feasible. A zero-artificial-variable solution recovers original feasibility, and a positive recovered x can initialize phase II.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Warm-start boundary for LP interior-point methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Addresses the mathematically meaningful initialization claim; historical software discussion and time-dependent solver comparisons are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When an estimate of an LP solution is available, it may be modified into a theoretically valid interior-point start so that a complexity bound depends on the quality of the estimate. Nevertheless, interior-point methods generally exploit warm-start information less effectively than simplex reoptimization, particularly for sequences of slightly changed LPs; this is a structure-dependent practical tendency, not a universal rule, and the improvement over a cold start may be only modest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate LP solution can be converted into a theoretically valid interior-point starting point, allowing complexity results that reflect the estimate's quality. In practice, however, interior-point methods generally benefit less from warm starts than simplex methods on sequences of nearby LPs. This tendency depends on problem structure, and improvement over a cold start may be only modest.
assumptions_latex: \text{A linear program or a sequence of slightly perturbed linear programs is to be solved.}
\text{Prior information, such as an approximate solution or optimal-basis estimate, is available.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{A valid interior start with quality-dependent complexity can be constructed, but no uniformly strong practical warm-start advantage follows; simplex reoptimization is generally more effective in this regime.}

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasible-Start Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization regime allowing positive primal and dual slack vectors with nonzero feasibility residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), define \(r_p(x)=Ax-b\), \(r_d(y,s)=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), and \(\mu(x,s)=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). An infeasible-start regime permits an initial triple \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(x_0>0\) and \(s_0>0\) without requiring \(r_p(x_0)=0\) or \(r_d(y_0,s_0)=0\). An associated infeasible-start interior-point method reduces the two residuals and complementarity while preserving \(x>0\) and \(s>0\), and terminates for prescribed tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_\mu>0\) when \(\|r_p(x)\|\leq\varepsilon_p\), \(\|r_d(y,s)\|\leq\varepsilon_d\), and \(x^{\mathsf T}s\leq\varepsilon_\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infeasible-start regime requires positive primal variables and dual slacks but allows nonzero primal and dual residuals, which the method reduces together with complementarity.
assumptions_latex: The chosen interior-point method maintains strict positivity.
The Newton systems and neighborhood conditions required by that method are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The initialization may have nonzero \(r_p(x_0)\) and \(r_d(y_0,s_0)\), while termination requires the prescribed residual and complementarity tolerances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the displayed iteration, including initialization, residual construction, direction computation, and parity-dependent step selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbb{R}^m, c\in\mathbb{R}^n, with X=\operatorname{Diag}(x), Y=\operatorname{Diag}(y), Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z), W=\operatorname{Diag}(w). Initialize (x,y,\phi,z,w,\psi)=(e,e,1,e,e,1). At each iteration set \mu=(z^Tx+w^Ty+\psi\phi)/(n+m+1) and \delta=0 on odd iterations or \delta=1 on even iterations. Form \widehat\rho=-(1-\delta)(Ax-b\phi+w)+w-\delta\mu Y^{-1}e, \widehat\sigma=-(1-\delta)(-A^Ty+c\phi+z)+z-\delta\mu X^{-1}e, and \widehat\gamma=-(1-\delta)(b^Ty-c^Tx+\psi)+\psi-\delta\mu/\phi. With K=\begin{bmatrix}-Y^{-1}W&A\\A^T&X^{-1}Z\end{bmatrix}, solve K\binom{f_y}{f_x}=\binom{\widehat\rho}{-\widehat\sigma} and K\binom{g_y}{g_x}=\binom{-b}{-c}. Then compute \Delta\phi=(c^Tf_x-b^Tf_y+\widehat\gamma)/(c^Tg_x-b^Tg_y-\psi/\phi), \binom{\Delta x}{\Delta y}=\binom{f_x}{f_y}-\binom{g_x}{g_y}\Delta\phi, \Delta z=-X^{-1}Z\Delta x+\delta\mu X^{-1}e-z, \Delta w=-Y^{-1}W\Delta y+\delta\mu Y^{-1}e-w, and \Delta\psi=-(\psi/\phi)\Delta\phi+\delta\mu/\phi-\psi. On odd iterations choose \theta=\max\{t:(x(t),\ldots,\psi(t))\in\mathcal N(1/2)\}; on even iterations set \theta=1. The displayed update is x\leftarrow x+\theta\Delta x and z\leftarrow z+\theta\Delta z.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize all primal, dual, slack, and homogeneous variables at one. Alternate odd predictor iterations with even centering iterations. Each iteration computes the average complementarity, constructs three residual terms, solves two systems with the same quasidefinite matrix, recovers the full search direction, and uses the largest neighborhood-preserving step on odd iterations and a full step on even iterations. The displayed final update advances x and z.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb{R}^m,\quad c\in\mathbb{R}^n
x,z\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++},\quad y,w\in\mathbb{R}^m_{++},\quad \phi,\psi>0
X=\operatorname{Diag}(x),\quad Y=\operatorname{Diag}(y),\quad Z=\operatorname{Diag}(z),\quad W=\operatorname{Diag}(w)
K\text{ is solvable and }c^Tg_x-b^Tg_y-\psi/\phi\ne0
\mathcal N(1/2)\text{ is the prescribed central-path neighborhood}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,z)\leftarrow(x,z)+\theta(\Delta x,\Delta z),\qquad \theta=\begin{cases}\max\{t:(x(t),\ldots,\psi(t))\in\mathcal N(1/2)\},&\text{odd iterations},\\1,&\text{even iterations}.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conditional geometric decay of path-following residuals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon convergence bound under a uniform step-size lower bound and uniformly bounded primal-dual iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose there exist \(t>0\), \(M<\infty\), and an integer \(K\) such that, for every iteration index \(k\le K\), \(\theta^{(k)}\ge t\), \(\lVert x^{(k)}\rVert_\infty\le M\), and \(\lVert y^{(k)}\rVert_\infty\le M\). Then there exists \(\bar M<\infty\) such that, for every \(k\le K\), \(\lVert\rho^{(k)}\rVert_1\le(1-t)^k\lVert\rho^{(0)}\rVert_1\), \(\lVert\sigma^{(k)}\rVert_1\le(1-t)^k\lVert\sigma^{(0)}\rVert_1\), and \(\gamma^{(k)}\le(1-\widetilde t)^k\bar M\), where \(\widetilde t=t(1-\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the path-following step parameters are uniformly bounded below by a positive number and the primal and dual iterates remain uniformly bounded through iteration K, then the two residual norms and the complementarity quantity admit geometric upper bounds through iteration K.
assumptions_latex: \(t>0\), \(M<\infty\), and \(K\in\mathbb Z\) exist.
\(\theta^{(k)}\ge t\) for every iteration index \(k\le K\).
\(\lVert x^{(k)}\rVert_\infty\le M\) and \(\lVert y^{(k)}\rVert_\infty\le M\) for every iteration index \(k\le K\).
\(\widetilde t=t(1-\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar M<\infty\;\forall k\le K:\;\lVert\rho^{(k)}\rVert_1\le(1-t)^k\lVert\rho^{(0)}\rVert_1,\;\lVert\sigma^{(k)}\rVert_1\le(1-t)^k\lVert\sigma^{(0)}\rVert_1,\;\gamma^{(k)}\le(1-\widetilde t)^k\bar M.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-scaling Phase I auxiliary problem and feasibility direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase I construction for a standard-form linear program when the positive initial point need not satisfy the equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0>0\), set \(\rho=b-Ax^0\), and solve \(\max\{-x_0:Ax+x_0\rho=b,\ x\ge0,\ x_0\ge0\}\). The point \((x^0,1)\) is strictly positive and feasible. At an optimum \((x^*,x_0^*)\), \(x_0^*>0\) certifies infeasibility of \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\), whereas \(x_0^*=0\) makes \(x^*\) feasible for that system. For a positive current auxiliary iterate \((x,x_0)\), with \(X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)\) and \(AX^2A^T\) nonsingular, the affine-scaling feasibility direction may be chosen, up to positive scaling, as \(\Delta x=X^2A^T(AX^2A^T)^{-1}\rho\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form the residual rho=b-Ax0 and introduce a nonnegative auxiliary variable multiplying rho. The positive point (x0,1) starts the auxiliary affine-scaling problem. A positive optimal auxiliary variable certifies that the original equality-and-nonnegativity system is infeasible; a zero optimum supplies a feasible original point. When the indicated matrix inverse exists, the feasibility direction is X squared times A transpose times the inverse of A X squared A transpose times rho, up to positive scaling.
assumptions_latex: x^0\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++}
\rho=b-Ax^0
(x,x_0)\in\mathbb{R}^n_{++}\times\mathbb{R}_{++}
X=\operatorname{Diag}(x)
AX^2A^T\text{ is nonsingular}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0^*>0\Rightarrow\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}=\varnothing;\quad x_0^*=0\Rightarrow Ax^*=b,\ x^*\ge0;\quad \Delta x\propto X^2A^T(AX^2A^T)^{-1}\rho.

children.title: Start-Regime Complexity Gap
children.top_down_role: Additional work or representation requirements caused by unavailable strict feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Start-Regime Complexity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates short-step complexity from the additional work needed to obtain a central strictly feasible start.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a primal-dual path-following method for an LP with an initial point satisfying strict feasibility and a prescribed central-neighborhood condition. Its usual iteration bound applies only after such a point is available. If the input instead supplies an arbitrary positive but infeasible point, the same bound does not follow merely by running identical Newton updates: primal and dual residuals must also be controlled, and initialization may require a Phase-I problem or a self-dual embedding. Thus a bound of the form \(O(\sqrt n\log(\mu_0/\varepsilon))\) is a conditional start-regime bound unless the cost and correctness of initialization are included explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A short-step iteration bound assumes a central strictly feasible start; an arbitrary infeasible start requires a separate initialization or embedding analysis whose work is not covered automatically.
assumptions_latex: The LP has \(n\) complementary primal-slack pairs.
The stated short-step bound assumes strict primal-dual feasibility and membership in a fixed central neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strictly feasible-start complexity guarantee cannot be transferred unchanged to an arbitrary infeasible-start regime without accounting for residual reduction and initialization.

children.title: Initialization Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where assumed starting information cannot be efficiently supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to initialization by a strictly positive feasible primal-dual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict feasibility can fail even when an LP has an optimal solution. For example, consider \(\min\{x_2:x_1=0,\ x_1+x_2=1,\ x\geq0\}\). Its unique feasible, hence optimal, point is \(x=(0,1)\), so no feasible point satisfies \(x>0\). Consequently, an initialization procedure that requires a strictly positive primal feasible point cannot start on this instance. More generally, if the feasible region lies in a proper face of the nonnegative orthant, a full-dimensional interior start does not exist; facial reduction, a relative-interior formulation, or an embedding is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP may lie entirely on an orthant face, so a strictly positive feasible initializer can fail despite existence of an optimum.
assumptions_latex: Strict positivity means componentwise positivity in \(\mathbb R^2_+\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility and attainment alone do not guarantee existence of the strictly feasible initialization required by a standard feasible-start interior-point method.

notation.meaning: every component of x is strictly positive

source_refs.locator: A Strictly Interior Point p. 29

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An LP with a finite attained optimum and strictly positive primal feasible points but no strictly positive dual slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\{0:x_1-x_2=0,\ x_1,x_2\ge0\}.\] It has strictly positive primal feasible points, such as \(x=(1,1)\), and every feasible point is optimal. Its dual equations are \[y+s_1=0,\qquad -y+s_2=0,\qquad s_1,s_2\ge0.\] Strict dual slack would require simultaneously \(y<0\) and \(y>0\), which is impossible. Thus strict primal feasibility and finite attainment do not guarantee a joint strictly feasible primal-dual initializer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict primal feasibility does not guarantee strict dual feasibility; a simple equality-form LP has positive primal points but no positive dual slack.
assumptions_latex: Strict dual feasibility requires every component of the dual slack vector to be positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LP admits \(x>0\) with \(Ax=b\), but no \((y,s)\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) and \(s>0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Interior Initialization Can Fail Independently

children.title: Self-Dual Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Embedded LP representations unifying primal and dual status.

knowledge_statements.title: Self-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedding representation that converts initialization and status determination into one primal-dual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), a self-dual embedding introduces auxiliary variables and constructs a single primal-dual system whose dual has the same structural form. The construction is chosen to possess a known strictly positive starting point. From a terminal embedded solution, a positive scaling variable yields primal-dual feasible solutions after normalization, while an appropriate zero-scaling terminal solution yields a certificate of primal infeasibility or dual infeasibility/unboundedness. The embedding therefore represents optimization, initialization, and alternative-system certification within one interior-point trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-dual embedding supplies a known interior start and encodes either normalized primal-dual solutions or infeasibility and unboundedness certificates in one system.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\).
The chosen embedding includes the auxiliary shifts needed for a known positive start.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the embedded self-dual problem determines an optimal primal-dual pair or an alternative-system certificate under the embedding's recovery conditions.

notation.meaning: primal variable, dual multiplier, and dual slack

children.title: Homogeneous Self-Dual Embeddings
children.top_down_role: Homogeneous embedded representations supporting unified status recovery.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decoding of the nondegenerate branches of the sign-consistent homogeneous system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonzero solution of the sign-consistent HSD system: if \(\tau>0\), then \(\kappa=0\), and \((x/\tau,y/\tau,s/\tau)\) is primal feasible, dual feasible, complementary, and optimal. If \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa>0\), then \[Ax=0,\quad x\geq0,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y=-s\leq0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y-c^{\mathsf T}x=\kappa>0.\] Thus at least one of \(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\) or \(c^{\mathsf T}x<0\) holds. The first is a Farkas certificate of primal infeasibility; the second is a Farkas certificate of dual infeasibility. If dual feasibility is independently known, the first direction also certifies dual unboundedness; if primal feasibility is independently known, the second direction certifies primal unboundedness. Each declared status requires its corresponding strict inequality and exact equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive tau recovers an optimal pair; zero tau and positive kappa produce a primal- or dual-infeasibility certificate, with unboundedness following on the opposite side when feasibility there is known.
assumptions_latex: The embedded point satisfies the sign-consistent HSD equations.
The embedded point is nonzero.
An unboundedness declaration additionally requires feasibility of the corresponding optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau>0\Rightarrow\text{optimal recovery};\qquad \tau=0,\ \kappa>0\Rightarrow\bigl(b^{\mathsf T}y>0\ \lor\ c^{\mathsf T}x<0\bigr).
knowledge_statements.title: HSD Solution and Alternative-Certificate Branches

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-explicit terminal homogeneous system for the stated primal minimization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\geq0\},\] consider \[Ax-b\tau=0,\qquad -A^{\mathsf T}y+c\tau-s=0,\qquad -c^{\mathsf T}x+b^{\mathsf T}y-\kappa=0,\] with \(x,s,\tau,\kappa\geq0\) and \(y\) free. The system is homogeneous and satisfies \[x^{\mathsf T}s+\tau\kappa=0.\] Hence nonnegativity forces \(x^{\mathsf T}s=0\) and \(\tau\kappa=0\), and every nonnegative scalar multiple of an embedded solution is again an embedded solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This sign-consistent HSD system homogenizes primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the objective alternative while enforcing complementarity at terminal solutions.
assumptions_latex: The primal is a minimization problem with dual equation \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\).
All three displayed sign conventions are used together.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{\mathsf T}s=0,\qquad \tau\kappa=0,\qquad \lambda(x,y,s,\tau,\kappa)\text{ is feasible for every }\lambda\geq0.
knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Consistent Homogeneous Self-Dual System
Homogeneous Self-Dual Embeddings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical homogeneous embedding and its solution-or-certificate normalization rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min\,c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(x\geq0\), with dual \(A^Ty+s=c\), introduce \(\tau,\kappa\geq0\) and impose
\[Ax-b\tau=0,\qquad A^Ty+s-c\tau=0,\qquad c^Tx-b^Ty-\kappa=0,\qquad x,s\geq0.\]
These equations are homogeneous and imply \(x^Ts=\tau\kappa\). If an embedded solution has \(\tau>0\) and \(\kappa=0\), then \((x/\tau,y/\tau,s/\tau)\) is primal-dual feasible with zero duality gap. If \(\tau=0\) and \(\kappa>0\), its nonzero components encode an alternative-system certificate, subject to the certificate's sign conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogeneous embedding uses two scalars: positive tau recovers an optimal primal-dual solution, while zero tau and positive kappa can expose an infeasibility certificate.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual use the displayed equality-form sign convention.
A nonzero embedded terminal solution is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signs of \(\tau\) and \(\kappa\) separate the solution-recovery and alternative-certificate regimes.

children.title: Embedding Variant Comparison
children.top_down_role: Differences in initialization, output interpretation, and complexity accounting across embedding variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Embedding Variant Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares ordinary self-dual and homogeneous self-dual formulations by initialization and recovery behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A shifted self-dual embedding and a homogeneous self-dual embedding serve the same logical purpose but use different recovery interfaces. A shifted embedding incorporates residual offsets selected so that a prescribed positive point is feasible; its terminal variables are decoded using the particular shifts. A homogeneous embedding instead preserves scale: every positive multiple of an embedded solution is again a solution, and recovery is governed by normalization with \(\tau\). Thus the variants may have comparable polynomial iteration theory, but their dimensions, initial residuals, Newton systems, degeneracy cases, and certificate decoding rules are not interchangeable. Complexity or recovery claims must be stated for the selected embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shifted embeddings manufacture a known feasible start; homogeneous embeddings preserve scale and recover results through tau. Their decoding and degeneracy rules cannot be mixed.
assumptions_latex: Both embeddings represent the same primal-dual LP pair.
Each variant is equipped with its own terminal decoding rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalence of represented LP status does not imply identity of initialization, linear algebra, or recovery formulas across embedding variants.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a homogeneous self-dual embedding, the usual decoding alternatives require either \(\tau>0\) or \(\kappa>0\). A nonzero terminal point satisfying \(\tau=\kappa=0\) lies on a degenerate boundary: division by \(\tau\) is undefined, while positivity of \(\kappa\), used to normalize the standard alternative certificate, is absent. Such a point can contain recession or other degenerate directions of the embedded system, but the two vanishing scalars alone do not identify the status of the original LP. Therefore satisfaction of the embedded equations and vanishing complementarity do not by themselves justify declaring an optimal solution or infeasibility; a separately verified certificate or an additional recovery condition is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When both homogeneous scalars vanish, neither solution normalization nor the usual certificate normalization is valid, so the embedded terminal point alone does not determine LP status.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be a strictly complementary optimal solution, and define \(B=\{i:x_i^*>0\}\), \(N=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\), and \(\Delta=\min\{\min_{i\in B}x_i^*,\min_{i\in N}s_i^*\}>0\). For an approximation \((x,y,s)\), let \(E=\max\{\lVert x-x^*\rVert_\infty,\lVert s-s^*\rVert_\infty\}\), and suppose \(E<\Delta/2\). Choose any threshold \(t\) satisfying \(E<t<\Delta-E\), and output \(\widehat B=\{i:x_i>t\}\) and \(\widehat N=\{i:s_i>t\}\). Then \((\widehat B,\widehat N)=(B,N)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under strict complementarity, if the uniform primal-and-slack error is less than half the smallest positive component, thresholding at any value between the error and the remaining separation recovers the exact optimal partition.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Partition Recovery

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic optimal-face definition of the partition recovered from a strictly complementary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume finite primal and dual optima are attained. Let \(X^*\) be the primal optimal face and \(S^*\) the set of optimal dual slack vectors, and define \[B^*=\{i:\exists x\in X^*\text{ with }x_i>0\},\qquad N^*=\{i:\exists s\in S^*\text{ with }s_i>0\}.\] Complementarity between primal and dual optima gives \(B^*\cap N^*=\varnothing\). Strict complementarity gives \(B^*\cup N^*=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and every strictly complementary optimal pair satisfies \(B^*=\{i:x_i>0\}\) and \(N^*=\{i:s_i>0\}\). Thus this maximal optimal partition is independent of the selected strictly complementary pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximal optimal partition is intrinsic to the primal and dual optimal faces, and every strictly complementary optimum realizes it.
assumptions_latex: Finite primal and dual optima are attained.
The LP uses the standard primal-dual form of the seed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B^*\mathbin{\dot\cup}N^*=\{1,\ldots,n\},\qquad (B^*,N^*)\text{ is intrinsic to the optimal faces}.

notation.meaning: primal optimal face and set of optimal dual slack vectors

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a target rational vector \(z^*\in\mathbb Q^d\) has every reduced coordinate denominator at most \(D\), and an approximation \(\widehat z\) satisfies \(\lVert\widehat z-z^*\rVert_\infty<1/(2D^2)\). For each coordinate, use continued fractions to find the unique rational number with denominator at most \(D\) in the interval of radius \(1/(2D^2)\) about \(\widehat z_i\). Assemble these values as \(z^{\mathrm{rec}}\), then verify the original linear equalities, inequalities, and objective or complementary conditions exactly using rational arithmetic. Output \(z^{\mathrm{rec}}\) only if verification succeeds; otherwise report that the rounding certificate is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A denominator bound and coordinate error below 1/(2D^2) permit unique rational reconstruction, followed by exact feasibility and optimality verification.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat z\in\mathbb Q^d\) and \(D\geq1\) be explicitly encoded. Continued-fraction reconstruction of denominator-at-most-\(D\) candidates for all coordinates takes time polynomial in \(d\), \(\operatorname{size}(\widehat z)\), and \(\log D\). For rational LP data, exact feasibility, complementarity, and objective checks on the reconstructed vector also take polynomial bit time in the combined encoding length. Thus certified reconstruction and verification are polynomial-time, excluding the work needed to produce \(\widehat z\) or derive \(D\).

\(D\) is supplied in binary.

children.top_down_role: Use of recovered partition information to identify exact optimal output.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition-to-Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converts a certified complementary partition into an exact primal-dual optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a partition \(B\mathbin{\dot\cup}N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), solve exactly the reduced system
\[Ax=b,\qquad A^Ty+s=c,\qquad x_N=0,\qquad s_B=0.\]
Require the returned vectors to satisfy \(x_B\geq0\) and \(s_N\geq0\). If the system is consistent, output any such \((x,y,s)\); otherwise reject the proposed partition. For every accepted output, \(x^Ts=0\), and primal-dual feasibility implies \(c^Tx=b^Ty\). Hence the output is primal-dual optimal. If uniqueness is required, impose an additional rank condition or select a basic solution of the reduced system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set primal variables and dual slacks to zero on complementary partition blocks, solve the remaining equations exactly, and verify nonnegativity to obtain an optimal pair.
assumptions_latex: The LP is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) with dual slack equation \(A^Ty+s=c\).
The proposed sets \(B\) and \(N\) form a disjoint exhaustive partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted reduced-system solution is primal feasible, dual feasible, complementary, and therefore optimal.

notation.meaning: subvector of primal variables indexed by N
subvector of dual slacks indexed by B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct exact-feasibility implementation and bit complexity of recovery from a certified partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational \(A,b,c\) and a supplied partition \(B\mathbin{\dot\cup}N\), solve the rational feasibility problem \[Ax=b,\qquad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\qquad x_N=0,\qquad s_B=0,\qquad x_B\geq0,\qquad s_N\geq0.\] Linear consistency alone is insufficient when the reduced system is underdetermined: the algorithm must find a solution satisfying the displayed sign restrictions. An exact polynomial-time rational LP-feasibility algorithm either returns such a rational point of polynomial encoding length or certifies that none exists. Every returned point is complementary and primal-dual feasible, hence optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover a solution by solving the reduced equations together with nonnegativity, not by testing linear consistency alone; exact rational LP feasibility performs this task in polynomial bit time.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are explicitly encoded rationals.
The supplied sets form a disjoint exhaustive partition.
An exact polynomial-time rational LP-feasibility algorithm is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{decode}}=\operatorname{poly}(\operatorname{size}(A,b,c),m,n),\quad \text{and every accepted output is optimal}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: No uniform positive numerical tolerance identifies an exact optimal partition over all rational LPs of unbounded encoding length. For \(0<\delta<1\), consider \(\min 0\) subject to \(x_1=\delta\), \(x_1+x_2=1\), and \(x\geq0\). The unique feasible point has \(x_1=\delta>0\), but an approximation with absolute error at least \(\delta\) may report that component as zero and misclassify its partition index. Since \(\delta\) can be arbitrarily small, exact recovery requires precision below an instance-dependent positive-component separation, or an encoding-derived rational-reconstruction bound followed by exact verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small positive optimal components defeat every fixed threshold; exact recovery needs instance-dependent separation or encoding-based rational-reconstruction precision.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an LP with \(n\) complementary primal-slack pairs, suppose a primal-dual short-step path-following method starts at a strictly feasible point in a fixed central neighborhood and each Newton step remains in that neighborhood while satisfying \(\mu_{k+1}\leq(1-\gamma/\sqrt n)\mu_k\), where \(\gamma>0\) is independent of \(n\). Then the number of Newton iterations needed to reduce complementarity from \(\mu_0\) to at most \(\varepsilon\in(0,\mu_0)\) is
\[O\!\left(\sqrt n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right).\]
This counts iterations only; initialization, arithmetic precision, and the cost of solving each Newton system are separate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible short-step method needs O(sqrt(n) log(mu_0/epsilon)) Newton steps to reduce complementarity to epsilon, excluding initialization and per-step linear algebra.

Then, for \(0<\varepsilon<\mu_0\), it reaches \(\mu_k\leq\varepsilon\) in \[O\!\left(n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\] iterations. Initialization, finite-precision control, and Newton-system work are excluded.
