children.title: Newton-System Solution Work
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic cost of solving interior-point Newton systems.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whole-solve arithmetic and storage decomposition, leaving detailed sparse-factor formulas to the sibling leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a direct interior-point Newton solve at iteration \(k\), let \(W_{\mathrm{form},k}\), \(W_{\mathrm{fact},k}\), \(W_{\mathrm{tri},k}\), and \(W_{\mathrm{rec},k}\) denote system formation, numerical factorization, one triangular solution, and eliminated-variable recovery work. If \(q_k\) right-hand sides use the same numerical factors, then \[W_{\mathrm{solve},k}=W_{\mathrm{form},k}+W_{\mathrm{fact},k}+q_kW_{\mathrm{tri},k}+W_{\mathrm{rec},k}.\] A fixed structural pattern permits reuse of ordering and symbolic analysis, but changing interior-point diagonal scalings generally changes numerical factor entries and requires numerical refactorization. Storage includes the system representation, filled factors, right-hand sides, and work arrays.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One direct Newton solve pays formation, numerical factorization, backsolves, and recovery; fixed sparsity can reuse symbolic analysis but generally not the changing numerical factors.
assumptions_latex: A direct factorization method is used for the chosen augmented or reduced Newton system.
The declared arithmetic model separately charges system formation, numerical factorization, triangular solves, and recovery.
Symbolic reuse is asserted only while the structural sparsity pattern and ordering remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{solve},k}=W_{\mathrm{form},k}+W_{\mathrm{fact},k}+q_kW_{\mathrm{tri},k}+W_{\mathrm{rec},k}.

notation.meaning: number of right-hand sides solved with the iteration-k factors
total arithmetic work for the Newton-system solve stage

knowledge_statements.title: Direct Newton-System Solve Accounting
Newton-System Solution Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic work of a sparse direct solve after forming an interior-point normal equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let an interior-point Newton direction be obtained from a symmetric positive-definite normal equation \(H\Delta y=r\), and let a fixed ordering produce a Cholesky factor \(H=LL^T\). Ignoring numerical pivoting and coefficient bit complexity, numeric factorization requires
\[O\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m \operatorname{nnz}(L_{:,j})^2\right)\]
arithmetic operations, while the two triangular solves require \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\) operations and factor storage requires \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\). Symbolic analysis may be reused while the sparsity pattern remains fixed, but numerical factorization is repeated as the interior-point scaling changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For sparse Cholesky, factorization work depends on squared factor-column counts; triangular solves and storage are linear in the factor's nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: The reduced Newton matrix \(H\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is symmetric positive definite.
A sparse Cholesky ordering is fixed and no dynamic pivoting changes the pattern.
The bound counts real-arithmetic operations, not finite-precision bit operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Per Newton step, direct-solve work is governed by fill in \(L\), not solely by \(\operatorname{nnz}(H)\).

notation.meaning: sparse Cholesky factor of the Newton matrix
number of stored nonzero entries of a matrix M

children.title: Sparse Factorization Work
children.top_down_role: Computational cost when Newton systems admit sparse factorizations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural arithmetic and storage model for a fixed sparse Cholesky ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be structurally symmetric positive definite and let \(PHP^{\mathsf T}=LL^{\mathsf T}\) be its Cholesky factorization under a fixed ordering. If \(\ell_j\) is the number of structural nonzeros in column \(j\) of \(L\), including the diagonal, then conventional sparse Cholesky numerical factorization requires \(\Theta(\sum_{j=1}^m\ell_j^2)\) arithmetic operations up to the chosen flop convention and stores \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\) numerical entries. One forward-and-backward substitution pair costs \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\). Thus the filled factor pattern, rather than \(\operatorname{nnz}(H)\) alone, controls sparse direct-solve work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse Cholesky factorization work is governed by squared filled-column counts, while factor storage and a triangular-solve pair are linear in factor nonzeros.
assumptions_latex: H is structurally symmetric positive definite.
P is a fixed symmetric permutation.
Structural cancellations and dynamic pivoting are excluded.
Costs are real-arithmetic and structural-storage costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{fact}}=\Theta\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^m\ell_j^2\right),\qquad M_{\mathrm{fact}}=\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L)),\qquad W_{\mathrm{tri}}=\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L)).

notation.meaning: structural nonzero count in column j of L

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symbolic sparse Cholesky work for a fixed elimination ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be the symmetric positive-definite matrix of a primal-dual Newton system after any reductions, and let \(PHP^{\mathsf T}=LL^{\mathsf T}\). If \(\ell_j\) counts the structural nonzeros in column \(j\) of \(L\), including its diagonal, then a conventional column-oriented numerical factorization uses \(\Theta(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\ell_j^2)\) arithmetic operations and \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\) storage. Once \(L\) is available, solving one right-hand side by forward and backward substitution costs \(\Theta(\operatorname{nnz}(L))\). Thus input sparsity alone does not determine Newton-step work; the filled factor pattern does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse Newton work is governed by the nonzeros created in the Cholesky factor, not merely by nonzeros in the original Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Factorization Work

children.title: Sparsity Preservation
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing whether matrix sparsity survives interior-point linear algebra.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph-theoretic condition for preservation of structural sparsity in Cholesky elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G(H)\) be the undirected structural sparsity graph of a structurally symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\), and let \(P\) specify an elimination ordering. Cholesky elimination introduces no new off-diagonal structural nonzeros if and only if, for every eliminated vertex, its neighbors occurring later in the ordering form a clique. Equivalently, \(P\) is a perfect elimination ordering of \(G(H)\). Such an ordering exists if and only if \(G(H)\) is chordal; consequently every ordering of a nonchordal graph creates some symbolic fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cholesky preserves the original structural sparsity exactly for perfect elimination orderings, and such an ordering exists exactly for chordal sparsity graphs.
assumptions_latex: H is structurally symmetric positive definite.
P is a fixed symmetric elimination ordering.
Fill is interpreted symbolically, without numerical cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{no symbolic fill under }P\iff P\text{ is a perfect elimination ordering of }G(H),\qquad \exists P\iff G(H)\text{ is chordal}.

notation.meaning: undirected structural sparsity graph of H

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Elimination No-Fill Criterion

assumptions_latex: \(H\) is structurally symmetric positive definite with sparsity graph \(G(H)\).
\(P\) specifies the elimination order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No symbolic fill occurs if and only if \(P\) is a perfect elimination ordering of \(G(H)\).

notation.meaning: Undirected structural sparsity graph of H

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact symbolic no-fill criterion for sparse Cholesky elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\) of \(G(H)\), let its later neighbors be the neighbors eliminated after \(v\) under \(P\). The Cholesky factorization \(PHP^{\mathsf T}=LL^{\mathsf T}\) preserves the original structural sparsity, meaning that elimination introduces no new off-diagonal structural nonzeros, if and only if the later neighbors of every \(v\) form a clique. Equivalently, \(P\) must be a perfect elimination ordering of \(G(H)\). Such an ordering exists exactly when \(G(H)\) is chordal; otherwise every ordering produces some symbolic fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cholesky introduces no symbolic fill exactly when the chosen ordering is a perfect elimination ordering of the sparsity graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity Preservation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The no-fill/perfect-elimination-ordering characterization is standard and the condition kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no source for the exact equivalence and chordality assertion.

children.title: Fill-In Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Loss of sparsity benefits through factorization fill-in.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adverse Star Elimination Produces Dense Fill
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit sparse positive-definite family showing that an adverse ordering can destroy sparse-factorization complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_{\mathrm{star},d}\) be the adjacency matrix of a star with one center and \(d-1\) leaves, and set \(H_d=I+\alpha A_{\mathrm{star},d}\), where \(0<\alpha<1/\sqrt{d-1}\). Then \(H_d\succ0\) and \(\operatorname{nnz}(H_d)=3d-2\). If the center is eliminated first, the Schur complement on the leaves has every off-diagonal entry equal to \(-\alpha^2\), so its structural graph is complete. Conventional Cholesky factorization under this ordering therefore has \(\Theta(d^2)\) factor entries and \(\Theta(d^3)\) arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearly sparse positive-definite star matrix becomes dense after eliminating its center first, causing quadratic factor storage and cubic conventional factorization work.
assumptions_latex: d\geq3.
0<\alpha<1/\sqrt{d-1}.
The star center is eliminated before its leaves.
Structural nonzeros are counted without cancellation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{nnz}(H_d)=\Theta(d),\qquad \operatorname{nnz}(L_d)=\Theta(d^2),\qquad W_{\mathrm{fact}}=\Theta(d^3).

notation.meaning: adjacency matrix of the d-vertex star

knowledge_statements.title: Adverse Star Elimination Produces Dense Fill

assumptions_latex: \(d\ge 3\) and \(0<\alpha<1/\sqrt{d-1}\).
The center of the star is eliminated first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(\operatorname{nnz}(H_d)=\Theta(d)\), the factor has \(\operatorname{nnz}(L_d)=\Theta(d^2)\) and factorization work \(\Theta(d^3)\).

notation.meaning: Adjacency matrix of the star on d vertices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sparse matrix can produce a dense factor under an adverse ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_d=I+\alpha A_{\mathrm{star},d}\), where the star has one center and \(d-1\) leaves. The bound \(0<\alpha<1/\sqrt{d-1}\) makes \(H_d\) positive definite, while \(\operatorname{nnz}(H_d)=3d-2\). If Cholesky elimination removes the center first, its Schur complement on the leaves has a nonzero entry between every distinct pair of leaves. The remaining symbolic graph is therefore complete, giving \(\operatorname{nnz}(L_d)=\Theta(d^2)\) and conventional factorization work \(\Theta(d^3)\). Hence linear input sparsity does not ensure nearly linear factorization work without an ordering or graph-structure hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the center of a sparse star first creates a dense Schur complement, causing quadratic storage and cubic factorization work.
knowledge_statements.title: Fill-In Complexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a rational LP of dimensions \(m,n\), binary encoding length \(L\), and target accuracy \(\varepsilon\). Suppose an interior-point method performs at most \(N=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations, and suppose each rounded Newton solve using \(p=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\) bits preserves the method's neighborhood, residual, and progress inequalities. If each iteration uses polynomially many arithmetic operations on \(p\)-bit numbers, then the complete implementation has bit complexity \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L,\log(1/\varepsilon))\). Iteration bounds alone do not establish this conclusion without precision and rounding control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial iteration complexity yields polynomial bit complexity only when polynomial working precision suffices to preserve feasibility, neighborhood membership, and progress.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial and strongly polynomial complexity for integer-data LP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the chapter's complexity definitions and applies them to the interior-point methods under consideration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer-data problem of dimension \(n\) and input length \(L>n\), an algorithm is polynomial when its running time is polynomial in \(L\). Thus, for every \(\omega\ge 0\), the stated interior-point bound \(O(n^{\omega}L)\) is polynomial in \(L\). An algorithm is strongly polynomial if it is polynomial and its total number of arithmetic operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\) alone. Consequently, the interior-point methods under consideration are not strongly polynomial when their arithmetic-operation bounds depend on \(L\), which can be arbitrarily larger than \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer data, polynomial time is measured in the encoded input length L. Since L exceeds the dimension n, an interior-point bound of order n^omega L is polynomial in L for every nonnegative omega. Strong polynomiality additionally requires an arithmetic-operation bound polynomial in n alone, so the interior-point methods considered here are not strongly polynomial when their bounds depend on the potentially much larger input length L.
assumptions_latex: \text{The problem data are integer-encoded.}
L>n
\omega\ge 0
\text{The interior-point bound is }O(n^{\omega}L).
\text{The arithmetic-operation bound depends on }L\text{ rather than being bounded polynomially in }n\text{ alone.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: O(n^{\omega}L)\text{ is polynomial in }L,\qquad \text{but the stated }L\text{-dependence prevents strong polynomiality.}

children.title: Ellipsoid Method Exemplar
children.top_down_role: The ellipsoid route as an encoding-dependent polynomial LP algorithm.

knowledge_statements.title: Ellipsoid Method Exemplar
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-cut ellipsoid feasibility method, its geometric oracle bound, and the additional conditions needed for weak polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\ge 2\) and represent the current ellipsoid by \(E_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:(x-a_k)^{\mathsf T}B_k^{-1}(x-a_k)\le 1\}\), where \(B_k\) is symmetric positive definite. If \(a_k\) is infeasible and a separation oracle returns a nonzero \(g_k\) satisfying \(g_k^{\mathsf T}(x-a_k)\le 0\) for every feasible \(x\), define \(q_k=B_kg_k/\sqrt{g_k^{\mathsf T}B_kg_k}\), \(a_{k+1}=a_k-q_k/(n+1)\), and \(B_{k+1}=\frac{n^2}{n^2-1}\left(B_k-\frac{2}{n+1}q_kq_k^{\mathsf T}\right)\). If the feasible region is contained initially in a radius-\(R\) ball and every nonempty feasible region under consideration contains a radius-\(r\) ball, the method finds a feasible center or establishes emptiness after \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) oracle calls. For rational LP, this gives a weakly polynomial algorithm when \(\log(R/r)\), oracle outputs, ellipsoid encodings, and per-iteration bit work are polynomially bounded by the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The central-cut ellipsoid method has a geometric oracle bound of order n squared times log(R/r); obtaining a weakly polynomial LP algorithm additionally requires polynomial encoding and bit-work bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge 2\), \(0<r\le R\), and \(B_0\) is symmetric positive definite.
The feasible region is contained in the initial radius-\(R\) ellipsoid, and every nonempty feasible region under consideration contains a Euclidean ball of radius \(r\).
The oracle returns a nonzero valid central-cut normal whenever the current center is infeasible.
For the rational-LP complexity conclusion, all maintained encodings and per-iteration bit operations are polynomially bounded in the input length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method uses \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) oracle calls; with the stated encoding conditions, its rational-LP implementation is weakly polynomial.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Method Exemplars
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly feasible short-step primal-dual path-following exemplar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank. Let \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) be the all-ones vector, \(X=\operatorname{diag}(x)\), \(S=\operatorname{diag}(s)\), and \(\mu=x^{\mathsf T}s/n\). Starting from a strictly feasible point in a fixed standard short-step neighborhood, choose \(\sigma_k=1-\Theta(1/\sqrt n)\) and solve \(A\Delta x=0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}\Delta y+\Delta s=0\), and \(S_k\Delta x+X_k\Delta s=\sigma_k\mu_ke-X_kS_ke\). Take the prescribed neighborhood-preserving short step and stop when \(x_k^{\mathsf T}s_k\le\varepsilon\). For \(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\), a standard short-step realization requires \(O(\sqrt n\log((x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0)/\varepsilon))\) Newton steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly feasible short-step primal-dual method solves the linearized complementarity equations while remaining in a fixed central-path neighborhood and reaches the requested duality gap in order square-root n times a logarithmic gap ratio Newton steps.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, and the primal-dual pair has a strictly feasible point.
The initial point \((x_0,y_0,s_0)\) lies in a fixed standard short-step central-path neighborhood.
\(0<\varepsilon<x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Polynomial Exemplar Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of polynomial iteration measures, without asserting a universal runtime ordering or deriving bit complexity from iteration counts alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under their respective standard hypotheses, the central-cut ellipsoid method uses \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) separation-oracle iterations, whereas a short-step primal-dual path-following method uses \(O(\sqrt n\log(
u_0/\varepsilon))\) Newton iterations, where \(
u_0=x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\) and \(0<\varepsilon<
u_0\). These bounds count different resources: an ellipsoid iteration invokes separation and updates a shape matrix, while an interior-point iteration solves a structured Newton system. Therefore the displayed iteration bounds do not establish a uniform runtime ordering. Weak polynomiality follows only after the relevant radii, encodings, oracle work, linear-algebra work, and finite-precision requirements are also shown to have polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid and short-step interior-point methods have polynomial iteration bounds measured in different units; neither universal runtime dominance nor weak bit complexity follows without per-iteration encoding and precision analysis.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\), \(0<r\le R\), and the ellipsoid instance satisfies the stated outer- and inner-radius hypotheses.
The short-step interior-point instance starts in a standard central-path neighborhood with \(\nu_0=x_0^{\mathsf T}s_0\) and \(0<\varepsilon<\nu_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exemplar bounds are \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) oracle iterations and \(O(\sqrt n\log(\nu_0/\varepsilon))\) Newton iterations, but these different counts alone imply neither runtime dominance nor polynomial bit complexity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Weak polynomiality permits an operation or bit bound \(T=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,L)\), where \(L\) measures coefficient encoding length. knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Lower-Bound Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a rule-specific exponential simplex lower-bound family and the canonical Dantzig-rule instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed deterministic simplex pivot rule \(R\), call a sequence of LP instances \((I_d)\) an exponential lower-bound family for \(R\) if each \(I_d\) has \(O(d)\) variables and inequalities, a designated initial basis and tie-breaking convention, and \(N_R(I_d)\ge 2^{cd}\) for some constant \(c>0\) and infinitely many \(d\). The Klee–Minty distorted-cube construction is the canonical such family for Dantzig's largest-reduced-cost rule and, under its standard starting-basis and nondegeneracy convention, has \(N_R(I_d)=2^d-1\). Thus linear formulation size does not guarantee a polynomial pivot count for that specified rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exponential lower-bound family is defined relative to a particular pivot rule and its conventions; Klee–Minty cubes give the canonical exponential family for Dantzig's rule.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a specified deterministic simplex pivot rule.
Each instance \(I_d\) includes a designated initial basis, tie-breaking rule, and perturbation convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a primal-feasible basis \(B\), choose an entering nonbasic index \(j\) having improving reduced cost and set \(u=B^{-1}a_j\). If \(u_i\leq0\) for every row \(i\), report that the objective is unbounded along the corresponding improving direction. Otherwise, for every row \(i\) with \(u_i>0\), form \(q_i=u_i^{-1}((B^{-1}b)_i,(B^{-1})_{i1},\ldots,(B^{-1})_{im})\), select a row whose \(q_i\) is lexicographically smallest, and pivot on \((i,j)\). If the initial tableau rows are lexicographically positive, every resulting tableau retains lexicographic feasibility, so no feasible basis repeats. Thus the process terminates finitely at an optimal basis or by detecting unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lexicographic ratio test compares entire normalized tableau rows, consistently resolves degeneracy, prevents repetition of a feasible basis, and separately detects an unbounded improving direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Bland's Pivot Rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smallest-index deterministic anticycling rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a total ordering of all variables in \(\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\). At a feasible basis, choose as entering variable the smallest-index nonbasic variable \(j\) with \(\bar c_j>0\). Among rows attaining the minimum feasible ratio \((B^{-1}b)_i/(B^{-1}a_j)_i\) with \((B^{-1}a_j)_i>0\), choose the row whose current basic variable has smallest index. If there is no improving reduced cost, stop with the current optimal basis. Bland's rule never repeats a basis and hence terminates whenever an optimum exists and the feasible pivot sequence is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bland's rule selects the smallest-index eligible entering and leaving variables; this deterministic convention prevents simplex cycling.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), let \(B_0\) be an initial primal-feasible basis, and suppose the objective is bounded above on the feasible region. Replace \(b\) symbolically by \(b(\varepsilon)=b+B_0(\varepsilon,\varepsilon^2,\ldots,\varepsilon^m)^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\varepsilon>0\) is treated as smaller than every positive real constant. Run primal simplex with improving reduced-cost selection and ratio tests performed on lexicographically ordered coefficient vectors in \(\varepsilon\). The generic symbolic ordering makes the perturbed basic solutions nondegenerate, so each pivot strictly improves the perturbed objective and no basis repeats. The sequence therefore terminates finitely; after infinitesimal terms are discarded, its terminal basis is optimal for the original problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symbolic infinitesimal right-hand-side perturbation removes ratio ties and prevents cycling; for a bounded feasible objective, the finite perturbed sequence yields an optimal basis for the original problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Anticycling Complexity Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite termination does not imply polynomial pivot complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a standard-form linear program with \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) of rank \(m\). Any anticycling simplex rule that never repeats a basis performs at most \(\binom{n}{m}-1\) pivots before termination, because every basis is an \(m\)-element subset of the \(n\) variable indices. This is only a combinatorial finite bound: \(\binom{n}{m}\) is exponential when \(m\) grows proportionally with \(n\). Therefore, a proof that a rule avoids cycling supplies termination but does not by itself supply polynomial or strongly polynomial pivot complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Anticycling bounds pivots by the number of bases, which can be exponential; finite termination alone is not a polynomial complexity guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) has rank \(m\).
The pivot rule never revisits a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generic bound is \(T\leq\binom{n}{m}-1\), which is not polynomial in variable dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\) be the complete algorithmic state space and let \(\mathcal P(s)\) be the finite set of admissible pivots at state \(s\). At every nonterminal state, a randomized pivot rule assigns a probability distribution \(q_s\) supported on \(\mathcal P(s)\), samples \(p\sim q_s\), and updates the state according to its declared pivot and history-update convention. Terminal states and their reported statuses are specified separately. The process is Markovian on \(\mathcal S\), although its projection onto the current basis or vertex need not be Markovian.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational linear programs with \(m\) constraints, \(n\) variables, and binary encoding length \(L\), a bit-polynomial simplex method must reach an appropriate terminal outcome using at most \(p(m,n,L)\) pivots and polynomially many bit operations for some fixed polynomial \(p\). A strongly polynomial simplex method must use a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in \(m+n\), independently of \(L\), while the sizes of all intermediate rational numbers remain polynomially bounded in the input encoding length. Polynomial-time solvability of linear programming by a method allowed to leave the polytope's edge graph does not imply the existence of either type of polynomial simplex pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polynomial-time linear-programming algorithm need not yield a polynomial simplex rule. Strong polynomiality additionally requires an operation bound independent of coefficient encoding length and controlled intermediate number sizes.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The \(d\)-dimensional cube has \(2d\) facets and graph diameter \(d\). Consequently, if \(\Delta(d,m)\) is the maximum diameter of a \(d\)-polytope with at most \(m\) facets, then \(\Delta(d,2d)\ge d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The d-cube has diameter d and 2d facets, giving a linear lower-bound family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(d,2d)\ge d.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge d\ge2\), Todd's refinement gives \(\Delta(d,m)\le (m-d)^{\log_2 d}\), with the zero-excess simplex case interpreted separately. This remains quasipolynomial when both parameters vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Todd refined the general bound to a quasipolynomial expression in the facet excess m-d.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kalai and Kleitman bounded polyhedral diameter quasipolynomially in the dimension and number of facets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-in-facet-count bound when dimension is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(d\ge3\), the maximum graph diameter \(\Delta(d,m)\) of a \(d\)-dimensional polytope with at most \(m\) facets satisfies \(\Delta(d,m)\le 2^{d-3}m\). Thus diameter is linear in \(m\) for every fixed dimension, although the coefficient is exponential in \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Larman's bound is linear in the number of facets for fixed dimension, with an exponential dimension-dependent coefficient.

knowledge_statements.title: Larman Fixed-Dimension Diameter Bound
Polyhedral Diameter Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary vertex-count bound for bounded polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:Ax\leq b\}\) be a nonempty bounded full-dimensional polytope described by \(m\) inequalities, and let \(G(P)\) be its vertex-edge graph. Every vertex is uniquely determined by some linearly independent set of \(d\) active inequalities, so \(|V(P)|\leq\binom{m}{d}\). Since \(G(P)\) is connected, its graph diameter satisfies \[\operatorname{diam}G(P)\leq |V(P)|-1\leq\binom{m}{d}-1.\] This universal bound is finite but generally exponential when \(d\) varies with \(m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded d-polytope with m facets has at most binomial(m,d) vertices, giving the same elementary upper scale for graph diameter.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded, nonempty, and full-dimensional.
The inequality description contains \(m\) rows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}G(P)\leq\binom{m}{d}-1\).
review_flags: polyhedral graph and vertex-count source needed

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role and elementary vertex-count/diameter inequalities fit the container, but no inspectable source is supplied for the polyhedral graph facts and counting bound.

children.title: Monotone Path Bounds
children.top_down_role: Objective-monotone path lengths relevant to simplex trajectories.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acyclic orientation and reachability of an objective-maximizing vertex under a generic linear objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope and let \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) take distinct values on adjacent vertices. Orient each edge toward increasing objective value. This orientation is acyclic. Every nonmaximizing vertex has an outgoing edge, and every vertex therefore lies on a directed path ending at an objective-maximizing vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generic linear objective acyclically orients the graph, and every vertex can reach an objective maximizer along improving edges.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty bounded polytope.
\(c^{\mathsf T}u\ne c^{\mathsf T}v\) for every edge \(uv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v\in V(P)\;\exists\text{ a strictly }c\text{-monotone edge path from }v\text{ to an objective maximizer}.
knowledge_statements.title: Existence of Objective-Monotone Paths
Monotone Path Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counting bound for strictly objective-monotone edge paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be a bounded polytope with vertex set \(V(P)\), and let \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) take distinct values on adjacent vertices. Orient every edge \(uv\) from \(u\) to \(v\) when \(c^{\mathsf T}v>c^{\mathsf T}u\). Any directed path is strictly objective-monotone and cannot repeat a vertex; hence its length is at most \(|V(P)|-1\). If \(P\) has an irredundant description with \(m\) facets and is full-dimensional, then every such path has at most \(\binom{m}{d}-1\) edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly objective-increasing edge path cannot revisit a vertex, so its length is bounded by the number of vertices minus one.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded and full-dimensional.
The objective is nonconstant on every edge.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(c\)-monotone edge path has length at most \(|V(P)|-1\leq\binom{m}{d}-1\).

notation.meaning: linear objective defining the edge orientation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role is correct, and the strict objective orientation yields the stated vertex-count bound. An authoritative locator for monotone paths and the supporting polyhedral count is still required.

children.title: Diameter-to-Pivot Complexity Gap
children.top_down_role: Why short graph paths need not yield efficiently selectable pivot paths.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bounded Undirected Diameter with Long Monotone Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separating family showing that undirected graph diameter alone does not control shortest objective-monotone distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrarily large \(n\), take a pyramid over a convex \(n\)-gon and choose a linear objective for which the apex lies below every base vertex and the two boundary chains from a base minimum \(u\) to a base maximum \(v\) each contain \(\Omega(n)\) edges. The pyramid graph has undirected diameter at most \(2\), because every two base vertices share the apex as a neighbor. Nevertheless, no directed path from \(u\) can use the lower-valued apex, so every objective-increasing path from \(u\) to \(v\) follows a base boundary chain and has length \(\Omega(n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pyramids can have graph diameter two while selected base vertices are separated by linearly many objective-increasing edges.
assumptions_latex: The base is a convex polygon with both objective-monotone boundary chains of length \(\Omega(n)\).
The apex has objective value below every base vertex.
Adjacent vertices have distinct objective values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{diam}G(P_n)\le 2\quad\text{while}\quad d_c^+(u_n,v_n)=\Omega(n).

notation.meaning: shortest distance in the objective-oriented graph

review_flags: explicit separating family added because the deferred seed's implication boundary requires more than the elementary distance inequality
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Undirected Diameter with Long Monotone Distance
Diameter-to-Pivot Complexity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected shortest paths do not control monotone rule paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a bounded polytope, let \(v^*\) maximize a generic linear objective \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), and let \(D=\operatorname{diam}G(P)\). For every vertex \(v\), an undirected path from \(v\) to \(v^*\) has length at most \(D\), but its edges need not all increase the objective. A simplex rule must follow an oriented, objective-nondecreasing path and may choose a path longer than the shortest oriented path. Therefore an upper bound on \(D\) alone gives neither an upper bound on monotone diameter nor a pivot bound for a specified simplex rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small undirected diameter guarantees short unrestricted paths, not short objective-monotone paths or short paths selected by a particular pivot rule.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is bounded.
The objective has a unique maximizing vertex \(v^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A diameter bound for \(G(P)\) does not by itself imply a simplex pivot-complexity bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role exactly matches the diameter-to-pivot gap. The distinction among undirected shortest paths, oriented monotone paths, and paths selected by a specified rule is mathematically coherent, but the record has no dedicated source.

children.title: Monotonicity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Restrictions imposed when admissible paths must remain objective-monotone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why vertex-count termination follows from strict improvement but not merely from nondecrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite polyhedral graph, a path satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}v_{k+1}>c^{\mathsf T}v_k\) cannot revisit a vertex and has at most \(|V(P)|-1\) edges. If only \(c^{\mathsf T}v_{k+1}\ge c^{\mathsf T}v_k\) is required, zero-improvement edges permit repeated vertices; weak monotonicity alone therefore proves neither termination nor the vertex-count bound without a nonrepetition or anti-cycling condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict improvement prevents repeated vertices; nondecrease alone permits zero-improvement cycling and requires an additional safeguard.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has finitely many vertices.
Successive vertices are adjacent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Strict monotonicity implies nonrepetition, whereas weak monotonicity alone does not.}
knowledge_statements.title: Strict-versus-Weak Monotonicity Boundary
Monotonicity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates undirected polyhedral diameter from objective-monotone simplex paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a polytope whose graph is \(G(P)\), and orient every edge from lower to higher value of a linear objective \(c^\top x\), assuming adjacent vertices have distinct values. For vertices \(u,v\) with a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be their undirected graph distance and \(d_c^+(u,v)\) the shortest directed distance. Then \(d_G(u,v)\le d_c^+(u,v)\). Consequently, an upper bound on the undirected diameter alone does not upper-bound the length of an objective-monotone pivot path or the path selected by a pivot rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Undirected diameter can be smaller than every objective-monotone route, so diameter bounds alone do not control simplex pivot complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope with a finite vertex-edge graph.
\(c^\top x\) takes distinct values at adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_G(u,v)\le d_c^+(u,v)\), and an undirected diameter bound alone gives no corresponding pivot-rule bound.

children.title: Empirical Simplex Performance

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Simplex Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines observed pivot-count and runtime summaries for a fixed implementation and test sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a simplex implementation \(R\), including its pivot rule, initialization, degeneracy handling, and stopping convention. For a finite test sample \(S=(I_1,\ldots,I_N)\), let \(T_R(I_i)\) denote a specified resource count, such as pivots or arithmetic time. The empirical mean performance is \[\widehat\mu_{R,S}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_R(I_i).\] An empirical performance report must identify \(R\), the resource counted, the sample construction, and any treatment of failures or censored runs; otherwise \(\widehat\mu_{R,S}\) does not define a reproducible statistic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical performance is the sample mean of a declared resource count for a fully specified simplex implementation and benchmark sample.
assumptions_latex: Each \(T_R(I_i)\) is recorded under the same resource and stopping conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\mu_{R,S}=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}T_R(I_i)\).

children.title: Average-Case Simplex Performance
children.top_down_role: Expected simplex behavior under specified input distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Average-Case Simplex Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines distribution-dependent expected simplex resource usage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a probability distribution \(\mathcal D\) on encoded linear-programming instances and a simplex implementation \(R\). If \(T_R(I)\) is a nonnegative measurable resource count, its average-case performance under \(\mathcal D\) is \[\mu_R(\mathcal D)=\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[T_R(I)].\] The value may be infinite. Thus average-case complexity is not intrinsic to the simplex method alone: it depends on the instance distribution, encoding, implementation, resource measure, and conventions for infeasible, unbounded, degenerate, or nonterminating inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average-case simplex performance is expected resource usage under an explicitly specified distribution and implementation; it may be infinite.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal D\) is a probability distribution on encoded LP instances.
\(T_R\) is nonnegative and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_R(\mathcal D)=\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[T_R(I)]\in[0,\infty]\).

The implementation \(R\) has polynomial average-case complexity for this ensemble if constants \(C,k,n_0\) satisfy \(A_R(n)\le Cn^k\) for all \(n\ge n_0\).

\(T_R\) is nonnegative and measurable.

children.title: Empirical-to-Average-Case Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relationship between measured workloads and distribution-based complexity conclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical-to-Average-Case Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives an elementary sampling guarantee connecting benchmark averages to a distributional mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\) be independent samples from \(\mathcal D\), and put \(X_i=T_R(I_i)\). If \(\mu=\mathbb E[X_i]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_i)=v<\infty\), then the empirical mean \(\widehat\mu=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_i\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[\widehat\mu]=\mu,\qquad \Pr\!\left(|\widehat\mu-\mu|\ge\varepsilon\right)\le\frac{v}{N\varepsilon^2}\quad(\varepsilon>0).\] Hence empirical and average-case performance are quantitatively comparable only relative to a sampling model and a tail or moment condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent representative runs with finite variance, the sample mean is unbiased and obeys a Chebyshev error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal D\).
\(X_i=T_R(I_i)\) has finite mean and variance \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu]=\mu\) and \(\Pr(|\widehat\mu-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le v/(N\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: resource count on sampled instance i

children.title: Distributional Representativeness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on using a chosen probability model to explain observed LP workloads.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Representativeness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why a favorable finite benchmark need not estimate performance under a target distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_R(I_0)=0\) and \(T_R(I_1)=H\) for two instances, where \(H>0\), and let the target distribution assign probabilities \(1-\eta\) and \(\eta\) to them, with \(0<\eta<1\). Then \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[T_R]=\eta H\), but an independent sample of size \(N\) contains only \(I_0\), and therefore has empirical mean zero, with probability \((1-\eta)^N>0\). Without representative sampling or distributional assumptions, small empirical pivot counts do not certify small target average-case complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark can miss rare hard instances and report zero cost even when the target distribution has arbitrarily large mean cost.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark instances are sampled independently from \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[T_R]=\eta H\), while \(\Pr(\widehat\mu=0)=(1-\eta)^N\).

notation.meaning: resource cost of the hard instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies transfer from a proxy distribution and its failure for uncontrolled costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be instance distributions and suppose \(0\le T_R(I)\le M\) almost surely under both. With \(\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\), \[|\mathbb E_P T_R-\mathbb E_Q T_R|\le M\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}.\] Without a uniform bound or other tail control, total-variation distance alone gives no finite bound on the mean difference: for every \(\delta>0\) and \(B>0\), some \(P,Q,T_R\ge0\) satisfy \(\|P-Q\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\delta\) and \(|\mathbb E_PT_R-\mathbb E_QT_R|\ge B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded costs transfer between nearby distributions, but total-variation closeness alone cannot control an unbounded runtime mean.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shadow Path as a Two-Objective Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation underlying shadow-vertex pivot counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a polytope and let \(u,c\in\mathbb R^n\) be linearly independent objectives. Define \(\pi(x)=(u^\top x,c^\top x)\). Under a general-position convention giving unique lifted adjacency, the shadow-vertex path from a vertex selected by \(u\) toward one selected by \(c\) follows the corresponding monotone boundary chain of the polygon \(\pi(P)\); its pivot count equals the number of traversed chain edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shadow-vertex simplex follows a monotone boundary chain in the two-dimensional projection defined by an auxiliary and target objective.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polytope.
\(u\) and \(c\) are linearly independent.
General position or an equivalent tie convention makes the lifted path unambiguous.

Shadow-Vertex Smoothed Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative polynomial smoothed bound under normalized independent Gaussian perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider normalized LP data \(I=(A,b,c)\) and perturb every scalar coefficient independently by a centered Gaussian of standard deviation \(\sigma>0\), followed almost surely by a nondegenerate shadow-vertex run with a prescribed auxiliary objective. If \(T_{\mathrm{sh}}(I+G_\sigma)\) counts traversed shadow edges, the Gaussian smoothed complexity is \[S_{m,n}(\sigma)=\sup_{\lVert I\rVert_F\le1}\mathbb E[T_{\mathrm{sh}}(I+G_\sigma)].\] The shadow-vertex smoothed-analysis theorem asserts that, for its specified normalization and initialization model, \(S_{m,n}(\sigma)\le p(m,n,1/\sigma)\) for a polynomial \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a specified normalized Gaussian perturbation model, the expected shadow-vertex pivot count is polynomial in dimensions and inverse noise scale.
assumptions_latex: \(\lVert(A,b,c)\rVert_F\le1\) and \(\sigma>0\).
Perturbed coefficients are independent Gaussians under the theorem's normalization.
The auxiliary objective and initialization follow the shadow-vertex model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{m,n}(\sigma)\le p(m,n,1/\sigma)\) for some polynomial \(p\).

notation.meaning: independent Gaussian perturbation of the LP data

children.title: Perturbation Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes unconditional perturbations from perturbations conditioned to preserve an LP property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K(z,\cdot)\) be a perturbation kernel and let \(E\) be measurable with \(K(z,E)>0\). The conditioned law is \[K_E(z,A)=\frac{K(z,A\cap E)}{K(z,E)}.\] Unless \(K(z,E)=1\), this is generally a different law; independence, centering, and original marginal distributions need not be preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioning perturbations to preserve feasibility, boundedness, rank, or encoding restrictions generally creates a different probability model.
assumptions_latex: \(K(z,\cdot)\) is a probability law.
\(E\) is measurable and \(K(z,E)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_E(z,A)=K(z,A\cap E)/K(z,E),\quad K_E\ne K\text{ in general.}

notation.meaning: required property of the perturbed instance

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Changes the Perturbation Law

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Perturbation Kernels and Common Noise Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents LP perturbations without treating the listed forms as an exhaustive taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbation regime is a probability kernel \(K_\sigma(z,\cdot)\) on encoded LP instances, together with a declared data representation and scale convention. Common forms include additive noise \(\widetilde z=z+\sigma Z\), bounded-support additive noise \(\widetilde z=z+U\) with \(\|U\|\le\sigma\) almost surely, and componentwise multiplicative noise \(\widetilde z_j=z_j(1+\sigma Z_j)\). The law, coordinates, perturbed components, norm or component scaling, and any conditioning must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP perturbation model is a fully specified probability kernel; additive, bounded-support, and componentwise multiplicative noise are common nonexhaustive forms.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is a declared finite-dimensional encoding of the LP data being perturbed.
\(\sigma\ge0\).
Each displayed construction induces a probability law on the stated input space.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Kernels and Common Noise Forms
Perturbation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes additive, bounded-support, and relative perturbation models for LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Encode an LP by a data vector \(z\in\mathbb R^q\). Three common perturbation regimes are: additive noise \(\widetilde z=z+\sigma Z\); bounded absolute noise \(\widetilde z=z+U\) with \(\lVert U\rVert\le\sigma\) almost surely; and componentwise relative noise \(\widetilde z_j=z_j(1+\sigma Z_j)\). Each regime is determined only after specifying the law of \(Z\) or \(U\), the norm or coordinate scaling, which data components are perturbed, and whether conditioning preserves feasibility or encoding restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbation models differ by additive, bounded, or relative noise and require an explicit distribution, scale, coordinates, and conditioning convention.
assumptions_latex: \(z\in\mathbb R^q\) encodes all LP data selected for perturbation.
\(\sigma\ge0\).

children.title: Input Distribution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Probability models governing unperturbed or perturbed LP instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-Case, Average-Case, and Smoothed Input Quantifiers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the three input-distribution regimes, including internal algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(I,\omega)\ge0\) be algorithmic cost on input \(I\), with internal random seed \(\omega\), and write \(\bar T(I)=\mathbb E_\omega[T(I,\omega)]\). For an input class \(\mathcal I\), input law \(\mathcal D\), and perturbation kernel \(K_\sigma(I,\cdot)\), define \[W=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\bar T(I),\qquad A(\mathcal D)=\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[\bar T(I)],\qquad S(\sigma)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\mathbb E_{J\sim K_\sigma(I,\cdot)}[\bar T(J)].\] The regimes differ by the order and scope of adversarial and probabilistic quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case, average-case, and smoothed complexity differ in whether inputs are maximized, sampled, or adversarially centered and then perturbed.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is nonnegative and measurable for every expectation used.
\(\mathcal D\) is a probability law and \(K_\sigma\) is a probability kernel.
Internal algorithmic randomness is averaged in \(\bar T\); for deterministic algorithms this expectation is omitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W,\ A(\mathcal D),\text{ and }S(\sigma)\text{ are distinct complexity functionals with different quantifier order.}

notation.meaning: expected algorithmic cost on a fixed input, averaging internal randomness
perturbation kernel centered at input I
worst-case, average-case, and smoothed cost functionals

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case, Average-Case, and Smoothed Input Quantifiers
Input Distribution Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes worst-case, average-case, and smoothed input quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative algorithmic cost \(T(I)\), a fixed input class \(\mathcal I\), a distribution \(\mathcal D\), and perturbation kernels \(K_\sigma(I,\cdot)\), define \[W=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}T(I),\qquad A(\mathcal D)=\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D}[T(I)],\qquad S(\sigma)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}\mathbb E_{J\sim K_\sigma(I,\cdot)}[T(J)].\] These are respectively worst-case, average-case, and smoothed regimes. They are not interchangeable because their adversarial and probabilistic quantifiers occur in different orders.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case, average-case, and smoothed complexity use different supremum and expectation quantifiers and therefore describe distinct input regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\mathcal I\to[0,\infty]\) is measurable where expectations are used.
\(K_\sigma(I,\cdot)\) is a probability kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W\), \(A(\mathcal D)\), and \(S(\sigma)\) are distinct complexity functionals with different quantifier order.

notation.meaning: average cost under the input distribution

children.title: Perturbation Scale Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of smoothed complexity on the magnitude of input perturbations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives sufficient local-stability and tail conditions for recovering unperturbed expected cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_\sigma=z+\sigma Z\). If \(T(J_\sigma)\to T(z)\) in probability as \(\sigma\downarrow0\) and \(\{T(J_\sigma):0<\sigma\le\sigma_0\}\) is uniformly integrable, then \[\lim_{\sigma\downarrow0}\mathbb E[T(J_\sigma)]=T(z).\] Convergence in probability alone does not control expectations when rare perturbations carry unbounded cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected cost converges to the unperturbed cost at zero noise when local probabilistic stability is accompanied by uniform tail control.
assumptions_latex: \(T(J_\sigma)\to T(z)\) in probability as \(\sigma\downarrow0\).
\(\{T(J_\sigma):0<\sigma\le\sigma_0\}\) is uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{\sigma\downarrow0}\mathbb E[T(J_\sigma)]=T(z).
knowledge_statements.title: Small-Noise Expectation Limit

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the normalization under which additive smoothed cost depends on relative scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(T(\alpha z)=T(z)\) for every \(\alpha>0\), and define \(M(z,\sigma)=\mathbb E[T(z+\sigma Z)]\) for a fixed noise law. Then \[M(\alpha z,\alpha\sigma)=M(z,\sigma)\qquad(\alpha>0).\] For \(z\ne0\), a normalized formulation may therefore use a dimensionless scale such as \(\sigma/\|z\|\). This covariance does not imply monotonicity of \(M(z,\sigma)\) in \(\sigma\), and \(z=0\) requires a separate normalization convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling scale-invariant LP data and additive noise together preserves expected cost, but does not make cost monotone in noise or define a relative scale at zero data.
assumptions_latex: \(T(\alpha z)=T(z)\) for every \(\alpha>0\).
The law of \(Z\) is fixed independently of \(z\), \(\sigma\), and \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M(\alpha z,\alpha\sigma)=M(z,\sigma).

notation.meaning: a possible dimensionless relative scale when z is nonzero

knowledge_statements.title: Scale Covariance of Additive Perturbations
Perturbation Scale Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses the scale covariance governing meaningful smoothed-complexity comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let LP encodings be positively homogeneous and let the pivot count satisfy \(T(\alpha z)=T(z)\) for every \(\alpha>0\). For additive perturbations \(\widetilde z=z+\sigma Z\), define \(M(z,\sigma)=\mathbb E[T(z+\sigma Z)]\). Then \[M(\alpha z,\alpha\sigma)=M(z,\sigma).\] Thus perturbation sensitivity is governed by a dimensionless relative scale, such as \(\sigma/\lVert z\rVert\), rather than by \(\sigma\) alone. This covariance does not imply that \(M(z,\sigma)\) is monotone in \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For scale-invariant pivoting, scaling both data and additive noise equally preserves expected pivots; no general monotonicity in noise follows.
assumptions_latex: \(T(\alpha z)=T(z)\) for all \(\alpha>0\).
The noise law of \(Z\) is independent of \(z\) and \(\sigma\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(\alpha z,\alpha\sigma)=M(z,\sigma)\), while monotonicity in \(\sigma\) is not guaranteed.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance identity follows from the stated scale invariance, and the warning that covariance does not imply monotonicity is correct. However, no source supports its use as an LP smoothed-complexity property or the accompanying relative-scale interpretation, including the required normalization and the exceptional case of zero data.

children.title: Distribution Robustness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on transferring smoothed conclusions across distribution families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when total-variation closeness controls expected algorithmic cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\le T\le M<\infty\), then for probability laws \(P,Q\), \[\left|\mathbb E_P[T]-\mathbb E_Q[T]\right|\le M d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q),\] where \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\). Without a uniform bound or suitable tail control on \(T\), arbitrarily small total-variation distance does not uniformly control the expectation difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total-variation closeness transfers expected-cost bounds for bounded costs, but not for arbitrary unbounded costs without tail control.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\) are probability laws on the same measurable space.
For the positive bound, \(T\) is measurable and \(0\le T\le M<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\mathbb E_P[T]-\mathbb E_Q[T]\right|\le M d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q).

notation.meaning: total-variation distance defined by the supremum over measurable events

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Variation Transfer Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient domination condition for transferring expected smoothed-cost bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\ge0\) be measurable. If \(Q\ll P\) and \(dQ/dP\le C<\infty\) \(P\)-almost surely, then \[\mathbb E_Q[T]\le C\mathbb E_P[T].\] Thus a finite or polynomial expectation bound under \(P\) transfers to \(Q\) with multiplicative loss \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniformly bounded likelihood ratio transfers a nonnegative expected-cost bound between perturbation laws.
assumptions_latex: \(T:\Omega\to[0,\infty]\) is measurable.
\(Q\ll P\) and \(dQ/dP\le C<\infty\) \(P\)-almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_Q[T]\le C\mathbb E_P[T].

notation.meaning: essential upper bound on the likelihood ratio

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Likelihood-Ratio Transfer
Distribution Robustness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rare hard perturbations prevent distribution-free transfer of smoothed bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a pivot rule have costs \(T(I_0)=a\) and \(T(I_1)=H\), where \(0\le a<H\). For the mixture \(Q_\eta=(1-\eta)\delta_{I_0}+\eta\delta_{I_1}\), \[\mathbb E_{Q_\eta}[T]=(1-\eta)a+\eta H.\] Even when \(\eta\) is arbitrarily small, the expectation can be arbitrarily large by increasing \(H\). Therefore a smoothed bound proved for one perturbation law does not automatically transfer to another law merely because both have small variance or concentrate near the same nominal input; a quantitative domination, coupling, or tail condition is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tiny probability of extremely hard instances can destroy expected pivot bounds, so robustness requires quantitative control between perturbation laws.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le a<H<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_{Q_\eta}[T]=(1-\eta)a+\eta H\), which is unbounded as \(H\to\infty\) for fixed \(\eta>0\).

notation.meaning: cost of a rare hard instance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixture expectation and its divergence with increasing hard-instance cost are correct. The example supports failure of distribution-free expectation transfer, but it does not by itself establish the stronger assertion about laws having small variance or concentrating near the same nominal input because no metric, input separation, or second comparison law is specified. A source or a more fully parameterized construction is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected pivot-count representation for the uniform geometric Random-Edge rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a finite acyclic improving graph, let \(H(v)\) be the expected number of uniform Random-Edge pivots needed to reach a sink from \(v\). Then \[H(v)=0\quad(N^+(v)=\varnothing),\qquad H(v)=1+\frac1{|N^+(v)|}\sum_{w\in N^+(v)}H(w)\quad(N^+(v)\ne\varnothing).\] These values are uniquely determined in reverse topological order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected Random-Edge pivot count is the unique hitting-time solution obtained by averaging over improving neighboring vertices.
assumptions_latex: The improving graph is finite and acyclic.
Selection is uniform over distinct improving neighboring vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(v)=1+|N^+(v)|^{-1}\sum_{w\in N^+(v)}H(w)\text{ off sinks, with }H=0\text{ on sinks}.
knowledge_statements.title: Random-Edge Hitting-Time Recurrence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes weighted and history-dependent Random-Edge variants without conflating their state with the current vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal S\) be a finite state space with vertex projection \(

u(s))=\varnothing\). Uniform geometric Random-Edge is recovered by taking \(\mathcal S=V(P)\), \(q_v(w)=1/|N^+(v)|\), and deterministic update to \(w\).

The vertex set of \(P\) is finite.
Each nonterminal \(q_s\) is supported on distinct improving geometric neighbors.

knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-State Weighted Random-Edge Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination for geometric Random-Edge and weighted variants on a finite vertex graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have finite vertex set \(V\), and suppose every transition moves from \(v\) to an adjacent vertex \(w\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}w>c^{\mathsf T}v\). Then every sample path reaches a vertex having no improving neighbor after at most \(|V|-1\) transitions. If \(P\) is a bounded polytope, every such terminal vertex maximizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict improvement on a finite vertex graph prevents revisits, so every trajectory terminates; on a bounded polytope its terminal vertex is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is finite.
Every sampled transition follows a strictly improving geometric edge.
The optimality conclusion assumes that \(P\) is a bounded polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\le |V|-1,\qquad v_T\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite Strictly Improving Random-Edge Termination
Random-Edge Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the canonical random-edge pivot rule and its admissible variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current vertex \(v\) of a polytope \(P\) and a linear objective to maximize, form the set \(E^+(v)\) of incident edges whose opposite endpoint has strictly larger objective value. If \(E^+(v)=\varnothing\), stop and output \(v\). Otherwise select an edge \(e\in E^+(v)\) according to a declared probability distribution \(p_v\), pivot to its opposite endpoint, and repeat. Canonical Random-Edge uses \(p_v(e)=1/|E^+(v)|\); weighted and history-dependent random-edge families replace this uniform law while retaining selection among improving incident edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-Edge repeatedly chooses an improving incident edge uniformly; related families use other declared probabilities over improving edges.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has a finite vertex-edge graph.
Adjacent vertices with equal objective value are excluded or handled by a declared tie convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a vertex \(v\) with \(E^+(v)=\varnothing\); canonical selection is uniform on \(E^+(v)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical uniform Random-Edge step is stated coherently and algorithm is the appropriate content kind. No primary or authoritative source is supplied, however, and the extension to history-dependent families is not represented by the vertex-indexed distribution p_v alone. Degeneracy and tie conventions also require source verification.

children.title: Random-Facet Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Randomized simplex behavior based on facet selection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclicity Does Not Imply the Face Unique-Sink Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal orientation counterexample to an insufficient hypothesis for Random-Facet recursion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orient the four-cycle on vertices \(\{00,10,11,01\}\) by \(00\to10\), \(00\to01\), \(11\to10\), and \(11\to01\). This orientation is acyclic, but the square has two sinks, \(10\) and \(01\). Consequently, acyclicity alone does not define a unique sink for every recursive face and cannot justify a Random-Facet conclusion requiring such a sink.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclically oriented square can have two sinks, so acyclicity alone is insufficient for a face-by-face unique-sink Random-Facet recursion.
assumptions_latex: The four vertices and four edges form a two-dimensional cube graph.
Sink means a vertex having no outgoing edge within the face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Acyclic orientation}\not\Rightarrow\text{unique sink on every face}.

notation.meaning: binary labels of the square's vertices

knowledge_statements.title: Acyclicity Does Not Imply the Face Unique-Sink Property
Random-Facet Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive Random-Facet rule stated for an acyclic orientation of a hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a vertex \(v\) of an acyclically oriented cube and a set \(S\) of available coordinate directions, define \(\operatorname{RF}(v,S)\) recursively. If \(S=\varnothing\), return \(v\). Otherwise choose \(i\) uniformly from \(S\), set \(u=\operatorname{RF}(v,S\setminus\{i\})\), and inspect the edge from \(u\) in direction \(i\). If that edge is outgoing, replace \(u\) by its opposite endpoint. Return \(\operatorname{RF}(u,S\setminus\{i\})\). The initial call uses all coordinate directions; recursion terminates because each call reduces \(|S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an oriented cube, Random-Facet recursively optimizes a random lower-dimensional facet, tests the omitted direction, then recursively continues.
assumptions_latex: The cube orientation is acyclic and supplies a unique direction for every edge.
\(S\) is a finite set of coordinate directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{RF}(v,S)\) terminates after finite recursion and returns the recursively selected sink over the subcube generated by \(S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, but the canonical Random-Facet recursion cannot be verified without a source. Mere acyclicity does not ensure a unique sink on every subcube, so the claim that the procedure returns the relevant subcube sink requires stronger orientation hypotheses, such as the appropriate unique-sink property, or a different conclusion. The repeated recursive call and omitted-direction convention also need verification against the canonical algorithm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed qualitative complexity guarantee pending verification of its exact parameters and algorithmic hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a canonical Random-Facet rule on a \(d\)-dimensional linear program with \(m\) facets, the proposed classical bound is \[\mathbb E[\mathrm{pivots}]\le\exp\!\bigl(O(\sqrt{d\log m})\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A classical subexponential expected-pivot bound is claimed for Random-Facet, but its exact formulation is not verified by the packet.
assumptions_latex: The canonical Random-Facet recursion and its exact orientation hypotheses are used.
All recursive pivots are included in the count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[\mathrm{pivots}]\le\exp(O(\sqrt{d\log m}))\quad\text{subject to source verification}.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Random-Facet Subexponential Pivot Bound

Expansion is required to resolve the recursion, orientation domain, bound, and counterexample. Variant taxonomy and generic complexity-interpretation boundaries are excluded to siblings.

children.title: Recursive Randomized Pivoting
children.top_down_role: Randomized simplex families organized through recursive subproblem structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Randomized Pivoting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract recursive template underlying Random-Facet simplex rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a bounded polytope \(P\), a linear objective \(c\), and a current vertex \(v\). If no edge incident to \(v\) improves \(c^\top x\), output \(v\). Otherwise randomly select an eligible facet \(F\) according to the variant's prescribed distribution, recursively optimize \(c^\top x\) over \(P\cap F\) from a reachable vertex, and obtain \(w\). If an improving pivot from \(w\) leaves \(F\), perform that pivot and recursively continue on \(P\); otherwise output \(w\). The recursion terminates when its optimality test succeeds, and its output is the final vertex returned by the outermost call.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-Facet recursively optimizes on a randomly selected facet, pivots away when improvement is possible, and repeats until a vertex passes the optimality test.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is a bounded polytope with a finite vertex-edge graph.
Every recursive restriction has a specified reachable starting vertex and an anti-cycling convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The outermost call returns a vertex at which the algorithm's optimality test succeeds.
review_flags: Exact Random-Facet eligibility distribution and recursion convention require a dedicated source.
Variant-dependent initialization and anti-cycling details need confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the terminal container, but no evidence is supplied for the eligible-facet rule, recursive initialization, outer continuation, or termination convention. These details distinguish Random-Facet algorithms and materially affect the statement, so the candidate requires a dedicated source.

children.title: Random-Facet Variants
children.top_down_role: Variants differing in sampling, recursion, or subproblem handling.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Facet Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric representation of common recursive Random-Facet choices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Random-Facet variant is specified by a tuple \((\mathcal E,\pi,\sigma,\tau)\). For every recursive state \((Q,x)\), \(\mathcal E(Q,x)\) is the set of eligible facets, \(\pi(\cdot\mid Q,x)\) is a probability distribution on that set, \(\sigma(Q,x,F)\) supplies the initial state for the recursive call on \(Q\cap F\), and \(\tau\) prescribes tie-breaking and termination. Uniform Random-Facet has \(\pi(F\mid Q,x)=1/|\mathcal E(Q,x)|\). Two implementations belong to the same parameterized variant only when these four components agree on every reachable state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random-Facet variants differ through eligible facets, their sampling distribution, recursive initialization, and tie-breaking or termination rules.
assumptions_latex: Every reachable state has a finite eligible set \(\mathcal E(Q,x)\).
The initialization map \(\sigma\) produces a valid state on the selected recursive face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The tuple \((\mathcal E,\pi,\sigma,\tau)\) determines the variant's recursive transition law.
review_flags: This abstract taxonomy needs comparison with named Random-Facet variants in a dedicated source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is an appropriate knowledge kind for this variants container, but the proposed four-component tuple appears to be a synthesized taxonomy rather than a cited standard representation. A source is needed to establish that it faithfully covers the intended Random-Facet variants.

children.title: Recursive Complexity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of expected-complexity guarantees for recursive randomized pivot families.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that bounded recursion depth does not bound the total number of recursive calls polynomially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a recursion in which every nonleaf call at depth less than \(d\) creates two child calls and leaves occur at depth \(d\). Its recursion depth is \(d\), but its total number of calls is \(1+2+\cdots+2^d=2^{d+1}-1\). Hence a depth bound alone does not imply a polynomial bound on total recursive work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary recursion can have depth d and exponentially many total calls.
assumptions_latex: Each nonleaf call creates exactly two child calls.
All leaves occur at depth \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{depth}=d,\qquad\operatorname{calls}=2^{d+1}-1.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Depth Branching Counterexample

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarifies the asymptotic status of a Random-Facet-style subexponential bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound of the form \(T(d,m)\le\exp(C\sqrt{d\log m})\) is not bounded by \((d+m)^k\) for any fixed \(k\) over all \(d,m\). Therefore such a bound does not establish a polynomial pivot rule or a strongly polynomial LP algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Random-Facet-style subexponential bound remains superpolynomial in general.
assumptions_latex: \(C>0\) is constant.
\(d,m\) range jointly without an additional restriction making the exponent logarithmic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exp(C\sqrt{d\log m})\notin(d+m)^{O(1)}\text{ in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Subexponential-Is-Not-Polynomial Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates expected recursive pivot bounds from per-run and strong tail guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\ge0\) be the total number of pivots made by all calls of a recursive randomized simplex method. If \(\mathbb E[X]\le B\), then \[\Pr(X\ge B/\delta)\le\delta\qquad(0<\delta<1).\] The expectation bound alone gives neither a deterministic bound \(X\le B\) nor an exponential tail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expected recursive pivot bound yields a Markov tail bound but does not control every run or imply exponential concentration.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the nonnegative total pivot count over the entire recursive execution.
\(\mathbb E[X]\le B<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr(X\ge B/\delta)\le\delta,\quad\text{while }X\le B\text{ need not hold}.

notation.meaning: total pivot count over all recursive calls
upper bound on expected pivot count

knowledge_statements.title: Expected-Pivot Tail Boundary
Recursive Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between recursive termination and a polynomial pivot bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T(d,m)\) denote the worst-case expected number of pivots of a recursive randomized facet rule on \(d\)-dimensional instances with \(m\) facets. Almost-sure termination on every finite instance establishes only \(T(d,m)<\infty\); it does not establish a polynomial bound in \(d+m\). A polynomial-time conclusion requires an independently proved recurrence and base cases whose solution is polynomial, together with polynomial work per pivot. Consequently, recursion depth bounded by \(d\), without sufficient control of repeated outer calls or branching, lies outside the polynomial-complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite recursive depth or almost-sure termination alone does not yield polynomial complexity; repeated calls, pivot counts, and per-pivot work must also be bounded.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm runs on finite noncycling simplex states.
\(T(d,m)\) counts expected pivots, including all recursive calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Termination alone implies no bound of the form \(T(d,m)\leq (d+m)^k\) for a fixed \(k\).
review_flags: A source specific to recursive randomized simplex complexity is required.
No numerical Random-Facet bound is asserted because its exact version is unresolved.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role matches the container, and the general distinction between termination and polynomial complexity is sound. However, the claim is framed specifically for recursive randomized facet rules without a supporting source for their recurrence, state counting, or termination model.

children.title: Pivot Counts
children.top_down_role: Iteration counts across simplex variants, pivot rules, instance classes, and termination regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Pivot Counts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivot count as a combinatorial simplex resource measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simplex execution producing bases \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_K\), where each transition replaces one basic index by one nonbasic index, the pivot count is \(K\). If no basis repeats, then \(K\leq N_B-1\), where \(N_B\) is the number of feasible bases reachable from \(B_0\). In standard form with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) of row rank \(m\), one has \(N_B\leq {n\choose m}\), hence \(K\leq {n\choose m}-1\). This bound counts pivots, not arithmetic operations or bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noncycling simplex run makes at most one fewer pivot than its number of reachable feasible bases, hence at most binomially many pivots.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
The pivot rule never revisits a basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\leq N_B-1\leq {n\choose m}-1\).
