knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the classical worst-case pivot boundary for Dantzig pricing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every dimension \(d\), there is a Klee--Minty-type linear program with a prescribed initial feasible basis on which primal simplex using Dantzig's largest-reduced-cost entering rule follows an exponentially long path and performs \(\Omega(2^d)\) pivots before reaching the optimum. Thus finite nonrepetition cannot generally be strengthened to a polynomial pivot bound for that rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Klee–Minty instances force Dantzig’s simplex rule to make exponentially many pivots, so finite termination does not imply a polynomial pivot bound.
assumptions_latex: Primal simplex uses the Dantzig largest-reduced-cost entering rule under the construction’s sign convention.
The prescribed initial feasible basis and Klee--Minty-type instance are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K(d)=\Omega(2^d).

notation.meaning: pivot count on the constructed instance

knowledge_statements.title: Klee–Minty Exponential Pivot-Count Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex pivot rule and improving variable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the maximization-tableau sign convention in which a positive objective-row coefficient indicates improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a simplex tableau, let \(I=\{j\notin B:\bar c_j>0\}\) be the set of improving nonbasic variables. A pivot rule selects an entering variable from \(I\), and may also specify a leaving variable when the ratio test has multiple minimizers. The number of pivots required to solve an LP can depend substantially on these selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An improving variable is a nonbasic variable with a positive coefficient in the objective row. A pivot rule chooses the entering variable among such candidates and may resolve ties for the leaving variable. The resulting pivot count can depend substantially on the rule.
assumptions_latex: \text{A simplex tableau for a maximization problem is given.}
I=\{j\notin B:\bar c_j>0\}\neq\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: j_{\mathrm{enter}}\in I\text{ is selected by the pivot rule, possibly together with a leaving-variable choice.}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A dense factorization costs \(O(m^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(m^2)\) storage, while each subsequent solve costs \(O(m^2)\) arithmetic operations.

source_refs.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be a nonsingular simplex basis matrix. Computing a dense factorization \(PB=LU\) by Gaussian elimination requires \(O(m^3)\) arithmetic operations and \(O(m^2)\) stored scalars. Once the factors are available, solving either \(Bx=b\) or \(B^\top y=c_{\mathcal B}\) requires \(O(m^2)\) arithmetic operations per right-hand side. These are real-arithmetic bounds; they do not account for sparse fill, numerical-pivoting overhead, or finite-precision bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense basis factorization costs cubic arithmetic and quadratic storage; each subsequent triangular solve costs quadratic arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Factorization Work

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Factor Solve and Fill Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses sparse basis-solve work through factor nonzeros and identifies the fill boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(PBQ=LU\) be a computed nonsingular sparse LU factorization of an \(m\times m\) basis. Applying permutations and solving one basis or transposed-basis system costs \(O(m+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+\operatorname{nnz}(U))\) arithmetic operations and storage proportional to the factors. Input sparsity alone does not control these costs: ordering and pivoting can create fill, and the factors can be dense in the worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse triangular-solve work scales with the computed factors’ nonzeros; sparse input alone does not prevent dense fill.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
A sparse factorization \(PBQ=LU\) has been computed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{solve}}=O\!\left(m+\operatorname{nnz}(L)+\operatorname{nnz}(U)\right),\quad \operatorname{nnz}(B)\text{ alone does not control fill}.

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros in M

children.title: Basis Update Work
children.top_down_role: Computational cost of maintaining basis representations between refactorizations.

assumptions_latex: \(B,B'\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) are nonsingular.
The dense inverse \(B^{-1}\) is available, and the entering-column update data are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Updating the stored dense inverse and applying it to one right-hand side each require \(O(m^2)\) arithmetic operations, with \(O(m^2)\) storage.

notation.meaning: basis matrices before and after the pivot
nonsingular elementary matrix representing the column replacement
stored inverse of the updated basis

review_flags: The replacement uses a dense stored-inverse model; product-form update sequences require a separate length-dependent analysis.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost of updating a dense stored inverse after one simplex pivot.

source_refs.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one simplex pivot replaces one column of a nonsingular basis \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\), producing the nonsingular basis \(B'=BE\), where \(E\) is the corresponding elementary column-replacement matrix. If the dense inverse \(B^{-1}\) is stored, the rank-one inverse-update formula computes \((B')^{-1}\) in \(O(m^2)\) arithmetic operations and retains \(O(m^2)\) storage. Multiplying the updated inverse by one right-hand side also costs \(O(m^2)\). This real-arithmetic bound does not imply numerical stability, so implementations may periodically refactor the basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a dense stored inverse, a nonsingular single-column basis replacement can be incorporated in quadratic arithmetic and storage, and a subsequent solve also costs quadratic arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Update Work

source_witnesses.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the length-dependent storage and solve costs of retained eta updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_k=B_0E_1\cdots E_k\), where each nonsingular eta matrix \(E_i\) differs from the identity in one column, and retain a factorization of \(B_0\). Then \(B_k^{-1}=E_k^{-1}\cdots E_1^{-1}B_0^{-1}\). Storing dense eta vectors for \(k\) updates uses \(O(km)\) additional scalars, and applying the chain to one right-hand side costs \(O(km)\) arithmetic operations in addition to the \(B_0\) solve. Hence an unrestarted chain becomes progressively more expensive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chain of k dense eta updates adds order km storage and per-solve work until refactorization restarts it.
assumptions_latex: \(B_0,\ldots,B_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) are nonsingular.
Each update is stored as an eta matrix differing from the identity in one column.
A factorization or inverse action for \(B_0\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{\mathrm{updates}}=O(km),\qquad T_{\mathrm{updates\ per\ solve}}=O(km).
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Form Update Chain Work

children.title: Per-Pivot Work Coupling
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs linking pivot counts, update frequency, refactorization frequency, and total computational work.

assumptions_latex: All work components are measured in the same arithmetic-operation model.
The execution has finite pivot count \(K\) and finite refactorization count \(R\).
For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), \(p_k\leq p\), \(u_k\leq u\), and \(s_k\leq s\); for every \(r\in\{1,\ldots,R\}\), \(f_r\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The total work satisfies \(W\leq W_{\mathrm{init}}+K(p+u+s)+Rf\).

notation.meaning: pricing, update, and remaining work at pivot k
uniform upper bounds on the corresponding work components

review_flags: The decomposition is an accounting identity; the source is provisional for the arithmetic-work model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decomposition coupling pivot count to total arithmetic work.

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a simplex run with \(K\) pivots and \(R\) basis refactorizations. Let \(W_{\mathrm{init}}\) be its initialization work; let \(p_k\), \(u_k\), and \(s_k\) be the pricing, basis-update, and remaining arithmetic work of pivot \(k\); and let \(f_r\) be the work of refactorization \(r\). The total arithmetic work is \[W=W_{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}(p_k+u_k+s_k)+\sum_{r=1}^{R}f_r.\] If \(p_k\leq p\), \(u_k\leq u\), and \(s_k\leq s\) for every pivot, and \(f_r\leq f\) for every refactorization, then \(W\leq W_{\mathrm{init}}+K(p+u+s)+Rf\). Thus a pivot-count bound yields an arithmetic-work bound only when the component costs and refactorization count are also controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total simplex work is initialization plus all pricing, update, auxiliary, and refactorization costs; under uniform component bounds it is bounded by initialization plus the pivot and refactorization counts times their respective costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Per-Pivot Work Coupling

source_witnesses.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the coupling between a periodic rebuild schedule and average pivot work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(K\geq1\) pivots are partitioned into consecutive blocks of at most \(q\geq1\) pivots and at most one scheduled basis refactorization occurs per block. If each scheduled refactorization costs at most \(f\), then \(R\leq\lceil K/q\rceil\), so scheduled rebuilds contribute at most \(\lceil K/q\rceil f\) total work and at most \(f/q+f/K\) amortized work per pivot. Diagnostic-triggered refactorizations outside this schedule must be counted separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one scheduled rebuild per block of q pivots, refactorization contributes about f/q work per pivot; extra diagnostic rebuilds require separate accounting.
assumptions_latex: The run has \(K\geq1\) pivots partitioned into blocks of at most \(q\) pivots.
At most one scheduled refactorization occurs per block.
Each scheduled refactorization costs at most \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\leq\lceil K/q\rceil,\qquad \frac{Rf}{K}\leq\frac{f}{q}+\frac{f}{K}.

notation.meaning: upper bound on one refactorization’s work

knowledge_statements.title: Periodic Refactorization Amortization

children.title: Pricing Work
children.top_down_role: Candidate-selection cost across full, partial, approximate, and structured pricing regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is stored densely.
\(\mathcal B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) has cardinality \(m\), and \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\) is nonsingular.
A dense factorization of \(B\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dense full pricing requires \(O(m^2+m(n-m))=O(mn)\) arithmetic operations per iteration.

notation.meaning: constraint matrix and its jth column
reduced cost of nonbasic index j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-pricing arithmetic cost for one dense revised-simplex iteration.

source_refs.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a standard-form minimization problem with dense matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), basic index set \(\mathcal B\) of cardinality \(m\), nonbasic set \(\mathcal N=\{1,ldots,n\}\setminus\mathcal B\), and nonsingular basis \(B=A_{[:,\mathcal B]}\). Full pricing computes \(y\) from \(B^\top y=c_{\mathcal B}\) and then computes \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^\top y\) for every \(j\in\mathcal N\), where \(a_j\) is column \(j\) of \(A\). With a dense stored factorization of \(B\), the solve costs \(O(m^2)\), and scanning the \(n-m\) dense nonbasic columns costs \(O(m(n-m))\). Therefore full pricing costs \(O(m^2+m(n-m))=O(mn)\) arithmetic operations and reads every nonbasic column.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense full pricing solves once for the simplex multipliers and scans every nonbasic column, costing quadratic solve work plus a dense column scan, or order mn overall.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Work

source_witnesses.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost of evaluating an explicitly selected subset of reduced costs in dense revised simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathcal N\) be the set of nonbasic columns inspected in one pricing search. With a stored dense factorization of \(B\), computing \(y\) from \(B^\top y=c_{\mathcal B}\) costs \(O(m^2)\), and evaluating \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^\top y\) for all \(j\in S\) costs \(O(m|S|)\). Hence that search costs \(O(m^2+m|S|)\) arithmetic operations when the multiplier solve is charged, or \(O(m|S|)\) after \(y\) is available.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense subset pricing costs one dense basis solve plus one length-m dot product per inspected column.
assumptions_latex: \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular and has a stored dense factorization.
Every inspected column is stored densely.
\(S\) is explicitly available; candidate-set construction is excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{price}}(S)=O(m^2+m|S|),\qquad W_{\mathrm{eval}}(S\mid y)=O(m|S|).
knowledge_statements.title: Dense Subset-Pricing Work

children.title: Sparsity-Exploiting Work
children.top_down_role: Work reductions and overhead arising from sparse constraint matrices, bases, and iterates.

assumptions_latex: Columns are stored in a sparse format that permits iteration over their stored nonzeros.
The multiplier vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) has already been computed.
One unit-cost objective-coefficient access and scalar subtraction are charged for each inspected index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pricing over \(S\) costs \(O\!\left(|S|+\sum_{j\in S}\operatorname{nnz}(a_j)\right)\) arithmetic operations.

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros in column j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation bound for sparse reduced-cost evaluation after the basis solve.

source_refs.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite set of inspected nonbasic indices, let \(a_j\in\mathbb{R}^m\) be column \(j\) of the constraint matrix, and let \(\operatorname{nnz}(a_j)\) be its number of stored nonzeros. Once the multiplier vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) is available, computing \(\bar c_j=c_j-a_j^\top y\) for every \(j\in S\) requires \(O\!\left(|S|+\sum_{j\in S}\operatorname{nnz}(a_j)\right)\) arithmetic operations in a sparse-column model. For full sparse pricing with \(S=\mathcal N\), this is \(O\!\left(|\mathcal N|+\operatorname{nnz}(A_{[:,\mathcal N]})\right)\). The bound excludes the basis solve and fill in the basis factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After the multiplier solve, sparse pricing costs one scalar amount of work per inspected column plus work proportional to the stored nonzeros in those columns; basis-solve and factor-fill costs are excluded.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparsity-Exploiting Work

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a finite set of inspected nonbasic indices, let \(a_j\) be the explicitly stored sparse column for \(j\in S\), and let \(y\) be the multiplier vector. In a direct sparse-column model that computes each \(a_j^\top y\) by reading every stored entry of \(a_j\), evaluating the reduced costs for \(S\) performs \(\Omega(|S|)\) column-level accesses and \(\Omega\!\left(\sum_{j\in S}\operatorname{nnz}(a_j)\right)\) stored-entry accesses. Full pricing uses \(S=\mathcal N\), where \(\mathcal N\) is the complete nonbasic index set. Partial pricing can reduce the current scan by choosing a proper subset of \(\mathcal N\), but then leaves the other reduced costs unevaluated in that scan.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the stated direct sparse-column model, pricing accesses every inspected column and every stored entry used in its dot product; partial pricing reduces the current scan by leaving some reduced costs unevaluated.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translates a contiguous sparse-column scan into an idealized memory-traffic bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an ideal cache-line model with \(L\geq1\) consecutive stored entries per line, a cold sequential scan of \(M\) contiguous entries transfers either \(\lceil M/L\rceil\) or \(\lceil M/L\rceil+1\) lines, depending on alignment. Hence its compulsory entry-data traffic is \(\Theta(\lceil M/L\rceil)\). This excludes index streams, multiplier-vector accesses, cache conflicts, prefetch behavior, and latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cold sequential scan of M contiguous entries needs order M/L cache-line transfers in the ideal model, excluding indices and irregular auxiliary accesses.
assumptions_latex: Each cache line contains \(L\) consecutive stored entries.
The \(M\) entries are contiguous and scanned once from a cold cache.
Conflict, prefetch, and latency effects are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{lines}}=\Theta\!\left(\left\lceil M/L\right\rceil\right).

source_refs.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a primal-feasible basis for a minimization problem, with complete nonbasic index set \(\mathcal N\) and reduced costs \(\bar c_j\) for \(j\in\mathcal N\). Let \(S\subsetneq\mathcal N\) be the indices inspected in the current pricing round. Finding \(\bar c_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in S\) does not certify optimality, because an uninspected index can have \(\bar c_j<0\). Partial pricing recovers the full-pricing optimality test only after every relevant omitted index is examined or a valid auxiliary certificate establishes \(\bar c_j\geq0\) for every \(j\in\mathcal N\setminus S\). Inspecting fewer columns reduces the direct reduced-cost evaluation performed in the current round, but may require later pricing rounds to examine omitted indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a primal-feasible minimization basis, nonnegative reduced costs on only the inspected subset do not certify optimality; omitted costs must eventually be checked or covered by a valid certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Pricing Locality Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 2. Exploiting Sparsity p. 127

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when smaller individual pricing scans reduce aggregate access work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let pricing round \(t\) inspect \(S_t\subseteq\mathcal N\), and let \(w_j\geq0\) be the charged work for column \(j\). Through round \(T\), localized work is \(W_{\mathrm{loc}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j\in S_t}w_j\), while one full scan costs \(W_{\mathrm{full}}=\sum_{j\in\mathcal N}w_j\). Proper-subset rounds may each be cheaper, but locality reduces aggregate work relative to one full scan only when \(W_{\mathrm{loc}}<W_{\mathrm{full}}\); repeated scans can erase the saving.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cheaper partial scans reduce aggregate pricing work only when their cumulative inspected-column cost remains below one full scan.
assumptions_latex: Each inspected column \(j\) has nonnegative charged work \(w_j\).
Repeated inspection is charged again.
All work is measured in the same model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{loc}}<W_{\mathrm{full}}\iff\sum_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{j\in S_t}w_j<\sum_{j\in\mathcal N}w_j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential improving simplex path on the specified LP family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded theorem for the LP family defined by the omitted constraints (3.7)–(3.8).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the linear program minimizing \(-x_n\) subject to (3.7)--(3.8), the feasible set has \(2^n\) vertices. The vertices can be ordered \(v^0,\ldots,v^{2^n-1}\) so that each \(v^{k+1}\) is adjacent to \(v^k\) and has strictly lower cost. Moreover, there exists a simplex pivoting rule requiring \(2^n-1\) basis changes before termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The specified LP has 2^n vertices admitting a strictly cost-decreasing adjacent-vertex ordering. There also exists a simplex pivoting rule that requires 2^n−1 basis changes before terminating.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies the referenced constraints (3.7)--(3.8).
The objective is \(\min -x_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\operatorname{vert}(P_n)|=2^n,\quad \exists (v^k)_{k=0}^{2^n-1}\ \forall k<2^n-1:\ v^{k+1}\sim v^k\ \text{and}\ -v^{k+1}_n<-v^k_n,\quad \exists\text{ a pivoting rule requiring }2^n-1\text{ basis changes}.

children.title: Degeneracy Work
children.top_down_role: Extra computational burden associated with degenerate bases, zero-length moves, and repeated objective values.

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computational work caused by degenerate simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form feasible basis \(B\), the basic solution is \(x_{\mathcal B}=B^{-1}b\). The basis is degenerate when at least one component of \(x_{\mathcal B}\) is zero. If the ratio test selects a leaving basic variable whose value is zero, the step length is \(\theta=0\); the basis changes, but the primal point and objective value do not. Such a pivot still incurs pricing, ratio-test, and basis-update work. Without an anti-cycling rule, repeated degenerate pivots may revisit a basis; with a finite anti-cycling rule, they terminate but may still add pivots without objective progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate pivot changes the basis with zero step and no objective improvement, yet still incurs the usual computational work and may cause cycling.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a feasible nonsingular basis for \(Ax=b\), \(x\geq0\).
The leaving variable selected by the ratio test has value zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pivot has \(\theta=0\), leaves the primal point unchanged, and nevertheless incurs nonzero iteration work.

children.title: Stalling Work
children.top_down_role: Iteration overhead from prolonged weak progress, cycling avoidance, and tie handling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accounts for pivot-count overhead accumulated during a zero-progress episode.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a simplex run contains a stalling episode of \(s\) completed pivots, those pivots contribute exactly \(s\) to the pivot count even though the specified progress measure has not improved during the episode. Consequently, a bound based only on the number of distinct primal points or strictly improving objective values need not bound the pivot count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An s-pivot stalling episode adds s iterations without measured progress, so progress-event counts alone do not control simplex work.
assumptions_latex: The episode contains \(s\) completed simplex pivots.
The specified progress measure remains unchanged or nonimproving throughout the episode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_{\mathrm{stall}}=s\), independently of the number of strict progress events in the episode.

notation.meaning: pivots performed during the stalling episode
number of pivots in the episode

knowledge_statements.title: Stalling Iteration Overhead

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a finite zero-progress episode from a repeated-basis cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simplex execution stalls over iterations \(k,\ldots,k+s-1\) relative to a specified progress measure when it performs \(s\geq1\) pivots while that measure does not improve. It cycles when some basis repeats, \(B_i=B_j\) for \(i<j\). A finite sequence of distinct degenerate bases can therefore stall without cycling; cycling is a stronger recurrence condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stalling is a specified zero-progress episode, whereas cycling requires a repeated basis; finite stalling need not be cycling.
assumptions_latex: A simplex execution produces a sequence of bases and values of a specified progress measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis repetition is required for cycling but not for finite stalling.
knowledge_statements.title: Stalling and Cycling Are Distinct
Stalling Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degenerate simplex pivots can consume work without changing the represented primal solution or objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a primal simplex iteration at a feasible basis with entering direction \(d\) and ratio-test step \(\alpha\). If \(\alpha=0\), the pivot changes the basis but leaves the basic feasible solution and objective value unchanged. Consequently, a sequence of \(s\) such degenerate pivots incurs \(s\) pivot operations while making zero primal or objective progress. Thus an iteration bound based only on the number of distinct visited vertices is invalid; without a terminating anti-cycling rule, repeated degenerate pivots may even revisit a basis indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each zero-step degenerate pivot costs an iteration without changing the solution or objective, so vertex counting does not control work and cycling is possible.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a feasible nonsingular simplex basis.
The ratio test returns \(\alpha=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^{+}=x\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x^{+}=c^{\mathsf T}x\), although the basis may change.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and zero-step-pivot claim fit the terminal container, but no inspectable source supports the degeneracy, work, and cycling assertions.

children.title: Finite-Precision Work
children.top_down_role: Numerical safeguards, residual control, refactorization, and reliability costs under finite precision.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic safeguard workflow for controlling accumulated basis-solve error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Monitor scaled residuals of basis solves produced by the maintained factorization. If a residual fails its declared tolerance, apply iterative refinement while it reduces the monitored error; if refinement fails or factor-update diagnostics exceed their thresholds, rebuild the factorization from the current basis matrix and recompute the affected quantities. Accept a pivot decision only after its declared feasibility, reduced-cost, and ratio-test tolerances are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-precision simplex monitors basis solves, refines inaccurate results, and refactorizes when accumulated update error cannot be controlled.
assumptions_latex: All tolerances are declared relative to data scaling and working precision.
The current basis is nonsingular and can be refactorized at the chosen precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Pivot decisions are accepted only after the monitored numerical tests pass.}
review_flags: Concrete tolerances and update-growth diagnostics are implementation-dependent.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Triggered Refinement and Refactorization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes residual and backward accuracy from conditioning-dependent forward accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a computed solution \(\widehat x\) of \(Bx=b\), let \(r=b-B\widehat x\). Then \(\widehat x\) exactly solves \(B\widehat x=b-r\), so \(\|r\|/\|b\|\) is an exact right-hand-side relative backward-error certificate when \(b\ne0\). If \(B\) is nonsingular and \(x=B^{-1}b\), then in a subordinate norm \[\frac{\|\widehat x-x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa(B)\frac{\|r\|}{\|b\|}.\] Thus a small residual alone need not imply small forward error for an ill-conditioned basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled basis residual certifies backward accuracy, while forward accuracy additionally depends on the basis condition number.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is nonsingular.
The matrix and vector norms are compatible subordinate norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat x\text{ solves }B\widehat x=b-r,\quad \|\widehat x-x\|/\|x\|\le\kappa(B)\|r\|/\|b\|.

notation.meaning: condition number of the basis matrix in the declared norm

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Solve Residual Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates nominal pivot work from safeguards and precision escalation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a run performs \(N_p\) pivots, \(N_r\) full refactorizations, and \(N_f\) refinement steps at working precisions \(p_k\), then its charged work has the form \[W=W_{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=1}^{N_p}W_{\mathrm{pivot}}(p_k)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_r}W_{\mathrm{refac}}(p_j)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_f}W_{\mathrm{refine}}(p_\ell)+W_{\mathrm{verify}}.\] Consequently, a pivot-count bound alone gives no finite-precision or bit-complexity bound without bounds on safeguard counts, working precision, and precision-dependent operation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-precision work includes pivots, refinement, refactorization, verification, and precision-dependent arithmetic, so pivot count alone is insufficient.
assumptions_latex: All terms are charged in one declared arithmetic or bit-cost model.
\(p_k\) records the working precision of the corresponding operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Bounding }N_p\text{ alone does not bound }W.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Work Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A local reliability test for sign-dependent simplex decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q\) be an exact decision quantity and \(\widehat q\) its computed value with \(|\widehat q-q|\le\eta\). If \(\widehat q>\eta\), then \(q>0\); if \(\widehat q<-\eta\), then \(q<0\). When \(|\widehat q|\le\eta\), its sign is not certified and the implementation must treat the test as numerically ambiguous, refine the computation, or increase precision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed simplex test has a certified sign only when its distance from zero exceeds its justified error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(|\widehat q-q|\le\eta\) with \(\eta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat q>\eta\Rightarrow q>0,\qquad \widehat q<-\eta\Rightarrow q<0.
knowledge_statements.title: Certified Finite-Precision Sign Test
Finite-Precision Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision simplex work requires numerical separation and error control beyond exact-arithmetic pivot counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose every tableau quantity used in a sign, feasibility, or ratio-test decision is computed with absolute error at most \(\eta\), and every nonzero exact quantity entering such a decision has magnitude at least \(\delta\). If \(2\eta<\delta\), rounding cannot change its sign or confuse it with zero. When no positive separation \(\delta\) is available, finite-precision arithmetic may alter pivot eligibility, declare false degeneracy, or require refactorization and higher precision. Hence an exact-arithmetic pivot bound alone does not bound bit operations or numerical-recovery work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact pivot counts omit precision costs. Reliable pivot decisions require errors smaller than a positive separation from zero; degeneracy removes that margin.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta\ge 0\) bounds absolute computational error.
\(\delta>0\) bounds the magnitude of each relevant nonzero exact test quantity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(2\eta<\delta\) preserves the signs of relevant nonzero tests; without such separation, exact pivot complexity does not control finite-precision work.

source_refs.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: The Turing Machine and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited interior-point complexity section does not adequately support the simplex-specific sign, ratio-test, refactorization, and precision claims. The stated separation condition is sufficient, but its interpretation also depends on the zero-testing rule.

children.title: Pathology Interaction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where degeneracy, stalling, and numerical error reinforce or remain distinct from one another.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Universal Decision Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates primal degeneracy from a zero margin in every simplex comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible basis is degenerate when some basic component is zero. This alone does not imply that every reduced-cost or ratio-test comparison is tied. If a selected comparison value is separated from every alternative by \(\delta>0\), perturbing each compared scalar by less than \(\delta/2\) preserves the winner. Arbitrarily small perturbations can reverse the decision only when its comparison gap is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degeneracy alone does not make every pivot decision unstable; a positive comparison gap provides a positive robustness radius.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is primal feasible and degenerate.
The decision compares finitely many exact scalars.
The selected value is separated from every alternative by \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_i|\widehat v_i-v_i|<\delta/2\) preserves the selected candidate.

notation.meaning: gap between the selected value and its nearest alternative

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Universal Decision Instability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precise interaction boundary between exact pivot ties and finite-precision path changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a simplex decision compares two candidates with exact values \(v_1=v_2\), and the perturbed computation does not reproduce the exact tie rule. For every \(\tau>0\), perturbations \(|e_i|<\tau\) can make either \(v_1+e_1<v_2+e_2\) or \(v_1+e_1>v_2+e_2\). Thus the decision has no positive robustness radius, although this local sensitivity alone implies no bound on either resulting pivot path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact pivot tie can be broken either way by arbitrarily small perturbations, but this alone does not imply a long global pivot path.
assumptions_latex: Two candidates have equal exact comparison values.
The perturbed computation need not enforce the exact symbolic tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\tau>0\), perturbations smaller than \(\tau\) can reverse the comparison outcome.
knowledge_statements.title: Tied Pivot Decisions Are Perturbation-Sensitive
Pathology Interaction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy eliminates the numerical margin needed to transfer exact-arithmetic simplex behavior to floating-point computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a degenerate simplex basis, at least one basic variable or exact ratio-test quantity equals \(0\), so the decision margin \(\delta\) is zero. For every tolerance \(\tau>0\), perturbations of magnitude below \(\tau\) can then place that quantity on either side of zero, potentially changing the leaving variable, pivot path, and number of pivots. Therefore exact anti-cycling and finite-precision stability are separate requirements: finite termination in exact arithmetic does not by itself imply a stable or polynomially bounded floating-point implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At degeneracy the decision margin is zero, so arbitrarily small perturbations may change the pivot path; exact anti-cycling does not ensure numerical complexity control.
assumptions_latex: The simplex basis is degenerate.
Pivot decisions depend on comparisons with zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta=0\), and arbitrarily small perturbations may change the selected pivot and subsequent work.

notation.meaning: minimum exact decision margin from zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A degenerate basis has a zero basic variable, but this does not automatically make the decision margin zero for every particular pivot decision. A source is needed to delimit the perturbation and pivot-path claims precisely.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Only Arithmetic-Operation Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The arithmetic-operation component of strong polynomiality for rational linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational linear programs with \(m\) constraints and \(n\) variables, an algorithm has dimension-only arithmetic-operation control if there exists a polynomial \(p\), independent of all input coefficient values and their encoding lengths, such that every instance is solved or correctly classified after at most \(p(m,n)\) exact arithmetic operations and comparisons. The counted operations are additions, subtractions, multiplications, divisions, and order comparisons in the real-arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension-controlled LP algorithm uses at most a polynomial in the numbers of constraints and variables, regardless of coefficient bit lengths.
assumptions_latex: The input LP has rational data and dimensions \((m,n)\).
Arithmetic operations and comparisons have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ops}}\le p(m,n)\) for some polynomial \(p\) independent of the input values.

notation.meaning: number of arithmetic operations and comparisons

source_refs.locator: More on the Real-Number Model and Algebraic Complexity p. 60
Complexity of Simplex, Ellipsoid, and Interior-Point Methods p. 57

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate Encoding-Size Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bit-growth component required alongside a dimension-only arithmetic-operation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) be the binary encoding length of a rational LP instance. An exact-arithmetic algorithm has intermediate encoding-size control if there exists a polynomial \(q\) such that every rational number stored during its execution has numerator and denominator binary lengths at most \(q(L,m,n)\). Together with polynomially many arithmetic operations, this condition permits simulation in the Turing model with polynomial bit complexity; an operation-count bound alone does not provide that conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intermediate rational numerators and denominators must retain polynomial encoding length; otherwise few arithmetic operations can still require excessive bit work.
assumptions_latex: Input data and intermediate quantities are represented as reduced binary rationals.
\(L\) is the total input encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_t \operatorname{size}(z_t)\le q(L,m,n)\) for every stored intermediate rational \(z_t\).

notation.meaning: an intermediate rational at step t

knowledge_statements.title: Independence from Numerical Data Magnitudes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong polynomiality excludes operation bounds depending on coefficient values or their bit lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP algorithm applied to rational data \((A,b,c)\), numerical-magnitude independence means that a single polynomial \(p(m,n)\) bounds its arithmetic operations and comparisons for every choice of encoded values with those dimensions. In particular, the bound contains no factor involving \(\|A\|\), \(\|b\|\), \(\|c\|\), the largest numerator or denominator, or the input length \(L\). This requirement concerns the operation count; polynomial intermediate encoding size remains a separate necessary criterion for strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The arithmetic-operation bound must depend only on dimensions, not coefficient norms, bit lengths, numerators, denominators, or the total input length.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm accepts every rational LP of dimensions \((m,n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{ops}}(A,b,c)\le p(m,n)\) uniformly over all rational \((A,b,c)\) of those dimensions.

notation.meaning: constraint matrix, right-hand side, and objective data

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the complexity definition with the unrestricted-LP open boundary and the Gaussian-elimination comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An LP algorithm is strongly polynomial if it is polynomial in encoded input size and there is a fixed polynomial $p$ such that every rational LP with $m$ constraints and $n$ variables is solved using at most $p(m+n)$ arithmetic operations, independently of the numerical magnitudes. A suitable Gaussian-elimination implementation uses at most $Cn^3$ arithmetic operations and is strongly polynomial for square linear systems. No strongly polynomial algorithm is known for unrestricted linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires ordinary polynomial bit complexity and a polynomial bound in only the numbers of constraints and variables on arithmetic operations, independent of coefficient magnitudes. Gaussian elimination satisfies the analogous condition for square linear systems, while existence of such an algorithm for unrestricted LP remains open.
assumptions_latex: A,b,c\text{ are rational LP data}
m=\text{number of constraints},\quad n=\text{number of variables}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{arith}}(L)\le p(m+n)\ \text{and}\ T_{\mathrm{bit}}(L)\le q(\langle L\rangle);\quad \text{no such algorithm is known for unrestricted LP}

children.title: Bounded-Coefficient Regime
children.top_down_role: Strong-polynomial consequences tied to bounded combinatorial coefficient data.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tardos Bound in the Bounded-Coefficient Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong-polynomial consequence when the integer constraint matrix has dimension-controlled encoding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an LP with integer constraint matrix \(A\), the Tardos framework has an arithmetic-operation bound polynomial in \(m,n\), and the binary encoding length of \(A\), independent of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of the right-hand side and objective. If \(\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\) and \(\log\Delta\le\operatorname{poly}(m+n)\), this dependence is polynomially controlled by the dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tardos-type complexity ignores right-hand-side and objective magnitudes; bounded matrix coefficients make the remaining matrix dependence dimension controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
\(\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\).
\(\log\Delta\le\operatorname{poly}(m+n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,\log\Delta),\quad T\text{ independent of }\langle b\rangle,\langle c\rangle.

notation.meaning: encoding lengths of right-hand-side and objective data

knowledge_statements.title: Tardos Bound in the Bounded-Coefficient Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coefficient Parameter Must Be Dimension Controlled
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between parameterized matrix dependence and strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complexity bound polynomial in \(m,n,\log\Delta\) is not dimension-only when \(\Delta\) is unrestricted. A finite instancewise coefficient bound therefore does not alone prove strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coefficient-parameter bound is strongly polynomial only when its parameter dependence is controlled by dimension or eliminated.
assumptions_latex: The algorithmic bound has nonconstant dependence on \(\log\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta\text{ unrestricted}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{poly}(m,n,\log\Delta)\text{ need not be strongly polynomial}.
knowledge_statements.title: Coefficient Parameter Must Be Dimension Controlled
Bounded-Coefficient Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer constraint matrices whose entries are uniformly bounded by a structural parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer constraint matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) belongs to the bounded-coefficient regime with parameter \(\Delta\ge1\) when \(\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\). In the Tardos framework, complexity may depend polynomially on \(m\), \(n\), and the encoding size of \(A\), while remaining independent of the numerical magnitudes and encoding lengths of \(b\) and \(c\). If \(\Delta\) is fixed or polynomially bounded in \(m+n\), the matrix-data contribution is dimension controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The integer constraint entries are bounded by a parameter; Tardos-type bounds may depend on this matrix structure but not magnitudes of right-hand-side or objective data.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
\(\Delta\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|A\|_{\max}=\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-coefficient definition is sound, but the claims about Tardos-framework dependence and when matrix-data complexity becomes dimension controlled require a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Bounded-Subdeterminant Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes controlled by bounds on relevant matrix subdeterminants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic consequence of uniformly bounded nonsingular minors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) have every square minor bounded in absolute value by \(\Delta\), and let \(B\) be a nonsingular square submatrix. For integral \(b_B\), every coordinate of \(B^{-1}b_B\) has a reduced denominator dividing \(|\det B|\), and hence at most \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic solutions with integral right-hand sides have denominators bounded by the subdeterminant parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(b_B\) are integral.
\(B\) is a nonsingular square submatrix of \(A\).
Every square minor of \(A\) has absolute determinant at most \(\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{den}((B^{-1}b_B)_i)\mid|\det B|\le\Delta.

notation.meaning: positive denominator of a reduced rational number

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Denominators of Basic Solutions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The parameter-one specialization of the all-subdeterminants regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer matrix is totally unimodular exactly when every square subdeterminant belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\), equivalently when its largest absolute square subdeterminant is at most one. Consequently, for integral \(b\), every vertex of \(\{x:Ax\le b\}\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subdeterminant bound one is total unimodularity and yields integral vertices for integral right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is integral.
\(b\) is integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(A)\le1\Longleftrightarrow A\text{ is totally unimodular},\qquad\operatorname{vert}\{x:Ax\le b\}\subseteq\mathbb Z^n.

notation.meaning: largest absolute square subdeterminant of A

knowledge_statements.title: Totally Unimodular Specialization
Bounded-Subdeterminant Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer matrices whose square minors are uniformly bounded in absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is in the bounded-subdeterminant regime with parameter \(\Delta\ge1\) when every square submatrix \(A_{I,J}\) satisfies \(|\det(A_{I,J})|\le\Delta\), including all nonsingular minors of every order. Since the minors of order one are the entries of \(A\), this condition also implies \(|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\). The parameter controls determinant-based arithmetic quantities arising from bases and Cramer's rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every square minor has determinant at most the parameter in absolute value; this automatically bounds individual entries and determinants of basis submatrices.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
\(\Delta\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{I,J:\,|I|=|J|}|\det(A_{I,J})|\le\Delta\).

notation.meaning: square submatrix indexed by equally sized row and column sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and its implication for entries are standard and fit the container, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the bounded-subdeterminant regime or its computational interpretation.

children.title: Coefficient–Subdeterminant Regime Comparison
children.top_down_role: Containment, incomparability, parameter translation, and complexity implications across the two restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A boundary under which bounded coefficients yield uniformly bounded subdeterminants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(|A_{ij}|\le C\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\le r\), then every nonzero square minor has order \(k\le r\), and Hadamard's inequality gives \(|\det M|\le(\sqrt{k}C)^k\le(\sqrt r C)^r\). Thus fixed rank converts a coefficient bound into a uniform subdeterminant bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed rank, bounded coefficients imply bounded subdeterminants; without a rank bound the implication is not uniform.
assumptions_latex: \(\max_{i,j}|A_{ij}|\le C\).
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)\le r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta(A)\le(\sqrt r C)^r.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Rank Parameter Translation
Coefficient–Subdeterminant Regime Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform minor bounds imply entry bounds, whereas entry bounds alone permit determinants growing with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every square minor of \(A\) has absolute determinant at most \(\Delta\), then every entry satisfies \(|A_{ij}|\le\Delta\), because entries are first-order minors. Conversely, if \(|A_{ij}|\le C\), then Hadamard's inequality gives \(|\det M|\le(\sqrt{k}C)^k\) for each \(k\times k\) submatrix \(M\), but no dimension-independent subdeterminant bound follows. Indeed, the \(k\times k\) matrices with diagonal entries \(1\), superdiagonal entries \(1\), and all other entries \(-1\) have entries bounded by \(1\) and determinant magnitude \(2^{k-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform bound on all minors bounds entries, but bounded entries do not uniformly bound minors; determinants can grow exponentially with submatrix order.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is an integer matrix.
Subdeterminant bounds include minors of order one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{bounded subdeterminants}\Rightarrow\text{bounded coefficients}\), while the converse fails uniformly in dimension.

notation.meaning: a square submatrix of order k

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison, Hadamard bound, and displayed exponential-determinant family are mathematically plausible and appropriately classified as a property, but none has an inspectable citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Polynomial Solvability in the Totally Unimodular Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tardos's combinatorial-coefficient framework specialized to totally unimodular constraint matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular and \(b,c\) are rational, Tardos's combinatorial LP algorithm solves the problem or correctly reports infeasibility or unboundedness using \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n)\) arithmetic operations. The bound is independent of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of \(b\) and \(c\); total unimodularity fixes the relevant subdeterminant bound at \(\Delta=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tardos's algorithm is strongly polynomial for LPs with a totally unimodular constraint matrix, independently of the sizes of the right-hand side and objective coefficients.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular.
\(b\) and \(c\) are explicitly represented rational vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{ops}}\le \operatorname{poly}(m,n)\quad\text{independently of the magnitudes of }b\text{ and }c.

notation.meaning: number of arithmetic operations and comparisons
maximum absolute subdeterminant of the constraint matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Solvability in the Totally Unimodular Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure of the integral-vertex consequence when the right-hand side is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matrix \(B=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) is totally unimodular, but with \(d=(0,\tfrac12)^\top\), the polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R:Bx\le d\}=[0,\tfrac12]\) has the fractional vertex \(x=\tfrac12\). Thus total unimodularity alone does not imply integral vertices without an integral right-hand side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular constraint matrix can produce fractional vertices when the right-hand side is fractional.
assumptions_latex: \(B=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(d=(0,\tfrac12)^\top\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ is totally unimodular, but }\tfrac12\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\setminus\mathbb Z.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Right-Hand-Side Boundary
Totally Unimodular Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The unit-subdeterminant specialization central to combinatorial linear programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matrix \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) is totally unimodular if every square submatrix \(M\) has determinant in \(\{-1,0,1\}\). Equivalently, its maximum absolute subdeterminant is at most \(1\). Consequently, if \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), every basic feasible solution of \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) is integral whenever the selected basis matrix is nonsingular. This regime is therefore the case \(\Delta=1\) of bounded-subdeterminant structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A totally unimodular matrix has every square minor in minus one, zero, or one; integral right-hand sides then give integral basic feasible solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ is totally unimodular}\iff \det(M)\in\{-1,0,1\}\) for every square submatrix \(M\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost flow as an LP with a directed node–arc incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), node balances \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), arc costs \(c\in\mathbb R^E\), and capacities \(u\in(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\})^E\), a network-structured LP has the form \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Nx=b,\ 0\le x\le u\},\] where the column of the node–arc incidence matrix \(N\) for arc \(e=(v,w)\) contains \(-1\) in row \(v\), \(1\) in row \(w\), and zeros elsewhere. It does not by itself prove strong polynomiality, which requires an arithmetic-operation bound depending only on \(m\) and \(n\), together with polynomially bounded intermediate encoding lengths.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an LP algorithm has a guarantee of the form \(T(I,\varepsilon)\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n,\log\kappa(I),\log(1/\varepsilon))\), or a bound polynomial in \(\kappa(I)\) itself. This is a condition-dependent guarantee: instances farther from ill-posedness may be solved faster, while arbitrarily ill-conditioned instances may make the bound arbitrarily large even at fixed \(m\) and \(n\). Unless \(\kappa(I)\) and the required accuracy are bounded solely by a polynomial in the dimensions, such a result does not supply a strongly polynomial worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A runtime depending on an instance condition number can be useful but does not prove strong polynomiality when conditioning is unbounded at fixed dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Condition-Dependent Guarantees

source_witnesses.locator: 5.7 Equivalent formulations of the interior-point condition p. 99
source_witnesses.source_title: Interior Point Methods for Linear Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic boundary statement is plausible, but κ is not tied to a defined LP condition measure. The cited 'interior-point condition' section may concern a feasibility condition rather than condition-number complexity, so it does not inspectably support the claimed bound.

children.title: Pseudopolynomial Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Bounds polynomial in numeric magnitudes or related value parameters rather than solely combinatorial dimensions.

assumptions_latex: Integer or rational input data have maximum absolute numerator or denominator magnitude \(U\ge 2\).
The input uses binary encoding, so representing \(U\) requires only \(O(\log U)\) bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n,U)\) is pseudopolynomial and may be exponential in the binary input length.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary-encoding distinction between pseudopolynomial and polynomial LP bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A guarantee is pseudopolynomial when it has the form \(T\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n,U)\), where \(U\) is a numerical value or coefficient-magnitude bound rather than its encoding length. Because binary input length satisfies \(L\ge\log_2 U\), a polynomial in \(U\) can be exponential in \(L\). Such a guarantee can be effective for numerically bounded instances, but it is neither a general weakly polynomial bit-complexity guarantee nor a strongly polynomial guarantee unless the dependence on \(U\) can be replaced by an appropriate dimension-only bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudopolynomial LP bound is polynomial in numerical magnitudes, which can be exponential in their binary encoding length.
knowledge_statements.title: Pseudopolynomial Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity_bound kind and binary-encoding distinction are appropriate, but the record supplies no citation for its LP-specific pseudopolynomial classification.

children.title: Strong-Polynomiality Exclusion Boundary
children.top_down_role: Reasons these parameter-dependent guarantees do not resolve strong polynomiality for general linear programming.

assumptions_latex: An LP algorithm is required to solve every rational instance exactly, including correct infeasibility and unboundedness decisions.
Its stated resource bound contains an instance-dependent parameter \(q(I)\) not uniformly bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(m,n)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated bound alone cannot certify strong polynomiality while its dependence on \(q(I)\) remains.

notation.meaning: an encoding-, magnitude-, conditioning-, or accuracy-dependent parameter

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary exclusion test for claims of strongly polynomial LP complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the only available estimate is \(N_{\mathrm{op}}(I)\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n,q(I))\), where \(q(I)\) may be the encoding length, a coefficient magnitude, a condition number, or \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\), then the estimate does not establish strong polynomiality when \(q(I)\) is unbounded at fixed \(m,n\). To cross the strongly polynomial boundary, one must prove an arithmetic-operation bound \(N_{\mathrm{op}}(I)\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n)\) for every rational instance and also polynomially bound the encoding lengths of intermediate quantities. Instance-dependent good behavior alone is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound involving unbounded encoding, magnitude, conditioning, or accuracy parameters cannot by itself establish strongly polynomial LP complexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong-Polynomiality Exclusion Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits and the exclusion test is coherent, but the precise two-part criterion for strong polynomiality is a nontrivial claim requiring a cited source.

children.title: Average-Case Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Expected complexity under specified input distributions and probabilistic instance models.

assumptions_latex: LP instances \(I\) are sampled from a fully specified probability distribution \(\mathcal D_{m,n}\).
The nonnegative cost \(T(I)\) measures operations, pivots, or bit time under a fixed algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The bound \(\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D_{m,n}}[T(I)]\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n)\) does not imply \(\sup_I T(I)\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n)\).

notation.meaning: distribution over LP instances of the stated dimensions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional expected complexity versus worst-case exact LP complexity.

source_refs.locator: Polynomial Versus Exponential, Worst Case Versus Average Case p. 50

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An average-case polynomial guarantee for an LP algorithm is a bound \(\mathbb E_{I\sim\mathcal D_{m,n}}[T(I)]\le p(m,n)\) under a specified distribution \(\mathcal D_{m,n}\), for some polynomial \(p\). This controls expected resource use for that distribution but permits exceptional instances with superpolynomial or exponential cost. Therefore it does not imply the worst-case bound \(\sup_I T(I)\le p(m,n)\) required for a strongly polynomial algorithm on unrestricted inputs. Changing the distribution can also change the guarantee, so the distribution is part of the mathematical statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial expected runtime under a chosen input distribution allows rare hard instances and therefore does not establish a worst-case strongly polynomial algorithm.
knowledge_statements.title: Average-Case Guarantees

source_witnesses.locator: Polynomial Versus Exponential, Worst Case Versus Average Case p. 50

children.title: Smoothed Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Complexity after controlled random perturbations of adversarial base instances.

assumptions_latex: An adversary chooses a normalized LP instance \(I\), after which its data receive an independent perturbation \(G_\sigma\) of scale \(\sigma>0\).
The resource cost \(T(I+G_\sigma)\) is measured for a fixed algorithm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bound polynomial in \(m,n,1/\sigma\) does not yield a dimension-only worst-case bound as \(\sigma\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic smoothed complexity under small random perturbations of adversarial LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smoothed complexity guarantee has the form \(\sup_{I}\mathbb E[T(I+G_\sigma)]\le\operatorname{poly}(m,n,1/\sigma)\), where \(I\) is an adversarial normalized LP instance and \(G_\sigma\) is a specified random perturbation of scale \(\sigma\). It shows that small random perturbations suppress difficult behavior in expectation. Because the bound may diverge as \(\sigma\downarrow0\), it does not control the unperturbed worst case and therefore does not establish strong polynomiality for every exact rational input. The perturbation law, normalization, and resource measure must be specified for the guarantee to be meaningful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smoothed polynomial complexity controls randomly perturbed instances but may deteriorate as perturbations vanish, so it does not imply worst-case strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Guarantees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits, but the displayed smoothed bound depends on normalization, perturbation law, and resource measure that are not fixed. No source is supplied to validate this particular formulation.

children.title: Approximate Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Complexity for prescribed approximate feasibility, optimality, or certificate targets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the approximation task without an invalid logarithmic normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization LP with nonempty feasible region \(P\), finite optimum \(v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\), an exactly feasible additive \(\varepsilon\)-solution is a point \(\hat x\in P\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-v^*\le\varepsilon\). If \(c=0\), every feasible point is a \(0\)-solution. If \(L\le v^*\le c^{\mathsf T}x\le U\) for every \(x\in P\), then every feasible point is an additive \(\varepsilon\)-solution whenever \(\varepsilon\ge U-L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive approximation requires exact feasibility and objective gap at most epsilon; zero objectives and tolerances covering the objective range need no logarithmic accuracy term.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty.
The optimum \(v^*\) is finite.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \hat x\in P,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-v^*\le\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the feasible objective range

knowledge_statements.title: Exactly Feasible Additive Objective Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why high-accuracy approximation does not itself establish strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose exact recovery from an additive approximation is justified only for \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta(A,b,c)\), where \(\Delta\) is an instance-dependent positive separation threshold. If only a bound \(\Delta\ge 2^{-p(L)}\) is available for a polynomial \(p\) of the binary input length \(L\), then choosing recovery accuracy in an algorithm polynomial in \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) introduces encoding-length dependence. Such an approximation guarantee alone therefore does not yield a strongly polynomial exact LP algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact recovery may require exponentially small tolerance, converting logarithmic accuracy dependence into input-length dependence.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational with binary encoding length \(L\).
Exact recovery requires \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta(A,b,c)\).
The approximation bound depends on \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta\ge 2^{-p(L)}\text{ only}\Longrightarrow\log(1/\varepsilon)=O(p(L))\text{ at recovery accuracy, not a dimension-only bound}.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-to-Exactness Dependence on Encoding Length

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicative Approximation Is Not Objective-Shift Invariant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on relative objective guarantees for general LP objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[0,1]\) and \(f(x)=x\), with optimum \(v^*=0\). The condition \(f(\hat x)\le(1+\varepsilon)v^*\) forces \(\hat x=0\). For the equivalent shifted objective \(f_K(x)=x+K\), where \(K>0\), the optimizer is unchanged, but \(f_K(\hat x)\le(1+\varepsilon)K\) permits every \(\hat x\le\min\{1,\varepsilon K\}\). Thus an unnormalized multiplicative objective guarantee is not invariant under additive objective shifts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative objective approximation can change under an irrelevant constant shift, so it requires explicit sign and normalization assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}f=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}f_K,\qquad\text{but their multiplicative acceptance sets differ}.

notation.meaning: objective f shifted by the constant K

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicative Approximation Is Not Objective-Shift Invariant
Approximate Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity guarantee for additive approximation of a bounded rational linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over a nonempty rational polytope \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) contained in a known ball of radius \(R\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), polynomial-time LP methods can return a feasible \(\hat x\in P\) satisfying \[c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\le\varepsilon.\] Their bit-operation count is polynomial in \(m\), \(n\), the input encoding length \(L\), and \(\log(R\lVert c\rVert_2/\varepsilon)\). Dependence on \(L\) or \(\log(1/\varepsilon)\) prevents this guarantee alone from establishing a strongly polynomial exact LP algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Additive LP approximation is polynomial in dimensions, encoding length, and logarithmic accuracy, but those numerical dependencies do not establish exact strong polynomiality.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty, bounded, and rationally encoded.
A valid radius bound \(R\) and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c^{\mathsf T}\hat x-v^*\le\varepsilon\), with bit complexity polynomial in \(m,n,L,\log(R\lVert c\rVert_2/\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the rational LP data
known Euclidean radius bound for the feasible region

children.title: Worst-Case Exactness Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits preventing distributional, smoothed, or approximate results from settling exact worst-case strong polynomiality.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Exactness Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical boundary separating non-worst-case or approximate results from strong-polynomial exact solvability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A guarantee settles worst-case exact strong polynomiality for linear programming only if, for every rational LP instance, it returns an exact optimizer or an exact infeasibility or unboundedness certificate using a number of arithmetic operations bounded by a polynomial in \(m+n\), independently of coefficient magnitudes and encoding length, while all intermediate numbers have polynomially bounded encoding length. An average-case, smoothed, high-probability, or \(\varepsilon\)-approximate bound that lacks any one of these requirements does not imply such an algorithm, even when its expected or perturbed running time is polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong polynomiality requires exact, dimension-polynomial worst-case performance on every instance; average, smoothed, probabilistic, or approximate guarantees do not by themselves meet it.
assumptions_latex: The input is a rational linear program in a finite binary encoding.
Arithmetic and intermediate-number growth are both included in the complexity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A guarantee omitting universal worst-case coverage, exact output, dimension-only operation bounds, or controlled intermediate encoding does not establish strong polynomiality.
