children.title: Primal Feasibility Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Distance, sensitivity, and robustness measures for primal feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise conditioning of the feasibility status of an inequality system under an explicitly fixed data space and norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite-dimensional normed data space for \(D=(A,b)\), let \(\mathcal F_P=\{D:\exists x,\ Ax\le b\}\), and define the primal ill-posed set by \(\Sigma_P=\partial\mathcal F_P\). Then \[\rho_P(D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma_P),\qquad \kappa_P(D)=\frac{\lVert D\rVert}{\rho_P(D)},\] with \(\kappa_P(D)=+\infty\) when \(\rho_P(D)=0\). For \(D\notin\Sigma_P\), \(\rho_P(D)\) is the radius of the largest open data ball about \(D\) on which primal feasibility status is unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing the perturbation space and norm, primal feasibility conditioning is data size divided by distance to the boundary between feasible and infeasible systems.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(A,b)\) ranges over a fixed finite-dimensional data space with a fixed norm.
Feasibility means existence of \(x\) satisfying the displayed weak inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_P(D)>0\) exactly off the feasibility boundary, while \(\kappa_P(D)=+\infty\) on that boundary.

notation.meaning: boundary of the primal-feasible data set

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Distance-to-Ill-Posedness Condition
Primal Feasibility Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-ill-posedness condition number for an inequality feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For data \(D_P=(A,b)\), let \(F_P(D_P)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\). Let \(\Sigma_P\) be the boundary, in the chosen data norm, between instances having \(F_P(D_P)\ne\varnothing\) and instances having \(F_P(D_P)=\varnothing\). Define \[\rho_P(D_P)=\operatorname{dist}(D_P,\Sigma_P),\qquad \kappa_P(D_P)=\frac{\lVert D_P\rVert}{\rho_P(D_P)}.\] The convention is \(\kappa_P(D_P)=+\infty\) when \(\rho_P(D_P)=0\). Thus \(\rho_P\) is the smallest normwise perturbation that can reach primal ill-posedness, and large \(\kappa_P\) indicates fragile primal feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility conditioning is data size divided by the distance to systems lying on the boundary between feasible and infeasible instances.
assumptions_latex: A norm on the product data space of \((A,b)\) is fixed.
Feasibility includes weak inequalities and permits boundary feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_P(D_P)=\lVert D_P\rVert/\operatorname{dist}(D_P,\Sigma_P)\), with value \(+\infty\) on \(\Sigma_P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition-number role fits, but distance-to-ill-posedness depends materially on the selected perturbation space, norm, and definition of the primal ill-posed set. No source establishes those conventions.

children.title: Dual Feasibility Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Distance, sensitivity, and robustness measures for dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-ill-posedness for one explicitly fixed dual conic feasibility convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix the dual feasibility system
\[F_D(A,c)=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=c\}.\]
In a declared product norm on \((A,c)\), let \(\Sigma_D\) be the boundary between data with \(F_D(A,c)\ne\varnothing\) and data with \(F_D(A,c)=\varnothing\). Define
\[\rho_D(A,c)=\operatorname{dist}((A,c),\Sigma_D),\qquad
\kappa_D(A,c)=\frac{\lVert(A,c)\rVert}{\rho_D(A,c)},\]
with \(\kappa_D=+\infty\) when \(\rho_D=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility conditioning is data magnitude divided by the distance to the boundary where feasibility status can change, under a fixed conic sign convention and data norm.
assumptions_latex: The dual convention is \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\).
A product norm on \((A,c)\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_D(A,c)=\lVert(A,c)\rVert/\operatorname{dist}((A,c),\Sigma_D).
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Distance Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Status interpretation of positive and zero distance to dual ill-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\rho_D(A,c)>0\), every perturbation of \((A,c)\) with norm strictly below \(\rho_D(A,c)\) preserves dual feasibility status. If \(\rho_D(A,c)=0\), arbitrarily small data perturbations reach instances of the opposite status, and no positive robustness radius exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive distance protects dual feasibility status; zero distance is exactly the unstable boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(\Sigma_D\) is the feasibility-status boundary in the declared data norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_D>0\Rightarrow\text{status is locally invariant};\qquad\rho_D=0\Rightarrow\text{no positive status-invariance radius}.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Feasibility Robustness Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric and alternative-system representations of the fixed dual feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Writing \(a_i^{\mathsf T}\) for row \(i\) of \(A\),
\[F_D(A,c)\ne\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_1,\ldots,a_m\}.\]
Equivalently, by the theorem of alternatives,
\[F_D(A,c)=\varnothing\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists z\in\mathbb R^n:\ Az\ge0,\ c^{\mathsf T}z<0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility means that the objective vector lies in the cone generated by the rows of the constraint matrix; infeasibility has a strict separating-vector certificate.
assumptions_latex: The convention is \(y\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_D(A,c)\ne\varnothing\iff c\in\operatorname{cone}\{a_i\};\quad F_D(A,c)=\varnothing\iff\exists z:Az\ge0,\ c^{\mathsf T}z<0.

notation.meaning: transpose of row i of A, viewed in objective space

knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Hull Feasibility Representation
Dual Feasibility Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-to-ill-posedness condition number for dual equality feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dual-feasibility data \(D_D=(A,c)\), let \(F_D(D_D)=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:y\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y=c\}\). Let \(\Sigma_D\) be the boundary, in the chosen data norm, between instances having \(F_D(D_D)\ne\varnothing\) and instances having \(F_D(D_D)=\varnothing\). Define \[\rho_D(D_D)=\operatorname{dist}(D_D,\Sigma_D),\qquad \kappa_D(D_D)=\frac{\lVert D_D\rVert}{\rho_D(D_D)},\] with \(\kappa_D(D_D)=+\infty\) when \(\rho_D(D_D)=0\). It measures the relative perturbation margin protecting the dual feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual feasibility conditioning divides dual-data size by the distance to the boundary separating feasible and infeasible dual systems.
assumptions_latex: A norm on the product data space of \((A,c)\) is fixed.
The dual sign convention is \(y\ge0\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y=c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_D(D_D)=\lVert D_D\rVert/\operatorname{dist}(D_D,\Sigma_D)\), with value \(+\infty\) on \(\Sigma_D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical version depends on the LP sign convention and on the precise perturbation model for (A,c). No source supports the stated dual system or boundary definition.

children.title: Joint Feasibility Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Relations between primal and dual feasibility margins, perturbations, and ill-posedness.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint primal-dual robustness defined directly on the complete LP data space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D=(A,b,c)\). Lift the primal and dual ill-posed sets to full data space by
\[\widehat\Sigma_P=\{(A,b,c):(A,b)\in\Sigma_P\},\qquad
\widehat\Sigma_D=\{(A,b,c):(A,c)\in\Sigma_D\},\]
and define
\[\Sigma_{PD}=\widehat\Sigma_P\cup\widehat\Sigma_D,\qquad
\rho_{PD}(D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma_{PD}),\qquad
\kappa_{PD}(D)=\frac{\lVert D\rVert}{\rho_{PD}(D)},\]
with \(\kappa_{PD}=+\infty\) when \(\rho_{PD}=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint feasibility conditioning measures the distance of the full LP data to either the primal or the dual feasibility boundary.
assumptions_latex: Primal and dual ill-posed sets use fixed compatible conventions.
A norm on the full data triple \((A,b,c)\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{PD}(D)=\operatorname{dist}(D,\widehat\Sigma_P\cup\widehat\Sigma_D).

notation.meaning: joint ill-posed set in full data space

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Data Joint Feasibility Radius

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint failure when exactly one feasibility component reaches its boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If either \(\rho_P(A,b)=0\) or \(\rho_D(A,c)=0\), then \(\rho_{PD}(D)=0\) and \(\kappa_{PD}(D)=+\infty\), even when the other component has positive robustness radius. Thus joint robustness requires both component radii to be positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One ill-posed component makes the entire primal-dual feasibility system jointly ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: The compatible aggregation of Component-Radius Aggregation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\{\rho_P,\rho_D\}=0\Rightarrow\rho_{PD}=0\text{ and }\kappa_{PD}=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Joint Ill-Posedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between full-data and component feasibility radii under a compatible block norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose the full-data norm is a compatible block-maximum norm for which distance to \(\widehat\Sigma_P\) equals \(\rho_P(A,b)\) and distance to \(\widehat\Sigma_D\) equals \(\rho_D(A,c)\). Then
\[\rho_{PD}(D)=\min\{\rho_P(A,b),\rho_D(A,c)\}.\]
Using the common numerator \(\lVert D\rVert\), define \(\widehat\kappa_P(D)=\lVert D\rVert/\rho_P(A,b)\) and \(\widehat\kappa_D(D)=\lVert D\rVert/\rho_D(A,c)\). Then
\[\kappa_{PD}(D)=\max\{\widehat\kappa_P(D),\widehat\kappa_D(D)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a compatible block norm and common normalization, the nearer component boundary controls the joint radius and the larger component condition number controls joint conditioning.
assumptions_latex: The full-data block norm induces the stated component distances.
All relative condition numbers use the common numerator \(\lVert D\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{PD}=\min\{\rho_P,\rho_D\},\qquad\kappa_{PD}=\max\{\widehat\kappa_P,\widehat\kappa_D\}.

notation.meaning: component radii normalized by the common full-data norm

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Radius Aggregation
Joint Feasibility Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined condition number governed by the more fragile primal or dual feasibility system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For LP data \(D=(A,b,c)\), compute the primal and dual distances \(\rho_P(A,b)\) and \(\rho_D(A,c)\) using compatible product norms. Define the joint relative feasibility condition number by \[\kappa_{PD}(D)=\max\{\kappa_P(A,b),\kappa_D(A,c)\}.\] Equivalently, under separate normalization \(\lVert(A,b)\rVert=\lVert(A,c)\rVert=1\), \(\kappa_{PD}(D)=1/\min\{\rho_P(A,b),\rho_D(A,c)\}\). Hence joint conditioning is finite exactly when both component systems have positive distance from their respective ill-posed sets; the less stable side controls the joint measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint feasibility conditioning is the worse of the primal and dual condition numbers, so the nearer ill-posedness boundary controls stability.
assumptions_latex: Primal and dual condition numbers use compatible norms and the same scaling convention.
Both component data blocks are nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_{PD}(D)=\max\{\kappa_P(A,b),\kappa_D(A,c)\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Defining joint conditioning as the maximum of two separately normalized condition numbers is convention-dependent. The claimed reciprocal-distance equivalence requires exact norm and normalization hypotheses not established by a source.

children.title: Optimal-Solution Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Stability and sensitivity of optimal solutions or optimal faces under perturbation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hausdorff Discontinuity at an Objective Tie
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical collapse of a nontrivial optimal face under an arbitrarily small objective perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=[-1,1]\) and \(S(c)=\arg\min_{x\in P}cx\). Then
\[S(0)=[-1,1],\qquad S(c)=\{-1\}\quad(c>0),\]
and
\[d_H(S(c),S(0))=2\quad(c>0).\]
Thus \(S(c)\) does not converge to \(S(0)\) in Hausdorff distance as \(c\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily small perturbation can collapse an optimal interval to one endpoint while its Hausdorff displacement remains fixed.
assumptions_latex: Hausdorff distance is induced by absolute value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c\downarrow0\not\Rightarrow d_H(S(c),S(0))\to0.

notation.meaning: optimizer set for scalar objective c

knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff Discontinuity at an Objective Tie

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric local conditioning of the optimizer set under objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a compact polytope \(P\), effective objective space \(L\), and \(S(g)=\arg\min_{x\in P}g^{\mathsf T}x\), define
\[\operatorname{cond}_H S(g)=\limsup_{\substack{d\to0\\d\in L,\ d\ne0}}
\frac{d_H(S(g+d),S(g))}{\lVert d\rVert_*}.\]
This symmetric modulus detects both newly appearing optimizers and disappearance of members of the current optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hausdorff optimizer conditioning measures symmetric solution-set displacement per unit effective objective perturbation.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
Hausdorff distance uses a fixed primal norm and objective perturbations use its dual norm.
Perturbations are restricted to the effective objective space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cond}_H S(g)\in[0,+\infty].
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff Optimizer-Map Modulus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable unique-vertex regime versus discontinuous tied-optimum regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume \(P\) contains at least two points. If \(S(g)=\{x^*\}\), then \(S\) is locally constant at \(g\), so
\[\operatorname{cond}_H S(g)=0.\]
If \(S(g)\) contains more than one point, arbitrarily small generic objective perturbations select proper subfaces at a fixed positive Hausdorff distance from \(S(g)\), and
\[\operatorname{cond}_H S(g)=+\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed polytope under objective perturbations, a unique optimizer is locally constant, while a nontrivial optimal face is Hausdorff-ill-conditioned.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope containing at least two points.
The Hausdorff optimizer-map modulus is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S(g)|=1\Rightarrow\operatorname{cond}_H S(g)=0,\qquad |S(g)|>1\Rightarrow\operatorname{cond}_H S(g)=+\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Optimizer-Conditioning Dichotomy
Optimal-Solution Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local set-valued Lipschitz conditioning of the optimizer map under objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope and \(S(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). The local outer-Lipschitz condition modulus of the optimal-solution map at \(c\) is \[\operatorname{cond}_S(c)=\limsup_{\substack{d\to0\\d\ne0}}\frac{e(S(c+d),S(c))}{\lVert d\rVert_*},\qquad e(U,V)=\sup_{u\in U}\operatorname{dist}(u,V).\] A finite value bounds the first-order displacement of every optimizer created by a small objective perturbation; an infinite value records failure of this local stability property. The modulus depends on the chosen primal norm and its dual objective norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimal-solution conditioning measures the worst local optimizer-set displacement per unit objective perturbation, using excess distance between solution sets.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
The primal norm and its dual norm are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e(S(c+d),S(c))\le(\operatorname{cond}_S(c)+o(1))\lVert d\rVert_*\) as \(d\to0\), when the modulus is finite.

notation.meaning: set of minimizers for objective vector \(c\)
one-sided excess of set \(U\) over set \(V\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a fixed polytope, sufficiently small objective perturbations expose faces contained in the original exposed face, so the one-sided excess e(S(c+d),S(c)) can be identically zero even when optimizers disappear. This modulus therefore does not measure the claimed optimizer-set sensitivity and is unsuitable for this terminal container.

children.title: Objective-Data Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity associated with perturbations to objective coefficients and objective orientation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative distance of effective objective data from objectives producing an optimal tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a compact polytope containing at least two points, let \(L=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\), and work in the effective objective space \(L\). Define
\[\Sigma_{\rm obj}(P)=\{g\in L:|\arg\min_{x\in P}g^{\mathsf T}x|>1\}.\]
For \(g\ne0\), set
\[\rho_{\rm obj}(P,g)=\operatorname{dist}_*(g,\Sigma_{\rm obj}(P)),\qquad
\kappa_{\rm obj}(P,g)=\frac{\lVert g\rVert_*}{\rho_{\rm obj}(P,g)},\]
with \(\kappa_{\rm obj}=+\infty\) when \(\rho_{\rm obj}=0\). Then \(\kappa_{\rm obj}(P,\lambda g)=\kappa_{\rm obj}(P,g)\) for every \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-data conditioning is the effective objective magnitude divided by the distance to the nearest objective tie.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with at least two points.
Objective data are measured in the effective space \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa_{\rm obj}(P,\lambda g)=\kappa_{\rm obj}(P,g)\quad(\lambda>0).
knowledge_statements.title: Effective Objective-Degeneracy Condition Number

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Removal of objective components constant on the feasible affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\ne\varnothing\) and \(L=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\). If \(a\in L^\perp\), then \(a^{\mathsf T}x\) is constant on \(P\), so
\[\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+a)^{\mathsf T}x=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x.\]
Optimizer-relevant objective data therefore belong to \(\mathbb R^n/L^\perp\), represented after choosing an inner product by the projection of \(c\) onto \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective components orthogonal to every feasible direction carry no optimizer information and should be removed before measuring objective conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\).
An inner product is fixed for the projection representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\in L^\perp\Rightarrow S(c+a)=S(c).
knowledge_statements.title: Effective Objective Quotient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation of objective degeneracy and its perturbation radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the effective objective space, the objectives uniquely minimized at a vertex \(x^*\) form the relative interior of its minimizing normal cone \(N_P^-(x^*)\). The degeneracy set \(\Sigma_{\rm obj}(P)\) is the union of the boundaries separating these vertex cones. Hence, when \(g\) uniquely selects \(x^*\),
\[\rho_{\rm obj}(P,g)=\operatorname{dist}_*\bigl(g,\partial_L N_P^-(x^*)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nearest objective tie is the nearest boundary of the vertex normal cone containing the effective objective.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with at least two points.
All cones, interiors, and boundaries are taken relative to the effective objective space \(L\).
\(g\) uniquely minimizes at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{\rm obj}(P,g)=\operatorname{dist}_*(g,\partial_LN_P^-(x^*)).

notation.meaning: minimizing normal cone at x star
boundary relative to the effective objective space

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Fan Boundary Representation
Objective-Data Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative distance of an objective vector from objectives with nonunique minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a nonempty compact polytope \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\), and let \(S(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). Define the objective-degeneracy set \(\Sigma_{m obj}(P)=\{q\in\mathbb R^n:|S(q)|>1\}\). For \(c\ne0\), the objective-data condition number is \[\kappa_{m obj}(P,c)=\frac{\lVert c\rVert_*}{\operatorname{dist}_*(c,\Sigma_{m obj}(P))},\] with value \(+\infty\) when the denominator is zero. It quantifies the relative objective perturbation required to reach a tie between distinct feasible minimizers and is unchanged by positive scalar rescaling of \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective-data conditioning compares objective magnitude with the nearest perturbation producing multiple optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(c\ne0\), and a dual norm on objective space is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_{m obj}(P,\alpha c)=\kappa_{m obj}(P,c)\) for every \(\alpha>0\).

notation.meaning: objectives having more than one minimizer on \(P\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed conic degeneracy-set condition number is plausible and fits the leaf, but its precise convention, treatment of the zero objective, and interpretation as established conditioning theory require an authoritative source.

children.title: Optimal-Value Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity and stability of the optimal value across nearby instances.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for differentiability of the objective-value function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P=[-1,1]\),
\[v(c)=\min_{x\in[-1,1]}cx=-|c|.\]
At \(c=0\), the optimizer set is \([-1,1]\), the directional derivative is \(v'(0;d)=-|d|\), and \(v\) is not differentiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial optimal face can give different directional value slopes and destroy differentiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(0)=[-1,1]\quad\text{and}\quad v\text{ is not differentiable at }0.
knowledge_statements.title: Nondifferentiability at Multiple Optimizers

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global and Pointwise Value Lipschitz Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise conditioning of the optimal value under objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a nonempty compact polytope and \(v(c)=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). Then
\[|v(c_1)-v(c_2)|\le\Bigl(\max_{x\in P}\lVert x\rVert\Bigr)\lVert c_1-c_2\rVert_*.\]
Define the pointwise calmness modulus
\[\operatorname{clm}v(c)=\limsup_{d\to0,\ d\ne0}\frac{|v(c+d)-v(c)|}{\lVert d\rVert_*}.\]
With \(S(c)=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\),
\[\operatorname{clm}v(c)=\max_{x\in S(c)}\lVert x\rVert.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value function is globally Lipschitz, and its pointwise calmness modulus is the largest norm of a current optimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
The objective norm is dual to the norm on feasible points.
The pointwise modulus is explicitly the calmness modulus displayed above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{clm}v(c)=\max_{x\in S(c)}\lVert x\rVert.

notation.meaning: optimal value as a function of objective data

knowledge_statements.title: Global and Pointwise Value Lipschitz Bounds

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Derivative of the Objective Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order value sensitivity to objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every direction \(d\),
\[v'(c;d)=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{v(c+td)-v(c)}{t}=\min_{x\in S(c)}d^{\mathsf T}x.\]
In particular, if \(S(c)=\{x^*\}\), then \(v\) is differentiable at \(c\) and \(\nabla v(c)=x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional value change minimizes the perturbing objective over the current optimal face; a unique optimizer is the value gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v'(c;d)=\min_{x\in S(c)}d^{\mathsf T}x,\qquad S(c)=\{x^*\}\Rightarrow\nabla v(c)=x^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Derivative of the Objective Value
Optimal-Value Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz modulus of the LP value as the objective varies over a fixed polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope and \(v(c)=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). With a primal norm and its dual objective norm, \(v\) is globally Lipschitz and satisfies \[|v(c+d)-v(c)|\le\Bigl(\max_{x\in P}\lVert x\rVert\Bigr)\lVert d\rVert_*.\] Its pointwise local Lipschitz modulus is \[\operatorname{lip}v(c)=\max_{x\in S(c)}\lVert x\rVert,\qquad S(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x.\] Thus value sensitivity is controlled by the norm of active optimal solutions, rather than by objective magnitude alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal value changes Lipschitz-continuously with the objective; its local modulus is the largest norm among current optimal solutions.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
The objective norm is dual to the norm used on feasible points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lip}v(c)=\max_{x\in S(c)}\lVert x\rVert\).

notation.meaning: pointwise local Lipschitz modulus of the value function

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global Lipschitz bound is standard, but the exact equality for the pointwise local modulus depends on whether lip denotes a two-point local Lipschitz modulus, calmness modulus, or another convention. A source and explicit definition are required.

children.title: Objective–Optimizer Sensitivity Link
children.top_down_role: How objective perturbations, solution geometry, and value stability influence one another.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite certificate for preservation of a unique vertex optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V(P)\) be the vertex set of a compact polytope and let \(x^*\in V(P)\) uniquely minimize \(g^{\mathsf T}x\). Then
\[\rho(g,x^*)=
\min_{v\in V(P)\setminus\{x^*\}}
\frac{g^{\mathsf T}(v-x^*)}{\lVert v-x^*\rVert},\]
where the objective norm is dual to the displayed primal norm. Therefore any perturbation \(d\) smaller than this positive margin preserves the unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unique optimizer is stable up to the smallest normalized objective gap between it and another vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with at least two vertices.
\(x^*\) uniquely minimizes \(g^{\mathsf T}x\).
The objective and primal norms are dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert d\rVert_*<\min_{v\ne x^*}\frac{g^{\mathsf T}(v-x^*)}{\lVert v-x^*\rVert}\Rightarrow S(g+d)=\{x^*\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Gap Stability Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of point-valued optimizer invariance at a nontrivial optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(S(g)\) contains more than one point, then \(g\) lies on the boundary of normal-fan regions. Arbitrarily small generic effective objective perturbations select a proper exposed subface of \(S(g)\), so no positive radius can preserve the original optimizer set or identify one designated member of it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an objective tie, arbitrarily small objective perturbations can select a proper part of the current optimal face.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with at least two points.
\(S(g)\) is nontrivial.
Perturbations are allowed in the effective objective space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |S(g)|>1\Rightarrow\text{no positive optimizer-set invariance radius exists}.
knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Boundary Optimizer Instability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact link between objective perturbation size and preservation of a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a compact polytope with at least two points, work in \(L=\operatorname{span}(P-P)\), and suppose \(x^*\) uniquely minimizes \(g^{\mathsf T}x\). Define
\[\rho(g,x^*)=\operatorname{dist}_*\bigl(g,\partial_LN_P^-(x^*)\bigr).\]
Then \(\rho(g,x^*)>0\), every \(d\in L\) with \(\lVert d\rVert_*<\rho(g,x^*)\) preserves \(x^*\) as the unique optimizer, and perturbations of arbitrarily near size \(\rho(g,x^*)\) can reach an objective tie. Thus \(\rho(g,x^*)\) is the exact open-ball invariance radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance from an objective to the boundary of its vertex normal cone is exactly the radius within which the unique optimizer cannot change.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a compact polytope with at least two points.
Objective data and perturbations lie in the effective space \(L\).
\(x^*\) uniquely minimizes the current objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert d\rVert_*<\rho(g,x^*)\Rightarrow\arg\min_{x\in P}(g+d)^{\mathsf T}x=\{x^*\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Optimizer-Invariance Radius
Objective–Optimizer Sensitivity Link
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-cone margin characterizes local invariance of a unique LP optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty compact polytope, let \(x^*\) uniquely minimize \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\), and define the minimizing normal cone \(N_P^-(x^*)=\{q:q^{\mathsf T}(x-x^*)\ge0\ \text{for all }x\in P\}\). Set \[\rho(c,x^*)=\operatorname{dist}_*\bigl(c,\mathbb R^n\setminus N_P^-(x^*)\bigr).\] If \(\rho(c,x^*)>0\), then every perturbation \(d\) with \(\lVert d\rVert_*<\rho(c,x^*)\) leaves \(x^*\) as the unique optimizer. If \(\rho(c,x^*)=0\), arbitrarily small objective perturbations can leave this optimizer’s normal cone, so no positive invariance radius exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance of the objective to the boundary of the optimizer’s normal cone is exactly its local objective-perturbation stability radius.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(x^*\) is the unique minimizer for \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert d\rVert_*<\rho(c,x^*)\Rightarrow S(c+d)=\{x^*\}\), and \(\rho(c,x^*)=0\) precludes a positive invariance radius.

notation.meaning: normal cone using the minimization sign convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normal-cone stability statement is plausible, but it lacks a source and does not address the singleton-polytope case, where the complement of the normal cone is empty and the displayed distance needs a convention.

children.title: Scaling Dependence
children.top_down_role: Variation of condition measures under row, column, variable, or objective rescaling.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative dependence of an inequality residual error-bound constant on positive row scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\le b\}\), \(r(x)=\|(Ax-b)_+\|_\infty\), and let \(H\) be the least constant satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H r(x)\) for all \(x\). For a positive diagonal matrix \(R=\operatorname{diag}(r_i)\), the scaled system \(R(Ax-b)\le0\) defines the same set and has residual \(r_R(x)=\|R(Ax-b)_+\|_\infty\). If \(0<r_{\min}\le r_i\le r_{\max}\), then its least constant \(H_R\) satisfies \[\frac{H}{r_{\max}}\le H_R\le\frac{H}{r_{\min}}.\] In particular, for \(R=\alpha I\), \(H_R=H/\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive row scaling preserves the feasible set but changes fixed-coordinate residual error-bound constants; uniform scaling changes the constant inversely.
assumptions_latex: The same norm is used for distance before and after scaling.
All diagonal entries of \(R\) are strictly positive.
The unscaled global error-bound constant \(H\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H/r_{\max}\le H_R\le H/r_{\min}\), with \(H_{\alpha I}=H/\alpha\).

notation.meaning: least unscaled and scaled error-bound constants

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error-Bound Scaling Law
Scaling Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raw distance-based condition numbers generally depend on equivalent row and variable scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) encode an LP and let \(\kappa_{m raw}(D)=\lVert D\rVert/\operatorname{dist}(D,\Sigma)\) for an ill-posed set \(\Sigma\) and a fixed coordinate norm. Positive diagonal row scaling and invertible diagonal variable scaling produce equivalent formulations \(D'=T_{R,S}(D)\) with the same feasibility and optimality content after the corresponding variable transformation. In general, \[\kappa_{m raw}(T_{R,S}(D))\ne\kappa_{m raw}(D),\] because the transformation changes both the data norm and distances to \(\Sigma\). Consequently, a complexity estimate expressed through \(\kappa_{m raw}\) must specify its scaling convention or optimize over admissible scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent row or variable scalings can change a coordinate-based condition number, so its normalization must be stated explicitly.
assumptions_latex: Row scalings are positive diagonal and variable scalings are invertible diagonal.
The raw condition number uses a fixed coordinate norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent LP formulations may have unequal values of \(\kappa_{m raw}\).

notation.meaning: equivalence transformation induced by row scaling \(R\) and variable scaling \(S\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the scaling-dependence leaf, but the transformed data, ill-posed set, coordinate norm, and admissible equivalence transformations must be specified by a source before the inequality is reliable.

children.title: Encoding Dependence
children.top_down_role: Variation caused by algebraically equivalent formulations, coordinate choices, and input encodings.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit complexity may vary across encodings of the same mathematical linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a binary encoding of rational LP data \(D\), and let \(L(E)\) denote its bit length. Distinct encodings can represent the same rational coefficients, for example through unreduced fractions or redundant leading bits. Therefore \[D(E_1)=D(E_2)\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad L(E_1)=L(E_2).\] Any running-time guarantee polynomial in \(L(E)\) is an encoding-sensitive bit-complexity statement unless a canonical encoding is fixed. Such a guarantee does not become strongly polynomial merely because different encodings decode to the same LP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same rational LP data can have binary encodings of different lengths, so bounds involving input bit length are encoding-sensitive rather than strongly polynomial.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a finite binary encoding of rational LP coefficients.
The decoding map identifies strings representing the same rational data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(E_1)=D(E_2)\) need not imply \(L(E_1)=L(E_2)\), so a bound polynomial in encoding length is not encoding-independent.

notation.meaning: finite binary representation of rational LP data
mathematical LP data decoded from E

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods and Rational Arithmetic p. 52

children.title: Representation-Invariant Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Conditioning concepts designed for comparison across equivalent scalings or formulations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract but exact criterion for a condition measure to be independent of a declared LP representation equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an equivalence relation \(\sim\) on LP data whose classes preserve the optimization problem with a declared solution correspondence. A condition measure \(\kappa\) is representation-invariant relative to \(\sim\) when \[D\sim D'\Longrightarrow \kappa(D)=\kappa(D').\] Equivalently, there is a function \(\bar\kappa\) on the quotient data space such that \(\kappa(D)=\bar\kappa([D])\). This property is meaningful only relative to the specified equivalence relation; invariance under positive row scaling does not imply invariance under variable changes, redundant constraints, or arbitrary reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A condition measure is representation-invariant when it is constant on every declared class of equivalent LP formulations, equivalently when it factors through the quotient by that equivalence.
assumptions_latex: The representation-equivalence relation and preserved solution correspondence are fixed.
\(\kappa\) is defined on all representations under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa\) is representation-invariant exactly when it factors as \(D\mapsto[D]\mapsto\bar\kappa([D])\).

notation.meaning: declared equivalence relation on LP representations
equivalence class of the representation D
condition measure defined on equivalence classes

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning on Representation Classes
Representation-Invariant Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning minimized over a specified equivalence class of LP representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a transformation group \(G\) act on LP data so that every \(gD\) represents the same optimization problem as \(D\), up to an explicitly invertible change of variables and positive constraint rescaling. Given a raw condition measure \(\kappa_{m raw}\), define its representation-invariant envelope by \[\kappa_{m inv}([D])=\inf_{g\in G}\kappa_{m raw}(gD),\qquad [D]=\{gD:g\in G\}.\] For every \(h\in G\), the orbit equality \([hD]=[D]\) implies \(\kappa_{m inv}([hD])=\kappa_{m inv}([D])\). The definition is meaningful only after the admissible transformations, norm conventions, and preserved solution correspondence are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A representation-invariant condition number is the best raw condition over all explicitly equivalent formulations in a chosen transformation group.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a group of LP-equivalence transformations.
\(\kappa_{m raw}\) is defined on every transformed representation under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_{m inv}([hD])=\kappa_{m inv}([D])\) for every \(h\in G\).

notation.meaning: orbit-invariant envelope of the raw condition measure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The orbit-infimum construction is internally invariant and its definition role fits the leaf, but no source establishes it as the intended representation-invariant LP conditioning notion. Its meaning also depends essentially on the chosen transformation group and norm conventions.

children.title: Misleading-Conditioning Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where benign reformulations produce large reported changes without comparable changes in intrinsic difficulty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary family showing that identical feasible geometry can have arbitrarily different residual error-bound constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), let \[P_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb R:\alpha x\le0,\ -\alpha x\le0\}=\{0\}\] and \(r_\alpha(x)=\|((\alpha x)_+,(-\alpha x)_+)\|_\infty=\alpha|x|\). The least \(H_\alpha\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P_\alpha)\le H_\alpha r_\alpha(x)\) for every \(x\) is \(H_\alpha=1/\alpha\). Hence a fixed feasible set admits arbitrarily large or small displayed residual constants under harmless positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling leaves the singleton feasible set unchanged while changing its best residual error-bound constant by an arbitrary factor.
assumptions_latex: The displayed residual uses the fixed \(\ell_\infty\) norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_\alpha=\{0\}\) for every \(\alpha>0\), but \(H_\alpha=1/\alpha\).

notation.meaning: scaled representation of the singleton feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Misleading Residual Conditioning

assumptions_latex: The residual is measured in a fixed norm on the displayed inequality system.
The scalar \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent representations of one feasible set can have arbitrarily different residual error-bound constants, so such constants are not representation-invariant condition measures.

notation.meaning: Feasible set represented with scaling parameter alpha

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: elementary rescaling example for representation-sensitive error bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates residual conditioning of a representation from intrinsic geometry of its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), represent the singleton feasible set by \[P_\alpha=\{x\in\mathbb R:\alpha x\leq0,\ -\alpha x\leq0\}=\{0\}.\] With residual \(r_\alpha(x)=\|((\alpha x)_+,(-\alpha x)_+)\|_\infty=\alpha|x|\), the least constant satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P_\alpha)\leq H_\alpha r_\alpha(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\) is \(H_\alpha=1/\alpha\). Thus identical feasible geometry admits arbitrarily large or small residual conditioning under harmless positive rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint rescaling leaves the feasible set unchanged but changes the best residual error-bound constant by an arbitrary factor.
knowledge_statements.title: Misleading-Conditioning Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rescaling example is mathematically correct, precisely delimited, and appropriately classified as a failure boundary, but no inspectable source is supplied for the representation-sensitivity claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consistency Boundary of the Hoffman Distance Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why the standard distance-to-feasibility formulation requires a nonempty target polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P=\varnothing\), then under the extended-real convention \(\operatorname{dist}(x,P)=+\infty\) for every \(x\), whereas \(\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\|\) is finite for every finite \(x\). Hence no finite \(H\) can satisfy the standard Hoffman distance inequality. Inconsistent systems require a different target, such as distance to consistent data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard Hoffman distance bound cannot hold for an empty feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\varnothing\).
Residuals of finite vectors are measured by a finite norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists H<\infty\ \forall x:\ \operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\left\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\right\|.
knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Boundary of the Hoffman Distance Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hoffman Modulus as a Worst Residual Ratio
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representation of the least Hoffman constant for a fixed consistent linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nonempty \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\), define \(r(x)=\|((Ax-b)_+,Cx-d)\|\). The least admissible constant for this fixed system is \[H_P=\sup_{x\notin P}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,P)}{r(x)}<\infty.\] A coefficient-matrix-uniform Hoffman constant is the supremum of these least constants over all right-hand sides \((b,d)\) for which the system is consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal Hoffman constant is the worst ratio of distance to feasibility over measured linear-constraint violation.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax\le b,\ Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\).
Norms on the variable and residual spaces are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_P=\sup_{x\notin P}\operatorname{dist}(x,P)/r(x)<\infty.

notation.meaning: Least error-bound constant for the fixed system

knowledge_statements.title: Hoffman Modulus as a Worst Residual Ratio

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean specialization for a consistent system of linear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\), and use Euclidean norms. Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,P)=\|C^\dagger(Cx-d)\|_2\le \|C^\dagger\|_2\|Cx-d\|_2.\] If \(C\ne0\), the least constant is \(\|C^\dagger\|_2=1/\sigma_{\min}^+(C)\). If \(C=0\) and the system is consistent, \(P=\mathbb R^n\) and the least constant is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For consistent linear equations in Euclidean norm, the exact nontrivial Hoffman constant is the reciprocal of the smallest positive singular value.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:Cx=d\}\ne\varnothing\).
Euclidean norms are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\ne0\implies\inf\{H:\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\le H\|Cx-d\|_2\}=\|C^\dagger\|_2=1/\sigma_{\min}^+(C).

notation.meaning: Smallest positive singular value of C

knowledge_statements.title: Equality-System Hoffman Constant

assumptions_latex: The polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\leq b,\ Cx=d\}\) is nonempty.
Finite-dimensional norms are fixed on the variable and residual spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(H<\infty\), depending only on \(A\), \(C\), and the chosen norms, such that the displayed global error bound holds.

notation.meaning: Distance in the fixed variable-space norm

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical finite-dimensional Hoffman error-bound theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical global Hoffman bound for a consistent finite linear equality-inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite constant \(H=H(A,C)\) such that every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x,P)\leq H\left\|\big((Ax-b)_+,\ Cx-d\big)\right\|.\] The constant is uniform in \(x\) and in the right-hand sides whenever the corresponding system is consistent; it depends on the coefficient matrices and the selected norms. Hence linear constraint violation controls distance to the feasible polyhedron globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every consistent finite linear system, distance to feasibility is globally bounded by a constant times its equality and inequality violations.
knowledge_statements.title: Hoffman Error-Bound Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional Hoffman bound is stated with appropriate consistency, norm, and matrix-dependence qualifications, and theorem is the correct content kind. An authoritative source with a theorem, section, or page locator is still required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degenerate Product Residual Has No Linear Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a product-only complementarity residual at a degenerate complementary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,s)\in\mathbb R_+^2:xs=0\}\) and \(r(x,s)=|xs|\). For \(z_t=(t,t)\), \(t>0\), \[\operatorname{dist}_2(z_t,C)=t,\qquad r(z_t)=t^2.\] Hence no \(\kappa<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dist}_2(z,C)\leq\kappa r(z)\) for every nonnegative \(z\) with \(\|z\|_2\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a degenerate complementary point, the product residual is quadratic along the diagonal while distance to the complementary set is linear.
assumptions_latex: Complementarity is represented only by \(|xs|\).
Distance is Euclidean and \(x,s\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,\kappa,\varepsilon>0\ \forall z\in\mathbb R_+^2:\ \|z\|_2\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}_2(z,C)\leq\kappa|xs|.

notation.meaning: Diagonal approach to the degenerate point.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Product Residual Has No Linear Error Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-Subregularity Formulation of the KKT Error-Bound Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise local error-bound formulation for the standard-form primal-dual KKT generalized equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(x,y,s)\), define the set-valued KKT mapping \[\mathcal F(z)=\bigl(Ax-b,\ A^Ty+s-c,\ s+N_{\mathbb R_+^n}(x)\bigr),\] and let \(Z^*=\mathcal F^{-1}(0)\). The primal-dual KKT error-bound regime holds at \(\bar z\in Z^*\) when \(\mathcal F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar z,0)\): there exist \(\kappa<\infty\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar z\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq \kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\mathcal F(z))\qquad(z\in U).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local primal-dual KKT error-bound regime is metric subregularity of the KKT generalized equation: near a KKT point, distance to the solution set is bounded by a constant times the KKT residual distance.
assumptions_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and its standard dual.
The reference point \(\bar z\) is a primal-dual KKT solution.
Distances use fixed finite-dimensional norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\kappa<\infty,\ U\ni\bar z:\ \operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\mathcal F(z))\quad(z\in U).

notation.meaning: Normal cone to the nonnegative orthant at x.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local equivalence of minimum and product complementarity residuals near a strictly complementary primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z^*=(x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be strictly complementary, so \(x_i^*+s_i^*>0\) for every \(i\). On a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(z^*\) with \(x,s\geq0\), there are constants \(0<a\leq b<\infty\) such that \[a\|\min(x,s)\|\leq\|Xs\|\leq b\|\min(x,s)\|,\qquad X=\operatorname{Diag}(x).\] Consequently, KKT residuals that differ only by using \(\min(x,s)\) or \(Xs\) have a local linear error bound simultaneously, with possibly different constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a strictly complementary KKT point, product and componentwise-minimum complementarity residuals are linearly equivalent.
assumptions_latex: \(z^*\) is a strictly complementary primal-dual KKT point.
The comparison is restricted to a sufficiently small neighborhood with \(x,s\geq0\).
A fixed finite-dimensional norm is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_{\min}\asymp R_{\mathrm{prod}}\text{ locally.}

notation.meaning: KKT residuals using minimum and product complementarity components.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Complementarity Residual Equivalence

assumptions_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and its dual, with a nonempty primal-dual solution set.
Residuals are measured in fixed finite-dimensional norms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The instance is in the local primal-dual KKT error-bound regime exactly when the displayed residual controls distance to \(Z^*\) on some neighborhood of \(Z^*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(z=(x,y,s)\), define \[R(z)=\left\|\big(Ax-b,\ A^Ty+s-c,\ (-x)_+,\ (-s)_+,\ \min(x,s)\big)\right\|.\] The primal-dual KKT error-bound regime holds locally if there exist \(\kappa<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq\kappa R(z)\] whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(z,Z^*)\leq\varepsilon\). Here \(\min(x,s)\) is componentwise, so its vanishing together with nonnegativity expresses complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near the primal-dual solution set, distance to a KKT point is controlled linearly by feasibility, sign, and complementarity residuals.

children.title: Local Error-Bound Regime
children.top_down_role: Error-bound behavior restricted to neighborhoods of a solution, face, or reference set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise Local Error Bound and Local Modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reference-point version of local error-bound regularity and its exact asymptotic modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=R^{-1}(0)\) and \(\bar x\in S\). A pointwise local error bound holds at \(\bar x\) if some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa<\infty\) satisfy \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa R(x)\qquad(x\in U).\] Its exact local modulus is \[\operatorname{eb}(R;\bar x)=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\notin S}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,S)}{R(x)}.\] Pointwise locality is weaker than requiring one pair \((\kappa,\varepsilon)\) to work uniformly around the entire solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound may be imposed near one reference solution; its sharp modulus is the limiting worst distance-to-residual ratio.
assumptions_latex: \(R:X\to[0,\infty)\) is defined on a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{eb}(R;\bar x)=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\ x\notin S}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)/R(x).
review_flags: Distinguishes pointwise locality from the seed's uniform neighborhood of the complete zero set.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Local Error Bound and Local Modulus

assumptions_latex: The zero set \(S=\{x:R(x)=0\}\) is nonempty.
The residual \(R:X\to[0,\infty)\) is defined on a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A local error bound controls distance to \(S\) only within a specified neighborhood and need not control remote points.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard local metric error-bound definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local residual control around the entire solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((R,S)\) has a local error bound around \(S\) if there exist \(\kappa<\infty\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa R(x)\] for every \(x\in X\) satisfying \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\varepsilon\). The radius \(\varepsilon\) is part of the regime: no assertion is made for points outside this neighborhood. The least admissible \(\kappa\) at a fixed radius is the corresponding local error-bound modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound controls distance to the solution set by residual size only for points sufficiently near that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Error-Bound Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent definition of an error bound uniform on a neighborhood of the entire zero set, and definition fits the leaf. No inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Global Error-Bound Regime
children.top_down_role: Error-bound behavior valid throughout the full domain or prescribed feasible region.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Control Without a Global Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-flattening example separating local and global regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=\mathbb R\), let \(S=\{0\}\) and \[R(x)=\frac{|x|}{1+|x|}.\] For \(|x|\le1\), \(|x|\le2R(x)\), so a local error bound holds. However, \(|x|/R(x)=1+|x|\to\infty\), and therefore no finite \(\kappa\) satisfies \(|x|\le\kappa R(x)\) for all \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual that behaves like distance near the solution but saturates far away has a local error bound and no global one.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R\) and \(S=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (R,S)\text{ has a local error bound but no global error bound}.
review_flags: Generic residual example used only to delineate the global regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Control Without a Global Error Bound

assumptions_latex: The zero set \(S=\{x:R(x)=0\}\) is nonempty.
The residual \(R:X\to[0,\infty)\) is defined on a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A global error bound uses one finite constant for every point in the residual's domain.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard global metric error-bound definition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines uniform residual control over the full domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((R,S)\) has a global error bound if there exists \(\kappa<\infty\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa R(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] The infimum of all such constants is the global error-bound modulus. Unlike a local bound, the same \(\kappa\) must control sequences escaping every bounded neighborhood of \(S\); consequently, behavior along recession directions can determine whether the global regime holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global error bound uses one constant to control distance to the solution set by residual size throughout the entire domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Error-Bound Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed condition correctly defines a global error-bound regime and the content kind fits the leaf, but the record has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Local-to-Global Transition
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions, constants, and domain restrictions governing extension from local to global control.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary far-field ratio condition for extending a local error bound over a prescribed domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the prescribed domain and \(S=R^{-1}(0)\cap D\ne\varnothing\). If there exists a sequence \(x_k\in D\) with \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)>0\) and \[\frac{R(x_k)}{\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)}\longrightarrow0,\] then no finite global modulus exists on \(D\), regardless of whether a local error bound holds near \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence along which residual becomes negligible relative to distance prevents a local error bound from extending globally.
assumptions_latex: \(S=R^{-1}(0)\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
There is a sequence in \(D\) with positive distance to \(S\) and residual-to-distance ratio tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\kappa<\infty\ \forall x\in D:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa R(x).

notation.meaning: Prescribed domain of the proposed global bound

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Flattening Obstruction to Globalization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Globalization on a bounded-distance prescribed domain using separation of the residual from zero outside the local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq X\), \(S=R^{-1}(0)\cap D\ne\varnothing\), and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa_0R(x)\) whenever \(x\in D\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\rho\), where \(\rho>0\). If \[M=\sup_{x\in D}\operatorname{dist}(x,S)<\infty,\qquad m=\inf_{\substack{x\in D\\\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\ge\rho}}R(x)>0,\] then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\max\{\kappa_0,M/m\}R(x)\qquad(x\in D).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a bounded-distance domain, a local bound becomes global if the residual stays uniformly positive outside the local neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a prescribed residual domain and \(S=R^{-1}(0)\cap D\ne\varnothing\).
A local error bound with modulus \(\kappa_0\) holds through radius \(\rho>0\).
The quantities \(M\) and \(m\) defined in the statement satisfy \(M<\infty\) and \(m>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in D:\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\max\{\kappa_0,M/m\}R(x).

notation.meaning: Prescribed domain of the desired global bound
Supremal distance to the solution set on D

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Local-to-Global Upgrade

assumptions_latex: A local bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\kappa_0R(x)\) holds whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\rho\).
There is \(\gamma>0\) such that \(R(x)\geq\gamma\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\geq\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local bound extends globally with modulus at most \(\max\{\kappa_0,\gamma^{-1}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient transition criterion combining local regularity with far-field residual growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=R^{-1}(0)\). For points with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\rho\), use the local modulus \(\kappa_0\). For points with \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\geq\rho\), the far-field inequality gives \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\gamma^{-1}R(x)\). Therefore every \(x\) satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq\max\{\kappa_0,\gamma^{-1}\}R(x).\] Thus local regularity becomes global precisely when an adequate uniform estimate also excludes residual flattening away from the solution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound becomes global when the residual also grows proportionally to distance outside the local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-to-Global Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local-plus-far-field decomposition yields the displayed global modulus, but the record does not explicitly introduce the domain of R or X and supplies no source. A cited formulation should also state rho>0 and the residual domain explicitly.

children.title: Objective Sharpness
children.top_down_role: Objective growth away from the optimal set across global, local, and face-restricted regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of an objective-gap bound into a distance-to-optimal-set certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If objective sharpness holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\), then every feasible \(x\) satisfying \(c^Tx-f^*\le\varepsilon\) obeys \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le \varepsilon/\alpha.\] Equivalently, \[\{x\in P:c^Tx\le f^*+\varepsilon\}\subseteq X^*+(\varepsilon/\alpha)\mathbb B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective gap of at most epsilon certifies distance at most epsilon divided by the sharpness modulus from the complete optimal set.
assumptions_latex: Objective sharpness holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\).
\(x\in P\), \(\varepsilon\ge0\), and \(c^Tx-f^*\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon/\alpha.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the selected norm

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Distance Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence of a positive global weak-sharpness modulus for an attained nonconstant polyhedral linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron, suppose \(f^*=\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\) is finite and attained, and let \(X^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\). If \(P\ne X^*\), then for every fixed norm there exists \(\alpha>0\) such that \[c^Tx-f^*\ge \alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\qquad(x\in P).\] If \(P=X^*\), every feasible point is optimal and the growth inequality is vacuous; that case is treated separately rather than by inserting an infinite coefficient into the inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every attained nonconstant linear objective on a polyhedron has a positive global sharpness constant relative to its complete optimal set.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
The finite optimum is attained.
A finite-dimensional norm is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\alpha>0\ \forall x\in P:\ c^Tx-f^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*).
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Objective Sharpness

assumptions_latex: The feasible polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
The optimum \(f^*=\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\) is attained and \(X^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Objective sharpness holds exactly when the displayed modulus \(\alpha\) is positive.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak-sharp-minimum formulation specialized to linear programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Setwise objective sharpness for an attained linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the objective sharpness modulus by \[\alpha=\inf_{x\in P\setminus X^*}\frac{c^Tx-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)},\] with the infimum interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(P=X^*\). The program is objectively sharp when \(\alpha>0\), equivalently when every \(x\in P\) satisfies \[c^Tx-f^*\geq\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*).\] This is a setwise property and does not require the optimal solution to be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective sharpness means objective suboptimality grows at least linearly with distance from the entire optimal set.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Sharpness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The setwise sharpness formulation is standard and condition is an appropriate content kind. However, no source is supplied, and the P=X^* convention makes the subsequent inequality with alpha=+infinity formally ambiguous; a sourced formulation should treat that trivial case separately.

children.title: Optimal-Set Stability
children.top_down_role: Persistence and displacement of optimal solutions or faces under perturbations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact description of the perturbed optimal set once sharpness prevents escape from the original face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the original problem has sharpness modulus \(\alpha>0\), and let \(X_h^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+h)^Tx\) be nonempty. If \(\|h\|_*<\alpha\), then \[X_h^*=\arg\min_{x\in X^*}h^Tx.\] Consequently, small objective perturbations preserve the entire original optimal set exactly if and only if \(h^Tx\) is constant on \(X^*\); otherwise they select a proper exposed face of \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside the sharpness radius, the perturbed objective merely minimizes its perturbation over the old optimal face.
assumptions_latex: The original optimum is attained and has sharpness modulus \(\alpha>0\).
The perturbed optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_h^*=\arg\min_{x\in X^*}h^Tx.

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the objective perturbation

knowledge_statements.title: Small-Perturbation Face-Selection Formula

assumptions_latex: The attained linear program has sharpness modulus \(\alpha>0\).
The objective perturbation \(h\) is measured in the norm dual to the distance norm.
The perturbed problem attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\|h\|_*<\alpha\), every optimizer of the perturbed objective belongs to the original optimal set.

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the objective perturbation

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: perturbation consequence of weak sharpness and dual-norm inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided stability under objective-only perturbations with fixed feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_h^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+h)^Tx\). For \(x_h\in X_h^*\), comparison with a nearest point of \(X^*\), together with objective sharpness, yields \[(\alpha-\|h\|_*)\operatorname{dist}(x_h,X^*)\leq0.\] Consequently, if \(\|h\|_*<\alpha\), then \(X_h^*\subseteq X^*\). The perturbation may select a proper face of \(X^*\), so this assertion is outer stability rather than equality of the two optimal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective perturbation smaller than the sharpness modulus cannot create optimizers outside the original optimal set, though it may select a smaller face.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Set Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The objective-only perturbation inclusion follows from setwise sharpness and the dual-norm inequality, and property fits the leaf. The claim nevertheless lacks an inspectable source locator.

children.title: Sharpness–Stability Link
children.top_down_role: Geometric connections between objective growth, solution-set movement, and perturbation sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative extension of the sharpness–stability implication to approximate solutions of a perturbed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume objective sharpness with modulus \(\alpha>0\), let \(\|h\|_*<\alpha\), and suppose \(x\in P\) satisfies \[(c+h)^Tx\le \min_{z\in P}(c+h)^Tz+\varepsilon.\] Then \[\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha-\|h\|_*}.\] For \(\varepsilon=0\), this reduces to the exact inclusion \(X_h^*\subseteq X^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a perturbation smaller than the sharpness modulus, an epsilon-optimal perturbed solution stays within epsilon divided by the remaining sharpness margin of the old optimal set.
assumptions_latex: The original LP has sharpness modulus \(\alpha>0\).
The perturbed minimum is finite and attained.
\(x\in P\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal for the perturbed objective, with \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon/(\alpha-\|h\|_*).
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Perturbed-Optimizer Bound

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is fixed and the original optimum is attained.
Objective sharpness holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\).
The perturbed objective attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sharpness modulus is a certified lower bound on the radius of objective perturbations that preserve the inclusion \(X_h^*\subseteq X^*\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: weak sharpness implies objective-perturbation stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative implication from setwise sharpness to objective-perturbation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every perturbation \(h\) satisfying \(\|h\|_*<\alpha\), one has \[\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+h)^Tx\subseteq\arg\min_{x\in P}c^Tx.\] Indeed, the sharpness inequality contributes \(\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\), while the perturbation can offset at most \(\|h\|_*\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\). Hence the same geometric modulus that controls objective error also supplies a quantitative stability radius against objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive objective sharpness supplies a stability radius: smaller objective perturbations cannot introduce optimizers outside the original optimal face.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness–Stability Link

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantitative sharpness-to-stability implication is correctly scoped to objective perturbations with a fixed feasible set, and theorem fits the link container. No authoritative source with a precise locator is provided.

children.title: Flat-Face Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of sharpness-based stability when optimal faces are extended, weakly exposed, or nearly flat.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of Inner Stability on a Flat Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of persistence of individual points of a positive-dimensional optimal face under arbitrarily small objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=X^*\) be a nontrivial optimal face, let objective sharpness hold with modulus \(\alpha>0\), and choose \(h\) such that \(G=\arg\min_{x\in F}h^Tx\) is a proper exposed face of \(F\). For every \(0<\varepsilon<\alpha/\|h\|_*\), \[\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+\varepsilon h)^Tx=G.\] Thus points of \(F\setminus G\) disappear under arbitrarily small objective perturbations, and the optimizer mapping is not inner semicontinuous at \(c\) relative to those points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat optimal face can collapse to a proper subface under arbitrarily small objective perturbations, so its individual points need not persist.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron and \(F=X^*\) is a positive-dimensional attained optimal face.
Setwise objective sharpness holds with modulus \(\alpha>0\).
\(h\) exposes a proper nonempty face \(G\) of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0<\varepsilon<\alpha/\|h\|_*\implies X^*_{\varepsilon h}=G\subsetneq F.

notation.meaning: Proper face selected by the perturbation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes stability of an optimal face from stability of a selected optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(u,v\in X^*\) and \(u\neq v\), every point \(x_t=(1-t)u+tv\) with \(0<t\leq1\) is feasible and optimal. Therefore \[c^Tx_t-f^*=0\qquad\text{but}\qquad\|x_t-u\|>0.\] Thus no \(\beta>0\) can satisfy \(c^Tx-f^*\geq\beta\|x-u\|\) near \(u\). A flat optimal face destroys pointwise sharpness and single-solution stability, while an error bound using \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\) can still hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nontrivial optimal face eliminates sharpness relative to one chosen optimizer, even when sharpness relative to the whole optimal set survives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Error Ratio and Reciprocal Sharpness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total extended-real definition of the local distance-to-objective-error ratio, including isolated optimal sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be closed, let the finite optimum \(f^*\) be attained, and let \(X^*=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=f^*\}\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), set \[E_\varepsilon=\sup\left\{\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)}{c^{\mathsf T}x-f^*}:x\in P\setminus X^*,\ 0<\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon\right\},\] \[a_\varepsilon=\inf\left\{\frac{c^{\mathsf T}x-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)}:x\in P\setminus X^*,\ 0<\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon\right\}.\] With \(\sup\varnothing=0\) and \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\), define \(\mathcal E=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}E_\varepsilon\) and \(\alpha_{\rm loc}=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}a_\varepsilon\). Then \(\mathcal E=1/\alpha_{\rm loc}\), using \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local limiting ratio of optimizer distance to objective error is the reciprocal of local setwise sharpness; empty punctured neighborhoods give ratio zero and sharpness infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is closed and the finite optimum is attained.
Distances use a fixed norm.
Every \(x\in P\setminus X^*\) has strictly positive objective gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E=\alpha_{\rm loc}^{-1}\) with the stated extended-real and empty-set conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Error Ratio and Reciprocal Sharpness

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(P\) is closed, the optimum is attained, and \(X^*\) is the optimal set.
The denominator is positive for \(x\in P\setminus X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The limiting error ratio equals the reciprocal of the local objective-sharpness modulus, with reciprocal conventions at zero and infinity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local asymptotic ratio of distance error to objective error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mathcal E=\limsup_{\substack{x\to X^*\\x\in P\setminus X^*}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)}{c^Tx-f^*},\qquad \alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}=\liminf_{\substack{x\to X^*\\x\in P\setminus X^*}}\frac{c^Tx-f^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)}.\] Since the displayed ratios are positive reciprocals, \[\mathcal E=\alpha_{\mathrm{loc}}^{-1},\] using \(1/0=+\infty\) and \(1/(+\infty)=0\). Thus a finite limiting error ratio is equivalent to positive local setwise sharpness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting ratio of distance error to objective error is the reciprocal of the local objective-sharpness modulus.

children.title: Unique-Optimum Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity and stability behavior when the optimal solution or relevant optimal representation is unique.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique-Optimum Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard-form LP regime classified solely by uniqueness of the primal optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the linear program 
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\). Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), assume the optimal value \(v^*\) is finite and attained, and define \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^*\}\). The instance lies in the unique-optimum regime precisely when
\[F^*=\{x^*\}\]
for some \(x^*\in P\). This condition does not assert primal nondegeneracy, dual uniqueness, or strict complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP with attained finite value is in this regime exactly when its optimal solution set contains one point.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\).
\(v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\in\mathbb R\) is attained.

children.title: Nonunique Nondegenerate Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonunique Optimum with Nondegenerate Optimal Vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed regime defined using primal nondegeneracy of every optimal basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and suppose the finite minimum of \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) is attained. With \(F^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\), the LP is in the nonunique nondegenerate regime when \[\dim(F^*)\ge1\quad\text{and}\quad |\operatorname{supp}(v)|=m\ \text{for every extreme point }v\text{ of }F^*.\] Thus the optimizer set is nonunique while each optimal basic feasible solution is primal nondegenerate. This convention quantifies over optimal basic feasible solutions, not over all basic feasible solutions of \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal face has positive dimension, but every optimal vertex is a nondegenerate basic feasible solution; nonoptimal vertices are irrelevant to this regime label.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
The primal optimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(F^*)\ge1\) and every extreme point \(v\in F^*\) has exactly \(m\) positive components.

notation.meaning: indices of positive components of v

knowledge_statements.title: Nonunique Optimum with Nondegenerate Optimal Vertices

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal standard-form example proving that primal nondegeneracy does not imply a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\min\ 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\] Here \(m=1\), the optimal set is the entire segment \(F^*=\{x\ge0:x_1+x_2=1\}\), and its extreme points \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) each have exactly one positive component. Hence both optimal basic feasible solutions are nondegenerate although the optimizer is not unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero objective on the standard simplex segment has two nondegenerate optimal vertices and infinitely many optimal solutions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim(F^*)=1\), while every extreme point of \(F^*\) is primal nondegenerate.

Nonunique Nondegenerate Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness combined with nondegeneracy of every optimal extreme point in standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[\dim(F^*)\ge1\quad\text{and}\quad |\operatorname{supp}(x)|=m\ \text{for every extreme point }x\text{ of }F^*.\]
Thus the optimal face contains multiple solutions, while each of its optimal basic feasible solutions is nondegenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal set is a positive-dimensional face, but every optimal basic feasible solution has exactly m positive components.

The primal optimum is finite and attained.
