children.title: Unique Degenerate Regime
children.top_down_role: Cases separating uniqueness of the optimum from degeneracy of its active representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Degenerate Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique primal optimum that is a degenerate basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), and consider minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Assume the finite optimum is attained. The instance lies in the unique degenerate regime when
\[\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=\{x^*\}\quad\text{and}\quad |\operatorname{supp}(x^*)|<m.\]
Equivalently, the unique optimizer is a basic feasible solution possessing a basis whose associated basic vector has at least one zero component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LP has exactly one optimizer, and that optimizer is a degenerate basic feasible solution.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
The primal optimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*=\{x^*\}\) and \(|\operatorname{supp}(x^*)|<m\).

children.title: Near-Infeasibility
children.top_down_role: Conditioning and sensitivity near loss of primal or dual feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-infeasibility under right-hand-side perturbations with the matrix fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and a norm on \(\mathbb R^m\). The system \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) is feasible exactly when \(b\in C:=\operatorname{cone}(A_{[:,1]},\ldots,A_{[:,n]})\). For feasible \(b\), define \[\rho_A(b)=\sup\{r\ge0:B(b,r)\subseteq C\}.\] Then \(\rho_A(b)=\operatorname{dist}(b,\mathbb R^m\setminus C)\), with value \(+\infty\) when \(C=\mathbb R^m\). Otherwise \(\rho_A(b)=0\) exactly when \(b\) is not an interior point of \(C\); if \(C\) is full-dimensional, this is equivalent to \(b\in\partial C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With A fixed, feasibility is column-cone membership, and distance to the cone complement is the largest guaranteed RHS feasibility radius.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is fixed.
A norm on right-hand sides is fixed.
\(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\) is feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_A(b)=\operatorname{dist}(b,\mathbb R^m\setminus\operatorname{cone}(A)).
knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side Feasibility Radius
Near-Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric proximity of a feasible standard-form instance to infeasible data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a norm on data triples \(D=(A,b,c)\), and let \(P(D)=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). Define the infeasible-data set
\[\mathcal I=\{(A',b',c'):P(A',b',c')=\varnothing\}.\]
For a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), a feasible nonzero instance \(D\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-infeasible when
\[0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal I)\le \varepsilon\|D\|.\]
Equivalently, the relative perturbation radius preserving feasibility is at most \(\varepsilon\); arbitrarily small values indicate approach to the feasibility-status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP is near-infeasible when a small relative perturbation of its data can make its feasible set empty.
assumptions_latex: \(D\ne0\) and \(P(D)\ne\varnothing\).
A norm on the product data space is fixed.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal I)/\|D\|\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: distance induced by the fixed data norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed metric definition depends materially on the admissible perturbation model, product norm, and infeasible-data set. No cited source establishes those choices or the claimed equivalence with a feasibility-preserving radius.

children.title: Near-Unboundedness
children.top_down_role: Conditioning and certificate behavior near emergence of improving recession directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-unboundedness under objective perturbations with the feasible region fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\ne\varnothing\) and \(K=\{d:Ad=0,\ d\ge0\}\). The problem \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is bounded below exactly when \(c\in K^*:=\{z:z^{\mathsf T}d\ge0\ \forall d\in K\}\). For a fixed objective norm \(\|\cdot\|_c\) with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_{c,*}\), if \(K\ne\{0\}\) and \(c\in K^*\), then \[\rho_K(c)=\operatorname{dist}_{\|\cdot\|_c}(c,\mathbb R^n\setminus K^*)=\inf_{d\in K\setminus\{0\}}\frac{c^{\mathsf T}d}{\|d\|_{c,*}}.\] If \(K=\{0\}\), every objective is bounded below and the radius is \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed feasible region, the smallest normalized recession slope is the objective-perturbation radius to unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(P\ne\varnothing\).
Only the objective vector is perturbed in a fixed norm.
The finite margin formula assumes \(K\ne\{0\}\) and \(c\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_Pc^{\mathsf T}x>-\infty\iff c\in K^*,\qquad \rho_K(c)=\inf_{d\in K\setminus\{0\}}\frac{c^{\mathsf T}d}{\|d\|_{c,*}}.

notation.meaning: recession cone of the fixed feasible region
cone of objectives bounded below on K

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Space Boundedness Margin
Near-Unboundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric proximity of a finite-optimum instance to feasible data unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a norm on data triples \(D=(A,b,c)\), set \(P(D)=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), and define
\[\mathcal U=\{D':P(D')\ne\varnothing,\ \inf_{x\in P(D')}c'^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\}.\]
For \(\varepsilon>0\), a nonzero instance \(D\) having an attained finite optimum is \(\varepsilon\)-near-unbounded when
\[0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal U)\le\varepsilon\|D\|.\]
Thus a relative data perturbation of size at most \(\varepsilon\) can change the finite optimal-value status to unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-optimum LP is near-unbounded when a small relative data perturbation can produce a feasible problem unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(D\ne0\) has an attained finite optimum.
A norm on the product data space is fixed.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal U)/\|D\|\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: data of feasible LPs unbounded below
distance induced by the fixed data norm

children.title: Status-Transition Boundary
children.top_down_role: Perturbation regimes where feasible, infeasible, bounded, or unbounded classifications become unstable.

knowledge_statements.title: Status-Transition Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary in LP data space separating infeasible, finite-optimum, and unbounded-below statuses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a normed space of standard-form data \(D=(A,b,c)\), let \(\mathcal I\) be the infeasible instances, \(\mathcal O\) the feasible instances with finite attained optimum, and \(\mathcal U\) the feasible instances unbounded below. The status-transition boundary is
\[\mathcal B=\bigcup_{\substack{S,T\in\{\mathcal I,\mathcal O,\mathcal U\}\\S\ne T}}\overline S\cap\overline T.\]
Hence \(D\in\mathcal B\) exactly when every neighborhood of \(D\) contains instances from at least two distinct status classes. The definition is relative to the chosen data representation and norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The status-transition boundary consists of data approached by LP instances having two or more different feasibility or boundedness statuses.
assumptions_latex: The data space carries a fixed norm topology.
The three status classes are defined for the same LP representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\in\mathcal B\) iff every neighborhood of \(D\) meets at least two distinct status classes.

notation.meaning: infeasible, finite-optimum, and unbounded-below data classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary formula is topologically coherent, and definition is the appropriate content kind, but the exact three-class partition, attainment convention, data representation, and topology require an authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Farkas Margins Are Locally Status-Stable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-matrix certificate robustness proposed for the status boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\) and suppose \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-\gamma<0\). Then every \(b+\Delta b\) satisfying \(|y^{\mathsf T}\Delta b|<\gamma\) remains infeasible for \(Ax=b+\Delta b,\ x\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict Farkas certificate remains valid under RHS perturbations smaller than its decisive margin.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is fixed.
\(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-\gamma<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |y^{\mathsf T}\Delta b|<\gamma\Rightarrow\{x:Ax=b+\Delta b,\ x\ge0\}=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Farkas Margins Are Locally Status-Stable

intermediate_metadata.reason: The global boundary remains unreliable without a fixed representation, topology, and status partition. The proposed Farkas-margin claim is mathematically sound but deferred as belonging primarily to Weak Status Boundaries. Near-infeasibility and near-unboundedness remain sibling regimes.

children.title: Flat Optimal Faces
children.top_down_role: Extended or weakly exposed optimal faces and their implications for solution identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Optimal Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-dimensional exposed optimal faces of a polyhedral feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty polyhedron and suppose \(v^*=\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is finite and attained. Its optimal set
\[F^*=\{x\in P:c^{\mathsf T}x=v^*\}\]
is an exposed face of \(P\). It is a flat optimal face when
\[\dim(F^*)\ge1.\]
Equivalently, there exist distinct \(x,y\in P\) such that every point \((1-t)x+ty\), with \(t\in[0,1]\), is optimal. Consequently, the objective is constant on every direction parallel to the affine hull of \(F^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat optimal face is a positive-dimensional optimal face, so an entire feasible segment shares the same objective value.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
The minimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\) is flat iff \(\dim(F^*)\ge1\).

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

source_witnesses.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Structure of a Flat Optimal Face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes bounded and unbounded flat optimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a nonempty polyhedron and suppose \(F^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is nonempty with finite value. Then \[\operatorname{rec}(F^*)=\{d\in\operatorname{rec}(P):c^{\mathsf T}d=0\}.\] Consequently, a flat optimal face may be bounded or unbounded. It is unbounded exactly when \(P\) has a nonzero zero-cost recession direction belonging to \(\operatorname{rec}(F^*)\). Such a direction enlarges the optimizer set but does not certify objective unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal face's recession directions are exactly the feasible zero-cost recession directions, so the face may be unbounded while the optimal value remains finite.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty polyhedron.
The minimum is finite and attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rec}(F^*)=\operatorname{rec}(P)\cap\{d:c^{\mathsf T}d=0\}.

children.title: Weak Objective Sharpness
children.top_down_role: Small objective growth away from the optimal set and associated sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized LP family whose positive sharpness modulus tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P=[0,1]^2\), use Euclidean distance, and set
\[c_\varepsilon=\frac{(\varepsilon,1)}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}},\qquad0<\varepsilon\le1.\]
Then \(\lVert c_\varepsilon\rVert_2=1\), the unique optimizer is \((0,0)\), and
\[\alpha(P,c_\varepsilon)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}}\longrightarrow0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with unit-normalized objectives and unique optimizers, polyhedral sharpness constants can approach zero.
assumptions_latex: Euclidean norms are used.
\(0<\varepsilon\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert c_\varepsilon\rVert_2=1\quad\text{and}\quad\alpha(P,c_\varepsilon)\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Normalized Vanishing-Sharpness Family

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best global linear-growth constant relating objective gap to distance from the optimal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron with finite attained minimum \(v^*\), optimal set \(F^*\), and \(P\setminus F^*\ne\varnothing\). For a fixed norm define
\[\alpha(P,c)=\inf_{x\in P\setminus F^*}\frac{c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)}.\]
Equivalently, \(\alpha(P,c)\) is the largest \(\alpha\ge0\) such that
\[c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\ge\alpha\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)\quad(x\in P).\]
Weak objective sharpness means that this positive modulus is small relative to a declared normalization of the objective data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective-sharpness modulus is the best coefficient converting objective gap into distance to the optimal set; calling it weak requires an explicit objective normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is polyhedral and has a finite attained minimum.
\(P\setminus F^*\ne\varnothing\).
A norm and an objective normalization are declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\ge\alpha(P,c)\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)\quad\text{for all }x\in P.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective Sharpness Modulus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization dependence of the objective-sharpness modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\lambda>0\), the objectives \(c\) and \(\lambda c\) have the same optimal set and
\[\alpha(P,\lambda c)=\lambda\alpha(P,c).\]
Thus an absolute threshold for weak sharpness is not invariant under positive objective rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive objective rescaling preserves all optimizers but scales the sharpness modulus by the same factor.
assumptions_latex: The objective-sharpness modulus is defined.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F^*_{\lambda c}=F^*_c,\qquad\alpha(P,\lambda c)=\lambda\alpha(P,c).
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Scaling Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positivity of the objective-sharpness modulus for a nonconstant polyhedral linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the assumptions defining \(\alpha(P,c)\), polyhedrality implies
\[\alpha(P,c)>0.\]
Consequently every feasible point satisfies
\[\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)\le\frac{c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*}{\alpha(P,c)}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonconstant polyhedral linear program has a positive global linear error-bound constant, although that constant can be arbitrarily small across normalized instances.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron with a finite attained minimum.
\(P\setminus F^*\ne\varnothing\).
Distance is measured in a fixed norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha(P,c)>0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)\le(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*)/\alpha(P,c).
knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Global Linear Growth
Weak Objective Sharpness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small global error-bound modulus relating objective gap to distance from the optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron with nonempty optimal set \(F^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) and finite value \(v^*\). For a fixed norm define the objective-sharpness modulus
\[\alpha(P,c)=\inf_{x\in P\setminus F^*}\frac{c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*}{\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)}.\]
For a prescribed scale \(\varepsilon>0\), the instance has \(\varepsilon\)-weak objective sharpness when
\[0<\alpha(P,c)\le\varepsilon.\]
Then the best global bound \(c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\ge\alpha(P,c)\operatorname{dist}(x,F^*)\) has a small coefficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective sharpness is weak when objective gap controls distance to the optimal set only through a small positive modulus.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is polyhedral and \(F^*\ne\varnothing\).
A norm and a threshold \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\alpha(P,c)\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: distance to the optimal set in the fixed norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed global ratio is plausible, but the terminology, normalization, positivity convention, and treatment of the case P equals its optimal set require a direct error-bound or weak-sharpness source.

children.title: Face-Flatness Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Connections between optimal-face geometry, sharpness constants, and perturbation response.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrarily Small Objective Tilts Select Opposite Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal sensitivity example for a one-dimensional flat optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=[0,1]\) and let the unperturbed objective be zero, so \(F^*=P\). For every \(\delta>0\), set \(d_+=\delta/2\) and \(d_-=-\delta/2\). Then \(|d_\pm|<\delta\), but \[\arg\min_{x\in P}d_+x=\{0\},\qquad \arg\min_{x\in P}d_-x=\{1\}.\] Thus arbitrarily small objective perturbations can select disjoint proper subfaces of the same flat optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small positive and negative tilts of a constant objective on a segment select opposite endpoints.
assumptions_latex: The unperturbed objective is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \arg\min_Pd_+x=\{0\}\ne\{1\}=\arg\min_Pd_-x,\qquad |d_\pm|<\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Arbitrarily Small Objective Tilts Select Opposite Endpoints

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Fan Perturbation Selection of a Proper Optimal Subface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General objective-perturbation sensitivity of a bounded positive-dimensional optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron and let \(F=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^Tx\) be nonempty, bounded, and positive-dimensional. For every proper nonempty face \(G\) of \(F\) and every \(\delta>0\), there exists \(d\) with \(0<\|d\|<\delta\) such that \(c+d\in\operatorname{ri}N_P^{\min}(G)\), and consequently \[\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+d)^Tx=G.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper nonempty face of a bounded flat optimum can be selected as the entire optimum by an arbitrarily small objective perturbation.
assumptions_latex: P\text{ is a polyhedron}
F=\arg\min_Pc^Tx\text{ is nonempty, bounded, and positive-dimensional}
G\text{ is a proper nonempty face of }F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\delta>0\ \exists d:\ 0<\|d\|<\delta,\quad\arg\min_P(c+d)^Tx=G.

notation.meaning: Minimization normal cone consisting of objective vectors that expose a face containing G.

review_flags: Boundedness ensures the selected face is an attained optimum and excludes recession ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Fan Perturbation Selection of a Proper Optimal Subface
Face-Flatness Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily small objective perturbations can select proper subfaces of a flat optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a polyhedron, and suppose \(F^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) is nonempty, bounded, and satisfies \(\dim(F^*)\ge1\). For every \(\delta>0\), there exists \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(0<\|d\|_*<\delta\) such that
\[\arg\min_{x\in P}(c+d)^{\mathsf T}x\subsetneq F^*.\]
The perturbation may be chosen so that its restriction to \(F^*\) is nonconstant. Thus no positive perturbation radius can guarantee preservation of every optimizer on a flat optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any flat bounded optimal face can be reduced to a proper subface by an arbitrarily small objective perturbation.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is polyhedral.
\(F^*\) is nonempty, bounded, and positive-dimensional.
\(\|\cdot\|_*\) is the objective-data norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\delta>0\), some \(d\) with \(0<\|d\|_*<\delta\) yields \(\arg\min_P(c+d)^{\mathsf T}x\subsetneq F^*\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the sensitivity leaf, but the universal perturbation claim requires direct support, including justification that a sufficiently small perturbation retains an attained optimum contained in the original face.

children.title: Solution-Identification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where objective accuracy fails to determine proximity to a particular optimizer.

knowledge_statements.title: Solution-Identification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective-gap information cannot identify an individual optimizer on a nontrivial optimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be polyhedral and let \(F^*=\arg\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) contain distinct points \(x^1\) and \(x^2\). Then
\[c^{\mathsf T}x^1-v^*=c^{\mathsf T}x^2-v^*=0,\qquad \|x^1-x^2\|>0.\]
Hence no implication of the form
\[c^{\mathsf T}x-v^*\le\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ \|x-x^\dagger\|\le r(\varepsilon),\qquad r(\varepsilon)\to0,\]
can hold uniformly for all \(x\in P\) and any fixed \(x^\dagger\in F^*\). Objective accuracy can identify the optimal set, but not a designated member without an additional selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With multiple optimizers, even zero objective gap cannot identify a chosen optimal point; an extra selection criterion is necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(F^*\) contains at least two distinct points.
The distance is induced by a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No objective-gap bound alone forces convergence to a prescribed \(x^\dagger\in F^*\).

source_refs.locator: Optimality Conditions, Duality, and Solution Sets p. 23

children.title: Exact Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Conditioning behavior at instances with redundant active structure or degenerate basic representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal degeneracy of a basic feasible solution in full-row-rank standard form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), and let \(x\) be a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\). Thus some basis \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(|B|=m\) and \(A_B\) nonsingular, satisfies
\[x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0,\qquad x_j=0\ \text{for }j\notin B.\]
The basic feasible solution is exactly degenerate when at least one basic component vanishes:
\[\min_{i\in B}(x_B)_i=0.\]
Equivalently, \(x\) has fewer than \(m\) positive components; this intrinsic criterion is independent of which representing basis is selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basic feasible solution is exactly degenerate when at least one of its basic variables is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
\(x\) is a basic feasible solution represented by a basis \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is degenerate iff \(\min_{i\in B}(x_B)_i=0\), equivalently \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|<m\).

notation.meaning: index set of a nonsingular basis matrix

source_refs.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

source_witnesses.locator: 8.5 Analysis of Karmarkar's Algorithm: Convergence, Complexity, Sliding Objective Method, and Basic Optimal Solutions p. 417

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representing Bases of a Degenerate Basic Feasible Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basis representations of a fixed standard-form basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a basic feasible solution of \(Ax=b,\ x\ge0\), where \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and let \(S=\{j:x_j>0\}\). An index set \(B\) represents \(x\) exactly when \(|B|=m\), \(S\subseteq B\), and \(A_B\) is nonsingular. Thus, when \(|S|<m\), every representing basis contains \(m-|S|\) zero-valued basic indices. Degeneracy permits but does not guarantee multiple representing bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Representing bases are precisely the nonsingular size-m supersets of the positive support; a degenerate point need not have multiple such bases.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\).
\(x\) is a basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\text{ represents }x\iff |B|=m,\ S\subseteq B,\ \det(A_B)\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Representing Bases of a Degenerate Basic Feasible Solution

children.title: Near-Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity when active constraints, reduced costs, or basic values approach degenerate configurations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A fixed-basis diagnostic rather than an invariant distance between LP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a primal- and dual-feasible basis \(B\) of \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), with at least one nonbasic index, define \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\) and \(r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\). For fixed positive scales \(s_x,s_r\), let \[\mu_B=\min\left\{\min_{i\in B}\frac{(x_B)_i}{s_x},\min_{j\notin B}\frac{(r_N)_j}{s_r}\right\}.\] Then \(\mu_B=0\) exactly when this feasible basis is primal or dual degenerate. The condition \(0<\mu_B\le\varepsilon\) is basis- and scaling-relative and is not invariant under reformulation, rescaling, or selection of another basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest scaled basic value or reduced cost is a fixed-basis near-degeneracy margin, not an invariant instance distance.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular and there is at least one nonbasic index.
The basis is primal and dual feasible.
Positive scales \(s_x,s_r\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_B=0\iff\left(\exists i\in B:(x_B)_i=0\right)\lor\left(\exists j\notin B:(r_N)_j=0\right).
knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Relative Near-Degeneracy Margins
Near-Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small relative distance from nondegenerate LP data to an instance possessing a degenerate basic feasible solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a norm on standard-form data pairs \(D=(A,b)\), and let \(\mathcal G\) be the set of data for which \(\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) has a degenerate basic feasible solution. For \(\varepsilon>0\), a nonzero instance \(D\notin\mathcal G\) is \(\varepsilon\)-near-degenerate when
\[0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal G)\le\varepsilon\|D\|.\]
Thus a relative perturbation of size at most \(\varepsilon\) can create a feasible basis with a zero basic component. The notion depends on the standard-form representation and chosen data norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondegenerate standard-form instance is near-degenerate when a small relative perturbation can create a zero basic variable.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(A,b)\ne0\) and \(D\notin\mathcal G\).
A norm on the data space is fixed.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\operatorname{dist}(D,\mathcal G)/\|D\|\le\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: data admitting a degenerate basic feasible solution
distance in the fixed data norm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance-based notion is representation- and norm-dependent and lacks authoritative support. Also, distance at most epsilon need not produce an actual perturbation of that size unless the degeneracy set has the required closedness or the infimum is attained.

children.title: Degeneracy Transition Under Perturbation
children.top_down_role: Movement between regular, nearly degenerate, and exactly degenerate regimes under data changes.

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has full row rank and \(B=A_{[:,I]}\) is a nonsingular basis.
The data vary affinely as \(b(\varepsilon)=b+\varepsilon d\) and \(c(\varepsilon)=c+\varepsilon e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy transitions occur only at parameter values where a basic variable or nonbasic reduced cost vanishes.

notation.meaning: basic solution associated with basis I
reduced cost of nonbasic variable j

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric transition for a fixed simplex basis under affine data perturbations.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 10. FINITENESS OF THE SIMPLEX METHOD UNDER PERTURBATION
5.4. Global dependence on the cost vector p. 216

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the basis \(I\), both \(x_I(\varepsilon)=B^{-1}(b+\varepsilon d)\) and every reduced cost \(r_j(\varepsilon)\), \(j\notin I\), are affine functions of \(\varepsilon\). On any open interval containing no zero of these functions, the signs determining primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and degeneracy are constant. A transition into or out of degeneracy can therefore occur only at a critical value \(\varepsilon_*\) satisfying \((x_I(\varepsilon_*))_i=0\) for some \(i\in I\), or \(r_j(\varepsilon_*)=0\) for some \(j\notin I\). If none of these affine functions is identically zero, the critical values are finite on every bounded parameter interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed basis, feasibility signs remain constant between zeros of affine basic variables and reduced costs; degeneracy can change only at such critical perturbation values.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Transition Under Perturbation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 10. FINITENESS OF THE SIMPLEX METHOD UNDER PERTURBATION
5.4. Global dependence on the cost vector p. 216

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-basis classification along a scalar affine perturbation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(\varepsilon)\) be a basic component or nonbasic reduced cost for a fixed nonsingular basis under affine data perturbation. If \(g(\varepsilon_*)=0\) and \(g'(\varepsilon_*)\ne0\), then \(\varepsilon_*\) is an isolated zero and \(g\) changes sign there. If \(g(\varepsilon_*)=g'(\varepsilon_*)=0\), affine dependence implies \(g\equiv0\), so the associated primal or dual degeneracy persists along the parameter line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine basic value or reduced cost either crosses zero at an isolated critical value or is identically zero and persistently degenerate.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a fixed nonsingular basis.
The data depend affinely on a scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(\varepsilon_*)=0\Rightarrow\bigl(g'(\varepsilon_*)\ne0\text{ gives an isolated crossing}\bigr)\lor\bigl(g\equiv0\bigr).
knowledge_statements.title: Transversal and Persistent Degeneracy Events

children.title: Primal-Dual Saddle Representations
children.top_down_role: LP formulations organized through convex-concave primal-dual saddle structure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax Values of the LP Saddle Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual values induced by the extended Lagrangian of an equality-constrained box LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle+\delta_B(x)\). Then \(\inf_x\sup_y L(x,y)=\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in B\}\), while \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)\) is the Lagrangian-dual value and never exceeds the primal value. An attained common finite value at \((x^*,y^*)\) is equivalent to the saddle inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The min–max value is the primal LP value and the max–min value is its Lagrangian-dual value; attained equality characterizes saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed box.
\(L(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x+\langle y,Ax-b\rangle+\delta_B(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_y\inf_xL(x,y)\leq\inf_x\sup_yL(x,y)\), with attained finite equality at \((x^*,y^*)\) exactly when \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax Values of the LP Saddle Representation

assumptions_latex: \(B=[l,u]\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty box, allowing infinite endpoints.
The primal LP is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in B\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal-dual solutions are precisely saddle points of \(L(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x+y^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)+\delta_B(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form box-constrained LP represented as a convex-concave saddle problem.

source_refs.locator: 6.2 Primal-Dual Relationships p. 264
A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(L(x,y)=c^{\mathsf T}x+y^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b)+\delta_B(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\). A pair \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point when \(L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\). This is equivalent to \(Ax^*=b\) and \(0\in c+A^{\mathsf T}y^*+N_B(x^*)\). Consequently, \(x^*\) is primal optimal and \(y^*\), together with the normal-cone vector, supplies the associated dual optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A box-constrained equality-form LP is the saddle problem for its extended Lagrangian; saddle points satisfy primal feasibility and normal-cone stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Saddle Representations

source_witnesses.locator: 6.2 Primal-Dual Relationships p. 264
A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and content kind fit the leaf, and the stated saddle/KKT equivalence is standard. However, the cited LP duality and interior-point sections do not clearly support the exact extended-real Lagrangian, normal-cone formulation, and unrestricted box endpoints. A direct convex-analysis or saddle-point source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Monotone-Inclusion Representations
children.top_down_role: LP optimality systems represented through monotone operators, normal cones, and fixed-point interfaces.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product-space monotone-operator representation of equality-constrained linear optimization over a nonempty closed convex box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in B\}\), where \(B\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty closed convex box, define \(T(x,y)=\bigl(c+A^{\mathsf T}y+N_B(x),\ b-Ax\bigr)\) on \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\). Then \(0\in T(x,y)\) is equivalent to \(Ax=b\) and \(0\in c+A^{\mathsf T}y+N_B(x)\). The normal-cone component is maximally monotone, the linear coupling \((x,y)\mapsto(A^{\mathsf T}y,-Ax)\) is continuous and skew, and their sum plus the constant \((c,b)\) is maximally monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal feasibility and stationarity form the zero set of a maximally monotone operator built from a box normal cone and skew primal-dual coupling.
assumptions_latex: B is nonempty, closed, and convex.
A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbb R^m, and c\in\mathbb R^n.
The normal cone uses N_B(x)=\{v:\langle v,z-x\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in B\} for x\in B and is empty otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in T(x,y)\iff Ax=b\ \text{and}\ 0\in c+A^{\mathsf T}y+N_B(x),\qquad T\ \text{is maximally monotone}.

notation.meaning: convex-analytic normal cone of the box B

knowledge_statements.title: Box-Constrained LP Monotone Inclusion

assumptions_latex: \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty closed convex box.
The LP data are \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The LP optimality system is the monotone inclusion \(0\in T(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximally monotone inclusion for equality-form, box-constrained linear programming.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(Z=\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\), define the set-valued operator \(T\) by \(T(x,y)=\bigl(c+A^{\mathsf T}y+N_B(x),\ b-Ax\bigr)\). The normal-cone part \((x,y)\mapsto(N_B(x),0)\) is maximally monotone, while the linear coupling \((x,y)\mapsto(A^{\mathsf T}y,-Ax)\) is skew and monotone; adding the constant \((c,b)\) preserves monotonicity. Thus \(0\in T(x,y)\) means exactly \(Ax=b\) and \(0\in c+A^{\mathsf T}y+N_B(x)\), the primal-dual optimality system for the LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal feasibility and stationarity conditions combine into a single monotone inclusion formed from a normal cone, a skew linear coupling, and constant data.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotone-Inclusion Representations

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The operator has the correct signs and its zero set is the stated LP optimality system, so representation is the appropriate content kind. The cited interior-point section does not directly substantiate the normal-cone and skew-operator monotonicity claims, especially the scope note's maximal-monotonicity assertion. Supply a monotone-operator source with a precise theorem or section locator.

children.title: Saddle–Inclusion Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Translation of variables, residuals, certificates, and structural assumptions between the two representations.

assumptions_latex: \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), where \(f\) and \(g^*\) are proper closed convex functions.
A saddle point exists in the finite-dimensional primal-dual space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x^*,y^*)\) is a saddle point of \(L\) if and only if \(0\in T(x^*,y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex-concave saddle functions with bilinear coupling.

source_refs.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), the saddle inequalities \(L(x^*,y)\leq L(x^*,y^*)\leq L(x,y^*)\) for all \((x,y)\) hold if and only if \(0\in\partial f(x^*)+K^{\mathsf T}y^*\) and \(0\in\partial g^*(y^*)-Kx^*\). Equivalently, with \(T(x,y)=\bigl(\partial f(x)+K^{\mathsf T}y,\partial g^*(y)-Kx\bigr)\), one has \(0\in T(x^*,y^*)\). Hence the saddle formulation and its monotone inclusion have identical solution sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order optimality in each saddle variable is equivalent to a zero of the associated primal-dual monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle–Inclusion Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: Primal-Dual Methods: Development of the Fundamental Ideas p. 43

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The equivalence is mathematically standard and the duality kind is compatible with the correspondence leaf. Wright's LP-specific primal-dual discussion is not a direct source for the general proper closed convex Fenchel saddle formulation and its subdifferential inclusion. A specific convex-analysis or primal-dual splitting reference is needed.

assumptions_latex: A primal-dual LP optimality system is expressible as \(0\in F(z)\) on a finite-dimensional space.
The embedding uses a nonnegative homogenizing coordinate \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonzero homogeneous solution with \(\tau>0\) decodes to a primal-dual LP solution by division by \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract homogeneous embedding interface; a specific self-dual embedding variant remains to be sourced.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A homogeneous first-order embedding replaces the affine optimality system by a positively homogeneous inclusion \(0\in\mathcal{H}(w)\) in an augmented variable \(w=(z,\tau)\), with \(\tau\geq0\) and \(\mathcal{H}(\alpha w)=\alpha\mathcal{H}(w)\) for every \(\alpha>0\). The embedding must satisfy the decoding condition that every nonzero solution \((z,	au)\) with \(\tau>0\) yields an original primal-dual solution \(z/\tau\). Its zero-homogenizing solutions, when accompanied by the embedding's prescribed sign conditions, represent normalized infeasibility or unboundedness certificates rather than finite primal-dual solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmented homogeneous inclusion represents LP optimality; positive homogenizing coordinate decodes a solution, while properly signed zero-coordinate solutions may encode certificates.
knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous First-Order Embeddings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Representation is the appropriate kind, but no concrete homogeneous embedding is defined or cited. Positive homogeneity and division by the homogenizing coordinate alone do not establish equivalence to an LP optimality system, and the zero-coordinate certificate claim depends on variant-specific equations and sign conditions. An authoritative source and a specified embedding are required.

children.title: Sparse Matrix-Vector Interface
children.top_down_role: Storage, access, transpose multiplication, and sparsity behavior for LP linear operators.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint-Consistency Test for Sparse Operator Calls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar diagnostic for paired forward and transpose sparse-operator implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact calls representing the same matrix satisfy \(\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,A^{\mathsf T}y\rangle\) for every \(x\) and \(y\). Hence \(d(x,y)=\langle\widehat{Ax},y\rangle-\langle x,\widehat{A^{\mathsf T}y}\rangle\) must vanish in exact arithmetic and is a scale-dependent implementation diagnostic in floating-point arithmetic. Passing finitely many tests does not certify equality for every input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and transpose products must satisfy the adjoint identity; sampled discrepancies are useful but nonexhaustive implementation checks.
assumptions_latex: The two calls are intended to implement \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\).
Both inner products use the real Euclidean pairing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Ax,y\rangle-\langle x,A^{\mathsf T}y\rangle=0\) for all \(x,y\).
knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint-Consistency Test for Sparse Operator Calls

assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is stored in a sparse format containing each nonzero once.
Arithmetic and index operations have unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both \(Ax\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) are computable in \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\) time and storage linear in the sparse input.

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzero entries of A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost sparse matrix-vector products used by first-order LP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\), initialize \(p=0\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(q=0\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For every stored nonzero \(A_{ij}\), accumulate \(p_i\leftarrow p_i+A_{ij}x_j\) and \(q_j\leftarrow q_j+A_{ij}y_i\). After all entries are processed, output \(p=Ax\) and \(q=A^{\mathsf T}y\). The procedure performs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) multiply-add pairs, plus \(O(m+n)\) initialization and output work, and requires \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\) stored scalars and indices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single pass over stored nonzeros computes the forward and transpose products with work proportional to matrix sparsity and vector dimensions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Matrix-Vector Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-pass sparse-product algorithm is correct under the stated storage and unit-cost assumptions, but the record also asserts explicit work and storage bounds without any evidence. A sparse linear-algebra source with a precise locator is required. The algorithm kind is defensible for the interface, though a complexity-bound record would be preferable if the terminal emphasis is the asymptotic guarantee.

children.title: Bound-Projection Interface
children.top_down_role: Projection access for variable bounds, simple constraint sets, and separable domains.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variational Characterization and Firm Nonexpansiveness of Bound Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric oracle properties of Euclidean projection onto a nonempty closed box.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=P_B(v)\), the following are equivalent: \(p=P_B(v)\), \(v-p\in N_B(p)\), and \(\langle v-p,z-p\rangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in B\), using \(N_B(p)=\{q:\langle q,z-p\rangle\leq0\ \forall z\in B\}\). Moreover, \(\|P_B(v)-P_B(w)\|_2^2\leq\langle P_B(v)-P_B(w),v-w\rangle\), so \(P_B\) is firmly nonexpansive and therefore \(1\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Box projection is characterized by a normal-cone variational inequality and is firmly nonexpansive.
assumptions_latex: \(B=[l,u]\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty and closed.
\(v,w\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v-P_B(v)\in N_B(P_B(v))\) and \(P_B\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.title: Variational Characterization and Firm Nonexpansiveness of Bound Projection

assumptions_latex: \(B=[l,u]=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:l_i\leq x_i\leq u_i\}\) is nonempty.
Infinite lower or upper endpoints are permitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Euclidean projection onto \(B\) is coordinatewise clipping and costs \(O(n)\) operations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection oracle for finite or one-sided variable bounds.

source_refs.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the unique Euclidean projection \(P_B(v)=\arg\min_{x\in B}\tfrac12\|x-v\|_2^2\) is separable and satisfies \((P_B(v))_i=\min\{u_i,\max\{l_i,v_i\}\}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\), with the evident convention for infinite endpoints. Thus projection requires one independent clipping operation per coordinate, uses \(O(n)\) arithmetic and comparisons, and needs no linear-system solve or access to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection onto variable bounds clips each coordinate independently, taking linear work and requiring no matrix operation.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Projection Interface

source_witnesses.locator: A Primal-Dual Framework p. 8

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Coordinatewise clipping is mathematically correct, including for infinite endpoints, but the cited interior-point section does not directly support the Euclidean projection formula or its O(n) cost. The record functions as an algorithm or property rather than merely a representation. A direct projection source is needed before a content-kind correction can be reviewed.

children.title: Operator–Projection Cost Balance
children.top_down_role: Relative arithmetic, memory, and synchronization costs of sparse products versus projections.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slow-memory traffic for explicitly stored sparse products and coordinatewise projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each of \(k_A\) operator calls streams all stored entries and indices of \(A\), reads its input vector, and writes its output, while each of \(k_P\) box projections reads and writes \(\Theta(n)\) vector entries. If these data do not persist in fast memory, one iteration transfers \(\Theta(k_A(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)+k_Pn+m+n)\) words, up to format-dependent constants and any separately counted residual passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse products stream matrix and vector data while projections stream vectors, producing a bandwidth balance distinct from arithmetic work.
assumptions_latex: Sparse data and working vectors do not persist in fast memory between the counted passes.
Each operator call traverses every stored nonzero once.
Each projection performs one coordinatewise read/write pass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{move}}=\Theta(k_A(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)+k_Pn+m+n)\text{ words per iteration}.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator–Projection Data-Movement Balance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-cost arithmetic accounting for a first-order iteration composed of sparse products, box projections, and dense vector passes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an iteration performs \(k_A\) sparse products, \(k_P\) box projections, and a fixed number of full passes over its \(m\)- and \(n\)-dimensional work vectors, then its arithmetic work is \(O(k_A(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)+k_Pn+m+n)\). Over \(N\) such iterations the work is \(O(N[k_A(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)+k_Pn+m+n])\), excluding initialization and output work. This additive bound alone does not establish that either primitive dominates without constants and a specified implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Per-iteration arithmetic work adds sparse-product, projection, and vector-pass costs; asymptotic terms alone do not determine practical dominance.
assumptions_latex: Sparse products explicitly initialize or overwrite their output vectors.
Arithmetic and index operations have unit cost.
The counts \(k_A\) and \(k_P\) are fixed for the iteration being analyzed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{arith}}=O(k_A(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)+k_Pn+m+n)\text{ per iteration}.
knowledge_statements.title: Additive Operator–Projection Arithmetic Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Synchronization Contrast Between Products and Projections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel synchronization structure of the two primitive operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coordinatewise box projection has independent output coordinates and requires no inter-coordinate reduction. A parallel sparse product may require reductions when contributions to one output coordinate are produced by multiple workers. Thus equal arithmetic work need not imply equal synchronization cost; the comparison depends on storage orientation and work partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound projections are coordinate-separable, whereas parallel sparse products can require reductions.
assumptions_latex: The primitives are executed by multiple workers.
Sparse-product contributions may be partitioned across workers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\mathrm{sync}}(P_B)\text{ has no output-reduction term, whereas }C_{\mathrm{sync}}(A\cdot)\text{ may have one}.
knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Contrast Between Products and Projections

assumptions_latex: Each iteration performs \(k_A\) sparse products with \(A\) or \(A^{\mathsf T}\) and \(k_P\) box projections.
The iteration count to the chosen stopping criterion is \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total work is \(O\!\left(N\bigl(k_A\operatorname{nnz}(A)+k_Pn+m+n\bigr)\right)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic work model separating sparse operator calls from coordinatewise projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the unit-cost RAM model, one iteration costs \(O(k_A\operatorname{nnz}(A)+k_Pn+m+n)\): sparse operator applications contribute \(O(k_A\operatorname{nnz}(A))\), projections contribute \(O(k_Pn)\), and vector updates and residual checks contribute \(O(m+n)\). Therefore \(N\) iterations cost \(O\!\left(N(k_A\operatorname{nnz}(A)+k_Pn+m+n)\right)\). In particular, when \(k_A\) and \(k_P\) are fixed constants, sparse operator work dominates precisely when \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)=\Omega(m+n)\) with a sufficiently large constant relative to projection and vector-update costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration cost is the sum of sparse operator, projection, and vector-update costs; multiplying by the stopping iteration count gives total arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator–Projection Cost Balance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the cost-balance leaf, but no source is supplied. If k_A is not fixed, initializing or clearing outputs can add dimension-dependent work per sparse product, which the displayed bound does not account for. The final 'dominates precisely' claim also requires explicit constants and a sharper cost model than asymptotic Omega notation supplies.

children.title: Parallel Execution Interface
children.top_down_role: Concurrency patterns, synchronization requirements, and workload partitioning for first-order LP operations.

assumptions_latex: The rows or nonzeros of \(A\) are partitioned among \(p\) workers.
Each first-order iteration permits synchronization after local sparse products and reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A parallel iteration consists of local sparse products, associative reductions, independent bound projections, and a synchronized state update.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bulk-synchronous execution interface for sparse first-order LP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the stored entries of \(A\) among \(p\) workers. At iteration \(k\), broadcast or expose the current vectors, let each worker compute its assigned partial contributions to \(Ax^k\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k\), combine overlapping output coordinates by associative summation, and compute bound projections independently by coordinate. After completing required scalar reductions for step sizes, residuals, or stopping tests, synchronize and output the updated state \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\). Correctness requires the reductions to equal the corresponding serial sums, up to the adopted floating-point convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Workers compute sparse partial products and coordinate projections concurrently, reduce shared outputs, then synchronize before publishing the next iterate.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Execution Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct kind for this execution-interface leaf, but the proposed schedule has no supporting source and does not specify whether row, column, or nonzero partitioning determines the broadcasts, reductions, and ownership of output coordinates. A concrete bulk-synchronous communication model and first-order LP implementation reference are required.

children.title: Accelerator Execution Interface
children.top_down_role: GPU or specialized-device execution for sparse products, projections, reductions, and vector operations.

assumptions_latex: The accelerator supports sparse matrix-vector kernels, vector kernels, and reductions.
All arrays use compatible index and scalar formats and reside in addressable accelerator memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One first-order iteration is implementable as a finite kernel schedule whose outputs equal the serial operator-projection update under exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Device-kernel contract for operator-projection first-order LP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store \(A\), the bounds, and \(z^k=(x^k,y^k)\) on the accelerator. Launch sparse kernels for the required products \(Ax^k\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}y^k\), vector kernels for affine updates and coordinatewise clipping, and reduction kernels for residual norms or scalar step rules. Enforce a dependency between kernels exactly when a consumer reads a producer's output. Stop when the device-computed criterion satisfies the prescribed tolerance, and return the final state and residual scalars. In exact arithmetic, the scheduled kernels must realize the same algebraic update as the serial method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accelerator iteration schedules sparse products, vector updates, clipping, and reductions with explicit data dependencies and returns the same algebraic update as serial execution.
knowledge_statements.title: Accelerator Execution Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the accelerator-interface leaf, but the record does not identify a first-order method whose serial update the kernel schedule must reproduce. Sparse format, reduction semantics, hardware execution model, and floating-point behavior are also variant-dependent. A specific accelerator implementation or authoritative algorithm source is required.

children.title: Throughput–Synchronization Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Performance interaction between device throughput, communication, synchronization, and iteration granularity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bulk-synchronous lower-bound model separating arithmetic, limiting-memory traffic, and additive synchronization latency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a model with \(p\) workers of arithmetic rate \(\rho\), aggregate sustainable bandwidth \(\beta\), \(s\) nonoverlapped global synchronizations of latency \(\lambda\), \(W\) operations, and \(M>0\) bytes of limiting-memory traffic, iteration time satisfies \(T_p\ge\max\{W/(p\rho),M/\beta\}+s\lambda\). The arithmetic and bandwidth terms cross at \(p=W\beta/(\rho M)\); the additive synchronization term does not move this crossover. The model-imposed floor as \(p\) grows is \(M/\beta+s\lambda\). These consequences require the stated overlap, bandwidth, and load-balance assumptions and are lower bounds rather than predictions of attained time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arithmetic time decreases with workers, while bandwidth and nonoverlapped synchronization impose a fixed floor; synchronization does not alter the arithmetic-bandwidth crossover.
assumptions_latex: Arithmetic and limiting-memory transfer may overlap, producing the maximum of their lower bounds.
Global synchronization does not overlap the preceding maximum term.
Work is perfectly balanced and \rho, \beta, and \lambda are fixed within the modeled regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_p\ge\max\left\{\frac{W}{p\rho},\frac{M}{\beta}\right\}+s\lambda,\qquad \liminf_{p\to\infty}T_p\ge\frac{M}{\beta}+s\lambda.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonoverlapped Synchronization Floor

assumptions_latex: An iteration performs \(W\) parallelizable operations and transfers \(M\) bytes.
It incurs \(s\) global synchronization events on \(p\) workers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under the stated performance model, iteration time is bounded below by \(\max\{W/(p\rho),M/\beta\}+s\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Latency-bandwidth performance model, not an oracle-complexity theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a bulk-synchronous model with perfect load balance, worker rate \(\rho\), aggregate bandwidth \(\beta\), and nonoverlapped synchronization latency \(\lambda\), any iteration performing \(W\) operations, moving \(M\) bytes, and executing \(s\) global synchronizations has time \(T_p\geq\max\{W/(p\rho),M/\beta\}+s\lambda\). Increasing \(p\) improves only the first term. Consequently, useful throughput scaling ends once \(W/(p\rho)\leq M/\beta+s\lambda\); beyond that point, additional workers cannot reduce the bandwidth and synchronization contributions in this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel speedup stops when arithmetic time falls below fixed memory-transfer and synchronization costs; more workers then cannot improve the modeled bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.title: Throughput–Synchronization Tradeoff

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the tradeoff leaf, but the record is unsourced and its scaling threshold does not follow from its own formula. For T_p >= max{W/(p rho), M/beta}+s lambda, the arithmetic-to-bandwidth crossover is W/(p rho) <= M/beta; adding s lambda inside that comparison is not justified merely because synchronization is additive. The model and corrected consequence need a direct source.

children.title: Memory-Bandwidth Scaling Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where data movement or sparse irregularity limits parallel and accelerator gains.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Roofline ceiling for a first-order LP kernel at a specified limiting memory level, without asserting ceiling attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a kernel performs \(W>0\) arithmetic operations and transfers at least \(M>0\) bytes through a specified limiting memory level. Let \(I=W/M\), let \(P_{\max}\) be peak arithmetic throughput, and let \(\beta\) be sustainable bandwidth at that memory level. Its attainable arithmetic throughput satisfies \(P_{\mathrm{att}}\le\min\{P_{\max},\beta I\}\). The ridge point is \(I=P_{\max}/\beta\): below it the bandwidth ceiling is lower, while above it the compute ceiling is lower. This comparison identifies the lower model ceiling but does not prove which resource limits a measured implementation. Reuse, compression, cache effects, irregular access, or a different memory level can change \(M\) and hence the classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Throughput is bounded by peak compute and bandwidth times arithmetic intensity; the lower ceiling changes at the ridge point, but this alone does not prove the observed bottleneck.
assumptions_latex: W and M count operations and compulsory or measured traffic for the same kernel execution.
P_{\max} and \beta refer to the same hardware and execution regime.
The limiting memory level is specified explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_{\mathrm{att}}\le\min\{P_{\max},\beta W/M\},\qquad I_{\mathrm{ridge}}=P_{\max}/\beta.

notation.meaning: arithmetic intensity at the selected memory level

knowledge_statements.title: Roofline Memory-Bandwidth Boundary

assumptions_latex: A kernel performs \(W\) arithmetic operations while transferring at least \(M>0\) bytes from limiting memory.
Peak arithmetic throughput is \(P_{\max}\) and sustainable bandwidth is \(\beta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Attainable throughput is at most \(\min\{P_{\max},\beta W/M\}\), with a bandwidth boundary at \(W/M=P_{\max}/\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Roofline-style boundary for sparse first-order LP kernels.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the arithmetic intensity be \(I=W/M\). Since execution requires at least \(W/P_{\max}\) seconds for arithmetic and at least \(M/\beta\) seconds for memory traffic, attainable arithmetic throughput is at most \(\min\{P_{\max},\beta I\}\). The kernel is bandwidth-limited when \(I<P_{\max}/\beta\) and compute-limited only when \(I\geq P_{\max}/\beta\). Thus sparse matrix-vector kernels with intensity bounded independently of processor count cannot sustain proportional scaling after their aggregate demand reaches \(\beta\), unless data reuse or compression reduces \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Throughput is capped by peak compute or bandwidth times arithmetic intensity; sparse kernels stop scaling when memory traffic saturates available bandwidth.
knowledge_statements.title: Memory-Bandwidth Scaling Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is an appropriate kind for this leaf, and the roofline ceiling min{P_max, beta I} is standard. No source is supplied, however, and crossing the ridge point classifies which roofline ceiling is lower rather than proving that an actual kernel is compute-limited. The processor-scaling conclusion additionally requires a defined memory level and validated traffic M.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral-data iteration bound for the network primal-dual method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite iteration bound expressed using the displacement D of the initial flow vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every demand b_j, every finite upper bound u_{ij}, and every component x_{ij} of the initial vector \mathbf{x} are integers, then the primal-dual method terminates within D^2 iterations, where D is the displacement of \mathbf{x}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If all demands, all finite arc upper bounds, and all components of the initial flow vector are integers, the primal-dual method terminates within D squared iterations, where D denotes the displacement of that vector.
assumptions_latex: b_j\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for all }j
u_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for every finite }u_{ij}
x_{ij}\in\mathbb Z\quad\text{for every component of the initial }\mathbf{x}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The primal-dual method terminates in at most }D^2\text{ iterations, where }D\text{ is the displacement of }\mathbf{x}.

source_evidence.locator: The Primal-Dual Method / 23. The Primal-Dual Method / Theorem 23.1

source_refs.locator: The Primal-Dual Method / 23. The Primal-Dual Method / Theorem 23.1

knowledge_statements.title: Integral-data iteration bound for the network primal-dual method

source_witnesses.locator: The Primal-Dual Method / 23. The Primal-Dual Method / Theorem 23.1

directory_assessment.rationale: The bound concerns an integral network-flow primal-dual method rather than the general first-order LP family or an LP interior-point method. Its primary ownership should be reconciled with network-flow algorithms, with an LP cross-index retained if useful.

children.title: PDHG Family
children.top_down_role: Primal-dual hybrid gradient variants used for saddle formulations of linear programs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone-inclusion representation underlying the generic PDHG family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \min_x\max_y\ f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y), define z=(x,y), \mathcal A z=(\partial f(x),\partial g^*(y)), and \mathcal Bz=(K^*y,-Kx). Then z is a saddle point exactly when 0\in(\mathcal A+\mathcal B)z. PDHG evaluates the separate resolvents associated with \partial f and \partial g^* while coupling the blocks through applications of K and K^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PDHG targets the saddle KKT inclusion formed by separable subdifferentials and a skew linear primal-dual coupling.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g^*\text{ are proper, closed, and convex}
K\text{ is linear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in(\mathcal A+\mathcal B)z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z\text{ is a saddle point}.
review_flags: This record states the common optimality system, not a specific preconditioned splitting identity or convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: PDHG Saddle Optimality Inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict positive-definiteness condition for primal and dual step operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\succ0\) and \(S\succ0\) be primal and dual step operators. Then \(H=\begin{pmatrix}T^{-1}&-K^*\\-K&S^{-1}\end{pmatrix}\succ0\) if and only if \(S^{-1}-KTK^*\succ0\), equivalently \(\lVert S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert<1\). For \(T=\tau I\) and \(S=\sigma I\), this becomes \(\tau\sigma\lVert K\rVert^2<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict preconditioned PDHG metric regime is equivalent to the scaled coupling operator having norm below one.
assumptions_latex: T\succ0
S\succ0
K\text{ is linear between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H\succ0\iff S^{-1}-KTK^*\succ0\iff\lVert S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert<1.
review_flags: This states the strict metric regime; boundary cases require separate analysis.
knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric PDHG Admissibility Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preconditioned PDHG with unit primal extrapolation and positive-definite primal and dual step operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_x\max_y f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\), let \(T\succ0\), \(S\succ0\), and \(\bar x^0=x^0\). Define \(\operatorname{prox}^{Q}_{h}(a)=\arg\min_w\{h(w)+\tfrac12\|w-a\|_Q^2\}\). Iterate \[y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{S^{-1}}_{g^*}(y^k+SK\bar x^k),\quad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}^{T^{-1}}_f(x^k-TK^*y^{k+1}),\quad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable-metric PDHG alternates dual and primal metric-proximal updates and then extrapolates the primal block.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g^*\text{ are proper, closed, and convex}
T\succ0
S\succ0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\text{ is the preconditioned PDHG update associated with }(T,S).

notation.meaning: Proximal map in the metric induced by Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Variable-Metric PDHG Updates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: PDHG Instability for an Unrestricted Step Product
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar bilinear example showing divergence for a step product outside the strict admissible regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(L(x,y)=xy\), \(f=g^*=0\), \(K=1\), \(\bar x^k=2x^k-x^{k-1}\), and scalar steps with \(a=\tau\sigma=4\). Eliminating the dual variable gives \[x^{k+1}=(2-2a)x^k+(a-1)x^{k-1},\] whose characteristic polynomial at \(a=4\) is \(\lambda^2+6\lambda-3\). Its root \(-3-2\sqrt3\) has modulus greater than one, so an initialization with a component in the corresponding mode diverges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar bilinear PDHG can diverge when the step product is chosen outside the admissible regime.
assumptions_latex: \tau\sigma=4
\bar x^k=2x^k-x^{k-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{\mathrm{iter}}\ge|-3-2\sqrt3|>1.

notation.meaning: Spectral radius of the linear recurrence.

review_flags: This example establishes failure for an inadmissible choice but does not classify every equality-boundary case.
knowledge_statements.title: PDHG Instability for an Unrestricted Step Product

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative convergence for the accepted unit-extrapolation variable-metric PDHG convention in the strict metric regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x\max_y f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)\) and the accepted variable-metric PDHG iteration. If \(T\succ0\), \(S\succ0\), \(\lVert S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert<1\), and the saddle-point set is nonempty, then in finite dimensions the full sequence \((x^k,y^k)\) converges to a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a nonempty saddle set and the strict variable-metric step condition, the accepted finite-dimensional PDHG sequence converges to a saddle point.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g^*\text{ are proper, closed, and convex}
K\text{ is linear between finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces}
T\succ0,\quad S\succ0
\lVert S^{1/2}KT^{1/2}\rVert<1
\operatorname{zer}(\mathcal A+\mathcal B)\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^k,y^k)\to(x^\star,y^\star),\qquad 0\in(\mathcal A+\mathcal B)(x^\star,y^\star).

notation.meaning: Block subdifferential operator from the accepted saddle inclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Variable-Metric PDHG Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict PDHG Step Condition Is Not Necessary in Every Instance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-boundary scalar example for unit-extrapolation PDHG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=g^*=0\), \(K=1\), \(\tau\sigma=1\), and \(\bar x^k=2x^k-x^{k-1}\), elimination of \(y\) gives \(x^{k+1}=0\) for every \(k\ge1\). Moreover, \(y^{k+1}=(x^k-x^{k+1})/\tau\), so \((x^k,y^k)\to(0,0)\). Thus equality in \(\tau\sigma\lVert K\rVert^2\le1\) can be convergent although the general accepted theorem assumes strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar bilinear PDHG converges at the equality boundary, so the strict norm condition is sufficient but not necessary for every instance.
assumptions_latex: \tau\sigma=1
\bar x^k=2x^k-x^{k-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x^k,y^k)\to(0,0)\quad\text{with}\quad\tau\sigma\lVert K\rVert^2=1.
review_flags: This establishes possible equality-boundary convergence, not a general equality-boundary theorem.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict PDHG Step Condition Is Not Necessary in Every Instance

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable saddle-stationarity residual for the accepted variable-metric, dual-first, unit-extrapolation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the accepted updates, define \[r_x^{k+1}=T^{-1}(x^k-x^{k+1}),\qquad r_y^{k+1}=S^{-1}(y^k-y^{k+1})+K(\bar x^k-x^{k+1}).\] Exact proximal optimality gives \[r_x^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})+K^*y^{k+1},\qquad r_y^{k+1}\in\partial g^*(y^{k+1})-Kx^{k+1}.\] Hence \(r_x^{k+1}=r_y^{k+1}=0\) certifies that \((x^{k+1},y^{k+1})\) is a saddle point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive-iterate differences and the extrapolation correction give computable elements of both saddle KKT inclusions; both vanishing certifies a saddle point.
assumptions_latex: Both proximal subproblems are solved exactly.
T\succ0,\ S\succ0.
The dual block is updated before the primal block using the accepted unit-extrapolation convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_x^{k+1}=0\ \text{and}\ r_y^{k+1}=0\Longrightarrow 0\in\partial f(x^{k+1})+K^*y^{k+1},\quad0\in\partial g^*(y^{k+1})-Kx^{k+1}.
knowledge_statements.title: PDHG Proximal KKT Residual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ergodic Restricted-Gap Bound for Strict-Metric PDHG
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard O(1/N) saddle-gap bound for bounded test sets under the accepted unit-extrapolation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N x^k\) and \(y_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^N y^k\). Under the accepted variable-metric PDHG assumptions, for every \((x,y)\), \[L(x_N,y)-L(x,y_N)\le\frac{\|x-x^0\|_{T^{-1}}^2+\|y-y^0\|_{S^{-1}}^2}{2N}.\] Consequently, for bounded test sets \(X\) and \(Y\), the restricted gap \[\sup_{y\in Y}L(x_N,y)-\inf_{x\in X}L(x,y_N)\] is at most \(C_{X,Y}/N\), where \(C_{X,Y}=\tfrac12\sup_{(x,y)\in X\times Y}(\|x-x^0\|_{T^{-1}}^2+\|y-y^0\|_{S^{-1}}^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cesàro averages of strict-metric PDHG have an O(1/N) restricted saddle-gap bound on bounded comparison sets.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g^*\text{ are proper, closed, and convex}.
T\succ0,\ S\succ0.
The accepted dual-first, unit-extrapolation PDHG iteration is used.
X\text{ and }Y\text{ are bounded for the restricted-gap conclusion}.

knowledge_statements.title: PDLP Family

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^Tx:x\in X,\ Ax=b\}\), where \(X=[l,u]\), choose positive diagonal matrices \(T,S\), initialize \(x^0\in X,y^0\), and set \(\bar x^0=x^0\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Scaling Conjugacy for the LP Saddle Model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of primal equality residuals, multipliers, and smooth stationarity vectors between scaled and original LP coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=D_x\hat x\) and scale \(Ax=b\) to \(D_y(AD_x\hat x-b)=0\), where \(D_x,D_y\) are nonsingular diagonal matrices. The scaled saddle term \(\hat y^TD_y(AD_x\hat x-b)\) equals \(y^T(Ax-b)\) under \(y=D_y^T\hat y\). Hence, with \(\hat r_p=D_y(Ax-b)\), \(r_p=Ax-b=D_y^{-1}\hat r_p\). If \(d=c+A^Ty\) and \(\hat d=D_x^Tc+D_x^TA^TD_y^T\hat y\), then \(d=D_x^{-T}\hat d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=[l,u]\), \(f(x)=c^Tx+\delta_X(x)\), \(K=A\), and \(g(z)=\delta_{\{b\}}(z)\). Since \(g^*(y)=b^Ty\), the PDHG saddle function is \(f(x)+\langle Ax,y\rangle-g^*(y)=c^Tx+\delta_X(x)+y^T(Ax-b)\). Consequently, scalar-step PDHG specializes to \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\sigma(A\bar x^k-b)\) and \(x^{k+1}=\Pi_X(x^k-\tau(c+A^Ty^{k+1}))\). Replacing scalar steps by compatible positive diagonal metrics yields the matrix-free PDLP core; averaging, adaptive scaling, and restart policies do not change this underlying saddle representation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \min_{x,z}f(x)+g(z) subject to Ax+Bz=b, suppose f and g are proper closed convex functions, an unaugmented-Lagrangian saddle point exists, every ADMM subproblem is solved exactly, and \rho>0 is fixed. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Primal and Dual Residuals for Exact Scaled ADMM
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT-residual interpretation for the declared update order and multiplier convention in exact two-block scaled ADMM.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For exact scaled ADMM applied to \(\min f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=b\), set \(y^{k+1}=\rho u^{k+1}\) and define \[r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-b,\qquad s^{k+1}=\rho A^{\mathsf T}B(z^{k+1}-z^k).\] Under the update \(x\) then \(z\) then \(u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}\), exact block optimality gives \(0\in\partial g(z^{k+1})+B^{\mathsf T}y^{k+1}\) and \(s^{k+1}\in\partial f(x^{k+1})+A^{\mathsf T}y^{k+1}\). Thus \(r^{k+1}\) is the coupling-feasibility residual and \(s^{k+1}\) is the remaining first-block stationarity residual for this convention.

\rho>0.

knowledge_statements.title: ADMM–Splitting Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: ADMM identified with Douglas–Rachford splitting on the Fenchel dual inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x,z} f(x)+g(z)\) subject to \(Ax+Bz=b\), and its dual objective \(f^*(-A^Ty)+g^*(-B^Ty)+b^Ty\). Define \(F(y)=f^*(-A^Ty)\) and \(G(y)=g^*(-B^Ty)+b^Ty\). Whenever the ADMM subproblems and the corresponding resolvents are well defined, two-block ADMM with penalty \(\rho\) is equivalent, after the standard affine identification of the multiplier and shadow variables, to Douglas–Rachford splitting with parameter \(\rho\) for \(0\in\partial F(y)+\partial G(y)\). Thus the ADMM multiplier sequence is the recovered dual sequence of the splitting iteration, up to indexing convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two-block ADMM on a linearly constrained LP is Douglas–Rachford splitting applied to its dual subdifferential inclusion, after an affine change of variables.

Strong duality holds and a primal–dual solution exists
The ADMM subproblems and dual resolvents are well defined
