children.title: Active-Set Identification Regime
children.top_down_role: Geometric conditions and complexity consequences associated with identifying the active constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the permanent stabilization event underlying the two-stage complexity split.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A^*\) be the target active index set and \(A_k\) the set predicted from iterate \(z^k\). Finite identification means that some \(K_{\mathrm{id}}<\infty\) satisfies \[A_k=A^*\qquad\text{for every }k\ge K_{\mathrm{id}}.\] Equality at one iteration is not identification unless later updates preserve the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite identification means that, after a finite iteration, the predicted active set permanently equals the target active set.
assumptions_latex: A target solution or optimal face determines an unambiguous active set \(A^*\).
The prediction rule defining \(A_k\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K_{\mathrm{id}}<\infty\ \forall k\ge K_{\mathrm{id}}:\ A_k=A^*.

notation.meaning: active set predicted at iteration k

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Active-Set Identification

assumptions_latex: The LP is in standard form and has a strictly complementary solution \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\).
The primal-dual iterates converge to that solution in the infinity norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Once \(\max\{\lVert x^k-x^*\rVert_\infty,\lVert s^k-s^*\rVert_\infty\}<\gamma/2\), thresholding at \(\gamma/2\) exactly identifies the positive-primal and positive-slack index sets.

notation.meaning: Indices positive in the primal solution
Indices positive in the dual slack

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite threshold identification near a fixed strictly complementary primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) with dual slack \(s=c-A^\top y\ge0\). Let \((x^*,y^*,s^*)\) be strictly complementary and define \(B=\{i:x_i^*>0\}\), \(N=\{i:s_i^*>0\}\), and \(\gamma=\min\bigl(\min_{i\in B}x_i^*,\min_{i\in N}s_i^*\bigr)>0\). If \((x^k,s^k)\to(x^*,s^*)\) in \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty\), then every iterate satisfying \[\max\{\lVert x^k-x^*\rVert_\infty,\lVert s^k-s^*\rVert_\infty\}<\gamma/2\] obeys \(B=\{i:x_i^k>\gamma/2\}\) and \(N=\{i:s_i^k>\gamma/2\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity creates a positive margin; sufficiently accurate primal-dual iterates identify the positive primal and positive slack indices by thresholding.
knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Identification Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The threshold conclusion is mathematically correct for convergence to the fixed strictly complementary solution, and condition fits the regime leaf. No cited source supports the identification result or its applicability to an LP algorithm.

children.title: Pre-Identification Complexity Phase
children.top_down_role: Global behavior before the relevant active structure becomes stable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a certified iterate-distance rate into a strict-threshold identification time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[e_k=\max\{\|x^k-x^*\|_\infty,\|s^k-s^*\|_\infty\}\le\frac{D}{(k+1)^p}\qquad(k\ge0),\] where \(D,p>0\), and let \(\gamma>0\) be a strict-complementarity separation. If classification is correct whenever \(e_k<\gamma/2\), then it is correct for every \[k\ge K_{\mathrm{id}}:=\left\lfloor(2D/\gamma)^{1/p}\right\rfloor.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An algebraic iterate-distance rate yields an exact strict-threshold identification index; the floor handles equality correctly.
assumptions_latex: \(e_k\le D/(k+1)^p\) for all relevant indices.
The classifier is correct whenever \(e_k<\gamma/2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\ge\left\lfloor(2D/\gamma)^{1/p}\right\rfloor\Longrightarrow e_k<\gamma/2.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Algebraic-Rate Identification Index

assumptions_latex: The target solution has strict-complementarity margin \(\gamma>0\).
Before identification, the method guarantees \(\max\{\lVert x^k-x^*\rVert_\infty,\lVert s^k-s^*\rVert_\infty\}\le D/(k+1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Identification occurs no later than iteration \(K_{\mathrm{id}}=\lceil2D/\gamma\rceil\), up to the endpoint convention for strict thresholding.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification time obtained by combining a global iterate-distance rate with the strict-complementarity margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((x^*,s^*)\) have strict-complementarity margin \(\gamma>0\), and suppose the pre-identification iterates satisfy \[\max\{\lVert x^k-x^*\rVert_\infty,\lVert s^k-s^*\rVert_\infty\}\le\frac{D}{k+1}.\] The threshold identification condition is reached whenever \(D/(k+1)<\gamma/2\). Thus identification occurs by \(K_{\mathrm{id}}=\lceil2D/\gamma\rceil\), with one additional iteration if equality occurs and strict thresholding is required. The pre-identification work is therefore \(O(D/\gamma)\) first-order iterations, independently of the later requested optimization tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an inverse-linear iterate-distance rate, the time to identify a strictly complementary active set scales as the rate constant divided by the complementarity margin.
knowledge_statements.title: Pre-Identification Complexity Phase

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The phase-bound kind fits, but the assumed inverse-linear iterate-distance rate is method-specific and uncited. The exact identification index also depends on the strict inequality: the first valid k satisfies k+1>2D/gamma, so the endpoint convention must be stated precisely.

children.title: Post-Identification Complexity Phase
children.top_down_role: Local behavior after stabilization of the active structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the structural reduction available after a correct active set becomes invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), suppose the invariant identified zero set is \(N\), and let \(B=\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus N\). Every later iterate on the identified face has \(x_N=0\), leaving the reduced primal problem \[\min\{c_B^\top x_B:A_Bx_B=b,\ x_B\ge0\}.\] Residuals and updates may be formed in the reduced variables when the algorithm preserves \(x_N=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After correct permanent identification, fixed zero variables can be removed and subsequent work performed on the reduced LP face.
assumptions_latex: The identified zero set is correct and remains invariant.
The chosen update is compatible with eliminating the fixed coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_N^k=0\ (k\ge K_{\mathrm{id}})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{the reduced primal LP uses }A_Bx_B=b,\ x_B\ge0.
knowledge_statements.title: Face-Restricted Reduced Problem After Identification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Face-restricted stationary iteration after a complementary partition has become invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual, let \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), impose \(x_N=0\) and \(s_B=0\), and define \(u=(x_B,y)\), \[K=\begin{bmatrix}A_B&0\\0&A_B^\top\end{bmatrix},\qquad h=\binom b{c_B}.\] For any dimensionally compatible residual preconditioner \(M\), set \[u^{t+1}=u^t-M(Ku^t-h),\qquad s_N^{t+1}=c_N-A_N^\top y^{t+1}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After identification, the fixed-zero coordinates may be eliminated and a stationary iteration applied to the remaining primal and dual equations.
assumptions_latex: \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) is correct and invariant.
The reduced equations \(Ku=h\) are consistent.
\(M\) maps reduced residuals to reduced-variable corrections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_N^t=0,\quad s_B^t=0,\quad u^{t+1}=u^t-M(Ku^t-h).
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Complementary-System Iteration

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact update count for a contractive reduced stationary iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u^*\) satisfy \(Ku^*=h\), and suppose an induced norm satisfies \(\|I-MK\|\le q<1\). Then \[\|u^t-u^*\|\le q^t\|u^0-u^*\|.\] For \(\varepsilon>0\), it suffices to take \[T(\varepsilon)=\max\left\{0,\left\lceil\frac{\log(\|u^0-u^*\|/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/q)}\right\rceil\right\}.\] Without a uniform contraction, no logarithmic post-identification bound follows from identification alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verified contraction gives logarithmic post-identification complexity, with zero updates when the initial reduced error already meets tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: t\ge T(\varepsilon)\Longrightarrow\|u^t-u^*\|\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Post-Identification Contraction Bound

assumptions_latex: The correct active partition is fixed after iteration \(K_{\mathrm{id}}\).
On the identified face, the update contracts a reduced residual \(R_Fully developed??\) by a factor \(q\in(0,1)\) per iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After identification, \(R_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}+t})\le q^tR_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}})\), so \(\lceil\log(R_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}})/\varepsilon)/\log(1/q)\rceil\) further iterations suffice.

notation.meaning: Residual restricted to the identified face

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional linear phase after exact active-set identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that iteration \(K_{\mathrm{id}}\) identifies the correct LP face and all subsequent iterates remain on it. Let \(R_F\) be a residual for the reduced primal-dual system. If the face-restricted update satisfies \[R_F(z^{k+1})\le qR_F(z^k)\qquad(k\ge K_{\mathrm{id}}),\quad 0<q<1,\] then \(R_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}+t})\le q^tR_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}})\). Consequently, at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\log(R_F(z^{K_{\mathrm{id}}})/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/q)}\right\rceil\] post-identification iterations suffice to attain \(R_F\le\varepsilon\). Total work is the identification cost plus this logarithmic term.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once the correct face is fixed, a contractive reduced update reaches high accuracy in logarithmically many additional iterations.
knowledge_statements.title: Post-Identification Complexity Phase

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The geometric consequence is valid conditional on contraction, and complexity_bound fits. However, the reduced update and residual are unspecified and uncited, while the assumptions contain the malformed expression “R_Fully developed??”.

children.title: Identification Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Degeneracy or instability regimes that prevent a clean two-stage interpretation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Identification Bound Without a Margin Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that instancewise strict complementarity does not yield a uniform identification complexity bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta>0\), consider \(\min\{\delta x:x\ge0\}\). Its unique optimum is \(x^*=0\), and the complementary dual slack is \(s^*=\delta\), so the identification margin is \(\gamma=\delta\). Any sufficient threshold rule requiring slack error below \(\gamma/2\) therefore requires error below \(\delta/2\). Since \(\delta\downarrow0\) is possible, no finite margin-independent iteration bound can uniformly guarantee identification over this family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity may hold with an arbitrarily small margin, so uniform identification complexity requires a quantitative margin lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Identification uses complementary slack information to classify a zero primal variable.
The sufficient accuracy threshold is proportional to the smallest positive complementary component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{\delta>0}\gamma_\delta=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{no margin-independent uniform finite identification bound}.

notation.meaning: objective coefficient and optimal dual slack

knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Identification Bound Without a Margin Lower Bound

assumptions_latex: Active indices are defined as zero coordinates at a selected optimal solution.
Identification is required to be locally constant around that solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without an isolated active pattern or a positive complementarity margin, finite identification need not be well-defined or stable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by nonunique optimal faces and absence of a strict-complementarity margin at the selected limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the LP \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}} 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x\ge0.\] Its solution set is \(X^*=[0,\infty)\). At the optimal point \(x^*=0\), the inequality is active, whereas at every arbitrarily close optimal point \(x>0\) it is inactive. Hence no neighborhood of \(x^*=0\) has a constant optimal active set. A convergent sequence \(x^k>0\) with \(x^k\downarrow0\) never identifies the active status of its limit in finite time. Thus finite active-set identification requires additional isolation, nondegeneracy, or strict-complementarity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When nearby optima have different active sets, convergence alone cannot ensure finite identification; a sequence may approach an active constraint while remaining strictly interior.
knowledge_statements.title: Identification Failure Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed LP is a valid counterexample to finite identification from convergence alone, and failure_boundary is the correct kind. A cited source or explicit standard-field rationale is required for the broader identification-boundary claim.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resource conditions distinguishing the huge-scale first-order regime from factorization-based regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order LP implementation is matrix-free when each iteration accesses \(A\) through products \(Av\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}u\), while storing sparse \(A\), the current iterates, and \(O(m+n)\) auxiliary scalars. Under this storage model, working memory is \[O(\bigl(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n\bigr),\] without storing an explicit KKT factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The huge-scale matrix-free regime uses sparse matrix-vector products and linear-size vectors instead of explicit KKT factors.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is stored sparsely.
Each iteration uses a constant number of \(A\)- and \(A^{\mathsf T}\)-products and only linear-size auxiliary vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\), with no explicit KKT-factor storage.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Huge-Scale Applicability Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Accuracy Boundary of a Sublinear Matrix-Free Rate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional loss of competitiveness caused by sublinear residual convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a matrix-free method guarantees \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)^\alpha\) for \(C>0\) and \(0<\alpha\le1\), then \[k\ge \left(\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\right)^{1/\alpha}-1\] is sufficient to guarantee \(R(z^k)\le\varepsilon\). Thus this guarantee has polynomial, rather than logarithmic, dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sublinear residual guarantee yields a polynomial inverse-tolerance iteration bound, delimiting the low-accuracy regime.
assumptions_latex: \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)^\alpha\).
\(C>0\), \(0<\alpha\le1\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=O((C/\varepsilon)^{1/\alpha})\) iterations suffice under the stated guarantee.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy Boundary of a Sublinear Matrix-Free Rate

assumptions_latex: A first-order iteration uses a constant number of products by \(A\) and \(A^\top\).
The method has residual guarantee \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)\).
Sparse matrix-vector products cost \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual accuracy \(\varepsilon\) is attained in \(O(C/\varepsilon)\) iterations, \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)C/\varepsilon)\) arithmetic operations, and linear sparse-storage memory.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse matrix-vector oracle model for moderate residual accuracy on very large LPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) be stored sparsely. Suppose each first-order iteration uses at most a constant number of multiplications by \(A\) and \(A^\top\), vector operations of cost \(O(m+n)\), and satisfies \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)\). Then achieving \(R(z^k)\le\varepsilon\) requires \(k=O(C/\varepsilon)\) iterations and \[O\!\left((\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\frac{C}{\varepsilon}\right)\] arithmetic operations. Storage is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)\). This regime is computationally relevant when \(\varepsilon\) is moderate and sparse matrix-vector products remain feasible while factorization is not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At moderate accuracy, a matrix-free first-order LP method trades inverse-accuracy iteration growth for sparse, linear-memory iterations suitable for extremely large problems.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Accuracy Huge-Scale Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The arithmetic and storage bounds follow from the stated oracle model, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. The underlying LP method, residual normalization, and O(1/k) guarantee are not identified or sourced.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: PDLP: A Practical First-Order Method for Large-Scale Linear Programming
top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Feasibility polishing and high-accuracy large-scale experiments
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: PDLP: A Practical First-Order Method for Large-Scale Linear Programming

children.title: High-Accuracy Optimization Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity considerations when stringent objective accuracy is required.

assumptions_latex: The first-order residual bound is \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)\).
A polishing procedure costs \(P\) equivalent first-order iterations once its local assumptions hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuing the first-order phase is cost-dominated by polishing whenever \(C/\varepsilon-k>P\), subject to successful active-set or local-model validation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-based boundary between continued first-order optimization and a validated local polishing phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a first-order LP method guarantees \(R(z^k)\le C/(k+1)\), so its worst-case target iteration is \(K_\varepsilon=\lceil C/\varepsilon\rceil-1\). Let a locally valid polishing method have cost \(P\) measured in equivalent first-order iterations. At iteration \(k\), the high-accuracy regime favors polishing when its active-set or local-model assumptions are certified and \[K_\varepsilon-k>P.\] In particular, from the initial iterate the crossover scale is approximately \(\varepsilon<C/P\). This inequality is a cost criterion, not a guarantee that polishing assumptions are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: High accuracy favors polishing when the predicted remaining inverse-accuracy first-order work exceeds the validated local solver's cost.
knowledge_statements.title: High-Accuracy Optimization Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate role, but the crossover is only a constructed cost heuristic. The polishing method, basin assumptions, cost equivalence, and source supporting this regime boundary are absent.

children.title: Feasibility-Polishing Regime
children.top_down_role: Postprocessing focused on reducing primal or dual feasibility residuals.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine and nonnegative feasibility tests after fixing candidate primal zeros.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), impose \(x_{F^c}=0\). The reduced affine equations are consistent if and only if \[b\in\operatorname{range}(A_{:,F}),\] equivalently \(\min_u\lVert A_{:,F}u-b\rVert_2=0\). The corresponding nonnegative LP face is feasible if and only if there exists \(u\ge0\) satisfying \(A_{:,F}u=b\); zero unconstrained least-squares residual alone does not certify that sign condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Range membership tests the reduced equations, while feasibility of the nonnegative LP face additionally requires a nonnegative reduced solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\).
\(F\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x:Ax=b,\ x_{F^c}=0\iff b\in\operatorname{range}(A_{:,F})\), while LP-face feasibility additionally requires \(x_F\ge0\).

notation.meaning: indices allowed to be nonzero on the candidate primal face

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Primal Feasibility Test

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank Deficiency and Sign Failure in Face Polishing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness and sign failure for reduced feasibility corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A_{:,F}\) is rank deficient and \(A_{:,F}u=b\) is consistent, its solutions need not be unique. The minimum-norm solution \(A_{:,F}^{\dagger}b\) is unique but need not be nonnegative, even when a nonnegative solution exists. For example, \(A_{:,F}=[1\ -1]\) and \(b=1\) admit the nonnegative solution \((1,0)\), whereas the minimum-norm solution is \((1/2,-1/2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient reduced system may have feasible nonnegative solutions even though its minimum-norm representative violates nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A_{:,F})\).
\(A_{:,F}\) is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{:,F}^{\dagger}b\not\ge0\) may hold even when \(\{u\ge0:A_{:,F}u=b\}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Deficiency and Sign Failure in Face Polishing

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-robust face polishing using constrained primal and dual feasibility problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Find \(x_B\) satisfying \(A_Bx_B=b\), \(x_B\ge0\), and set \(x_N=0\). Independently find \(y\) satisfying \(A_B^\top y=c_B\), \(A_N^\top y\le c_N\), and set \(s_B=0\), \(s_N=c_N-A_N^\top y\). Reject the partition if either feasibility problem is infeasible; otherwise return \((x,y,s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polish a candidate complementary face by solving constrained primal and dual feasibility problems, rejecting the face when either side fails.
assumptions_latex: \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
The feasibility subproblems are solved exactly under the declared arithmetic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{accept}\Longrightarrow Ax=b,\ x\ge0,\ A^\top y+s=c,\ s\ge0,\ x_N=0,\ s_B=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Complementary-Face Polishing Algorithm

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined exact acceptance test for a polished face-restricted tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tuple \((x,y,s)\) is an exact primal-dual optimality certificate when \[Ax=b,\quad x\ge0,\quad A^\top y+s=c,\quad s\ge0,\quad x^\top s=0.\] Under \(x_N=0\), \(s_B=0\), and \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), complementarity is automatic. Failure of any required predicate mandates rejection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polished tuple is accepted only after primal feasibility, dual feasibility, signs, and complementarity all hold.
assumptions_latex: The stated equality-form primal-dual sign convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax=b,\ x\ge0,\ A^\top y+s=c,\ s\ge0,\ x^\top s=0\Longrightarrow c^\top x=b^\top y\text{ and }(x,y,s)\text{ is optimal}.
knowledge_statements.title: Complete Post-Polishing Optimality Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual feasibility conditions on a candidate complementary face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), a dual-feasible point with \(s_B=0\) exists if and only if some \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfies \[A_B^\top y=c_B,\qquad A_N^\top y\le c_N.\] Then \(s_N=c_N-A_N^\top y\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A candidate dual face is feasible exactly when its equality and remaining inequality conditions admit a common multiplier.
assumptions_latex: \(B\dot\cup N=\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(y,s):A^\top y+s=c,\ s\ge0,\ s_B=0\iff\exists y:A_B^\top y=c_B,\ A_N^\top y\le c_N.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Dual-Face Feasibility Characterization

assumptions_latex: Candidate zero sets \(N_x\) and \(N_s\) are fixed and disjoint.
The reduced primal and dual linear systems are consistent or are interpreted in least-squares form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the displayed reduced systems returns a face-restricted primal-dual point whose remaining feasibility residual is minimized before complementarity and sign checks.

notation.meaning: Indices fixed to zero in the primal variable
Indices fixed to zero in the dual slack

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Least-squares feasibility correction on a candidate complementary face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), input candidate sets \(N_x\) and \(N_s\) with \(N_x\cap N_s=\varnothing\). Set \(x_{N_x}=0\) and \(s_{N_s}=0\). Compute \(x_{N_x^c}\) as a minimum-norm minimizer of \[\min_u\lVert A_{:,N_x^c}u-b\rVert_2,\] and compute \((y,s_{N_s^c})\) as a minimum-norm minimizer of \[\min_{y,v}\lVert A^\top y+E_{N_s^c}v-c\rVert_2.\] Accept the polished point only if \(x\ge0\), \(s\ge0\), the requested feasibility tolerances hold, and \(x_i s_i\) satisfies the complementarity tolerance; otherwise reject the candidate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility polishing fixes candidate zero variables and slacks, solves reduced primal and dual systems, then accepts only after sign, feasibility, and complementarity checks.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility-Polishing Regime

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the polishing leaf, but disjointness alone does not make the candidate sets a complete complementary partition. The least-squares construction, rank-deficient cases, tolerances, and acceptance rule require an inspectable algorithmic source.

children.title: Accuracy-to-Polishing Transition
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which the computational emphasis shifts from global progress to residual refinement.

assumptions_latex: A candidate face has remained unchanged for a prescribed validation window.
A polishing map is defined and has an estimated cost \(P\).
The current point lies within the stated local residual threshold \(\rho\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transition occurs only when face stability, basin membership, and the cost inequality \(K_\varepsilon-k>P\) all hold; otherwise the first-order phase continues.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validated switching rule from matrix-free iterations to face-restricted feasibility polishing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At first-order iteration \(k\), form a candidate complementary face by thresholding the primal variables and dual slacks. Transition to polishing only if: \(\mathrm{(i)}\) the candidate face has remained unchanged over the prescribed validation window; \(\mathrm{(ii)}\) the normalized KKT residual satisfies \(R(z^k)\le\rho\), where \(\rho\) is a certified polishing-basin threshold; and \(\mathrm{(iii)}\) the predicted remaining first-order work satisfies \(K_\varepsilon-k>P\). Apply the polishing map and accept its output only after feasibility, sign, and complementarity checks. If any test fails, retain \(z^k\) and continue the first-order method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Switch to polishing only after the candidate face stabilizes, the iterate enters a validated local basin, and polishing is cheaper than predicted remaining first-order work.
knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-to-Polishing Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is suitable for the transition leaf, but the validation window, certified basin threshold, work predictor, and polishing cost are method-specific and have no supporting citation.

children.title: Poor Scaling Effects
children.top_down_role: Complexity degradation caused by unfavorable row, column, or coefficient scales.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute Residual Noninvariance under Row Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent equality systems can give arbitrarily different unnormalized residuals at the same point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equations \(x=1\) and \(\delta x=\delta\), with \(0<\delta\le1\), have the same feasible set \(X^*=\{1\}\). At \(x=0\), \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)=1\), whereas the absolute residual of the scaled equation is \(|\delta x-\delta|=\delta\). Thus, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), choosing \(0<\delta\le\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\) makes this infeasible point pass the unnormalized residual test while remaining unit distance from feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row scaling can make an absolute residual arbitrarily small without moving the candidate closer to the unchanged feasible set.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\delta\le1\)
Acceptance uses the unnormalized absolute residual of the displayed equation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |\delta x-\delta|\le\varepsilon\text{ at }x=0\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad\operatorname{dist}(x,X^*)\le\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: common feasible set of the equivalent equations

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute Residual Noninvariance under Row Scaling

assumptions_latex: Algorithmic constants depend monotonically on the spectral condition number of the scaled linear operator.
No compensating row or column equilibration is applied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(A_\delta=\operatorname{diag}(1,\delta)\), \(\kappa_2(A_\delta)=1/\delta\); thus rate constants depending on \(\kappa_2\) become unbounded as \(\delta\downarrow0\), although the system remains nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete nonsingular family showing how row-scale disparity degrades condition-dependent first-order guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\delta\le1\), consider the nonsingular constraint matrix \[A_\delta=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&\delta\end{pmatrix}.\] Its singular values are \(1\) and \(\delta\), hence \(\kappa_2(A_\delta)=1/\delta\). Therefore any first-order LP complexity estimate whose constant grows with \(\lVert A_\delta\rVert_2/\sigma_{\min}(A_\delta)\), or with a positive power of that ratio, deteriorates without bound as \(\delta\downarrow0\). The underlying equations remain exactly solvable for every \(\delta>0\); the degradation is caused by representation scaling rather than combinatorial problem size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple diagonal rescaling can make the operator condition number arbitrarily large, degrading condition-dependent first-order bounds even though every scaled system remains nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.title: Poor Scaling Effects

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition-number calculation is correct and failure_boundary fits. The claimed effect on first-order LP complexity remains conditional and needs a source tying a specific method's rate constant to this spectral condition number.

children.title: Weight Imbalance Effects
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity arising from disproportionate primal-dual or residual weighting.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp Coordinatewise Interpretation of a Weighted Residual Test
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-coordinate accuracy implied by a positive diagonal weighted Euclidean certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_q)\) with \(w_i>0\). If \(\lVert Wr\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\), then \[|r_i|\le \frac{\varepsilon}{w_i}\qquad(i=1,\ldots,q).\] Each bound is sharp: for fixed \(i\), equality holds for \(r=(\varepsilon/w_i)e_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted residual tolerance gives the sharp coordinatewise bound epsilon divided by the corresponding weight.
assumptions_latex: \(r\in\mathbb R^q\).
\(w_i>0\) for every \(i\).
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Wr\rVert_2\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow |r_i|\le\varepsilon/w_i\) for every \(i\), and each bound is sharp.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Coordinatewise Interpretation of a Weighted Residual Test
Weight Imbalance Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of diagonal residual weights on a first-order LP stopping certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the unweighted certificate residual be \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_q)\), and let \(W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_q)\) with \(w_i>0\). Then \[w_{\min}\lVert r\rVert_2\leq \lVert Wr\rVert_2\leq w_{\max}\lVert r\rVert_2.\] Consequently, accepting when \(\lVert Wr\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\) guarantees only \(\lVert r\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon/w_{\min}\). The distortion factor is \(\kappa_W=w_{\max}/w_{\min}\); hence severe weight imbalance can make a small weighted residual coexist with a large componentwise or unweighted residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal residual weights distort certificate accuracy by as much as their largest-to-smallest weight ratio; a small weighted residual need not imply uniformly small residual components.
assumptions_latex: \(r\in\mathbb{R}^q\).
\(0<w_{\min}\leq w_i\leq w_{\max}<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert Wr\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow \lVert r\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon/w_{\min}\), with distortion \(\kappa_W\).

notation.meaning: vector of primal, dual, and gap certificate residuals

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The norm inequalities are correct, and the property kind fits the leaf. A source is still required for interpreting this diagonal weighting as the local first-order LP certificate model.

children.title: Weak Error-Bound Effects
children.top_down_role: Slow local progress associated with unfavorable error-bound geometry.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearly Parallel Constraints Force a Large Error-Bound Constant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-norm constraint geometry whose violation residual is arbitrarily smaller than distance to feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0<\delta\le1\), let \(X_\delta=\{(x_1,x_2):x_2\ge0,\ x_2\le\delta x_1\}\) and \(R_\delta(x)=\max\{(-x_2)_+,(x_2-\delta x_1)_+\}\). At \(\bar x=(-1,0)\), \(R_\delta(\bar x)=\delta\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(\bar x,X_\delta)=1\). The two constraint normals have norms between \(1\) and \(\sqrt2\). Hence every bound \(\operatorname{dist}(x,X_\delta)\le H_\delta R_\delta(x)\) valid at \(\bar x\) requires \(H_\delta\ge1/\delta\), which diverges as the boundary rays become nearly parallel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with bounded row norms, nearly parallel constraints can force the residual-to-distance constant to diverge.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\delta\le1\)
Distance is Euclidean
The residual is the maximum displayed inequality violation
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_\delta\ge\frac{\operatorname{dist}(\bar x,X_\delta)}{R_\delta(\bar x)}=\frac1\delta.
knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Parallel Constraints Force a Large Error-Bound Constant
Weak Error-Bound Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation of residual convergence into distance-to-solution convergence through an LP error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X^*\neq\varnothing\) be the LP solution set and suppose an error bound \(\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H\lVert R(z)\rVert\) holds on the iterates. To ensure \(\operatorname{dist}(z_k,X^*)\leq\varepsilon\), it suffices to drive the residual below \(\varepsilon/H\). Thus, if a first-order method guarantees \(\lVert R(z_k)\rVert\leq C/\sqrt{k}\), then \[k\geq C^2H^2/\varepsilon^2\] suffices. A weak error bound, represented by large \(H\), therefore amplifies the iteration requirement quadratically for this residual rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large error-bound constant forces proportionally smaller residuals; with a square-root residual rate, the resulting iteration bound grows quadratically in that constant.
assumptions_latex: \(X^*\neq\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H\lVert R(z)\rVert\).
\(\lVert R(z_k)\rVert\leq C/\sqrt{k}\) for \(k\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\geq C^2H^2/\varepsilon^2\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(z_k,X^*)\leq\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional derivation is mathematically correct and the complexity-bound kind is appropriate, but no source supports the selected LP error bound or residual-rate model.

children.title: Compounded Numerical Degradation
children.top_down_role: Regimes where multiple pathologies reinforce one another.

knowledge_statements.title: Compounded Numerical Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined effect of scaling, weighting, error bounds, and residual-evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=WS\) be an invertible scaling-and-weighting operator, and suppose \(\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H\lVert R(z)\rVert_2\). If a computed residual \(\widehat R(z)\) satisfies \(\lVert R(z)-\widehat R(z)\rVert_2\leq\eta\), then acceptance under \(\lVert T\widehat R(z)\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\) yields \[\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_{\min}(T)}+\eta\right).\] Hence the certificate cannot guarantee distance below \(H\eta\), and poor scaling or weight imbalance magnifies its nominal tolerance by \(H/\sigma_{\min}(T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling, weight imbalance, weak error bounds, and residual-evaluation error combine multiplicatively or additively, creating an accuracy floor and an amplified stopping tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(T=WS\) is invertible.
\(\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H\lVert R(z)\rVert_2\).
\(\lVert R(z)-\widehat R(z)\rVert_2\leq\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert T\widehat R(z)\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(z,X^*)\leq H(\varepsilon/\sigma_{\min}(T)+\eta)\).

notation.meaning: combined residual scaling and weighting operator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed bound follows from the stated norm and error-bound assumptions, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The combined certificate interpretation is synthetic and needs a source specifying the residual, scaling, and perturbation model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust Status Requires Separation from Ill-Posed Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correct uncertainty-set condition for status ambiguity near an ill-posed boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the definite LP-status regions be disjoint open subsets of a normed data space, and let \(\Sigma\) contain their boundary. For data \(d\), define \(\rho(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\). If the admissible uncertainty set is the full closed ball \(U=B[d,\delta]\), then \(\delta<\rho(d)\) guarantees that \(U\) remains in the status region containing \(d\). If \(\delta\ge\rho(d)\) and the distance is attained, \(U\) contains boundary data, so no procedure using only the uncertain representation can certify one definite status uniformly for every member of \(U\). Merely knowing that the unknown actual perturbation has norm at most \(\delta\) does not imply ambiguity unless all points in that ball remain admissible alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform status certification requires the entire admissible uncertainty set to stay inside one status region; a perturbation upper bound alone is not an impossibility result.
assumptions_latex: Definite status regions are disjoint and open in a fixed normed data space
\(\Sigma\) contains their boundary
The admissible alternatives equal the full closed radius-\(\delta\) ball
The distance to \(\Sigma\) is attained for the stated \(\delta\ge\rho(d)\) conclusion
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta<\rho(d)\Rightarrow B[d,\delta]\text{ lies in one status region};\qquad \delta\ge\rho(d)\Rightarrow B[d,\delta]\cap\Sigma\ne\varnothing.

notation.meaning: distance from d to the status boundary
set of all data compatible with the representation

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Status Requires Separation from Ill-Posed Data
Certificate Ambiguity near Ill-Posedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-precision limit on distinguishing nearby feasible, infeasible, and unbounded LP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) denote encoded LP data, let \(\Sigma\) be the boundary separating instances with different status, and define \(\rho(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\) in a fixed data norm. If the available data or arithmetic determines the instance only within radius \(\delta\geq\rho(d)\), then the uncertainty ball contains a point of \(\Sigma\) and may meet a neighboring status region. No certificate based solely on that uncertain representation can uniformly distinguish the statuses. A robust status certificate therefore requires a verified margin \(\delta<\rho(d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When data uncertainty reaches the distance to ill-posed instances, nearby problems may have different statuses, so finite-precision certificates cannot distinguish them uniformly.
assumptions_latex: LP status regions are defined in a fixed normed data space.
\(\Sigma\) is their common ill-posed boundary.
The represented data uncertainty is at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta\geq\rho(d)\) precludes uniform status certification from the uncertain data alone.

notation.meaning: distance from the instance to ill-posedness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A canonical condition/ill-posedness framework is needed. The record must also distinguish an uncertainty set equal to the full radius-delta ball from merely having an upper bound on the actual perturbation; only the former directly supports the uniform-impossibility conclusion.

children.title: Worst-Case Complexity Profile
children.top_down_role: Formal complexity behavior used to compare simplex and polynomial-time LP methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Complexity Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical worst-case contrast among simplex, ellipsoid, and interior-point LP methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational LP input of binary encoding length \(L\), the ellipsoid method and suitable interior-point methods admit arithmetic-operation bounds polynomial in \(L\). In contrast, there exist indexed LP families and deterministic simplex pivot rules for which the number of visited bases is \(2^{\Omega(n)}\). Thus polynomial worst-case complexity is an algorithm-specific guarantee: it applies to polynomial-time ellipsoid and interior-point schemes, but not uniformly to classical simplex pivot rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid and suitable interior-point algorithms have polynomial worst-case bounds in input length, whereas some simplex pivot rules require exponentially many basis changes.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational and have binary encoding length \(L\).
Each method uses the computational model specified by its complexity theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial worst-case bounds hold for suitable ellipsoid and interior-point methods, while some simplex rules have \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) pivot paths.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the LP instance
dimension parameter of the adverse simplex family

children.title: Practical Performance Profile
children.top_down_role: Empirical runtime behavior, iteration patterns, and implementation-sensitive outcomes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties and limits of the finite-benchmark profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each solver \(s\), \(\rho_s\) is a nondecreasing right-continuous step function with values in \([0,1]\). The value \(\rho_s(1)\) is the fraction of benchmark instances on which \(s\) ties for best measured cost, and \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\rho_s(\tau)\) is its success fraction on \(P\). These quantities can change when the benchmark set, solver set, resource metric, limits, or failure convention changes and therefore imply neither average-case nor worst-case complexity rankings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile is a monotone step function; its value at one measures best-cost ties and its limit measures benchmark success, all relative to the declared suite and protocol.
assumptions_latex: The ratios and failure convention are those of Empirical Solver Performance Profile.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_s(1)=\frac{|\{p:r_{p,s}=1\}|}{|P|},\qquad \lim_{\tau\to\infty}\rho_s(\tau)=\frac{|\{p:s\text{ succeeds on }p\}|}{|P|}.

notation.meaning: fraction of benchmark instances tied for best observed cost

knowledge_statements.title: Performance-Profile Interpretation and Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-benchmark performance-ratio profile with an explicit failure convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite nonempty benchmark set and \(S\) a finite nonempty solver set. For every successful run let \(t_{p,s}>0\) be its measured cost. Define \(t_p^*=\min\{t_{p,u}:u\in S\text{ succeeds on }p\}\) when at least one solver succeeds. Set \(r_{p,s}=t_{p,s}/t_p^*\) for a successful run and \(r_{p,s}=\infty\) otherwise; if every solver fails on \(p\), set all \(r_{p,s}=\infty\). Then \[\rho_s(\tau)=\frac1{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver's profile is the fraction of all benchmark instances on which it succeeds within factor tau of the best successful measured cost; failed runs, including universal failures, receive infinite ratio.
assumptions_latex: P\neq\varnothing and S\neq\varnothing are finite.
Successful measured costs are positive and use one declared resource and protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_s(\tau)\text{ is the empirical fraction of all benchmark instances solved by }s\text{ within factor }\tau\text{ of the observed best successful cost}.

notation.meaning: best successful measured cost on benchmark instance p
performance ratio, with infinity assigned to failure

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Solver Performance Profile
Practical Performance Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical benchmark profile comparing LP solvers by a chosen performance measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite benchmark set \(P\), solvers \(S\), and positive measured costs \(t_{p,s}\), define \(r_{p,s}=t_{p,s}/\min_{u\in S}t_{p,u}\), with \(r_{p,s}=\infty\) for failure. The practical performance profile of solver \(s\) is \[\rho_s(\tau)=\frac{1}{|P|}\left|\{p\in P:r_{p,s}\leq\tau\}\right|,\qquad \tau\geq1.\] It records the fraction of tested instances solved within factor \(\tau\) of the best observed cost and is benchmark-dependent rather than a worst-case complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver’s practical profile is the benchmark fraction on which its measured cost lies within a chosen factor of the best observed solver.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(S\) are finite and nonempty.
Successful measured costs satisfy \(t_{p,s}>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho_s(\tau)\) is the empirical fraction of instances for which \(s\) is within factor \(\tau\) of the observed best cost.

notation.meaning: measured cost of solver s on problem p
performance ratio relative to the observed best solver

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and formula are essentially the standard empirical performance profile, but an authoritative source is required. It should also specify how the denominator is handled when every solver fails on an instance.

children.title: Theory-to-Practice Divergence
children.top_down_role: Structural reasons formal rankings may differ from computational rankings.

knowledge_statements.title: Theory-to-Practice Divergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separation between worst-case guarantees and finite benchmark observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algorithms \(A\) and \(B\), let \(T_A(x)\) and \(T_B(x)\) denote costs measured in the same resource model, and define \(W_A(n)=\sup_{|x|=n}T_A(x)\) and \(W_B(n)=\sup_{|x|=n}T_B(x)\). For a finite nonempty benchmark set \(P\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1]\), let \(Q_{A,P}(\alpha)\) and \(Q_{B,P}(\alpha)\) be the corresponding empirical cost quantiles. Without assumptions connecting \(P\) to the input populations defining the suprema, an ordering of \(W_A\) and \(W_B\) does not imply the same ordering of the benchmark quantiles, nor does a benchmark ordering imply a worst-case ordering. Polynomial degree, constants, numerical kernels, and implementation overhead can further affect observed costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case complexity does not by itself determine benchmark rankings, and benchmark rankings do not determine worst-case rankings; a sampling model and a common cost model are required.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are evaluated using the same specified resource measure.
\(P\) is finite and nonempty and need not contain worst-case instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without additional sampling assumptions, an ordering of \(W_A\) and \(W_B\) implies no corresponding ordering of \(Q_{A,P}(\alpha)\) and \(Q_{B,P}(\alpha)\), or conversely.

notation.meaning: worst-case cost of algorithm A at input size n
empirical alpha-quantile of algorithm A's costs on P

children.title: Vertex-Solution Profile
children.top_down_role: Output structure associated with basic or extreme-point solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex-Solution Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimal-vertex output for a standard-form linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\), where \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(r\). A feasible point \(x\) is a vertex of \(P\) exactly when the columns \(\{A_i:x_i>0\}\) are linearly independent; consequently, every vertex has at most \(r\) positive components. A vertex-solution output represents an optimal such point through a basis, which may include zero basic variables under degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimal vertex solution has linearly independent positive-support columns, at most rank(A) positive entries, and a basis representation that may be degenerate.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\neq\varnothing\).
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=r\).
The linear program has an optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vertex output \(x\in P\) satisfies that \(\{A_i:x_i>0\}\) is linearly independent and \(|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\leq r\), and it admits a basis representation.

notation.meaning: indices of positive components of x

children.title: Interior-Solution Profile
children.top_down_role: Output structure associated with iterates or solutions in the relative interior.

knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Solution Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly interior primal-dual output in standard-form LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(\max\{b^Ty:A^Ty+s=c,\ s\geq0\}\), a strictly interior feasible output satisfies \(Ax=b\), \(A^Ty+s=c\), \(x>0\), and \(s>0\). For \(x,s\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n\geq1\), its duality gap is \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts>0\), so it is not an exact optimal primal-dual pair. Interior-point output is therefore naturally represented by interior iterates with decreasing positive gap rather than by a vertex at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly interior feasible primal-dual output has positive variables and slacks and a positive duality gap, so it represents an interior iterate rather than an exact optimal pair.
assumptions_latex: The displayed primal and dual problems are feasible and have a finite common optimal value.
\(x,s\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(n\geq1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal-dual feasibility together with \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) gives \(c^Tx-b^Ty=x^Ts>0\), so the strictly interior output is not exactly optimal.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier and nonnegative dual slack
primal-dual objective gap at a feasible pair

source_witnesses.locator: A Strictly Interior Point p. 29

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact points in the relative interior of an optimal face from strictly primal-dual interior iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\}\) have an attained finite optimum \(z^*\), and let \(F^*=\{x\in P:c^Tx=z^*\}\). Every \(x\in\operatorname{relint}(F^*)\) is exactly optimal. If \(\dim F^*>0\), then no point of \(\operatorname{relint}(F^*)\) is a vertex of \(F^*\), although it may lie on the boundary of \(P\) and need not satisfy \(x>0\). Thus relative interior of the optimal face is distinct from simultaneous strict primal-dual interiority, for which \(x>0\) and \(s>0\) imply the positive gap \(x^Ts>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact optimizer can lie in the relative interior of a positive-dimensional optimal face and need not be a vertex or strictly positive; this differs from a strictly primal-dual interior iterate, which has positive duality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty and its finite optimum is attained.
\(F^*\) is the resulting optimal face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{relint}(F^*)\Longrightarrow c^Tx=z^*,\qquad \dim F^*>0\Longrightarrow x\text{ is not a vertex of }F^*.

notation.meaning: optimal face of the primal feasible polyhedron
relative interior of the optimal face

children.title: Approximate-Solution Profile
children.top_down_role: Output structure when termination is based on finite accuracy tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Solution Profile
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-and-gap certificate for an approximate standard-form primal-dual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard-form primal-dual pair, a tuple \((x,y,s)\) is an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-certificate when \[\lVert Ax-b\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon,\qquad \lVert A^Ty+s-c\rVert_2\leq\varepsilon,\qquad x\geq-\varepsilon\mathbf1,\qquad s\geq-\varepsilon\mathbf1,\qquad |c^Tx-b^Ty|\leq\varepsilon.\] These directly checkable inequalities certify approximate primal feasibility, dual feasibility, nonnegativity, and objective agreement. They do not by themselves certify proximity to an exact optimizer unless an additional error bound or conditioning estimate is supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate solution is certified by small primal and dual residuals, bounded nonnegativity violations, and a small objective gap; optimizer distance needs conditioning information.
assumptions_latex: Primal and dual data are \((A,b,c)\).
\(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities constitute an absolute \(\varepsilon\)-optimality certificate, but imply no uniform optimizer-distance bound without conditioning assumptions.

notation.meaning: primal variable, dual multiplier, and dual slack
all-ones vector of the required dimension

children.title: Solution-Geometry Conversion Costs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-independent accounting for converting approximate or interior LP output into a verified exact vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an LP pipeline first produces an approximate output and then identifies an optimal face, constructs a basis, and verifies the resulting exact vertex, its end-to-end cost is \[T_{\mathrm{total}}=T_{\mathrm{approx}}+T_{\mathrm{id}}+T_{\mathrm{basis}}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.\] Consequently, a complexity bound for producing the approximate output alone is not a bound for exact-vertex output unless the other three terms are also bounded in the same computational model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-vertex production must additionally charge face identification, basis construction, and verification; approximate-solution complexity alone omits these costs.
assumptions_latex: All four costs are measured in one declared arithmetic or bit-complexity model.
The requested output is a verified exact optimal vertex rather than only a tolerance-certified point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{total}}=T_{\mathrm{approx}}+T_{\mathrm{id}}+T_{\mathrm{basis}}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.

notation.meaning: cost of identifying suitable active or optimal-face information
cost of constructing an exact candidate basis
cost of exact basis and optimality verification

knowledge_statements.title: End-to-End Geometry-Conversion Cost

knowledge_statements.statement_title: No Uniform Gap Threshold for Vertex Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of instance-independent vertex recovery from residual-and-gap accuracy alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(0<\delta\leq2\varepsilon\) and consider \[\min\{\delta x_2:x_1+x_2=1,\ x\geq0\}.\] Its unique optimum is \(e_1\), but \(\widehat x=(1/2,1/2)\), together with dual multiplier \(y=0\) and slack \(s=(0,\delta)\), is exactly primal-dual feasible and has duality gap \(\delta/2\leq\varepsilon\). Thus arbitrarily small residual-and-gap tolerance does not, uniformly over LP data, identify the optimal vertex or its support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point can have an arbitrarily small primal-dual gap while remaining far from the unique optimal vertex, so no instance-independent tolerance guarantees vertex identification.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\).
The stopping certificate controls feasibility residuals and primal-dual gap but supplies no instance-dependent separation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\,\bar\varepsilon>0\text{ independent of the LP data that guarantees optimal-vertex identification from gap at most }\bar\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: objective separation between the two feasible vertices

knowledge_statements.title: No Uniform Gap Threshold for Vertex Identification
Solution-Geometry Conversion Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost and instability of converting an interior approximate output into an exact optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an algorithm returns an approximate interior point \(\widehat x\), while an exact vertex is required. A crossover procedure must identify an optimal face and then select a basis or vertex on that face. If the smallest positive basic variable, reduced-cost separation, or active-constraint margin is at most \(\gamma\), residual uncertainty of order \(\gamma\) can change the inferred face. Therefore no iteration bound for merely reaching residual tolerance \(\varepsilon\) includes reliable vertex recovery unless \(\varepsilon<\gamma\) and the basis-identification and linear-system costs are separately accounted for.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Turning an approximate interior point into a vertex requires face identification and basis recovery; without a separation margin, this conversion is unstable and adds uncounted work.
assumptions_latex: An exact optimal vertex, rather than an approximate feasible point, is required.
\(\gamma>0\) bounds the relevant support or reduced-cost separation margin.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reliable vertex recovery requires residual uncertainty below \(\gamma\) plus explicit crossover and linear-algebra work.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Generality Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input-access contrast between ellipsoid and standard interior-point polynomiality results.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex feasible set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), an ellipsoid algorithm can use a separation oracle that, given \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), either certifies \(x\in K\) or returns a valid separating hyperplane. In a standard well-bounded rational oracle model, with polynomial-time oracle calls and the size and accuracy data required by the applicable theorem, this yields polynomial oracle complexity. Standard LP interior-point methods instead take an explicit equality or inequality representation and exploit it to evaluate barriers and solve Newton systems. Thus the ellipsoid model accommodates more general oracle descriptions, while the standard LP interior-point model assumes richer explicit algebraic access.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the usual well-bounded oracle assumptions, ellipsoid algorithms can use separation-oracle descriptions, whereas standard LP interior-point methods use explicit constraints, barriers, and Newton systems.
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is presented in the well-bounded rational oracle model required by the stated ellipsoid complexity theorem.
The separation oracle has polynomial encoding and evaluation cost.
The interior-point formulation supplies an explicit tractable barrier and the required numerical linear-algebra operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ellipsoid access model is representation-general within its oracle assumptions, whereas standard LP interior-point polynomiality exploits an explicit algebraic representation.

children.title: Numerical Stability Contrast
children.top_down_role: Finite-precision sensitivity of ellipsoid and interior-point computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Stability Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates exact-arithmetic polynomiality from floating-point stability for ellipsoid and primal-dual interior-point methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an LP algorithm have a polynomial iteration bound in exact arithmetic. This bound alone implies neither backward stability nor a polynomial finite-precision implementation. Ellipsoid iterations can amplify rounding through accumulated center and shape-matrix updates, while an interior-point iteration can amplify error through an ill-conditioned Newton system. If the respective updates are computed with perturbations \(\Delta E_k\) and \(\Delta H_k\), stability requires separate bounds relating these perturbations to maintained feasibility, positive definiteness, and progress. Thus neither method is numerically more stable solely because it is polynomial-time; stability depends on conditioning, scaling, update realization, and precision control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-arithmetic polynomiality does not rank numerical stability: ellipsoid updates and interior-point Newton solves have distinct rounding-error mechanisms requiring separate finite-precision analyses.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are finite and represented in floating-point or rational arithmetic.
The compared algorithms possess exact-arithmetic polynomial iteration bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact-arithmetic polynomiality \(\not\Rightarrow\) numerical stability for either method.

notation.meaning: rounding perturbation in the ellipsoid update at iteration k
perturbation in the interior-point Newton matrix at iteration k

children.title: Linear-Algebra Workload Contrast
children.top_down_role: Differences in matrix operations, system solves, and oracle-centered computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Algebra Workload Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares dense per-iteration kernels, excluding separation-oracle cost, iteration counts, and sparsity-dependent savings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\) be the ellipsoid decision-space dimension and let \(N\) be the order of the dense Newton or normal-equations matrix used by an interior-point implementation. A standard ellipsoid center-and-shape update requires \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic and \(O(n^2)\) storage per oracle call. Forming and factoring a dense interior-point Newton matrix requires up to \(O(N^3)\) arithmetic and \(O(N^2)\) storage per iteration, followed by triangular solves. Thus the dense ellipsoid update is quadratic in \(n\), whereas dense Newton factorization is cubic in its system order \(N\); sparsity and system formulation can materially change these costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dense ellipsoid shape update is quadratic in the decision dimension, while a dense interior-point Newton factorization is cubic in the order of its linear system; the two dimensions need not be equal.
assumptions_latex: The ellipsoid decision-space dimension is \(n\).
The dense interior-point Newton-system order is \(N\).
Oracle evaluation cost and sparsity-dependent savings are excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{ell}}(n)=O(n^2),\qquad W_{\mathrm{IP}}(N)=O(N^3).

notation.meaning: order of the dense interior-point Newton system

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Per-Iteration Work Does Not Determine Total Work
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on conclusions obtainable from the dense kernel comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K_{\mathrm{ell}},K_{\mathrm{IP}}\) be iteration counts, \(W_{\mathrm{oracle}}\) the cost of one separation-oracle call, and \(W_{\mathrm{ell}},W_{\mathrm{IP}}\) the respective per-iteration algebra costs. Up to separately accounted initialization and recovery costs,
\[T_{\mathrm{ell}}=K_{\mathrm{ell}}(W_{\mathrm{oracle}}+W_{\mathrm{ell}}),\qquad T_{\mathrm{IP}}=K_{\mathrm{IP}}W_{\mathrm{IP}}.\]
Therefore \(W_{\mathrm{ell}}=O(n^2)\) and \(W_{\mathrm{IP}}=O(N^3)\) alone imply no ordering of total workloads because dimensions, iteration counts, oracle costs, sparsity, and factorization reuse differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic-versus-cubic dense per-iteration kernels do not rank total ellipsoid and interior-point work without iteration, oracle, dimension, sparsity, and reuse information.
assumptions_latex: All workload components are measured in one declared arithmetic-cost model.
Initialization and recovery costs are accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{ell}}=O(n^2),\ W_{\mathrm{IP}}=O(N^3)\ \not\Rightarrow\ T_{\mathrm{ell}}\le T_{\mathrm{IP}}\ \text{or}\ T_{\mathrm{IP}}\le T_{\mathrm{ell}}.

notation.meaning: total arithmetic workloads under the declared model

knowledge_statements.title: Per-Iteration Work Does Not Determine Total Work

children.title: Precision Requirement Contrast
children.top_down_role: Accuracy demands placed on arithmetic and intermediate computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Precision Requirement Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts bit-model precision obligations rather than asserting a universal numerical advantage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rational LP data of binary encoding length \(L\), an ellipsoid bit-complexity proof explicitly maintains rational approximations whose word lengths are polynomial in \(L\), the dimension, and the iteration count. A real-arithmetic polynomial iteration bound for an interior-point method does not by itself provide this guarantee: a bit-complexity result additionally requires polynomially bounded rounding precision for Newton solves, residual evaluation, and step selection. Consequently, both methods can be polynomial in the Turing model, but the required precision control is part of the ellipsoid analysis and must be supplied separately for a real-arithmetic interior-point analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ellipsoid bit-complexity analyses explicitly control rational word length; interior-point iteration bounds need an additional finite-precision argument to imply Turing-model polynomiality.
assumptions_latex: The LP data are rational with total binary encoding length \(L\).
Complexity is measured in the Turing bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial real-arithmetic iteration bound alone does not imply polynomial bit complexity.

notation.meaning: binary encoding length of the rational LP instance

children.title: Memory Footprint Contrast
children.top_down_role: Storage requirements of factorization-based and matrix-free solver families.

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Footprint Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a sparse Newton-system model and a fixed-storage, short-recurrence matrix-free Krylov method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) have \(q=\operatorname{nnz}(H)\). A factorization-based solve whose triangular factors contain \(f\) stored entries requires \(O(q+f+n)\) words when the operator data are retained. A matrix-free, short-recurrence Krylov solve that stores only a fixed number of work vectors requires \(O(q+p+n)\) words when its preconditioner occupies \(p\) words. Hence the matrix-free implementation has lower storage in this model when \(q+p+n<q+f+n\), with a substantial advantage when \(p+n\ll f\); a large preconditioner or a growing Krylov basis can remove that advantage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct solves store factor fill, while fixed-storage matrix-free Krylov solves store operator data, a preconditioner, and a constant number of vectors; the latter saves memory when these are smaller than the factors.
assumptions_latex: The Newton system has dimension \(n\) and \(q\) stored nonzeros.
The direct factors contain \(f\) stored entries, including fill.
The matrix-free method uses a fixed number of length-\(n\) work vectors and a preconditioner occupying \(p\) words.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_{\mathrm{dir}}=O(q+f+n),\qquad M_{\mathrm{mf}}=O(q+p+n).

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros in the Newton operator
number of stored factor entries, including fill

children.title: Arithmetic Work per Iteration
children.top_down_role: Per-iteration computational effort across the two solver families.

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Work per Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares one Newton solve by sparse factorization and a short-recurrence preconditioned Krylov method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Newton system \(Hd=r\) of order \(n\), let \(F(H)\) be the arithmetic required to form and factor \(H\), and let \(S(H)\) be the work of the associated triangular solves. A factorization-based outer iteration costs \(F(H)+S(H)\). Suppose a short-recurrence matrix-free Krylov method takes \(k\) iterations, each product with \(H\) costs \(O(q)\), and each preconditioner application costs \(P\). Its solve then costs \(O(k(q+P+n))\). Matrix-free arithmetic is lower for that outer iteration only when this quantity is below \(F(H)+S(H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct Newton solve pays factorization plus triangular-solve work; a short-recurrence matrix-free solve pays operator, preconditioner, and vector work at every Krylov iteration.
assumptions_latex: The Newton system has order \(n\), and its matrix has \(q\) nonzeros.
A short-recurrence Krylov method performs \(k\) iterations.
One preconditioner application costs \(P\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{dir}}=F(H)+S(H),\qquad W_{\mathrm{mf}}=O\!\left(k(q+P+n)\right).

notation.meaning: arithmetic cost of one preconditioner application
number of nonzeros in the Newton matrix

children.title: Data-Movement Cost per Iteration
children.top_down_role: Memory-traffic implications that are not captured by arithmetic counts alone.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Movement Cost per Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts slow-memory word transfers for sparse, fixed-storage linear solves when operator and factor data exceed fast memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume a sparse Newton operator with \(q\) stored entries exceeds fast memory. In a fixed-storage, short-recurrence matrix-free implementation, each Krylov step streams the operator and a constant number of vectors, requiring \(\Theta(q+n)\) word transfers under the stated streaming model. Thus \(k\) steps require \(O(k(q+n)+Q_P)\) transfers, where \(Q_P\) is total preconditioner traffic. A factorization-based solve moves data while constructing the factors and traverses \(O(f+n)\) words per triangular solve when the \(f\) factor entries do not reside in fast memory. Matrix-free execution avoids factor-fill traffic but repeatedly streams the operator, whereas factorization may amortize construction when its factors serve multiple right-hand sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-storage matrix-free solve repeatedly streams the sparse operator and vectors; a direct solve moves factor data and may amortize factor construction over reused right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: The operator and factors do not fit entirely in fast memory.
The operator has \(q\) stored entries and the factors have \(f\) stored entries.
The matrix-free method uses a fixed-storage, short-recurrence Krylov implementation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q_{\mathrm{mf}}=O\!\left(k(q+n)+Q_P\right),\qquad Q_{\mathrm{tri}}=O(f+n)\ \text{per triangular solve}.

notation.meaning: total preconditioner data movement over the Krylov solve

children.title: Resource Tradeoff Boundary
children.top_down_role: Problem regimes in which storage or iteration cost becomes the dominant consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Resource Tradeoff Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the per-iteration feasibility and work boundary under explicit memory and arithmetic budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_M\) be available memory, \(B_W\) the permitted arithmetic per outer iteration, \(M_{\mathrm{dir}},M_{\mathrm{mf}}\) the two memory requirements, and \(W_{\mathrm{dir}},W_{\mathrm{mf}}\) their work. A direct factorization is resource-feasible exactly when \(M_{\mathrm{dir}}\le B_M\) and \(W_{\mathrm{dir}}\le B_W\); a matrix-free solve is feasible exactly when \(M_{\mathrm{mf}}\le B_M\) and \(W_{\mathrm{mf}}\le B_W\). The operative boundary is the union of the equalities \(M=B_M\) and \(W=B_W\). In particular, matrix-free execution is the sole feasible choice when \(M_{\mathrm{dir}}>B_M\ge M_{\mathrm{mf}}\) and \(W_{\mathrm{mf}}\le B_W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method is usable only within both memory and work budgets; matrix-free execution becomes mandatory when factor storage exceeds memory but its iterative work remains affordable.
assumptions_latex: Memory and arithmetic budgets \(B_M,B_W>0\) are fixed.
Both methods solve the same Newton system to the required tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal{F}_j=\{(B_M,B_W):M_j\le B_M,\ W_j\le B_W\},\qquad j\in\{\mathrm{dir},\mathrm{mf}\}.

notation.meaning: memory and work required by method j
resource-feasible budget region for method j

children.title: Achievable Accuracy Contrast
children.top_down_role: Attainable solution quality for factorization-based and matrix-free methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Achievable Accuracy Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares forward accuracy floors for backward-stable direct and residual-controlled iterative Newton solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Hd=r\) be nonsingular, with condition number \(\kappa(H)\), unit roundoff \(u\), and a normwise backward-stable factorization. Its computed solution ordinarily has relative forward error \(O(\kappa(H)u)\) while \(\kappa(H)u\ll1\). A matrix-free iterative solve stopped at relative residual \(\eta\) has a forward-error bound scaling as \(O(\kappa(H)(\eta+u))\), subject to stable operator and preconditioner applications. Thus direct factorization can usually attain near-machine residuals, whereas matrix-free accuracy is additionally limited by the chosen inner tolerance and attainable residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct solves can approach the conditioning-dependent floating-point floor; iterative solves also inherit their stopping tolerance and residual stagnation.
assumptions_latex: The Newton matrix \(H\) is nonsingular.
Operator, factorization, and preconditioner applications are normwise stable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\|\widehat d-d\|}{\|d\|}=O(\kappa(H)u)\ \text{directly},\qquad O(\!\left(\kappa(H)(\eta+u)\right))\ \text{iteratively}.

notation.meaning: condition number of the Newton matrix in the selected norm
