children.title: Conditioning Sensitivity Contrast
children.top_down_role: Performance degradation as problem or operator conditioning worsens.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning Sensitivity Contrast
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes direct-solve error sensitivity from unpreconditioned conjugate-gradient convergence sensitivity for symmetric positive-definite systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be symmetric positive definite with spectral condition number \(\kappa(H)\), and let \(u\) be unit roundoff. When \(\kappa(H)u\ll1\), a normwise backward-stable direct factorization has relative forward error of order \(O(\!\left(\kappa(H)u\right))\), while its arithmetic count is governed principally by dimension, sparsity, ordering, and fill. In exact arithmetic, unpreconditioned conjugate gradients satisfies \(\|e_k\|_H/\|e_0\|_H\le 2\rho^k\), where \(\rho=(\sqrt{\kappa(H)}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa(H)}+1)\). Thus poor conditioning affects the direct solve's attainable accuracy and also increases the iteration count required by unpreconditioned conjugate gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive-definite system, ill-conditioning limits the accuracy of a backward-stable direct solve and also slows unpreconditioned conjugate gradients.
assumptions_latex: The Newton matrix \(H\) is symmetric positive definite.
The direct factorization is normwise backward stable.
Conjugate gradients is unpreconditioned and analyzed in exact arithmetic.
The direct-solve error estimate is used in the regime \(\kappa(H)u\ll1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{direct forward error}=O\!\left(\kappa(H)u\right),\qquad \frac{\|e_k\|_H}{\|e_0\|_H}\le2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa(H)}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa(H)}+1}\right)^k.

notation.meaning: energy norm induced by the positive-definite matrix H

source_refs.locator: Linear Algebra Issues p. 16

source_witnesses.locator: Linear Algebra Issues p. 16

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpens the condition-number convergence estimate with exact-arithmetic finite termination for an SPD system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\times n\) symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\), exact-arithmetic conjugate gradients terminates with the exact solution in at most \(n\) iterations. If \(\kappa(H)>1\) and \(\rho=(\sqrt{\kappa(H)}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa(H)}+1)\), relative energy-norm error at most \(\varepsilon\) is therefore attained within \(\min\{n,\lceil \log(2/\varepsilon)/(-\log\rho)\rceil\}\) iterations; when \(\kappa(H)=1\), one iteration suffices from a nonexact initial iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-arithmetic CG has both a condition-number convergence bound and an at-most-n finite-termination cap.
assumptions_latex: H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\text{ is symmetric positive definite}.
\text{Conjugate gradients is executed in exact arithmetic}.
0<\varepsilon<1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\le \min\!\left\{n,\left\lceil\frac{\log(2/\varepsilon)}{-\log\rho}\right\rceil\right\}\quad(\kappa(H)>1).
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Cap on Unpreconditioned CG

children.title: Preconditioning Dependence
children.top_down_role: Reliance on scaling or preconditioning to obtain useful computational behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Preconditioning Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies exact-arithmetic preconditioned conjugate-gradient dependence for a symmetric positive-definite Newton system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) and \(M\) be symmetric positive definite, let \(d_*\) solve \(Hd=r\), and let \(d_k\) be the \(k\)-th preconditioned conjugate-gradient iterate. Define \(e_k=d_k-d_*\) and \(\kappa_M=\kappa(M^{-1/2}HM^{-1/2})\). In exact arithmetic, \(\|e_k\|_H/\|e_0\|_H\le 2((\sqrt{\kappa_M}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa_M}+1))^k\). Consequently, for \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \(k=O(\sqrt{\kappa_M}\log(1/\varepsilon))\) iterations suffice to make the relative energy-norm error at most \(\varepsilon\). Matrix-free efficiency therefore depends on reducing \(\kappa_M\) without making construction, storage, or application of \(M\) comparable to full factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioned conjugate-gradient complexity depends on the preconditioned condition number, balanced against the construction, storage, and application costs of the preconditioner.
assumptions_latex: The Newton matrix \(H\) and preconditioner \(M\) are symmetric positive definite.
Exact-arithmetic preconditioned conjugate gradients is used.
The target relative energy-norm error satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k=O\!\left(\sqrt{\kappa_M}\log(1/\varepsilon)\right),\qquad \kappa_M=\kappa(M^{-1/2}HM^{-1/2}).

notation.meaning: exact solution and kth preconditioned conjugate-gradient iterate
condition number of the symmetrically preconditioned system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adds the exact-arithmetic finite-termination cap to the preconditioned condition-number estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an \(n\times n\) symmetric positive-definite matrix \(H\) and symmetric positive-definite preconditioner \(M\), exact-arithmetic preconditioned conjugate gradients terminates in at most \(n\) iterations. With \(\kappa_M=\kappa(M^{-1/2}HM^{-1/2})>1\) and \(\rho_M=(\sqrt{\kappa_M}-1)/(\sqrt{\kappa_M}+1)\), relative energy-norm error at most \(\varepsilon\) is attained within \(\min\{n,\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)/(-\log\rho_M)\rceil\}\) iterations; if \(\kappa_M=1\), one iteration suffices from a nonexact initial iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact-arithmetic PCG is bounded both by the preconditioned condition number and by at most n iterations.
assumptions_latex: H,M\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\text{ are symmetric positive definite}.
\text{Preconditioned conjugate gradients is executed in exact arithmetic}.
0<\varepsilon<1.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: k\le \min\!\left\{n,\left\lceil\frac{\log(2/\varepsilon)}{-\log\rho_M}\right\rceil\right\}\quad(\kappa_M>1).

notation.meaning: condition number of the symmetrically preconditioned system

children.title: Accuracy-Limited Regime Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where conditioning prevents a solver family from reaching the desired accuracy efficiently.

knowledge_statements.title: Accuracy-Limited Regime Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when a normwise matrix-backward-error model cannot certify requested relative forward accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be nonsingular, let \(d\) solve \(Hd=r\), and suppose a computed solution \(\widehat d\) satisfies \((H+\Delta H)\widehat d=r\) with \(\|\Delta H\|/\|H\|\le\delta\). If \(\kappa(H)\delta<1\), the standard perturbation estimate gives \(\|\widehat d-d\|/\|d\|\le\kappa(H)\delta/(1-\kappa(H)\delta)\). Hence this estimate is unavailable when \(\kappa(H)\delta\ge1\), and it does not certify a requested tolerance \(\varepsilon\) when \(\kappa(H)\delta/(1-\kappa(H)\delta)>\varepsilon\). For a direct solve one may have \(\delta=O(u)\); for an iterative solve the same boundary applies only after establishing an effective backward-error bound \(\delta_{\mathrm{it}}\), which may depend on roundoff and the stopping criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A requested forward-accuracy guarantee becomes unavailable when the condition number times a justified backward-error bound is too large; an iterative residual tolerance must first be converted into such a bound.
assumptions_latex: The matrix \(H\) is nonsingular.
The computed solution obeys the matrix perturbation model \((H+\Delta H)\widehat d=r\) with \(\|\Delta H\|/\|H\|\le\delta\).
The requested tolerance satisfies \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \kappa(H)\delta\ge1\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{the standard bound is unavailable};\qquad \frac{\kappa(H)\delta}{1-\kappa(H)\delta}>\varepsilon\ \Longrightarrow\ \varepsilon\ \text{is not certified}.

notation.meaning: effective backward-error bound established for an iterative solve

children.title: Parallel Execution Potential
children.top_down_role: Available concurrency across factorization-based and matrix-free computations.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Execution Potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts concurrency in sparse matrix-free products with dependency-limited sparse factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(p\) processors apply a sparse Newton operator with \(q\) nonzeros. With balanced row partitioning, a matrix-vector product has local arithmetic \(O(q/p)\), followed by communication for shared vector entries; Krylov inner products additionally require global reductions. Sparse factorization exposes parallelism within an elimination tree but also imposes dependencies between fronts and may suffer load imbalance from fill. Hence matrix-free iterations offer broad operator-level parallelism but incur repeated synchronization, while factorization-based methods offer dependency-limited parallelism and can reuse factors across multiple right-hand sides. Neither dominates without a communication and sparsity model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free products parallelize broadly but synchronize repeatedly; sparse factorization has elimination-tree dependencies yet can reuse factors across right-hand sides.
assumptions_latex: The sparse operator has \(q\) nonzeros distributed across \(p\) processors.
Work is sufficiently balanced for the local product bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_{\mathrm{local}}(Hv)=O(q/p),\quad\text{with communication and reduction costs remaining method- and architecture-dependent}.

notation.meaning: number of nonzeros in the sparse Newton operator

source_refs.locator: Linear Algebra Issues p. 16

children.title: Data-Access Locality
children.top_down_role: Locality and reuse characteristics of the principal computational kernels.

knowledge_statements.title: Data-Access Locality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Idealized comparison of factorization-based and matrix-free LP iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\). A matrix-free iteration that evaluates only \(Av\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}u\) may stream the stored entries of \(A\), requiring \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) matrix-data accesses per product pair and no persistent factor storage. A factorization-based iteration using a nonsingular system matrix \(K\) must access the stored factors \(L,U\) during triangular solves, requiring \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(L)+\operatorname{nnz}(U))\) factor-data accesses after factorization. Hence fill-in can make factor access substantially less local than streaming access to \(A\); the comparison depends on ordering, caching, and reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free products can stream the original sparse matrix, whereas factorization-based solves access potentially much denser factors; fill-in therefore governs their relative data locality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and all factors are stored in sparse formats.
One matrix-free iteration uses a constant number of products with \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matrix-free access is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\) per product pair, while factor-solve access is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(L)+\operatorname{nnz}(U))\).

notation.meaning: number of stored nonzeros of matrix M
triangular factors of the factorization-based system

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the locality leaf, but the access-count and locality comparison depends on sparse storage, traversal, factor representation, caching, and reuse. No inspectable source is supplied to support this hardware-sensitive formulation.

children.title: Synchronization Burden
children.top_down_role: Coordination costs that limit effective parallel scaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Burden
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bulk-synchronous comparison of parallel factorization and matrix-free iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a bulk-synchronous model, suppose one matrix-free iteration performs \(q\) sparse matrix-vector products and \(r\) global reductions. Its synchronization depth is at least \(r\), plus communication phases required by the data distribution. A factorization-based iteration additionally incurs the dependency levels of factorization and triangular solves: if their elimination and solve dependency depths are \(d_f\) and \(d_s\), respectively, its critical synchronization depth is at least \(d_f+d_s\). Thus arithmetic parallelism alone does not determine scalability; global reductions and sequential dependency levels impose latency-sensitive barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix-free methods synchronize mainly for reductions and distributed products; factorization-based methods additionally inherit elimination and triangular-solve dependency barriers.
assumptions_latex: Execution follows a bulk-synchronous parallel model.
Each dependency level requires completion before its successor begins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The synchronization depth is bounded below by \(r\) for the matrix-free iteration and by \(d_f+d_s\) for the factorization-based computation.

notation.meaning: number of global reductions per iteration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the synchronization leaf, but the stated critical-depth lower bounds depend on the parallel execution model and on whether factorization and solves occur sequentially in the measured computation. No source supports these assumptions.

children.title: Hardware-Regime Suitability
children.top_down_role: Solver-family suitability across memory-bound, throughput-oriented, or distributed platforms.

knowledge_statements.title: Hardware-Regime Suitability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-model condition selecting between factorization-based and matrix-free LP methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For hardware regime \(H\), let \(T_F(H)=T_{\mathrm{fact}}(H)+k_FT_{\mathrm{solve}}(H)\) be the predicted time of a factorization-based solve and let \(T_M(H)=k_M(T_{A}(H)+T_{A^{\mathsf T}}(H)+T_{\mathrm{red}}(H))\) be that of a matrix-free solve to the same prescribed accuracy. The matrix-free method is suitable under this model exactly when \(T_M(H)\le T_F(H)\) and its working set fits available memory; otherwise the factorization-based method is preferred when its factors fit memory and \(T_F(H)<T_M(H)\). Comparisons are valid only when both times include communication and synchronization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the method with lower predicted time to the same accuracy, provided its working set fits memory and communication and synchronization costs are included.
assumptions_latex: Both methods target the same accuracy and problem instance.
The cost model includes computation, communication, and synchronization.
The selected method's working set fits hardware memory.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matrix-free suitability is characterized by \(T_M(H)\le T_F(H)\); factorization suitability is characterized by \(T_F(H)<T_M(H)\), subject to memory feasibility.

notation.meaning: global-reduction and synchronization time per matrix-free iteration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the hardware-suitability leaf, but the proposed time model and its claim of exact suitability are machine- and implementation-dependent. An inspectable performance-model source is required.

children.title: Basis Certificates
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial solution evidence represented through a selected LP basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic-feasibility certificate for equality-form linear programming.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\). A set \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) with \(|B|=m\) is a basis certificate for a basic feasible solution when \(A_B\) is nonsingular, \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), and \(x_N=0\) for \(N=B^c\). These equations are directly checkable and imply \(Ax=b\) and \(x\ge0\). The basis alone certifies primal basic feasibility, not optimality; an optimality certificate additionally requires compatible nonnegative reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular column basis whose basic solution is nonnegative certifies a basic feasible solution, but needs reduced costs to certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The LP is in equality form with nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(A_B\) is nonsingular and \(A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), then \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\) is a basic feasible solution.

notation.meaning: submatrix formed from columns indexed by B

children.title: Reduced-Cost Certificates
children.top_down_role: Optimality evidence conveyed through nonbasic-variable reduced costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-feasibility and optimality certificate associated with an LP basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and a basis \(B\), define \(y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), \(s_B=0\), and \(s_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\). If \(s_N\ge0\), then \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\) and \(s\ge0\), so \((y,s)\) is dual feasible. If the associated basic solution is also primal feasible, then \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s=0\); consequently, primal and dual feasibility plus these reduced costs certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative reduced costs give a dual-feasible certificate; paired with a feasible basic solution, zero complementarity certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The primal LP has equality constraints and nonnegative variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condition \(s_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\ge0\) certifies dual feasibility and, with primal basic feasibility, optimality.

notation.meaning: dual multiplier determined by the basis

children.title: Basis–Reduced-Cost Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Consistency between the selected basis and its associated reduced-cost evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Reduced-Cost Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility predicate joining primal basis and reduced-cost certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\). For the primal-dual pair \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0\}\), a basis \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and reduced-cost vector \(s\in\mathbb R^n\) are compatible when \(|B|=m\), \(A_B\) is nonsingular, \(N=B^c\), \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\ge0\), \(x_N=0\), \(y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B\), \(s_B=0\), and \(s_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\). Compatibility gives primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and \(x^{\mathsf T}s=0\), hence \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\) and both points are optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis and reduced costs are compatible when they generate feasible primal and dual points with complementary basic and nonbasic components; such compatibility certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The primal and dual use the displayed equality-form convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility implies \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s\ge0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Certificate Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness boundaries for basis and reduced-cost LP certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible basis \(B\) is primal degenerate when \((A_B^{-1}b)_i=0\) for some \(i\in B\); then the same basic feasible point may admit multiple bases. An optimal basis is dual degenerate when \(s_j=0\) for some \(j\in N\); then zero reduced cost permits alternative optimal adjacent bases or solutions, although their existence is not guaranteed. Thus degeneracy destroys uniqueness of the basis–reduced-cost representation, but it does not invalidate a certificate satisfying primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Zero basic variables or zero nonbasic reduced costs can make certificate representations nonunique, without invalidating feasible complementary optimality certificates.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a feasible basis for the equality-form LP.
\(s\) is the compatible reduced-cost vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a basic variable or nonbasic reduced cost is zero, uniqueness may fail, while feasibility and \(x^{\mathsf T}s=0\) still certify optimality.

Norms and tolerances are fixed before assessing an approximate certificate.

children.title: First-Order Residual Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Residual Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-based feasibility certificate for first-order LP iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^n\) define the primal LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and the dual constraints \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), \(s\ge0\). For an iterate \((x,y,s)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\), fix norms and positive scales \(\sigma_p,\sigma_d>0\). Define \(\rho_p=\|Ax-b\|/\sigma_p\) and \(\rho_d=\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|/\sigma_d\). Together with the checks \(x\ge0\) and \(s\ge0\), these quantities form a normalized residual certificate. For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the certificate establishes \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility under this convention when \(\max\{\rho_p,\rho_d\}\le\varepsilon\). It concerns constraint satisfaction only; without a gap or complementarity bound, it does not certify approximate optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a specified equality-form primal-dual LP, normalized primal and dual residuals and the sign checks certify approximate feasibility under the chosen convention, but a separate gap or complementarity test is needed for approximate optimality.
assumptions_latex: The residual norms are fixed.
\(\sigma_p>0\) and \(\sigma_d>0\).
The iterate satisfies \(x\ge0\) and \(s\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), if \(\max\{\rho_p,\rho_d\}\le\varepsilon\), then the iterate is \(\varepsilon\)-feasible under the specified normalized-residual convention.

notation.meaning: positive primal and dual scaling factors

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified finite-accuracy residual representation when iterates need not satisfy nonnegativity exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(z_-:=\max\{-z,0\}\) componentwise, positive scales \(\sigma_p,\sigma_d,\sigma_x,\sigma_s\), and fixed norms, define
\[R(x,y,s)=\max\left\{\frac{\|Ax-b\|}{\sigma_p},\frac{\|A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\|}{\sigma_d},\frac{\|x_-\|}{\sigma_x},\frac{\|s_-\|}{\sigma_s}\right\}.\]
Then \(R\le\varepsilon\) is the declared normalized \(\varepsilon\)-feasibility test, and \(R=0\) holds exactly when primal and dual feasibility both hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality residuals and negative-part norms combine into a normalized primal-dual feasibility certificate that vanishes exactly at feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \sigma_p,\sigma_d,\sigma_x,\sigma_s>0
All norms and scales are fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=0\iff Ax=b,\ x\ge0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge0.

children.title: First-Order Gap Certificates

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Gap Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual objective-gap certificate for first-order LP iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For primal-feasible \(x\) and dual-feasible \((y,s)\) satisfying \(Ax=b\), \(x\ge0\), \(A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c\), and \(s\ge0\), the computable gap is \(G=c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s\ge0\). Given a positive scale \(\sigma_g\), the inequality \(G/\sigma_g\le\varepsilon\) certifies that both feasible objective values lie within \(\varepsilon\sigma_g\) of the common optimal value. If feasibility is only approximate, the raw objective difference alone lacks this certification meaning unless residual-error terms are also controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For feasible primal-dual points, their nonnegative objective gap bounds both objective errors; approximate feasibility requires residual corrections.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual LPs have finite common optimal value.
The displayed primal and dual feasibility conditions hold.
The gap scale \(\sigma_g\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(G/\sigma_g\le\varepsilon\), then \(0\le c^{\mathsf T}x-p^*\le\varepsilon\sigma_g\) and \(0\le p^*-b^{\mathsf T}y\le\varepsilon\sigma_g\).

notation.meaning: positive normalization scale for the gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic decomposition explaining how infeasibility changes the interpretation of the objective difference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r_p=Ax-b\) and \(r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c\), every \((x,y,s)\) satisfies
\[c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y=x^{\mathsf T}s+y^{\mathsf T}r_p-x^{\mathsf T}r_d.\]
Consequently,
\[\left|c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y-x^{\mathsf T}s\right|\le \|y\|_*\|r_p\|+\|x\|_*\|r_d\|\]
for the corresponding paired dual norms. Thus a gap at infeasible iterates is interpretable only with residual bounds and bounds on the multiplying vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The raw objective difference equals complementarity plus explicit primal- and dual-residual corrections bounded by paired norms.
assumptions_latex: r_p=Ax-b
r_d=A^{\mathsf T}y+s-c
Each displayed multiplier norm is dual to the corresponding residual norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y-x^{\mathsf T}s\right|\le \|y\|_*\|r_p\|+\|x\|_*\|r_d\|.

notation.meaning: the applicable norm dual to a residual norm

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Ray Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas and recession-ray certificates recoverable from first-order LP iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(P=\{x\ge0:Ax=b\}\), a vector \(y\) satisfying \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certifies \(P=\varnothing\). Conversely, if \(x_0\in P\) and a nonzero vector \(d\) satisfies \(d\ge0\), \(Ad=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(x_0+td\in P\) for every \(t\ge0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}(x_0+td)\to-\infty\). Thus normalized limits of diverging first-order iterates are valid ray certificates only after these homogeneous inequalities and strict-sign conditions are verified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas multiplier certifies primal infeasibility, while a feasible negative-cost recession direction certifies primal unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: The primal LP is \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
Strict inequalities are assessed with exact arithmetic or certified margins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed \(y\) certifies infeasibility; the displayed pair \((x_0,d)\) certifies unboundedness below.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Status Interpretation of Certificate Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes an exact homogeneous ray from the feasible base point additionally needed to infer unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\},\]
a vector \(d\ge0\) with \(Ad=0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\) certifies dual infeasibility; if a primal-feasible base point exists, it also certifies primal unboundedness. Likewise, a vector \(v\) with \(A^{\mathsf T}v\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}v<0\) certifies primal infeasibility; if a dual-feasible base point exists, \(-v\) also certifies dual unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict homogeneous ray certifies infeasibility of the opposite system and certifies unboundedness on its own side when a feasible base point is known.
assumptions_latex: The primal is equality-form with nonnegative variables.
The dual is \(A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\).
All strict signs are certified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\Rightarrow D=\varnothing,\quad (P\ne\varnothing\wedge d)\Rightarrow\inf P=-\infty;\qquad v\Rightarrow P=\varnothing,\quad (D\ne\varnothing\wedge v)\Rightarrow\sup D=+\infty.

children.title: Certificate Consistency Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Consistency Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling and feasibility boundaries limiting first-order LP certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Residual and gap tests are jointly consistent only under fixed scaling and compatible feasibility conventions. Indeed, replacing \(Ax=b\) by \(\alpha Ax=\alpha b\) multiplies the absolute primal residual by \(|\alpha|\) without changing the feasible set; hence an unnormalized threshold \(\|Ax-b\|\le\varepsilon\) is not representation invariant. Moreover, for infeasible iterates the quantity \(c^{\mathsf T}x-b^{\mathsf T}y\) can be negative and need not bound suboptimality. Therefore a first-order optimality certificate must report normalized residuals, sign violations, and a gap bound whose interpretation explicitly accounts for residual error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute residuals change under equivalent scaling, and gaps at infeasible iterates need not bound suboptimality; consistent certificates must normalize and combine all errors.
assumptions_latex: Equivalent constraint scalings with \(\alpha\ne0\) are permitted.
Candidate iterates need not be exactly feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither an unnormalized residual threshold nor a raw infeasible objective gap alone is a representation-invariant approximate-optimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate Ray Tests Need a Certified Margin
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a tolerance-only Farkas-ray test when homogeneous violations are small but nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(P=\{x\ge0:x=1\}\), which is feasible. For every \(\delta>0\), the scalar \(y=-\delta\) satisfies \(A^{\mathsf T}y=-\delta\ge-\delta\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y=-\delta<0\). Thus a test accepting a negative decisive quantity together with an absolute homogeneous violation at most \(\delta\) would falsely declare infeasibility for arbitrarily small \(\delta\). An approximate ray becomes a valid status certificate only when error bounds establish the exact homogeneous inequalities and preserve a strict decisive margin, or when it is converted to an exactly verified ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily small homogeneous violation plus a negative ray margin can occur for a feasible LP, so tolerance-only ray tests do not certify infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \delta>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\ne\varnothing\quad\text{although}\quad A^{\mathsf T}y\ge-\delta\ \text{and}\ b^{\mathsf T}y<0.

notation.meaning: absolute tolerance and magnitude of the invalid candidate ray

children.title: Exact Solution Recovery

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal-dual certification for a standard-form rational LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal-dual pair 
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge 0\},\qquad \max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\ s\ge 0\},\]
an exactly represented triple \((x,y,s)\) recovers an optimal primal-dual solution whenever
\[Ax=b,\quad x\ge0,\quad A^{\mathsf T}y+s=c,\quad s\ge0,\quad c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y.\]
These equalities and inequalities form a finite, exactly checkable optimality certificate. If additionally the optimal primal solution is unique, the certified vector \(x\) is the exact solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact primal and dual feasibility together with a zero duality gap certify an exact LP optimum; uniqueness identifies the recovered primal solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^n\).
The candidate triple \((x,y,s)\) is represented exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) and \((y,s)\) are respectively primal and dual optimal, and their common value is \(c^{\mathsf T}x=b^{\mathsf T}y\).

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Solution Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-and-gap definition for approximate primal-dual LP recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For tolerances \(\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g\ge0\), a triple \((\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)\) is an \((\varepsilon_p,\varepsilon_d,\varepsilon_g)\)-approximate primal-dual solution of
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\]
if
\[\widehat x\ge0,\quad \widehat s\ge0,\quad \|A\widehat x-b\|\le\varepsilon_p,\quad \|A^{\mathsf T}\widehat y+\widehat s-c\|\le\varepsilon_d,\quad |c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-b^{\mathsf T}\widehat y|\le\varepsilon_g.\]
The norm is fixed as part of the accuracy convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate solution has nonnegative primal and dual slacks, small feasibility residuals, and a small primal-dual objective gap.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
A norm \(\|\cdot\|\) is fixed on each residual space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)\) satisfies the stated approximate-recovery criterion.

children.title: Approximate-to-Exact Recovery
children.top_down_role: Structural settings in which approximate solver output supports exact reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit precision and postprocessing cost once a denominator bound and sufficiently accurate approximation are available.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The threshold \(1/(2D^2)\) requires \(O(\log D)\) fractional bits of absolute coordinate accuracy. Given exactly represented approximations or certified intervals of that width, continued-fraction rational reconstruction of all \(n\) coordinates uses time polynomial in \(n\), \(\log D\), and the input encoding length of the approximations. This bound concerns reconstruction postprocessing and does not include the cost of producing the approximation or of exact final certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded-denominator reconstruction needs logarithmically many accuracy bits in the determinant bound and polynomial-time coordinate postprocessing.
assumptions_latex: A valid denominator bound \(D\ge1\) is available.
Each coordinate approximation is represented exactly or by a certified interval narrow enough for the reconstruction theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The required coordinate precision is \(O(\log D)\) bits, and coordinatewise rational reconstruction has polynomial bit complexity in its encoded input and \(\log D\).
knowledge_statements.title: Precision and Reconstruction Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes approximate numerical acceptance from a certified reconstruction radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Bounds on primal residual, dual residual, and primal-dual objective gap do not by themselves imply \(\|\widehat x-x^*\|_\infty<1/(2D^2)\). Approximate-to-exact reconstruction therefore requires an independently justified distance or separation bound; after reconstruction, the candidate must satisfy an exact optimality certificate before it is accepted as an exact LP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small residuals and gap alone do not justify rational reconstruction; a certified separation bound and exact final validation are required.
assumptions_latex: The approximate output is evaluated using residual-and-gap tolerances.
Exact recovery targets a rational optimal solution with a stated denominator or separation bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without a certified reconstruction radius, rational reconstruction is inconclusive; exact acceptance requires exact feasibility and optimality verification.

notation.meaning: denominator bound used by the reconstruction theorem

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-and-Gap Recovery Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise reconstruction of a unique integer-data LP vertex from a certified distance bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), where \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) has rank \(m\), \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\), and the unique optimal solution \(x^*\) is a basic feasible solution. Let \[D=\max\{|\det A_B|:A_B\text{ is a nonsingular }m\times m\text{ column submatrix of }A\}.\] Every coordinate of \(x^*\) has reduced denominator at most \(D\). If \(\widehat x\) satisfies \(\|\widehat x-x^*\|_\infty<1/(2D^2)\), then each coordinate of \(x^*\) is the unique rational number with denominator at most \(D\) within that radius of the corresponding coordinate of \(\widehat x\), so bounded-denominator rational reconstruction recovers \(x^*\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certified approximation within one half of the inverse squared basis-determinant bound uniquely determines every coordinate of a rational optimal vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb Z^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\), and \(b\in\mathbb Z^m\).
The LP has a unique optimal basic feasible solution \(x^*\).
\(D\ge1\) is the displayed maximum absolute basis determinant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coordinatewise bounded-denominator rational reconstruction returns \(x^*\) exactly.

notation.meaning: maximum absolute determinant of a nonsingular basis submatrix
approximation with a certified distance to the optimal vertex

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Denominator Approximate-to-Exact Recovery
Approximate-to-Exact Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise rational reconstruction of a unique optimal vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a standard-form LP with integer data and a unique optimal basic feasible solution \(x^*\). Define
\[D=\max\{|\det A_B|:A_B\text{ is a nonsingular }m\times m\text{ submatrix of }A\}.\]
Every coordinate of \(x^*\) has reduced denominator at most \(D\). Consequently, if an approximation \(\widehat x\) satisfies
\[\|\widehat x-x^*\|_\infty<\frac{1}{2D^2},\]
then coordinatewise rational reconstruction among fractions with denominator at most \(D\) returns \(x^*\) exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sufficiently accurate approximation to a unique rational optimal vertex can be converted to the exact vertex by bounded-denominator rational reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\), and \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^m\), \(c\in\mathbb{Z}^n\).
The LP has a unique optimal basic feasible solution \(x^*\).
\(D\ge1\) is the displayed determinant bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded-denominator rational reconstruction applied to \(\widehat x\) recovers \(x^*\) exactly.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovery Ambiguity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonuniqueness prevents an approximate point from selecting a distinguished exact optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min 0\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=1,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\]
Every point \(x(t)=(t,1-t)\) with \(0\le t\le1\) is exactly optimal. The approximation \(\widehat x=(1/2,1/2)\) has zero feasibility residual and zero objective error, yet the LP data provide no rule selecting either endpoint or any other distinguished optimum. Thus vanishing residuals and objective error do not imply recovery of a particular exact solution unless uniqueness or an explicit selection rule is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the optimal face is nontrivial, even zero residual and zero objective error cannot identify a particular exact optimizer.
assumptions_latex: Approximate recovery is judged only by feasibility and objective error.
No tie-breaking or optimizer-selection rule is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery of a distinguished optimizer is ambiguous despite zero approximation error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Objective Accuracy Does Not Uniformly Control Optimizer Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharpness boundary for recovering an optimizer from objective accuracy, distinct from nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\varepsilon>0\), consider \(\min\{\delta x:0\le x\le1\}\) with \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon\). The unique optimizer is \(x^*=0\), but the feasible point \(\widehat x=1\) satisfies \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-c^{\mathsf T}x^*=\delta\le\varepsilon\) while \(|\widehat x-x^*|=1\). Hence no instance-independent bound on optimizer distance follows from feasibility and objective error alone; a sharpness or conditioning modulus is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even with a unique optimizer, arbitrarily small objective error need not imply uniformly small optimizer error without a sharpness or conditioning bound.
assumptions_latex: \varepsilon>0
0<\delta\le\varepsilon
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le\varepsilon\quad\text{but}\quad |\widehat x-x^*|=1.

Moderate-Scale High-Accuracy Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Short-step interior-point complexity when explicit linear systems fit available resources.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible bounded LP possessing a strictly feasible primal-dual point, a short-step path-following method reduces the duality measure from \(\mu_0\) to at most \(\varepsilon\) in
\[O\!\left(\sqrt n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\]
Newton iterations. If forming and solving one Newton system costs \(F(A)\) arithmetic operations and \(M(A)\) memory, the corresponding bounds are
\[O\!\left(F(A)\sqrt n\log\frac{\mu_0}{\varepsilon}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad O(M(A)).\]
This characterizes the moderate-scale, high-accuracy regime when these factorizations fit memory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Short-step interior-point methods attain high accuracy in logarithmically many accuracy-dependent iterations when Newton systems can be stored and solved.
assumptions_latex: The LP admits a strictly feasible primal-dual starting point.
The short-step neighborhood and exact-arithmetic Newton model are used.
Each Newton system can be solved within costs \(F(A)\) and \(M(A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated iteration, arithmetic, and memory bounds hold for reaching duality measure at most \(\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: arithmetic cost of one Newton-system solution
memory required for the Newton-system solve

knowledge_statements.title: Huge-Scale Sparse Approximation Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse first-order saddle-point complexity under bounded-domain assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write a bounded LP as the bilinear saddle problem
\[\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}\;c^{\mathsf T}x+y^{\mathsf T}(Ax-b),\]
where \(X\) and \(Y\) are compact convex sets of diameters \(D_X\) and \(D_Y\). A standard ergodic primal-dual first-order method with an admissible fixed step size produces an averaged iterate with saddle gap at most \(C/k\) after \(k\) iterations, where \(C\) depends on \(D_X,D_Y\) and \(\|A\|\). If each iteration uses one multiplication by \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\), an \(\varepsilon\)-gap costs \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)C/\varepsilon)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On bounded saddle domains, sparse first-order primal-dual methods reach an epsilon gap using order one-over-epsilon sparse matrix passes.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonempty compact convex sets with computable projections or proximal maps.
The selected primal-dual method has the standard ergodic \(C/k\) gap guarantee.
Sparse matrix-vector products cost \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An averaged iterate with saddle gap at most \(\varepsilon\) is obtained in \(O(C/\varepsilon)\) iterations and \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)C/\varepsilon)\) arithmetic work.

notation.meaning: number of nonzero entries of the constraint matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, the claimed bounded-domain saddle problem is not generally equivalent to an equality-constrained LP, and the unspecified method does not determine the asserted constant or rate.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates separation-oracle query count from oracle evaluation and processing costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an oracle algorithm makes \(N\) queries, incurs non-oracle processing cost \(T_{\mathrm{proc}}\), and query \(q_j\) costs \(T_{\mathcal O}(q_j)\), then \[T_{\mathrm{total}}=T_{\mathrm{proc}}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}T_{\mathcal O}(q_j).\] Thus polynomial oracle-call complexity implies polynomial total time only when query and response lengths, oracle evaluation costs, and intervening bit lengths are polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many oracle calls imply polynomial running time only when oracle evaluation, response encoding, and processing costs are also polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Queries and oracle responses have finite encodings.
The computational model separately charges oracle evaluation and non-oracle processing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N\in\operatorname{poly}(L,n)\ \not\Rightarrow\ T_{\mathrm{total}}\in\operatorname{poly}(L,n)\text{ without polynomial oracle and bit-work bounds}.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Call and End-to-End Cost Decomposition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which an implicitly represented rational polyhedron belongs to the polynomial oracle-solver regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P\subseteq\mathbb R^n be given implicitly. The standard polynomial oracle-defined-polyhedron regime applies only after specifying (i) a strong separation oracle that, for each rational query z, either confirms z\in P or returns a polynomially encoded valid separating inequality, (ii) polynomial bounds on oracle evaluation and response length, and (iii) localization or rational-size promises sufficient to bound the search and distinguish the requested outcome. Separation access without these computational and size promises does not by itself yield a polynomial-time optimization guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Implicit constraints form a polynomial oracle-solving regime only when strong separation, polynomial oracle cost and encoding, and sufficient localization or rational-size promises are all available.
assumptions_latex: P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is an implicitly represented rational polyhedron}.
Queries and oracle responses use finite rational encodings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Strong separation}+\text{polynomial oracle/encoding bounds}+\text{localization or size promises are required for the standard polynomial oracle regime}.
knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Defined Regime Applicability Conditions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Incumbent–Lower-Bound Certificate for Approximate Oracle Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance test for an approximate minimizer once a valid global lower bound has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*=\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\). If an oracle-based procedure produces \(\widehat x\in P\) and a certified scalar lower bound \(L\le p^*\), then \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies \(c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-p^*\le\varepsilon\). Membership of \(\widehat x\), validity of \(L\), and the displayed gap are separate obligations; a small localization volume alone supplies none of them without an accompanying size theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible incumbent is epsilon-optimal when its objective lies within epsilon of a valid global lower bound; volume reduction alone is not such a certificate.
assumptions_latex: \widehat x\in P.
L\le p^*=\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x.
c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-L\le\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\le c^{\mathsf T}\widehat x-p^*\le\varepsilon.

notation.meaning: certified global lower bound on the optimal value

knowledge_statements.title: Incumbent–Lower-Bound Certificate for Approximate Oracle Optimization
Oracle-Defined Polyhedra Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ellipsoid optimization using separation rather than an explicit inequality matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational objective \(c\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), an initial ellipsoid containing a polyhedron \(P\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), and a strong separation oracle. At each ellipsoid center \(z_k\), query the oracle. If \(z_k\notin P\), update to an ellipsoid containing the returned separating half-ellipsoid; if \(z_k\in P\), retain it as an incumbent and add an objective cut excluding points whose objective cannot improve it. Continue until the maintained lower bound and incumbent value differ by at most \(\varepsilon\); output the incumbent, or an oracle-supported infeasibility certificate when the feasibility phase exhausts its rational size bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ellipsoid method optimizes over an implicitly represented polyhedron using separation cuts, objective cuts, and a certified stopping gap.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a rational polyhedron with known encoding-size and bounding-radius data.
The oracle returns either membership or a valid strong separating hyperplane.
Oracle calls and rational arithmetic are charged in the oracle bit-complexity model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal feasible point or a certified infeasibility conclusion within polynomially many oracle operations.

notation.meaning: polyhedron represented by a separation oracle

children.title: Basis-Recovery Regime
children.top_down_role: Solver settings where obtaining a stable optimal basis is a primary requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis-Recovery Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict primal and dual margins certify a unique recovered optimal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
let \(B\) index \(m\) columns with nonsingular \(A_B\), and let \(N\) be its complement. Compute
\[x_B=A_B^{-1}b,\quad x_N=0,\quad y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B,\quad r_N=c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}y.\]
If \(x_B>0\) and \(r_N>0\) componentwise, then \(B\) is the unique optimal basis and \(x\) is the unique optimal solution. These strict margins make the basis exactly verifiable after numerical recovery.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive basic variables and strictly positive nonbasic reduced costs certify a unique optimal basis and solution.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
\(A_B\) is nonsingular.
All displayed quantities are evaluated exactly or with certified error bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) is the unique optimal basis, and \((x_B,x_N)=(A_B^{-1}b,0)\) is the unique primal optimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict-Margin Stability of a Recovered Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed perturbation theorem is mathematically sound but belongs to the postoptimality-analysis sibling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(A\) and a strictly certified basis \(B\). Let \(\alpha=\min_i(A_B^{-1}b)_i>0\) and \(\beta=\min_{j\in N}(c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B)_j>0\). If \(\|A_B^{-1}\Delta b\|_\infty<\alpha\) and \(\|\Delta c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}\Delta c_B\|_\infty<\beta\), then \(B\) remains uniquely optimal for the perturbed right-hand side and objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict margins define a neighborhood of right-hand-side and objective perturbations in which a fixed basis remains uniquely optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is fixed and has full row rank.
\(A_B\) is nonsingular.
The original primal and reduced-cost margins are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|A_B^{-1}\Delta b\|_\infty<\alpha\ \wedge\ \|\Delta c_N-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}\Delta c_B\|_\infty<\beta\Longrightarrow B\text{ remains uniquely optimal}.

children.title: Postoptimality Analysis Regime
children.top_down_role: Solver settings where sensitivity information after optimization is a primary requirement.

knowledge_statements.title: Postoptimality Analysis Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-basis optimality test after right-hand-side and objective perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a basis \(B\) for a standard-form LP and hold \(A\) fixed. Under perturbed data \((b',c')\), the same basis remains primal and dual feasible precisely when
\[A_B^{-1}b'\ge0,\qquad c_N'-A_N^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B'\ge0.\]
Whenever these inequalities hold, the basic solution \(x_B'=A_B^{-1}b'\), \(x_N'=0\) is optimal, the dual solution is \(y'=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B'\), and the perturbed optimal value is
\[v(b',c')={c_B'}^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b'.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed basis remains optimal exactly while its perturbed basic variables and nonbasic reduced costs stay nonnegative.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular and the constraint matrix \(A\) is unperturbed.
Only the right-hand side and objective coefficients change to \((b',c')\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequalities certify continued optimality of \(B\) and yield the stated perturbed solution and value.

notation.meaning: perturbed right-hand side and objective data
optimal value while the basis remains optimal

children.title: Recovered-Basis Sensitivity Interface
children.top_down_role: Use of recovered basis structure as the interface to postoptimality analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Recovered-Basis Sensitivity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local solution and value differentials induced by a stable recovered basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a recovered basis \(B\) satisfies strict primal and reduced-cost inequalities, so it remains optimal in a neighborhood of \((b,c)\) with \(A\) fixed. Within that neighborhood,
\[x_B=A_B^{-1}b,\quad x_N=0,\quad y=A_B^{-\mathsf T}c_B,\quad v=c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}b.\]
Consequently, its first-order sensitivity interface is
\[dx_B=A_B^{-1}db,\quad dx_N=0,\quad dy=A_B^{-\mathsf T}dc_B,\quad dv=y^{\mathsf T}db+x_B^{\mathsf T}dc_B.\]
The formulas apply only while the same basis remains optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Once a strict optimal basis is recovered, linear solves with its basis matrix give local solution, multiplier, and value sensitivities.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is fixed and nonsingular.
The recovered basis remains optimal throughout the perturbation neighborhood.
Perturbations affect only \(b\) and \(c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed representations and first differentials describe local postoptimality sensitivity while the recovered basis remains optimal.

children.title: Degenerate Basis Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nonuniqueness or instability limits basis-dependent analysis.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Basis Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy destroys identification of a unique basis from the optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[\min x_1+x_2\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_1+x_2=0,\qquad x_1,x_2\ge0.\]
The unique feasible and optimal solution is \(x^*=(0,0)\), but either singleton column set \(B=\{1\}\) or \(B=\{2\}\) is a feasible optimal basis, and its basic variable equals zero. Hence exact recovery of \(x^*\) does not determine a unique optimal basis. More generally, when a basic variable or a nonbasic reduced cost vanishes, strict-margin certification of a unique stable basis is unavailable without an additional basis-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At degeneracy, a unique optimal vector can correspond to multiple bases, so solution recovery alone does not identify a unique stable basis.
assumptions_latex: Basis recovery is required to identify an index set, not merely an optimal vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Degeneracy permits multiple optimal bases for the same recovered solution and prevents unique basis identification without an additional selection rule.

notation.meaning: unique optimal solution in the example

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Reduced-Cost Margin Causes Basis Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective perturbations can select different optimal bases on opposite sides of a dual-degenerate boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\delta\in\mathbb R\), consider \(\min\{\delta x_1:x_1+x_2=1,\ x_1,x_2\ge0\}\). If \(\delta>0\), the unique optimum is \((0,1)\) with basis \(\{2\}\); if \(\delta<0\), the unique optimum is \((1,0)\) with basis \(\{1\}\). At \(\delta=0\), every feasible point is optimal and the relevant reduced-cost margin is zero. Hence arbitrarily small objective perturbations on opposite sides select different optimal bases, so no open neighborhood preserving one unique optimal basis exists at the zero-margin instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a zero reduced-cost margin, arbitrarily small objective perturbations can switch the unique optimal basis between the two endpoint bases.
assumptions_latex: Basis stability is considered under objective perturbations with the constraint matrix and right-hand side fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta>0\Rightarrow B=\{2\},\qquad \delta<0\Rightarrow B=\{1\},
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Reduced-Cost Margin Causes Basis Instability

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Solver Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity and numerical behavior for LP instances with poor conditioning.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regime classification relative to a declared LP status task, data norm, and ill-posed boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a norm and normalization on LP data and a status task with ill-posed boundary \(\Sigma\). For \(d\notin\Sigma\), define \(\rho(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)\) and \(\mathcal C(d)=\|d\|/\rho(d)\). The instance is in the distance-based ill-conditioned regime when \(0<\rho(d)<\infty\) and \(\mathcal C(d)\) is large on the scale of the available relative data and arithmetic uncertainty. The reciprocal \(1/\mathcal C(d)\) is the relative distance to the declared ill-posed boundary; the definition does not identify basis conditioning, Newton-system conditioning, or poor scaling with status conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP is status-ill-conditioned when its normalized data are close, relative to their norm, to the declared ill-posed boundary.
assumptions_latex: A data representation, normalization, norm, and admissible perturbation model are fixed.
The status task and its ill-posed boundary \(\Sigma\) are explicitly declared.
\(d\notin\Sigma\) and \(0<\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(1/\mathcal C(d)=\operatorname{dist}(d,\Sigma)/\|d\|\) is the relative status-stability scale.

notation.meaning: ill-posed boundary for the declared LP status task
distance from the data to that boundary

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Based Ill-Conditioned Solver Regime
Ill-Conditioned Solver Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition-number criterion for instability near primal-dual ill-posedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d=(A,b,c)\) denote normalized LP data, and let \(\Sigma\) be the set of ill-posed instances at which arbitrarily small perturbations can change the relevant primal-dual feasibility status. Define
\[\rho(d)=\inf_{\widetilde d\in\Sigma}\|d-\widetilde d\|,\qquad \mathcal C(d)=\frac{\|d\|}{\rho(d)}.\]
The instance is in an ill-conditioned solver regime when \(\rho(d)>0\) but \(\mathcal C(d)\) is large relative to working precision. Perturbations of relative size comparable to \(1/\mathcal C(d)\) can then approach an ill-posed instance, so reliable classification or certification requires correspondingly finer data and arithmetic accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LP is ill-conditioned when its normalized data lie very near instances whose feasibility status changes under arbitrarily small perturbations.
assumptions_latex: A norm and normalization convention for the data space are fixed.
The ill-posed set \(\Sigma\) corresponds to the feasibility status being certified.
\(d\notin\Sigma\), so \(\rho(d)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reciprocal condition number \(1/\mathcal C(d)\) is the relative distance scale at which status and certification become unstable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distance-to-ill-posedness idea is standard, but no source fixes the normalization, data norm, status convention, or ill-posed set needed to validate this particular condition-number statement.

children.title: Nearly Infeasible Solver Regime
children.top_down_role: Complexity and certificate behavior near the feasibility boundary.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise regime of feasible LP data at a small positive relative distance from primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(d)\) be the primal feasible set for data \(d\ne0\), and fix a norm and admissible data-perturbation model. Define \(\rho_P(d)=\inf\{\|\Delta d\|:F(d+\Delta d)=\varnothing\}\). For a declared threshold \(\tau>0\), the nearly infeasible regime is \[F(d)\ne\varnothing,\qquad 0<\frac{\rho_P(d)}{\|d\|}\le\tau.\] Thus the current instance is feasible but infeasible instances occur within a small relative data perturbation. Actual infeasibility and the zero-distance ill-posed boundary are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP is nearly infeasible when its positive distance to infeasible data is small relative to the fixed data scale.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ne0\) and \(F(d)\ne\varnothing\).
A norm, data normalization, and admissible perturbation model are fixed.
The relative threshold \(\tau>0\) is declared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0<\rho_P(d)/\|d\|\le\tau\) characterizes the declared nearly infeasible regime.

notation.meaning: primal feasible set determined by data d
distance from d to primal-infeasible data

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Infeasible Feasible-Data Regime
Nearly Infeasible Solver Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise characterization of feasible standard-form LP data lying near primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For data \(d=(A,b)\) defining \(F(d)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), fix a norm on data perturbations and define
\[\rho_P(d)=\inf\{\|\Delta d\|:F(d+\Delta d)=\varnothing\}.\]
For a prescribed relative threshold \(\tau>0\), the nearly infeasible regime is
\[F(d)\neq\varnothing,\qquad 0<\rho_P(d)\leq\tau\max\{1,\|d\|\}.\]
Thus feasibility holds, but a perturbation small relative to the data scale can destroy it. The definition depends on the selected perturbation norm and admissible perturbation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible LP is nearly infeasible when the smallest admissible data perturbation destroying feasibility is positive but small relative to the data scale.
assumptions_latex: \(F(d)\neq\varnothing\).
A norm and admissible perturbation model for \(d=(A,b)\) are fixed.

notation.meaning: Primal feasible set for data d
Distance from d to primal infeasibility

children.title: Conditioning–Feasibility Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where poor conditioning obscures the distinction between feasible and infeasible instances.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility Radius and Reciprocal Condition Measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interaction between distance to primal infeasibility and the relative radius of guaranteed feasibility preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be the nonempty set of primal-infeasible data in a fixed normed data space, and let feasible \(d\ne0\) satisfy \(0<\rho_P(d):=\inf_{\widehat d\in\mathcal I}\|d-\widehat d\|<\infty\). Then \(\|\Delta d\|<\rho_P(d)\) implies that \(d+\Delta d\) remains primal feasible. For every \(\epsilon>0\), some infeasible \(\widehat d\) satisfies \(\|d-\widehat d\|<\rho_P(d)+\epsilon\). Hence, for \(\kappa_P(d):=\|d\|/\rho_P(d)\), the guaranteed relative feasibility radius is \(1/\kappa_P(d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to infeasibility is the largest open perturbation radius guaranteed to preserve feasibility, and its relative reciprocal is the primal condition measure.
assumptions_latex: \(d\ne0\) is primal feasible.
The infeasible-data set \(\mathcal I\) is nonempty and the fixed data norm gives \(0<\rho_P(d)<\infty\).
Perturbations use the same data space, admissibility rules, and norm used to define \(\rho_P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\Delta d\|/\|d\|<1/\kappa_P(d)\) guarantees primal feasibility, while infeasible data occur arbitrarily close to the boundary radius.

notation.meaning: set of primal-infeasible data under the fixed perturbation model
distance from d to primal-infeasible data

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Radius and Reciprocal Condition Measure
Conditioning–Feasibility Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-radius relation between feasibility stability and a distance-based condition number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(d\neq0\) be feasible LP data and let \(\rho_P(d)>0\) be its distance to primal infeasibility in a fixed norm. Define \(\kappa_P(d)=\|d\|/\rho_P(d)\). Every admissible perturbation satisfying
\[\|\Delta d\|<\rho_P(d)=\frac{\|d\|}{\kappa_P(d)}\]
preserves primal feasibility. Conversely, the definition of the infimum supplies infeasibility-producing perturbations with norms arbitrarily close to \(\rho_P(d)\). Hence increasing \(\kappa_P(d)\) shrinks the relative perturbation radius on which feasibility is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger distance-based condition number means a smaller relative perturbation neighborhood in which primal feasibility is guaranteed to persist.
assumptions_latex: \(d\neq0\), \(F(d)\neq\varnothing\), and \(\rho_P(d)>0\).
The data norm and admissible perturbations are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\Delta d\|/\|d\|<1/\kappa_P(d)\) implies \(F(d+\Delta d)\neq\varnothing\).

children.title: Reliable Certification Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits on trustworthy feasibility or optimality conclusions in adverse numerical regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact or outward-rounded verification boundary for a standard-form primal-infeasibility witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\), a candidate \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) certifies \(F=\varnothing\) when \[A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0.\] A finite-precision candidate is accepted only if exact evaluation establishes these inequalities or outward-rounded enclosures have nonnegative lower bounds for every component of \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) and a strictly negative upper bound for \(b^{\mathsf T}y\). If any required enclosure overlaps the forbidden side of zero, verification of that candidate is inconclusive and does not establish either feasibility or infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed Farkas vector is a reliable infeasibility certificate only when rigorous evaluation separates all required signs from their invalid sides.
assumptions_latex: The standard-form feasible set is \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\).
Certificate expressions are evaluated exactly or with valid outward-rounded enclosures.
The signs follow the displayed Farkas convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rigorous verification of \(A^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certifies \(F=\varnothing\); failure to separate the signs is indeterminate for this candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Rigorous Farkas-Certificate Acceptance Boundary
Reliable Certification Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and interval-verifiable Farkas certificates for standard-form primal infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying
\[A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0,\qquad b^{\mathsf T}y<0\]
is an infeasibility certificate, because these inequalities are incompatible with \(Ax=b\) and \(x\geq0\). In finite-precision computation the certificate is reliably verified only when exact arithmetic or outward-rounded interval evaluation proves every component of \(A^{\mathsf T}y\) nonnegative and proves a strictly negative upper bound for \(b^{\mathsf T}y\). If either interval contains zero, this test is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Farkas vector certifies infeasibility only when its nonnegative and strictly negative inequalities can be verified exactly or by separating intervals.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
Certificate evaluation uses exact arithmetic or outward-rounded intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Verified \(A^{\mathsf T}y\geq0\) and \(b^{\mathsf T}y<0\) imply \(F=\varnothing\).
