children.title: Pipeline-Dependent Solver Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity consequences of solver pipelines; detailed implementation mechanisms remain in the solver-architecture chapter.

children.title: Presolve Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Effects of model reduction and structural simplification on downstream solver work.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Soundness condition for outcomes reconstructed by an exact presolve pipeline; it does not specify particular reduction rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R map an LP P to a reduced LP P' and record reconstruction maps L_{\mathrm{sol}},L_{\mathrm{inf}},L_{\mathrm{unb}}. Postsolve preserves outcomes when every valid optimal primal-dual solution u' of P' maps to a valid optimal primal-dual solution L_{\mathrm{sol}}(u') of P, every valid Farkas infeasibility certificate q' for P' maps to a valid certificate L_{\mathrm{inf}}(q') for P, and every valid improving recession certificate d' for P' maps to a valid improving recession certificate L_{\mathrm{unb}}(d') for P. Only outcomes satisfying the applicable implication may be accepted for P.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced solution or status certificate is sound for the original LP only when the recorded postsolve map lifts it to a valid original-instance solution or certificate.
assumptions_latex: Presolve transformations are exact and record all information required by the applicable reconstruction map.
Each reduced output satisfies the defining conditions of its claimed outcome class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u'\in\mathcal S(P')\Rightarrow L_{\mathrm{sol}}(u')\in\mathcal S(P),\quad q'\in\mathcal I(P')\Rightarrow L_{\mathrm{inf}}(q')\in\mathcal I(P),\quad d'\in\mathcal U(P')\Rightarrow L_{\mathrm{unb}}(d')\in\mathcal U(P).

notation.meaning: postsolve maps for solutions, infeasibility certificates, and improving recession certificates
valid optimal-solution, infeasibility-certificate, and improving-recession-certificate classes

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Postsolve Lifting Condition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reduced Size Does Not Imply Reduced Solve Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on inferring downstream work solely from presolved dimensions or sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let presolve map an LP instance P to an outcome-equivalent reduced instance P'. Even if P' has no more rows, columns, or stored nonzeros than P, these inequalities alone imply no ordering T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P')\le T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P) in a fixed arithmetic or bit-complexity model. Presolve can change coefficient bit lengths, conditioning, factorization fill, and exploitable structure, so a complexity improvement requires a bound for the selected downstream algorithm on P'.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smaller presolved dimensions or sparsity do not alone guarantee a cheaper solve because encoding, conditioning, fill, and structure can change.
assumptions_latex: P'\text{ is an outcome-preserving presolved form of }P.
T_{\mathrm{solve}}\text{ is measured in one declared computation model.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (m'\le m,\ n'\le n,\ \operatorname{nnz}(P')\le\operatorname{nnz}(P))\not\Longrightarrow T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P')\le T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P).

notation.meaning: cost of the selected downstream solver in a fixed model

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced Size Does Not Imply Reduced Solve Complexity
Presolve Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive work accounting for an exact presolve–solve–postsolve pipeline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let presolve transform an LP instance \(P\) into \(P'\), while recording a map that reconstructs a solution or certificate for \(P\). If presolve, solution of \(P'\), and postsolve require respectively \(T_{\mathrm{pre}}(P)\), \(T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P')\), and \(T_{\mathrm{post}}(P',P)\) operations in one fixed computation model, then the pipeline cost is
\[T_{\mathrm{pipe}}(P)=T_{\mathrm{pre}}(P)+T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P')+T_{\mathrm{post}}(P',P).\]
Presolve improves total complexity precisely when its reduction in downstream solve work exceeds presolve and postsolve overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Presolve helps overall only when the solve work it removes is greater than the combined presolve and reconstruction cost.
assumptions_latex: Presolve and postsolve preserve the required solution or certificate.
All costs use the same computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{pipe}}(P)<T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P)\) exactly when \(T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P)-T_{\mathrm{solve}}(P')>T_{\mathrm{pre}}(P)+T_{\mathrm{post}}(P',P)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive accounting and break-even identity are coherent and fit the complexity-effects leaf, but no source supports the presolve/postsolve model or its preservation assumptions.

children.title: Scaling Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Effects of numerical rescaling on conditioning and solver progress.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse Arithmetic and Encoding Cost of Rational Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic, sparsity, and bit-length overhead of explicitly forming a rational diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), let \(q=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\), and suppose each numerator and denominator in positive rational diagonal matrices \(D_r,D_c\) has bit length at most \(s\). Forming \(D_rAD_c\), \(D_rb\), and \(D_cc\) uses \(O(q+m+n)\) rational multiplications and preserves the zero pattern of \(A\). If \(L\) is the binary length of \((A,b,c)\), the uncancelled scaled representation has length \(O(L+(q+m+n)s)\). Thus polynomial-length rational scaling preserves polynomial encoding size, whereas unrestricted scaling factors need not preserve a Turing-model complexity guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal scaling preserves sparsity and has linear sparse formation cost, but polynomial bit complexity also requires scaling factors of polynomial encoding length.
assumptions_latex: The LP data and scaling factors are explicitly encoded rationals.
Bit length is measured for an ordinary numerator-denominator encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\rm form}=O(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n),\qquad L_{\rm scaled}=O\!\left(L+(\operatorname{nnz}(A)+m+n)s\right).

notation.meaning: Number of nonzero entries of the constraint matrix
Maximum numerator or denominator bit length of a scaling factor
Binary length of the original LP data

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Arithmetic and Encoding Cost of Rational Scaling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Diagonal Scaling Can Arbitrarily Worsen Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of any unconditional spectral-conditioning improvement claim for diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=I_2\), \(D_r=I_2\), and \(D_c=\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\) with \(t\ge1\). Then \(\kappa_2(A)=1\), whereas \(\kappa_2(D_rAD_c)=t\). Positive diagonal scaling can therefore worsen the spectral condition number by an arbitrarily large factor while preserving the exact LP equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling the identity by diag(t,1) increases its spectral condition number from one to t, so scaling has no unconditional conditioning benefit.
assumptions_latex: Conditioning is measured by the spectral condition number \(\kappa_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{\kappa_2(D_rAD_c)}{\kappa_2(A)}=t\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Diagonal Scaling Can Arbitrarily Worsen Conditioning

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual and Certificate Transport Under Diagonal Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact transport of dual variables, slacks, objectives, and optimality certificates under positive diagonal scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) and its dual \(\max\{b^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le c\}\), let \(D_r,D_c\) be positive diagonal and set \(x=D_cz\). The scaled primal has data \((D_rAD_c,D_rb,D_cc)\) and dual variable \(w\). The correspondence \(y=D_rw\) is bijective on dual feasible points, preserves the dual objective, and maps the original slack \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\) to the scaled slack \(s'=D_cs\). Together with \(x=D_cz\), it preserves primal feasibility, dual feasibility, complementary slackness, duality gaps, and optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal scaling transports primal-dual solutions and certificates bijectively; slacks are rescaled componentwise while objectives and duality gaps are unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) are positive diagonal matrices.
The original and scaled LPs are interpreted in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y=D_rw,\qquad s'=D_c(c-A^{\mathsf T}y),
knowledge_statements.title: Dual and Certificate Transport Under Diagonal Scaling
Scaling Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal scaling preserves exact solutions while changing numerical conditioning and pipeline cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive diagonal matrices \(D_r\) and \(D_c\), the equality-form LP
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\]
is transformed by \(x=D_cz\) into
\[\min\{(D_c^{\mathsf T}c)^{\mathsf T}z:(D_rAD_c)z=D_rb,\ z\geq0\}.\]
The substitution is bijective, so exact feasibility and objective values are preserved. Its pipeline cost equals scaling formation and application, the solve cost for the scaled data, and unscaling. Numerical work may decrease or increase because the scaling changes coefficient ranges and the conditioning of the linear systems used by the solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive diagonal scaling preserves the exact LP but changes transformation overhead and the numerical conditioning governing practical solve work.
assumptions_latex: \(D_r\) and \(D_c\) are positive diagonal matrices.
Arithmetic and solver cost models are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=D_cz\) bijectively maps scaled feasible points to original feasible points with equal objective values.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal substitution is correct and the property kind fits, but the practical conditioning and solve-work claims require an inspectable source and a specified conditioning/cost model.

children.title: Presolve–Scaling Interaction
children.top_down_role: Dependence between structural reductions and subsequent numerical scaling quality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Absolute-Tolerance Presolve Does Not Commute with Row Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit order-dependence example in which both reduced pipelines retain exact logical equivalence because the thresholded row is redundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix 0<\tau<1 and let P contain the equalities x=1 and (\tau/2)x=\tau/2. Let a presolve rule delete a redundant equality a^{\mathsf T}x=b when \max\{\|a\|_\infty,|b|\}\le\tau. Applied directly, the rule deletes the second equality. If that redundant row is first multiplied by 4, giving 2\tau x=2\tau, the same threshold rule retains it. Thus presolve before scaling and scaling before presolve produce different reduced numerical instances, although the retained equation x=1 makes both pipelines exactly equivalent to P.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant equation can fall below an absolute presolve threshold before row scaling but exceed it afterward, so the two transformation orders produce different yet exactly equivalent reduced instances.
assumptions_latex: The presolve rule applies the stated absolute threshold only to an equality already known to be redundant.
Positive row scaling is an exact equivalence transformation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R(S(P))\ne S'(R(P))\text{ as numerical instances, while both have the exact solution set }\{x=1\}.

notation.meaning: threshold-based deletion rule for a redundant equality
scaling of the redundant row by four

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Tolerance Presolve Does Not Commute with Row Scaling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for exact presolve and nonsingular diagonal scaling to commute up to induced scaling and bookkeeping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a nonsingular diagonal row-and-column scaling and let an exact presolver \(R\) be composed of reduction rules whose applicability predicates are invariant under \(S\) and whose reduction and reconstruction maps are equivariant under \(S\). Then there is an induced scaling \(S_R\) of the reduced variables and constraints such that \[R(S(P))=S_R(R(P))\] up to permutation and recorded reconstruction data. Consequently, order dependence requires a failure of predicate invariance, reduction equivariance, or deterministic tie correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact presolve commutes with diagonal scaling when every rule detects and transforms scaled instances equivariantly; order dependence requires one of those invariances to fail.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonsingular diagonal equivalence scaling.
Every presolve applicability predicate is invariant under \(S\).
Every reduction and reconstruction map is equivariant under \(S\), including corresponding deterministic ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R\circ S=S_R\circ R\quad\text{up to permutation and reconstruction bookkeeping}.

notation.meaning: nonsingular diagonal scaling of the original instance
induced scaling of the reduced instance

knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Equivariance Criterion for Commuting Presolve

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Like-for-like cost accounting for the two transformation orders, without asserting universal dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Pi_{SR}\) scale and then presolve, and let \(\Pi_{RS}\) presolve and then apply the induced scaling. In one fixed computation model, define \[T_{SR}=T_S(P)+T_R(SP)+T_{\mathrm{solve}}(R(SP))+T_{\mathrm{lift}}^{SR}(P),\] \[T_{RS}=T_R(P)+T_{S_R}(RP)+T_{\mathrm{solve}}(S_R(RP))+T_{\mathrm{lift}}^{RS}(P).\] Then scaling first is cheaper exactly when \(T_{SR}<T_{RS}\). Logical equivalence of both pipelines to \(P\) alone implies no ordering of these sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cheaper order is determined by its complete transformation, solve, and reconstruction cost; semantic equivalence gives no cost dominance.
assumptions_latex: Both pipelines preserve the requested original-instance outcome.
All terms are charged in the same computation model.
Unscaling and postsolve reconstruction costs are included.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{SR}<T_{RS}\iff T_S(P)+T_R(SP)+T_{\mathrm{solve}}(R(SP))+T_{\mathrm{lift}}^{SR}(P)<T_R(P)+T_{S_R}(RP)+T_{\mathrm{solve}}(S_R(RP))+T_{\mathrm{lift}}^{RS}(P).

notation.meaning: Scaling induced on the presolved instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Specific Presolve–Scaling Cost Comparison
Presolve–Scaling Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order dependence of presolve and diagonal scaling in finite-precision solver pipelines.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) denote a presolve transformation and \(S\) a nonsingular diagonal scaling. Although exact scaling preserves the LP under a variable substitution, a tolerance-based presolver may make different reduction decisions on \(P\) and \(S(P)\). Consequently,
\[R(S(P))\neq S'(R(P))\]
may hold as transformed numerical instances, even when both pipelines are logically equivalent to \(P\). Their total costs must therefore be evaluated separately as transformation overhead plus solve and reconstruction costs; neither ordering has a universal complexity advantage without assumptions on \(R\), the tolerances, and the solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling can change tolerance-based presolve decisions, so scaling-before-presolve and presolve-before-scaling may produce different reduced instances and costs.
assumptions_latex: Scaling is nonsingular and presolve preserves the intended LP semantics.
Presolve decisions may depend on numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No universal equality \(R\circ S=S'\circ R\) or ordering advantage follows without additional invariance assumptions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property appropriately describes the interaction leaf, but tolerance-dependent noncommutation and the absence of a universal ordering advantage are implementation-sensitive claims with no cited evidence.

children.title: Transformation Overhead Boundary
children.top_down_role: Regimes where preprocessing cost offsets its downstream complexity benefit.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformation Overhead Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Break-even condition for preprocessing transformations in a solver pipeline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(T_0(P)\) be the cost of solving \(P\) directly. Let a transformation produce \(P'\) with preprocessing cost \(T_f\), solve cost \(T_s(P')\), and reconstruction or verification cost \(T_r\), all measured in the same resource model. The transformation is complexity-beneficial exactly when
\[T_f+T_s(P')+T_r<T_0(P).\]
Equality is the transformation-overhead boundary. Above this boundary the transformation can still improve stability or reliability, but it does not reduce the selected total resource.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transformation saves complexity exactly when reduced solve cost outweighs preprocessing and reconstruction overhead; equality is the break-even boundary.
assumptions_latex: The transformed problem preserves the requested output semantics.
Every cost is measured using one resource model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The break-even boundary is \(T_f+T_s(P')+T_r=T_0(P)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The break-even condition is internally correct and the condition kind matches the boundary leaf, but the pipeline model has no source and the selected resource measure is not instantiated.

children.title: Crossover Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Additional work required to move from an interior or approximate solution to basic structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic additional-work accounting for a crossover stage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose crossover initialization costs \(T_{\mathrm{init}}\), it performs \(K\) accepted or degenerate basis-processing iterations with costs \(C_1,\ldots,C_K\), and terminal verification costs \(T_{\mathrm{ver}}\). Then \[T_{\mathrm{cross}}=T_{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=1}^KC_k+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.\] If \(C_k\leq C_{\max}\), then \(T_{\mathrm{cross}}\leq T_{\mathrm{init}}+KC_{\max}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}\). Polynomial crossover work therefore requires compatible polynomial bounds on \(K\), per-iteration work, numerical precision, initialization, and verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover work is initialization plus all basis-processing iterations plus verification; a polynomial interior-point iteration bound does not control crossover unless these added quantities are also bounded.
assumptions_latex: All terms use one declared computational model.
The crossover procedure terminates after K<\infty basis-processing iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{cross}}\leq T_{\mathrm{init}}+KC_{\max}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Crossover Work

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why the generic crossover accounting does not itself establish polynomial complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Finiteness or polynomial complexity of the preceding bound cannot be inferred merely from the accuracy or iteration bound of the interior-point phase. A simplex-style crossover must separately specify a finite pivot rule or anti-cycling mechanism, and polynomial total work additionally requires a polynomial bound on its basis changes and charged linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior-point convergence does not imply finite or polynomial crossover; pivot termination and work require separate guarantees.
assumptions_latex: Crossover may use simplex-style basis changes, including degenerate changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Polynomial pre-crossover iteration complexity}\not\Rightarrow\text{polynomial crossover complexity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Pivot Crossover Boundary
Crossover Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive accounting for crossover from an approximate interior solution to a basic solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose crossover starts from an approximate primal-dual solution, performs initialization costing \(T_{\mathrm{init}}\), executes \(K\) basis-changing iterations with costs \(C_1,\ldots,C_K\), and verifies the recovered basis at cost \(T_{\mathrm{ver}}\). Its additional work is
\[T_{\mathrm{cross}}=T_{\mathrm{init}}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}C_k+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.\]
If each iteration costs at most \(C_{\max}\), then \(T_{\mathrm{cross}}\leq T_{\mathrm{init}}+KC_{\max}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}\). This is output-sensitive in \(K\); a polynomial bound requires an independent bound on the number of basis changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Crossover cost is initialization plus basis-change work plus verification; polynomial complexity additionally requires controlling the number of basis changes.
assumptions_latex: Crossover terminates after \(K<\infty\) basis-changing iterations.
All operation costs use one computation model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{cross}}\leq T_{\mathrm{init}}+KC_{\max}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The output-sensitive accounting is algebraically valid and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no source establishes this crossover decomposition or supports the statement about polynomial complexity.

children.title: Basis-Recovery Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Additional work required to identify and validate a useful LP basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-attempt arithmetic cost for selecting, solving, and verifying a basis from candidate columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have row rank \(m\), and let \(J\) contain \(q\) candidate columns. In a dense unit-cost arithmetic model, rank-revealing selection of \(m\) independent columns from \(A_J\), factorization of the resulting basis \(B\), primal and dual basis solves, and verification against all \(n\) columns can be performed in \[O(m^2q+m^3+mn)\] arithmetic operations per attempted candidate set. If \(a\) candidate sets are attempted without reusable factorizations, the bound is \(O(a(m^2q+m^3+mn))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense basis recovery costs rank-revealing selection, factorization, two basis solves, and full verification; rejected candidate sets multiply this work.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\text{ has row rank }m.
Dense unit-cost scalar arithmetic is charged.
Each attempted candidate set has at most q columns.
No factorization work is reused between attempts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{rec}}=O\!\left(a(m^2q+m^3+mn)\right).

notation.meaning: maximum number of candidate columns in an attempt

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Arithmetic Basis-Recovery Cost

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit of an arithmetic recovery bound for exact rational output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A unit-cost arithmetic bound for rank tests, factorization, solves, and verification is not by itself a Turing bit-complexity bound. Exact rational basis recovery additionally requires bounds on operand encoding lengths, intermediate growth, precision or exact-arithmetic costs, the number of rejected attempts, and the encoded output size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting dense arithmetic operations does not establish polynomial bit complexity for exact basis recovery.
assumptions_latex: The LP data and requested recovered basis certificate are exactly encoded rational objects.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Arithmetic-operation polynomiality}\not\Rightarrow\text{Turing bit polynomiality without size and precision bounds}.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic-to-Bit Recovery Boundary
Basis-Recovery Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic cost decomposition for selecting and verifying a basis from approximate active-set information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let basis recovery for an LP with \(m\) equality rows and \(n\) variables examine \(q\) candidate columns, select \(m\) independent columns, factor the resulting basis matrix \(B\), solve the associated primal and dual systems, and verify feasibility. If these stages cost \(T_{\mathrm{sel}}(m,q)\), \(T_{\mathrm{fac}}(B)\), \(T_{\mathrm{sol}}(B)\), and \(T_{\mathrm{ver}}(m,n)\), then
\[T_{\mathrm{rec}}=T_{\mathrm{sel}}+T_{\mathrm{fac}}+T_{\mathrm{sol}}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}.\]
Repeated rank failures or rejected bases add the corresponding selection and factorization costs for every attempted basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basis recovery costs candidate selection, basis factorization, primal-dual solves, and verification, with failed basis attempts adding repeated work.
assumptions_latex: The equality-constraint matrix has row rank \(m\).
Recovery outputs only after primal-dual basis verification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{rec}}=T_{\mathrm{sel}}+T_{\mathrm{fac}}+T_{\mathrm{sol}}+T_{\mathrm{ver}}\), plus analogous costs for rejected attempts.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stage-cost decomposition fits the complexity-effects leaf, but it is unsupported and leaves the arithmetic or bit-cost models for selection, factorization, solves, and failed attempts unspecified.

children.title: Crossover-to-Recovery Interface
children.top_down_role: Relationship between crossover output and subsequent basis reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact acceptance test at the crossover-to-recovery boundary for a standard-form minimization LP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a full-row-rank standard-form LP and candidate basis \(B\), set \(x_B=A_B^{-1}b\), \(x_N=0\), solve \(A_B^{\mathsf T}y=c_B\), and set \(s=c-A^{\mathsf T}y\). Accept \(B\) as an exact optimal recovered basis only if \(A_B\) is nonsingular, \(x_B\geq0\), and \(s_N\geq0\); then \(s_B=0\) and the reconstructed primal-dual pair is optimal. Under a tolerance-based contract, every relaxed inequality and residual threshold must instead be stated explicitly, and the output is only tolerance-certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact recovery accepts a nonsingular basis only after its basic solution and nonbasic reduced costs are nonnegative; tolerance-based acceptance must be labeled approximate.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\text{ has row rank }m.
B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\},\ |B|=m.
The exact and tolerance-based output contracts are not conflated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_B\text{ nonsingular},\ x_B\geq0,\ s_N\geq0\ \Longrightarrow\ (x,y,s)\text{ is an exact optimal primal-dual reconstruction}.

notation.meaning: nonbasic reduced costs or dual slacks

knowledge_statements.title: Recovered-Basis Acceptance Contract

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation-independent contract between approximate crossover information and basis reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), a crossover-to-recovery handoff consists of the LP data, approximate primal-dual data \((\widehat x,\widehat y,\widehat s)\), declared residual and rank tolerances, and optional candidate-index, active-set, or optimal-partition information. A conforming recovery stage returns either (i) a candidate basis \(B\) together with reconstructed primal-dual quantities and verification status, or (ii) an explicit failure status such as insufficient rank, failed feasibility or optimality checks, or unresolved identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The handoff carries approximate primal-dual data, tolerances, and optional candidate structure, and returns either a verified basis package or an explicit recovery failure.
assumptions_latex: The LP representation and exact or tolerance-based acceptance regime are declared.
A has the row rank required by the selected basis representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{handoff output}\in\{\text{verified basis package},\text{explicit recovery failure}\}.

notation.meaning: approximate primal variables, dual multipliers, and dual slacks
candidate basis index set or basis matrix

knowledge_statements.title: Crossover Recovery Handoff Contract
Crossover-to-Recovery Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Threshold-and-rank interface converting an approximate primal-dual point into a candidate basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input an LP \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\geq0\}\), an approximate primal-dual pair \((x,y,s)\), and thresholds \(\tau_x,\tau_s>0\). Form the candidate index set
\[J=\{j:x_j>\tau_x\}\cup\{j:s_j\leq\tau_s\}.\]
Select \(m\) indices \(B\subseteq J\) whose columns in \(A\) are numerically independent; if none exist, enlarge \(J\) or report recovery failure. Solve the basis primal and dual equations, perform feasibility-improving basis changes when necessary, and output the basis only after verifying primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and the requested optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface ranks threshold-selected variables, builds a candidate basis, corrects it if necessary, and returns it only after primal-dual verification.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has row rank \(m\).
Approximate variables satisfy \(x,s\geq0\).
Rank and optimality tolerances are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either a verified primal-dual basis or an explicit recovery-failure report.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the interface leaf, but the threshold rule is a particular crossover variant with no source, and the primal and dual basis equations and correction procedure are not explicitly specified.

children.title: Degenerate Recovery Boundary
children.top_down_role: Cases where degeneracy or instability increases cost or prevents reliable recovery.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Recovery Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of stable basis identification when strict-complementarity or rank margins vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min 0\) subject to \(x_1+x_2=1\) and \(x_1,x_2\geq0\). Every feasible point is optimal, and both singleton bases \(\{1\}\) and \(\{2\}\) are valid; at \(x=(1/2,1/2)\), both reduced costs are zero. Hence no positive threshold based only on primal variables and reduced costs uniquely identifies an optimal basis. More generally, when the smallest candidate-basis singular value or the strict-complementarity margin is zero, arbitrarily small perturbations can change the recovered basis, so uniform stable basis identification fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When rank or strict-complementarity margins vanish, arbitrarily small perturbations can change the recovered optimal basis; a simple two-variable LP demonstrates nonuniqueness.
assumptions_latex: Basis recovery uses approximate primal values, reduced costs, or numerical rank.
No positive rank or strict-complementarity margin is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A uniformly stable, uniquely determined recovered basis need not exist.

notation.meaning: Variables in the degenerate two-variable LP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example supports nonuniqueness of optimal bases and the failure-boundary kind fits. The broader assertion that either a zero singular-value margin or zero strict-complementarity margin causes perturbation instability needs a precise theorem and source.

children.title: Polishing Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Cost and benefit of final residual or accuracy refinement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polishing Decomposition Is Not a Complexity Guarantee
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of deriving asymptotic polishing complexity from a finite work decomposition alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An identity of the form \(T_{\rm polish}=T_{\rm init}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}(R_k+F_k+S_k)+T_{\rm ver}\) is only an output-sensitive accounting formula. It yields an asymptotic arithmetic or bit-complexity bound only after \(K\), every charged step cost, verification, and required numerical precision or intermediate encoding length are bounded in the selected model. Matrix conditioning affects such a bound only through a model that charges finite-precision accuracy or condition-dependent iterative linear algebra; it is not by itself a parameter of exact unit-cost arithmetic complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite polishing-cost sum is not an asymptotic complexity guarantee without bounds on correction count, charged step work, verification, and model-dependent precision or encoding growth.
assumptions_latex: All terms are measured in one specified resource model.
The claimed guarantee is asymptotic over a stated family of LP instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\rm polish}\text{ has no generic asymptotic bound from the decomposition alone}.

notation.meaning: Residual, factorization or update, and solve costs at correction k

knowledge_statements.title: Polishing Decomposition Is Not a Complexity Guarantee
Polishing Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Output-sensitive work bound for active-set polishing after an approximate LP solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose polishing initializes an active-set estimate at cost \(T_{m init}\), performs \(K\) correction steps, and verifies the final point at cost \(T_{m ver}\). If step \(k\) forms residuals at cost \(R_k\), factors or updates a correction system at cost \(F_k\), and solves it at cost \(S_k\), then
\[T_{m polish}=T_{m init}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}(R_k+F_k+S_k)+T_{m ver}.\]
If each step costs at most \(C_{m step}\), then \(T_{m polish}\leq T_{m init}+KC_{m step}+T_{m ver}\). Complexity guarantees require bounds on both \(K\) and correction-system conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polishing cost is initialization plus correction-system work and verification; a complexity guarantee also needs iteration and conditioning bounds.
assumptions_latex: Polishing terminates after \(K<\infty\) correction steps.
All costs use the same arithmetic or bit-complexity model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{m polish}\leq T_{m init}+KC_{m step}+T_{m ver}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The output-sensitive sum and upper bound fit the complexity-effects leaf, but no source supports the polishing model, and the claimed conditioning requirement is not tied to a formal arithmetic or bit-complexity bound.

children.title: Warm-Start Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Impact of reusable solution information on initialization and total solver effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Start Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic end-to-end cost comparison for a fixed LP solver and accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a solver \(M\), a cold-start state \(z^{\mathrm c}\), and a warm-start state \(z^{\mathrm w}\). Let \(C_M(z,\varepsilon)\) be the resources used by \(M\), initialized at \(z\), to return an accepted \(\varepsilon\)-accurate output, and let \(W\) be the cost of constructing and validating \(z^{\mathrm w}\). The end-to-end costs are \(T_{\mathrm{warm}}(\varepsilon)=W+C_M(z^{\mathrm w},\varepsilon)\) and \(T_{\mathrm{cold}}(\varepsilon)=C_M(z^{\mathrm c},\varepsilon)\). Thus warm starting improves end-to-end complexity exactly when \(W+C_M(z^{\mathrm w},\varepsilon)<C_M(z^{\mathrm c},\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Warm starting improves end-to-end complexity exactly when its construction and validation overhead plus the subsequent solver cost is less than the cold-start solver cost.
assumptions_latex: The LP instance and requested accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\) are fixed.
All costs are measured in one specified computation or oracle model.
The warm-start construction returns a state accepted by solver \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A warm start improves complexity exactly when \(W+C_M(z^{\mathrm w},\varepsilon)<C_M(z^{\mathrm c},\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: cost of constructing and validating the warm-start state
cost for method M to reach accuracy epsilon from state z

review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports warm-start complexity accounting; intervention construction and validation costs must be included.

children.title: Method-Switching Complexity Effects
children.top_down_role: Overhead and potential benefit of changing solver families during the pipeline.

knowledge_statements.title: Method-Switching Complexity Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: End-to-end resource accounting for one deterministic switch between two LP methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Run method \(M_1\) from state \(z_0\) until switching time \(\tau\), producing state \(z_\tau\), and transfer \(P_{12}(z_\tau)\) to method \(M_2\). If the first stage costs \(C_{M_1}^{\tau}\), switching and validation cost \(S_{12}^{\tau}\), and completion by \(M_2\) costs \(C_{M_2}(P_{12}(z_\tau),\varepsilon)\), then the total switched cost is \(T_{1\to 2}(\tau,\varepsilon)=C_{M_1}^{\tau}+S_{12}^{\tau}+C_{M_2}(P_{12}(z_\tau),\varepsilon)\). Relative to running \(M_1\) from \(z_0\) to the same accuracy and acceptance criterion, switching improves complexity exactly when \(T_{1\to 2}(\tau,\varepsilon)<C_{M_1}(z_0,\varepsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method switch improves end-to-end complexity exactly when first-stage work, switching and validation overhead, and second-stage completion together cost less than running the original method to the same accepted accuracy.
assumptions_latex: Methods \(M_1\) and \(M_2\) use compatible accuracy and acceptance criteria.
The transferred state is valid input to \(M_2\), possibly after conversion.
All stage and switching costs use the same resource model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Switching improves complexity exactly when \(C_{M_1}^{\tau}+S_{12}^{\tau}+C_{M_2}(P_{12}(z_\tau),\varepsilon)<C_{M_1}(z_0,\varepsilon)\).

notation.meaning: resource cost incurred by method M1 through switching time tau
cost of deciding, converting, and validating a switch from M1 to M2
state-conversion map from method M1 to method M2

children.title: Intervention Selection Boundary
children.top_down_role: Problem and accuracy regimes favoring polishing, reuse, or a solver-family transition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic refinement of weak argmin regions when predicted intervention costs tie.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a strict priority order \(\prec\) on interventions, with \(k\prec i\) meaning that \(k\) has higher tie priority than \(i\). For nonempty \(\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\), intervention \(i\) is selected exactly when \(i\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\), \(Q_i(s,\varepsilon)\le Q_k(s,\varepsilon)\) for every admissible \(k\), and \(Q_i(s,\varepsilon)<Q_k(s,\varepsilon)\) for every admissible higher-priority \(k\prec i\). These regions are disjoint and cover every state with a nonempty admissible set; the weak argmin regions without the priority inequalities may overlap on cost-indifference sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed priority rule turns overlapping weak argmin regions into disjoint deterministic selection regions by excluding tied higher-priority competitors.
assumptions_latex: The admissible intervention set is nonempty.
All predicted costs use common resource units.
The intervention priority order is fixed and strict.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\mathcal R}_i=\{s:i\in\mathcal I,\ Q_i\le Q_k\ \forall k\in\mathcal I,\ Q_i<Q_k\ \forall k\prec i\}\text{ forms a disjoint cover}.

notation.meaning: Tie-resolved selection region of intervention i

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Resolved Intervention Selection Regions
Intervention Selection Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise and global selection boundaries under a common deterministic resource model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For solver state \(s\), requested accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), and each intervention \(i\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\), define the predicted end-to-end cost \(Q_i(s,\varepsilon)=H_i(s)+R_i(s,\varepsilon)\). Select \(i^*(s,\varepsilon)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{i\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)}Q_i(s,\varepsilon)\), using the fixed tie rule. The selection region of \(i\) is \(\mathcal R_i(\varepsilon)=\{s:i\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon),\ Q_i(s,\varepsilon)\le Q_k(s,\varepsilon)\text{ for every }k\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\}\). The cost-indifference selection boundary between \(i\) and \(j\) is \(\mathcal B_{ij}(\varepsilon)=\{s:i,j\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon),\ Q_i(s,\varepsilon)=Q_j(s,\varepsilon)\le Q_k(s,\varepsilon)\text{ for every }k\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose an admissible intervention with minimum predicted total cost. Two interventions lie on a cost-indifference selection boundary where both are admissible, have equal predicted total cost, and no other admissible intervention has lower predicted cost.
assumptions_latex: The admissible intervention set \(\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\) is nonempty.
Every predicted remaining cost and intervention overhead is expressed in the same resource units.
Ties are resolved by a fixed deterministic rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cost-indifference selection boundary between interventions \(i\) and \(j\) is \(\mathcal B_{ij}(\varepsilon)=\{s:i,j\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon),\ H_i(s)+R_i(s,\varepsilon)=H_j(s)+R_j(s,\varepsilon)\le H_k(s)+R_k(s,\varepsilon)\text{ for every }k\in\mathcal I(s,\varepsilon)\}\).
